News.title: Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election
News.content:
The Treasury is disputing that Chancellor John Healey suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next general election.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election, with one suggesting Healey was explicitly attempting to avoid that impression being left.

It suggests, instead, that ministers are not committed to cutting the benefits bill by the next election.

The chancellor told Today: "I have said clearly and the prime minister has said as well, we have to bring the benefits bill down. You don't do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures."

He said two "big reports" next month would help the government "map out the way that we need to change the system for the long run" and the government has "been reducing the rate of increase in the welfare bill".

Healey said the current system was "unsustainable" and the government had a "moral duty" to help the almost one million young people out of work, education or training.

He said young people would be expected to take up offers of work or training "and that's the way we can take welfare bills down in the long term".

News.title: Poundland's future hangs in the balance as chain edges towards collapse
News.content:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as the discount chain edges towards collapse, the BBC understands.

The retailer's directors are filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which if approved by the High Court, will give the business 10 days breathing space to find a rescue deal.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams wrote a memo to his 12,000 staff across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland saying the US owner of the chain had limited Poundland's access to funding.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco in June last year for a nominal Â£1.

But a little over a year later it put the business up for sale.

Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG) put forward a bid to take the business on as a going concern, which was the preferred option for management, but it is understood this did not meet Gordon Brothers' expectations.

Gordon Brothers wants to recoup a Â£30m shareholder loan it inherited from the previous owners as part of a its deal, but it is understood the Martin Property Group offer was for Â£5m, with the rest of the payment deferred.

It means Poundland is now heading towards an insolvency process.

Gordon Brothers could secure a new owner through what is known as a pre-pack administration.

But the most likely option for the business to be broken up and for parcels of stores to be sold.

A Gordon Brothers insider said this would allow creditors to recover funds. Gordon Brothers is the main creditor, and has made Â£70m of loans to the business.

The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.

This type of process would let interested parties firm up offers.

Interested parties include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested to take on between 200 and 250 stores.

Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.

More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.

News.title: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment
News.content:
The environmental performance of water companies fell again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators into water companies.

Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.

Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".

The chair of the environmental regulator said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".

Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.

It is a nod to the commitment which Sir Keir Starmer's government made to merge the organisations into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation.

But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical - and damning.

Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.

Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.

The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".

And in Wales, DÅµr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by Natural Resources Wales.

Alan Lovell, chair of the EA, said the "results expose the scale of underperformance across the sector".

Water companies have committed record levels of investment up to 2030 to upgrade their networks and sewage treatment works. But customer bills are expected to rise 36% on average as a result.

There has already been Â£5bn invested over the last five years to try and tackle environmental pollution. But Lovell said "not all companies have delivered the environmental improvement schemes they have been funded for".

Moving forward, he said it was important that any further investment "delivers cleaner waters, healthier habitats and stronger public confidence".

In September, it was reported that the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the Consumer Council for Water rose by 84% in a year - the highest in 20 years.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing".

"We are getting on with the job of building a water system that finally works for the people who pay for it," she added.

Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough" but pointed to "the lowest level of leakage in history, as well as other areas of good performance".

"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.

News.title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
News.content:
Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

The 39-year-old told the jury at his rape and sexual assault trial that "the way he treats me is to know me", adding: "I feel very seen by him... I love him very much."

The media personality faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday, Laura Brand was asked by the defence barrister if her husband respected her when she didn't want to be sexual with him, and she replied: "Yes absolutely."

Meanwhile, a former girlfriend of Russell Brand described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".

Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, after meeting when she was training at a drama centre in London.

She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".

"When I said no, however, he accepted it", she said in a statement.

Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.

The trial continues.

News.title: Ofcom sets out social media age-checking methods ahead of ban
News.content:
Ofcom has set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

Under the UK's social media ban - which is due to come into force in March next year - those under that age will be prevented from accessing ten of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

Many UK adults are also likely to have to confirm that they are not under-age by using one of the proposed measures, which are subject to government approval.

A similar ban was introduced in Australia last year but many children there have found ways to get round it. The UK says it intends to take a tougher approach.

Age verification below 18 is challenging because 16 and 17 year olds don't have credit cards or full driving licences, and may not have passports either. They can also look significantly older or younger than they are.

To address that challenge, Ofcom has - in addition to traditional forms of ID - recommended four methods that it says would be "highly effective" at gauging people's ages:

photo ID matching, where relevant information on a photo ID document such as a passport is checked against a live image taken during an age check

banking-based checks, which involves using the information a financial institution has on record regarding a user's age

face age estimation technology (which the regulator argues has recently improved)

digital ID services, which enable people to digitally prove who they are or provide information about themselves, such as their age

The BBC has asked three of the UK's biggest banks whether they would have a process for assisting with social media requests for age verification if it did become an official measure.

However, ultimately it will be up to the tech companies to figure out how to implement the checks: the onus is on social network providers to come up with their own solutions and comply.

Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes said the regulator was drawing on its experience in introducing tougher age checks for porn sites last year:

"What we've learned in introducing age checks across the porn industry is that actually what a lot of countries did before us was say you need to do it this way and they were very prescriptive and it didn't work," she told the BBC.

"So what we've said all along is here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you."

News.title: Row over George Michael items up for auction - including Faith guitar
News.content:
Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.

She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.

"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.

"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."

The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.

The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".

It has an estimated price tag of between Â£60,000 and Â£120,000. Other less significant but more personal items have already exceeded their estimates.

A Filofax from the 1988 Faith tour with Siobhan's handwritten notes and annotations had a guide price of up to Â£600 and a current bid of Â£1,750.

Other items include a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.

The auction also includes the gold disc and platinum CD presented to her for sales milestones achieved by Michael's music.

"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.

He said "she would never have consented" to the sale of these items, adding that the auction "breaks my heart".

"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.

Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".

He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".

Bailey acknowledged that Belcher has a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

News.title: Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?
News.content:
From Milan, to Marseille, to Madrid and in so many other cities across Europe, streets have erupted in colourful, passionate protests in recent weeks. While most started peacefully, a large number ended in shocking scenes of violence and looting. There have been allegations of radical left-wing groups sparking riots intentionally and reports of police heavy-handedness.

We've seen thousands rallying in Rome and Florence. Hundreds of thousands across France. In Madrid, an encampment of tents has occupied a city-centre square since late September. In Lisbon, tens of thousands of mostly young people marched earlier this month. Tear gas and water cannon were used on protesters in Brussels, after young men dressed in black, their faces covered to hide their identities, threw rocks and firecrackers at police. In Albania, demonstrators alleging government corruption are demanding that their Prime Minister Edi Rama - already 13 years in power - stand down.

This continent feels volatile, socially and politically.

I've spent years in Europe reporting from a multitude of demonstrations, both peaceful and violent. I remember well the ardent Catalan pro-independence marches of 2017, the desperation and Molotov cocktails flying through Athens' streets during the 2015 Greek debt crisis, and various outbreaks of violence in France during President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office, sparked by fuel tax and pension reform proposals.

News.title: Watch: King dances in the streets of the Bahamas capital
News.content:
King Charles III danced in the street while taking part in a parade with officials in the Bahamas capital city of Nassau.

On Tuesday, the King gave a speech at an event celebrating local youth and acknowledged "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

The nine-day tour will end in the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, where the King says leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

News.title: I earn £30,000. I'm angry there was no fuel duty cut in the Budget
News.content:
Dave Herbert is a professional driver on Â£30,000 a year. He moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries and says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.

He spends around Â£350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.

He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."

The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.

The only measure Dave wanted to see was a cut to fuel duty, and he was disappointed this didn't happen.

"I'm pretty angry, really. Nothing has been thrown my way," he says.

The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 52.95p per litre until the summer, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."

News.title: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
News.content:
Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.

The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.

He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists.

"We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, president of the Bahamas National Trust Council.

"We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselvesâ¦ we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."

Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes.

The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.

A small protest near the parade, which had activists holding placards with the words "Pay us what you owe us", was moved on by the police.

The small group of protesters were from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.

The King acknowledged the "great suffering of the past" when he first arrived in the Bahamas, as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Noelle Nicholls, chair of the reparations committee, said :"We are demanding an apology for those crimes, and reparations for the harm that was done."

Nicholls said the protesters' presence "amidst the pomp and pageantry of the celebrations... are for us also a sombre occasion, because this is the King returning in a way that has still not atoned for the sins of the past."

The King has confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery at a major summit in Antigua next week.

News.title: Weight-loss jabs boom putting recycling centre workers at risk
News.content:
The boom in injectable weight-loss drugs, such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, is leading to more used needles turning up at recycling centres, putting workers at risk of serious injury and infection, bosses say.

At a recycling plant in Coventry, I watched staff sorting rubbish on a fast-moving conveyor belt when a crushed yellow sharps container suddenly appeared among the waste.

"A resident has put this in a wheelie bin," explained supervisor Paul Pagett.

"It then gets crushed by the recycling vehicle and then it comes to us open and obviously we've got needles then falling out on to the line putting my guys at risk."

The sharps box should never have been there.

Used needles should be disposed of separately through dedicated clinical waste services. Instead, recycling bosses say they are increasingly finding them mixed in with household waste.

"There are safe disposal routes for needles but the worst place to put them is in your recycling," said Richard Dobbs, managing director of Sherborne Recycling.

"It ends up in facilities like ours where it will be touched by people and that's inherently unsafe."

News.title: Tower block residents plagued by intruders in scaffolding 'nightmare'
News.content:
Natasha Dyett moved into the nine-storey block two years ago, with the scaffolding already in place.

"We've had the heatwave this summer; I've spent most of it with everything shut because we've had people breach the scaffolding all summer long," Dyett said.

She said that in July she was terrified to see someone outside her window.

"I climbed into bed, I turned over and I saw something outside. I rubbed my eyes because my vision is failing and I could still see it and it moved," she said. "I realised it was a person standing there."

She shouted at the person to go away and contacted her landlord, who advised her to call the police. However, she said the CCTV footage was wiped before it could be examined.

"It seems that every week someone is reporting people on the scaffolding," Dyett said. "They just walk around. I think they can get all the way up to the roof."

News.title: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
News.content:
A first-time mum was denied hospital meals while her baby was "fighting for her life" because she was not breastfeeding.

Sophie Price, 22, was "shocked" when staff refused to give her a meal while her daughter Florence was being treated on a paediatric ward at Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen.

Despite giving birth in the hospital five days earlier, she was told she was no longer classed as a patient as she was not breastfeeding, so she would not be provided with meals.

Aneurin Bevan health board said it was "sorry to hear about Sophie's experience" and was "committed to supporting families throughout their child's stay".

"It was just an awful experience. I just needed a hot meal to keep going for my daughter," said Sophie, from Newport.

Her family said they spent more than Â£1,000 on food from the canteen and takeaway meals during their three-week stay at the hospital while Florence was treated.

News.title: Russell Brand tells trial sexual consent is 'fundamental'
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

Russell Brand has told the jury at his trial he believes sexual consent is "fundamental" and "more important than sex itself".

Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Brand said the allegations had been "deeply traumatic" and had a "devastating" impact on him.

The media personality gave evidence as his defence case began at his trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

Asked whether consent was important to him, he told the court: "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself."

Brand told the court he had previously been "comfortable" allowing his fame to "facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong".

But asked by the prosecution whether he "needed and was prepared to go to any lengths", Brand replied: "Absolutely no."

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC suggested to Brand there were inconsistencies between his previous prepared police statement and what he told the jury.

"Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree," he replied. "Since these events occurred there's been escalating recollection.

"It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life. I've focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health.

"I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that."

He said: "I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.

"With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I've been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy."

He told the jury: "Regrettably I've had a lot of consensual sex, which I see has caused harm."

News.title: Huntingdon train attacker asked man 'do you want to die?', trial hears
News.content:
Train passengers fled "in sheer terror" from a knife attacker who asked one victim "do you want to die?", a trial has heard.

Jurors were shown CCTV footage of passenger Stephen Crean attempting to disarm Anthony Williams during the attack on the Doncaster to King's Cross train at Huntingdon on 1 November last year.

Opening the prosecution case at Cambridge Crown Court, Christopher Paxton KC said that of those on the train "some stood tall, to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage".

Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 train passengers and staff. He is also accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough the day before and then a boy at a London railway station.

Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder.

He is accused of attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett and Samir Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on that Saturday evening.

He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.

Williams was then seen swigging from a bottle of alcohol outside Ritzy Barber Shop in Fletton in Peterborough, before going into the shop brandishing a knife.

The jury heard he then travelled to east London, where he stabbed a 17-year-old on a Docklands Light Railway train at Pontoon Dock in Silvertown in the early hours of 1 November.

During that attack, jurors were told a witness said she heard the defendant repeatedly say: "Are you trying to beef with the devil?"

News.title: Chancellor says government has 'moral duty' to help young people out of work
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has pledged a reduction in the welfare bill ahead of the next general election, in an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

His comments come after the Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare", while Reform UK said the Budget did not address the "ballooning" benefits bill.

Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year to Â£353bn - and to Â£431bn in 2031/32, according to government spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Read more on the Budget on our live page.

News.title: Healey’s ‘risky’ budget slammed for failing to tackle worst decade for UK growth on record
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An influential think tank has criticised John Healey’s “risky” Budget for exposing Britain to further economic shocks and failing to tackle the “worst decade for growth” for household incomes on record.

The chancellor has been warned that the lower fiscal headroom left as a result of his first Budget could leave the country “more exposed to future bad news”, as government departments also face a real-terms value cuts to their spending.

In an exasperated tone, the IFS hit out: “temporary cost of living measures” being no substitute for “a strong economy” in a broadside against the approach taken by Andy Burnham since he became prime minister with a series of small measures on minor reductions to energy bills and capping the price of bus tickets to £2.

In its analysis of Mr Healey’s Budget, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said there are “risks” to his approach, which also come amid dismal growth for household incomes.

IFS director Helen Miller said the chancellor will need to do more, amid “depressing” growth, and said: “It’s depressing. No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy.”

She also criticised his “small, unhelpful fiddling with the tax system”, leaving it in a “mess” and calling his new Founders’ Relief “bonkers”.

( House of Commons )

“It is far more complex than it should be,” she said.

“And that is because, Budget after Budget, chancellors make seemingly small tweaks that lack principle and don’t systematically move us to a better place. This approach gives us more complexity and more instability. Both have real economic costs.”

More follows on this breaking news story...

News.title: Two young hikers found dead in remote Colorado basin after brutal mountain blizzard
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The search for two missing young hikers in Colorado ended in tragedy on Wednesday when a search party recovered the bodies of Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20, in the basin of West Apostle Mountain.

The pair planned to hike Ice Mountain and departed on October 23, intending to return on October 25, officials said earlier. Authorities found Matsuda’s car at the Mt. Huron trailhead, where hikers typically leave their vehicles. They also found their tent, but it had been covered with snow.

Authorities warn that anyone planning to climb in the area should be experienced, as it’s regarded as a “very technical” climb. At the time of the pair’s planned climb, Ice Mountain was covered in around two feet of snow. Officials described the area as having little or no cell phone service.

open image in gallery ( Chafee County Sheriff's Office )

Their bodies were found around 3:30 pm local time, some four miles from where Matsuda’s car was located, authorities said. Investigators do not suspect foul play was involved in the tragedy. An autopsy is pending. The search effort involved about 60 people, along with search dogs, drones, and helicopters.

Both were students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville.

open image in gallery Kaden Matsuda, 19, from Ridgway, Colorado, was an aspiring firefighter ( Chafee County Sheriff's Office )

Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich disclosed that Matsuda, a native of Ridgeway, Colorado, was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon, a native of New York, was studying to be a ‘Mountainar’ guide. The sheriff hoped that, despite the adverse weather conditions, the college students would be found “hunkered down” somewhere. Jackson was believed to be carrying an avalanche beacon.

“We are devastated by the loss of Kaden Matsuda and Jackson Donlon, two members of our Colorado Mountain College community,” the school said in a statement.

open image in gallery Jackson Donlon, 20, from New York, was an aspiring mountain guide ( Chafee County Sheriff's Office )

“Our hearts are with their families, friends, classmates, faculty and everyone who knew and cared about them. Our focus tonight is on supporting those closest to Kaden and Jackson and making sure our Leadville students, faculty and staff have the emotional support they need in the difficult days ahead. We are extraordinarily grateful to the search and rescue professionals and volunteers who devoted themselves to finding Kaden and Jackson.”

“Our heart aches for Kaden and Jackson's family and friends. We are very proud of our team's efforts to find them before this weekend's coming storm. Although this is a gut punch, our prayers were answered that we would find Kaden and Jackson, allowing some closure for the family. We ask that everyone give time and distance to family members and friends as they mourn their loss,” Sheriff Rohrich said in a statement.

News.title: The chaos inside Hegseth’s defense department that left Trump ‘concerned’ by scale of purge
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, at a time when President Donald Trump is openly musing about the prospect of further strikes on Iran after the midterms.

Sylvia was removed on October 28 as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, with no replacement named and no official reason given for his departure. He is the second person to be ousted from the all-important role: his predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement a year earlier.

A spokesperson for the Joint Staff said: “The Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation.” They added that they “wish him and his family the best.”

open image in gallery Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has endured a turbulent period in charge of the Department of Defense, defined by culture war vendettas and high staff turnover ( AP )

Sylvia is the latest casualty in what critics describe as an unprecedented purge of military leadership on Hegseth’s watch, which even Trump has reportedly expressed “concern” about in private.

The defense secretary addressed the broader issue of cuts during an ideology-heavy speech at Marine Corps Base Quantico in September. He announced additional 10 percent cuts to positions reserved for generals and admirals, having already made 10 percent cuts to those roles in 2025.

“The media calls that a purge,” Hegseth said. “I call it accountability and long overdue. And frankly, the bare minimum.

“The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in with testosterone testing on top. Diversity is not our strength. Unity is our strength.”

Below, we look at some of the high profile Pentagon departures during his tenure so far.

Gen. Charles Q Brown Jr

open image in gallery Gen. Charles Q Brown Jr was one of the first to be dismissed by Hegseth ( Getty )

The first casualty of Hegseth’s tenure was the 40-year Air Force veteran Gen. Charles Q Brown Jr, who was replaced by Lieutenant General Dan “Razin’” Caine as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in February 2025.

Brown, who had made history as the Air Force’s first African American chief of staff, had been in the post for 16 months and had expected to continue his term until the fall of 2027.

Trump said in a statement announcing Caine’s nomination that he had been “overlooked” by his predecessor Joe Biden, an apparent slight on Brown, who was nevertheless praised as “a fine gentleman and an outstanding leader.”

Adm. Lisa Franchetti

open image in gallery No reason was given for the removal of the trailblazing Amd. Lisa Franchetti ( Getty )

Hegseth also fired Franchetti – the first woman to serve as chief of naval operations and the first female member of the Joint Chiefs – that same month without explanation.

Biden had nominated her over the preference of his own defense secretary, Lloyd Austin, convinced by her vast experience in command and executive decision making.

Hegseth’s opposition invited concern from other women in the service, who feared they too could be blocked from advancing.

Gen. Tim Haugh

open image in gallery Gen. Tim Haugh was reportedly dismissed under the influence of MAGA influencer Laura Loomer ( Reuters )

Next to go was the director of the U.S. National Security Agency, who was fired along with his deputy Wendy Noble in April last year.

Haugh and Noble’s departures reportedly came after consultation with MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who beamed on X that they had been dismissed because they had been “disloyal to President Trump” and “handpicked” by former chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Gen. Mark Milley.

Loomer’s apparent role in the firings led to expressions of concern on Capitol Hill.

Vice Adm. Shoshana Chatfield

open image in gallery Vice Adm. Shoshana Chatfield was axed after reportedly appearing on a ‘woke’ list ( US Navy )

Four days after Haugh’s axing, the former Navy helicopter pilot and combat veteran was fired from her role as U.S. representative to the NATO Military Committee.

That came after she reportedly appeared on a “woke” list drawn up by the Trump administration, which took exception to her past advocacy for diversity in the Armed Forces.

According to the Associated Press, Chatfield was informed by Admiral Christopher Grady, the then-acting chairman of the Joint Chiefs, that the administration wanted to go in a different direction.

Gen. David Allvin

open image in gallery Former Air Force chief of staff Gen. David Allvin was persuaded to take retirement two years early ( Getty )

The following August, the Air Force chief of staff was dismissed with the same message as Chatfield, prompting him to retire two years into his four-year term.

Allvin was thanked for his “transformational” efforts in the role but an insider told The Washington Post his early retirement was “certainly not his choice.”

The general nevertheless issued a statement in which he said: “More than anything, I’m proud to have been part of the team of airmen who live out our core values of integrity, service and excellence every day as we prepare to defend this great nation.”

Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse

open image in gallery Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse led the Defense Intelligence Agency, which angered President Trump by undermining his rhetoric on Iran ( Getty )

There were to be more departures that month, including that of Kruse as head of the Defense Intelligence Agency, which had determined that the administration’s Operation Midnight Hammer airstrikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities were less effective than Trump and Hegseth had claimed.

While the president and his secretary had repeatedly insisted Iran’s capabilities had been “obliterated,” the DIA put out a report suggesting they had only been set back by a matter of months, infuriating Trump.

Also leaving their posts at this time were Vice Adm. Nancy Lacore and Rear Adm. Milton Sands, departing as chiefs of the Navy Reserve and Naval Special Warfare Command respectively.

Gen. Randy George

open image in gallery Army chief of staff Gen. Randy George’s dismissal a matter of weeks into the war was met with concern ( Reuters )

After a period of relative calm – other than the loss of the aforementioned three-star Lt. Gen. McGee from the Pentagon’s Joint Staff in October – Hegseth dismissed the Army’s chief of staff in April this year, perhaps his most controversial call coming a little over a month into the Iran conflict.

The decorated veteran’s firing reportedly came after another clash with Hegseth and was met with solemn scenes when he broke the news to colleagues and indignation in Congress, where the Senate Armed Forces Committee pressed the secretary for an explanation.

The Army’s top uniformed officer has since been replaced on an acting basis by Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who has yet to be confirmed by the Senate.

Navy Secretary John Phelan

open image in gallery Navy Secretary John Phelan came after Hegseth determined new leadership was needed ( Getty )

Three weeks after George was let go, Hegseth ousted the head of the Navy, replacing him with then-undersecretary Hung Cao on an acting basis, shortly after Iran’s move to shut off the Strait of Hormuz caused a spike in global oil prices.

“President Trump and Secretary Hegseth agreed new leadership at the Navy is needed,” a senior administration official told The Independent at the time.

The plight of sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, diverted to the Gulf because of the war and starved of necessities, has since come to light, drawing attention to the strain being placed on U.S. military resources by the war.

Gen. Christopher Donahue

open image in gallery Gen. Christopher Donahue is a legend in the U.S. military for being the last U.S. soldier to leave Afghanistan in 2021 ( U.S. Army Europe and Africa )

After Phelan, the next to leave the military’s hierarchy was the commander of U.S. Army forces in Europe and Africa.

Donahue was famously the last American soldier to leave Afghanistan in 2021 and enjoyed a distinguished career leading Delta Force units in Iraq and Afghanistan before commanding the 82nd Airborne Division.

Maj. Gen. Christopher Norrie, Donahue’s deputy, has since stepped in as his interim replacement.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll

open image in gallery Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is a close friend of Vice President JD Vance ( Getty )

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll then resigned on September 1 amid reports of tensions with Hegseth.

As with Sylvia, no official reason was offered for his departure after 18 months in the role but CNN and Reuters reported he had been butting heads with Hegseth for several months. The Atlantic reported he had raised concerns about the state of the military with Trump in the Oval Office, who was said to have been left “surprised and concerned” by what he heard.

Driscoll is an Iraq War veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vice President JD Vance, whom he befriended while they were contemporaries at Yale Law School.

When nominating him in 2024, Trump hailed Driscoll as “a disruptor and change agent.” He went on to make good on that reputation by championing the development of drone warfare technology – only for Hegseth to shut down a European unit focused on that field in August and order it to return to its “core” mission of airborne infantry.

He subsequently gave an interview to Rolling Stone in which he acknowledged differences of opinion with Hegseth, while adding: “If you polled us, we probably agreed on more than 50 percent of things. What’s been reported is all the things we disagree on.”

Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia

open image in gallery Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of planning with the president openly musing on further airstrikes against Iran ( AP )

Sylvia, who previously commanded the storied 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, was ousted after a year of serving as the Pentagon’s top military planner, having replaced the retired Lt. Gen. McGee.

His departure was controversial as it came with less than a week to go before the midterm elections, for which Trump had been touring the country and telling rally crowds he could launch further airstrikes against Iran aimed at ending the unpopular war he started the previous February.

The conflict remains mired in deadlock, having cost American lives and driven up domestic gas prices.

News.title: Healey’s Budget slammed as ‘scattergun’ by think tank formerly run by Treasury minister
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Budget has been dismissed as “scattergun” by an economic think tank formerly run by one of the chancellor John Healey's own Treasury ministers.

The Resolution Foundation, set up to help people on lower and middle incomes, says the Budget will do little to address “the sharp challenges facing Britain”.

And it warned that the decisions facing the government would “unavoidably get starker” next year because of the failure to tackle them now.

The rebuff for Mr Healey's package of measures is particularly embarrassing because until two years ago the think tank was headed by pensions minister Torsten Bell.

Mr Bell was one of six Treasury ministers who appeared alongside Mr Healey in Downing Street yesterday for the traditional photograph of the Chancellor holding the Red Box containing the Budget before heading to the Commons to unveil its contents.

open image in gallery Mr Bell (far left) was one of six Treasury ministers who appeared alongside Mr Healey in Downing Street yesterday ( Reuters )

Mr Bell played a key role in drawing up the measures. Until he became an MP in 2024 he was chief executive of the Resolution Foundation.

In its highly critical verdict on the Budget today, the think tank said the cost of living measures announced yesterday would not stop energy bills from leaping above levels seen during the last rises triggered by the Iran War and Middle East crisis.

Mr Bell's successor as Resolution Foundation, chief executive Ruth Curtice, said: “Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”

The think tank said that average annual energy bills are likely to rise to £1,750 as a result of government aid in 2026-27.

It also stated that typical disposable income can be expected to go down by £1,050 in the next two to three years when the next general election is due to take place.

open image in gallery The rebuff for Healey's package of measures is particularly embarrassing: until two years ago the think tank was headed by pensions minister Torsten Bell (far left) ( Reuters )

Ms Curtice added: “A more dramatic change of tactics may be needed, and we did not learn how the government will choose between public service ambitions and household incomes. Next year the choices will unavoidably get starker.”

She added that the Budget “did not live up to the scale of the challenges that Britain faces”, arguing that “in the face of what are really catastrophic forecasts for living standards” the government had taken “an approach to cost of living support that may be popular but is far from effective.”

Meanwhile, Greg Thwaites, interim chief economist at the think tank warned that the government’s move to provide £100 energy support for households in council tax band A to D is “extremely badly targeted”.

“£100 is nice, but the point is it’s extremely badly targeted … There are lots of people who are doing okay who probably can manage without that money”, he said.

He added that the support has “really nothing to do with how much energy people use” leaving lower income households which have high levels of energy consumption with the similar support to higher income households with smaller gas and electricity use.

Until he became a minister Mr Bell was best known as the brains behind one of the most derided stunts in modern political history.

As an aide to former Labour leader Ed Miliband he was credited with devising the notorious 'Edstone,' whereby Labour's six core 2015 election pledges would be carved into a massive 8 foot 6 inches tall limestone slab to be erected in Downing Street.

As pensions minister since 2024 Mr Bell was heavily involved in Andy Burnham’s controversial decision to end the pensions ‘triple lock.’

It comes as the budget watchdog, the Office of Budget Responsibility, said the UK’s “economic and fiscal position remains very challenging” after almost two decades of shocks and stagnation, pushing up the national debt.

Professor David Miles of its Budget Responsibility Committee (BRC) warned it marked a “pretty grim picture”.

“If you go back to just before Covid and take that as your base, where we are right now which is what some seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income,” he said.

“That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.” He added: “It’s been a dismal period in British economic history.”

News.title: Thousands of jobs at risk with Poundland on brink of administration
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

High street giant Poundland is on the brink of administration, putting around 12,000 jobs at risk.

The retailer is set to file a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which will give the business 10 working days of breathing space from creditors to secure a potential rescue deal.

It is understood Poundland has not yet filed the notice, but is preparing to do so imminently.

Poundland managing director Barry Williams told staff in a memo that the situation is “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”.

open image in gallery A Poundland store

The discount chain is due to enter insolvency after owner Gordon Brothers rejected a takeover offer from Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group, which management named as their preferred bidder earlier this month.

Gordon Brothers – which only bought Poundland last year for £1 – launched a sale process for the retailer at the start of September.

Wilko and The Range owner CDS Superstores, Poundstretcher owner Fortress and TG Jones owner Modella are all understood to be interested in buying parts of the Poundland business.

It is understood the retailer has appointed advisers at AlixPartners to oversee the insolvency process and assess offers to buy all or parts of the business.

Poundland currently runs around 600 stores across the UK.

Gordon Brothers had overseen a major turnaround programme at Poundland that included closing more than 100 shops over the past year in an effort to shore up its finances.

News.title: Trump says he will look at helping Netanyahu after Israeli prime minister claims election ‘stolen’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

US president Donald Trump has said he will “take a look” at helping Benjamin Netanyahu after the prime minister claimed the Israel election was “stolen”.

Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc secured the most seats in Israel's parliament but still lost its parliamentary majority on Tuesday despite a glowing endorsement from US president Trump.

His Likud party on Wednesday claimed voter fraud perpetrated by Arab citizens had stopped him from winning a clear victory in the election - claims already shot down by Israeli police.

Even as Netanyahu cried foul, Trump claimed that his endorsement had lifted Netanyahu in Tuesday’s vote.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump says that his endorsement of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu turned the latter's campaign around ( Reuters )

“I heard my endorsement made a big difference for Bibi,” Trump told Axios in a brief interview on Wednesday, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.

Trump said he had initially received “horror reports” about his ally’s prospects in the polls, but felt he was “in pretty good shape now”.

Asked whether he might intervene in an effort to form a Netanyahu-led unity government in Israel, he said he hadn’t thought about it but would “take a look”.

With nearly 94% of votes tallied on Wednesday, Netanyahu's bloc was set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, well ahead of the 48 for rival Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc.

Parties representing Arab Israelis were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot little realistic path to power without their broad backing, which many Jewish political leaders reject.

open image in gallery Trump said he wanted Netanyahu to remain in power to help him soon "finish the job” against Iran ( AFP/Getty )

In a statement shared by Netanyahu, Likud insisted there was “evidence of election theft in many Arab polling stations” and urged law enforcement to “act harshly and swiftly”.

Israel police said they had no investigative or intelligence-based evidence supporting the allegations, however, after the party demanded and investigation into alleged voting irregularities.

Police received 48 complaints concerning fraud and impersonation nationwide as of Tuesday night, down from nearly 80 in the previous election.

They stressed that neither investigative findings nor intelligence supported the allegations raised.

In his October 18 endorsement, Trump said he wanted Netanyahu to remain in power to help him soon "finish the job” against Iran.

open image in gallery Israeli left-wing activists hold placards during a protest calling for a formation of a government, in Tel Aviv on Wednesday ( AFP/Getty )

The president said overnight that Netanyahu, who outperformed pre-election polls, had done "very well" and that his backing had boosted the Israeli leader.

Earlier on Wednesday, he shared a statement attributed to somebody called “Irving C. Schwartz” that assessed Trump’s endorsement had “turned the tide” in the election.

“When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu,” read the statement shared to his Truth Social profile.

While Netanyahu now seems in a stronger position, neither side is projected to have an outright path to form a new government after Israel’s first election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023.

The stage appears to be set for a period of painstaking coalition bargaining – or possibly another election – while Netanyahu remains in power in a caretaker capacity.

Experts say the caretaker role would still retain powers, including over the war in Iran.

open image in gallery Trump shared a post saying he deserved the credit for Netanyahu’s survival ( @RealDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

Consequently, the outcome of the election will have implications for US-Israeli relations, which have been dominated by the joint fight against Iran, stalled Gaza peace efforts and signs of eroding US public support for Israel.

“Israeli politics can be messy,” said Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East adviser in Democratic and Republican administrations.

From the US perspective, he said, “it would be good to get some clarity, but that's easier said than done”.

But Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy US national intelligence officer on the Middle East, said any future Israeli leadership would likely be on the same page as Trump if he decides to escalate from the current stalemate with Israel’s regional arch-foe.

“It’s hard to imagine any real daylight between them on that point,” said Panikoff, now at the Atlantic Council think tank in Washington.

News.title: Thailand revokes citizenship of chief rabbi Yosef Chaim Kantor over continued use of US passport
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thailand has revoked the citizenship of chief rabbi Yosef Chaim Kantor over the continued use of his US nationality for international travel.

Despite becoming a Thai citizen in 2013, Rabbi Kantor reportedly used his US passport, including on 16 trips to and from Australia, local media reports said. The order was signed by prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

Thai law allows the government to revoke naturalised citizenship if a person continues to use a former nationality. The move comes amid a wider crackdown on foreign nationals accused of breaking laws or circumventing regulations.

According to local media outlet Thairath, the announcement said Mr Kantor’s “Thai nationality was officially announced in the Royal Gazette on April 11, 2013, and his first national identity card was issued on May 2, 2013”.

“However, information from the Department of Special Investigation, Ministry of Justice, reveals that they have investigated foreign nationals who have been granted Thai citizenship for actions that may affect national security, both economically and socially.”

It added that Mr Kantor “has continuously used his American citizenship to travel in and out of Australia 16 times (the last time being January 26, 2026), which constitutes a violation of the conditions for obtaining Thai citizenship”.

Mr Anutin’s government, which won February’s elections on a nationalist, Thailand-first platform, has introduced rules allowing faster deportations of foreigners deemed harmful to public order and stepped up investigations into foreign-controlled businesses and land held through Thai proxies.

Mr Kantor has led the Chabad community of Thailand, an Orthodox Jewish group, since 1993. Chabad is a global Orthodox Jewish movement headquartered in New York.

JDN, a Hebrew-language news outlet, reported that Chabad is challenging the decision through legal channels. It said that its centres across Thailand continued to operate as usual.

According to a statement carried by the outlet in Hebrew, Chabad said: “Rabbi Kantor has served the Jewish community in Thailand for more than 30 years, and Thailand is his and his family’s home. We respect the Kingdom of Thailand, its laws and institutions, and are grateful for its hospitality over the years.”

They “regretted” Thailand’s decision and said “the issue is being handled through the accepted legal channels, with full trust in the Thai system”.

Mr Kantor’s case comes soon after the revocation of a businessman’s Thai citizenship after authorities said he continued using an Israeli passport and failed to disclose his Uruguayan nationality when naturalised.

Investigators also searched Chabad and other Jewish-linked premises this month as part of an investigation into suspected nominee businesses and property holdings.

Officials have stressed that the investigation concerns possible legal violations rather than nationality, and no wrongdoing has been established against Mr Kantor or Chabad.

News.title: Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out
News.content:
It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

News.title: Burnham rules out calling early election
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has promised to offer households “breathing space” in his maiden Budget today.

The Chancellor insisted the economy has shown “resilience” in the face of the energy shock from the Iran war.

However, he admitted the conflict has pushed up the cost of living, “piling pressure on the families, on businesses, and on our public finances”.

Among the measures the Chancellor is expected to announce are plans to scrap standing charges on household gas bills – saving families up to £50 a year.

Mr Healey said: “We can’t stop these shocks that hit Britain, but we can make Britain more resilient when they do.

“So, this Budget is designed to give households breathing space from some of the everyday costs, provide targeted support for businesses and self-employed people, and to start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Healey prepares to slash household gas bills by £50 | Chancellor to scrap standing charges on gas bills and curb Energy Secretary’s power

2) Minimum wage rise will drive up food prices, Healey warned | Manufacturers say they are already struggling to cover soaring production costs

3) Poundland directors quit in stand-off over administration | Board members fear owner wants to steer retailer into insolvency

4) Google attacks UK over ‘unlawful’ AI plans | Search giant fights plans by competition regulator to force it to promote rivals

5) Netherlands to cut 25,000 civil service jobs in AI push | Police and defence will be exempt from plans to trim 15pc of government workforce in next decade

What happened overnight

Ahead of the Budget, oil prices rose after an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest crude exporter, which has renewed concerns around the risks to supply in the Middle East.

Brent crude was up 1.7pc to nearly $116 a barrel, maintaining inflationary pressure on the global economy. It traded around $70 before the start of the Iran war.

Meanwhile, Asia stocks rallied amid fresh enthusiasm about AI.

South Korea’s Kospi surged more than 6pc and was on track for its largest one-day gain since July, after chipmaker SK Hynix reported a more than seven-fold jump in quarterly profit and said it would return about $75 billion to shareholders this year.

The AI rally faces its next test when technology giants Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings after market close later today, with investors looking for evidence of returns that would justify the hefty cost of the AI build-out.

In Asia, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 1.7pc, with Japan’s Nikkei adding 1.1pc and ⁠China’s CSI300 blue-chip index climbing 0.7pc.

News.title: Government remains tight-lipped on aid spending in Autumn budget
News.content:
The government made no mention of plans to restore aid spending in the Autumn budget and is on track to miss its current aid commitment.

It had been rumoured that a Burnham government planned to reverse the overseas aid cuts made by Sir Keir Starmer, who reduced an already shrunken aid budget from 0.5 to 0.3 per cent of gross national income (GNI) in February 2025.

The current 0.3 per cent allocation is the lowest proportion of national income spent on aid since 1999.

It was expected the reversal would be drawn up as part of a wider shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) under Ed Miliband as foreign secretary, The Telegraph reported in September.

But there was no mention of any timeline for restoring Britain’s overseas development assistance to the legally enshrined 0.7 per cent of gross national income GNI target on Wednesday.

The UK is now also on track to miss its 0.3 per cent aid spending commitment, equivalent to £9.2 billion per year, following a failure to confirm any upwards adjustment to the UK aid budget to account for inflation.

The shortfall is estimated to fall at £410 million this year, an analysis from the Centre for Global Development (CGD) found.

Britain’s aid money is spent across the world in sectors like health, education, disaster relief, and helping to promote democracy.

News.title: Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history
News.content:
An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.



“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”



Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: High temperatures linked to more than 700,000 deaths in 2023, study estimates
News.content:
Record-breaking temperatures killed an estimated 710,00 people globally in 2023, an increase of more than 36 per cent since 2015, according to new research.

A report on climate change and health by the Lancet medical journal shows that since the Paris climate agreement was introduced in 2016 the number of deaths linked to heat has rocketed.

Between 2006 and 2015 the average annual number of deaths attributed to heat stood at around 398,400 but between 2016 and 2023 the number increased to an annual average of 540,800, hitting a high of 710,000 in 2023.

The authors of the Lancet study say that extreme heat, which is linked to cardiovascular problems and is particularly dangerous for older people, pregnant women and those with other health conditions, must be considered a global health emergency. And they warn that the risks from high temperatures have accelerated in recent years.

News.title: Nigeria’s women and girls impacted the most by British and US funding cuts, committee is told
News.content:
UK and US aid funding cuts in Nigeria have impacted the country’s women and girls more than other groups, MPs were told on Tuesday.

Nigeria has been among the hardest-hit countries as many Western governments have slashed overseas development budgets to increase defence spending.

At the International Development Committee’s first hearing on the impact of aid cuts on global health in Africa, MPs were told that UK government cuts had impacted water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programmes in Nigeria significantly, putting women and girls at risk.

“WASH is one of the lowest-funded areas in UK government support to Nigeria. WASH enables girls to stay in school, enables them to manage their menstruation effectively, enables women to give birth safely, and protects the lives of children under 5,” Evelyn Mere country director of Water Aid Nigeria said.

“The UK government says one of its priorities is that it will educate girls, empower women and make sure their voices are heard. It means that the UK says one thing, but with the aid cuts does another,” she added.

The British Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) announced earlier this year it would reduce its aid spending in Nigeria by 50.2 per cent over the next three years, from £136 million in 2025 to £68 million by 2029.

Nigeria has also faced substantial funding reductions from the US after the Trump administration shuttered USAID, the government’s foreign assistance arm. This included more than $600 million (£450 million) in health funding.

An FCDO internal impact assessment, published in July 2025, acknowledged that the biggest casualties of African funding cuts would be frontline WASH and women’s health programmes.

“Overall, any reductions to health spending risk an increase in disease burden and ultimately in deaths, impacting in particular those living in poverty, women, children and people with disabilities,” the assessment concluded.

Sports.title: England star Ivan Toney pleads not guilty to ‘headbutting and punching man in swanky nightclub brawl’
Sports.content:
CLUB 'ATTACK' England star Ivan Toney pleads not guilty to ‘headbutting and punching man in swanky nightclub brawl’







Next

ENGLAND star Ivan Toney has pleaded not guilty to headbutting and punching a man during an alleged brawl inside a swanky nightclub.

The former Brentford striker, 30, allegedly assaulted Saber Da Silva after a “confrontation” at 100 Wardour Street in Soho, London, last December.



Toney appeared at Southwark Crown Court today where he denied assault causing actual bodily harm.

A court was told previously the two men “squared up to each other” before Toney allegedly “lunged forward and headbutted the complainant, followed by a few punches”.



Mr Da Silva was left with injuries to his nose and finger, the prosecutor added.

Judge Chris Hehir set a provisional trial date of June 2028 as he released the star on unconditional bail.



He said: “That’s a long way, I’m sorry about that. As you may know the crown courts are operating under a great deal of pressure.”

The Sun revealed the footballer, who now plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was held following an alleged headbutt during the brawl.

Witnesses in the club claimed trouble erupting after a fan grabbed Toney for a selfie.

Officers arrived at the club within half an hour and quickly frogmarched the ex-Premier League star out of the venue.



The London Ambulance Service confirmed three people were assessed at the scene before one was taken to hospital.

Toney’s charge came just weeks after he started in England’s World Cup third-place play-off victory against France.

The Met Police said: “A man has been charged with assault following a Met investigation.



“Ivan Toney, 30, of Northampton, was charged on Thursday, 31 July with assault causing actual bodily harm.

“He will appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday, 24 September.

“The charge relates to an assault, which reportedly took place on 6 December 2025 at a nightclub on Wardour Street, W1.”

Toney began his career at his hometown club Northampton Town and made his first team debut in November 2012.

He then signed for Premier League club Newcastle United in August 2015 on a long-term contract for an undisclosed fee.



Toney enjoyed spells on loan at Barnsley, Shrewsbury Town, Scunthorpe United and Wigan Athletic before signing for League One club Peterborough.

In August 2020, the footballer signed for then-Championship side Brentford on a nine-year deal worth around £10million with add-ons.

He scored 67 goals across 128 games and was brought up with the team when they were promoted in 2021.



Toney completed a transfer to Saudi Pro League club Al Ahli in August 2024 for a reported £40million.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The striker has made ten appearances for England was taken to the World Cup this summer by Thomas Tuchel.

A spokesperson for Toney said previously: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

EMMANUEL EMEGHA was slammed after sensationally shoving Virgil van Dijk as Chelsea crashed out of the Carabao Cup.

The striker, 23, could not stop the West Londoners falling to a nail-biting penalty shootout defeat to Liverpool.



And Emegha, who joined Chelsea team-mate Wesley Fofana in missing from the spot, was at the centre of a major flashpoint at Anfield.

Sports.title: Carlos Tevez claims broken promise from Sir Alex Ferguson caused Man Utd exit and why he wanted to ‘kill Gary Neville’
Sports.content:
Next

CARLOS TEVEZ has claimed that Sir Alex Ferguson broke a promise to him ahead of his Manchester United exit in 2009.

The Argentine superstar spent two seasons with the Red Devils on loan from West Ham between 2007 and 2009.



But despite the Fergie allegedly promising him that United would look at buying him out of his West Ham deal, Tevez felt the club were not treating his situation with respect.

That’s when he then infamously jumped ship to join ‘noisy neighbours’ Manchester City.



The move understandably shocked and upset fans, but Tevez has now claimed on Rio Ferdinand Presents that the departure was in part due to a perceived betrayal by his own manager.

He explained: “They spoke to me (before) the two-year loan. After, if you play well, (we) pay the contract after one year.



“Fergie told me, ‘Carlos, now I’m going to pay out your contract and you’re going to stay in Manchester’.

“The team went to Los Angeles for pre-season. I remember this conversation with Fergie.

“He said ‘I’m going to pay for Berbatov but you, don’t worry, I’m going to buy you and we’ll do your contract.'”

But that promise never came to pass, and as time passed Tevez became convinced that he was not truly wanted by the club and should begin to look for other options.

That came despite a wealth of support among fans, including those who Tevez recalls chanting at Fergie to “sign him up”.

Tevez continued: “For me, the people, the United fans, understand.

“They don’t understand about Fergie speaking to me, or behind the scenes. What happened between Fergie and me, I think people don’t understand that.’

“I think that Ferguson had, from the day we talked, up to six months to keep his word. And he didn’t. On the contrary, he started leaving me on the bench.

“In my head, he started pushing me aside so he could bring down what I was worth. And that’s what hurt me the most.”



Tevez added: “It was hard Rio, because I felt like I had given my heart to United, and I didn’t feel the same in return.”

Sports.title: ‘Nothing justifies this’ – Chelsea fans rage as Xabi Alonso ‘makes popular star warm up twice then refuses to play him’
Sports.content:
Next

CHELSEA fans raged as Estevao was left on the bench against Liverpool.

The Brazilian, 19, did not come on before the Blues were dumped out of the Carabao Cup on penalties following a 1-1 draw at Anfield.



Estevao has not started a Premier League match under Xabi Alonso, but had previously begun both cup contests.

This time he could not get on, despite his name being chanted by travelling Chelsea fans, with forgotten man Emmanuel Emegha instead getting the nod during the second half.



After the game, several fans took to social media to fume over Estevao’s lack of minutes.

One wrote: “The way Alonso has treated Estevao is so disgusting. How is nobody talking about it”.

And a second blasted: “I’m sorry but nothing justifies why Estevao is not playing, we might lose him in January or maybe he will put in a transfer request next summer,he can’t even start in Carabao cup games, this is the face of Brazil football and he is being treated like a trash.”

A third raged: “Sorry but Xabi Alonso lost me today. What we saw today was a f***ing disgrace.

“Don’t tell me that he doesn’t have a problem with Steve. He made him warm up twice and didn’t play him. He heard our fans ask for him three times and didn’t play him.

“Steve is also a penalty taker.”



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

After the match, Alonso explained of the teenager: “I understand his situation and that he could be happier for sure.

“Every player wants to play, wants to be part of the team. We have had some intense games, and there will be moments for everything.

“I’m sure that Este will have his moment. It’s my responsibility and we need to deal with that.”

On the fans’ chants for Estevao, Alonso added: “The fans were saying a lot of things. We have started with Pedro [Neto], with Danny [Welbeck] and with Morgan [Rogers] up front. The game had very intense moments.



“We knew that it was going to be physical. And after we had to deal with Moi [Caicedo], he had little problems. Malo [Gusto], as well, he had cramps. So we were a little bit forced with substitutions.

“And now we know that the season is going to be long. And there will be moments for everyone.”

Alonso, 44, was then asked if Estevao’s lack of physicality was playing a significant role in his lack of minutes.

The Spaniard admitted: “Yes, we know that the Premier League and the game in England is really intense.



“You need to be up for it. Este has played, for sure, it’s his second season. But he had the injury and he’s in that process.

“Trust me, I’m sure the season is going to be long and Este is going to play his role.”

Sports.content:
WNBA Finals: Game 6 live on Sky Sports, Thursday at 4.30pm as Golden State Valkyries vs Atlanta Dream makes history

Game 6 of the WNBA Finals between Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream takes place live on Sky Sports on Thursday October 29 at 4.30pm

On Thursday, either the Golden State Valkyries will win a WNBA championship in just their second year of existence, live on Sky Sports, or the Atlanta Dream will force the first Game 7 in league history.

Amid scheduling drama, which has resulted in a 12.30pm tip off time in Atlanta - and 9.30am in San Francisco - the match is still a sell out and much anticipated.

"I'd like to see it be a national holiday for all WNBA championship games," Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said in jest this week.

"I hope everybody gets to see it, somehow. I know for some people, it's not realistic. They have jobs. They won't be able to make it. I'm disappointed for that, but I'm really hopeful that as many people can see the game as possible."

The game could have been played at Atlanta's 'usual' home court at the Gateway Center Arena on Thursday night. It would have been a great atmosphere, but nobody wanted the tiny crowd of 3,500 or so.

In the future, State Farm and its 17,000 capacity will become the full-time home of the Dream, which means potential WNBA Finals dates won't clash with Atlanta Hawks NBA games.

"It's better than, you know, having it at the YMCA that night in front of 75 people," the NBA's Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said. "They're doing what they've got to do."

The Valkyries, for their part, have some ideas on how fans can manage the early start time.

"Call in sick," guard Veronica Burton said. "I recommend it."

Forward Kiah Stokes added: "Don't y'all know how to fake a cough?"
