World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 29, 2026
World.content:
One Year After Tanzania's Election Crackdown, Victims' Families Demand Justice

One year after deadly election-related violence in Tanzania that left at least 518 people dead, families of victims are demanding justice, accountability and financial assistance for medical treatment. Survivors continue to struggle with injuries and mounting hospital bills. Families of those killed or missing say they have received little support or information. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have accused authorities of failing to hold security forces accountable and intensifying repression against critics, opposition supporters and journalists. The government denies widespread human rights abuses. President Samia Suluhu Hassan was elected with 98% of the vote. The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Hassan's two main challengers were excluded. Opposition leader Tundu Lissu remains on trial for treason amid growing concerns over political freedoms.

Rights Group Calls for Release of Missing Niger Journalist

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Human Rights Watch has urged Niger's authorities to disclose the whereabouts of prominent journalist Moussa Kaka, who disappeared in August 2026. He was later confirmed by the justice minister to be in detention. The authorities have not revealed where he is being held or provided details of the alleged offence. Kaka, director-general of Radio Télévision Saraounia and a former Radio France Internationale correspondent, has previously faced arrest over his journalism. His disappearance comes amid growing concerns about political repression under Niger's military junta, which has been accused of restricting press freedom, detaining critics and weakening democratic institutions. Rights groups are calling for his safe release unless he has been lawfully charged.

Kenya Anger Grows Over Delay in Ex-British Soldier's Extradition Hearing in Murder Case



The family of Agnes Wanjiru, a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by former British soldier Robert James Purkiss in 2012, has condemned the postponement of his extradition hearing in the United Kingdom until May 2027. Wanjiru's body was found in a septic tank near a British Army training camp in Kenya. Her family said that the latest delay prolongs their 14-year wait for justice. Purkiss, who was arrested in the UK in November 2025, denied the allegation. He is contesting extradition to Kenya. The family said it was not properly informed of the postponement and urged authorities to expedite proceedings so he can face trial. The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

Tanzania Discovers Major Natural Gas Reserves After a Decade

Tanzania has announced its first major natural gas discovery in a decade, with an estimated 223 billion cubic feet found at the Kasa-1X ST2 well in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country. Energy Minister Juma Homera described the discovery as a significant milestone expected to strengthen domestic energy supplies. Production is anticipated to begin early next month. Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet. The gas will support electricity generation, industrial activities and vehicles powered by compressed natural gas. Natural gas already accounts for nearly 80% of Tanzania's electricity generation. The discovery could help meet growing energy demand as the country expands its industrial sector.

Liberia to Lead UN Security Council for First Time in 65 Years

Liberia will assume the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December for the first time in 65 years, marking a significant milestone in its diplomatic history. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai is scheduled to chair a high-level debate on maritime security on 3 December. The government said that Liberia will draw on its experience of civil conflict, reconciliation and post-war recovery to contribute to international peace and security. Ahead of the presidency, the Foreign Affairs Ministry has announced events focused on diplomacy, women's leadership, youth participation and the country's peacebuilding legacy. Boakai also said the need for stronger international cooperation on challenges including climate change, poverty, migration and emerging technologies. He advocated for developing countries to have a greater voice in global decision-making.

Close 

WFP Chief Says Ending Conflict Is Key to Tackling Global Hunger

The new head of the World Food Programme (WFP), Executive Director Luke Lindberg, has said that reducing conflict is the most effective way to tackle global hunger, with conflict driving two-thirds of acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide. He warned that El Niño could push a further 49 million people into acute food insecurity, while supply chain disruptions are worsening the crisis. Lindberg outlined priorities including protecting humanitarian workers, strengthening donor partnerships, improving operations, investing in disaster preparedness and expanding school meal programmes. He identified Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia as areas of special concern, vowing to prevent famine and enhance food aid in the most vulnerable areas.

World.title: Kenya: Agnes Wanjiru Family Outraged as Extradition Hearing Delayed to 2027
World.content:
Fourteen years after a British soldier killed Agnes Wanjiru, her daughter is waiting for the UK to answer

The family of Agnes Wanjiru, a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by former British soldier Robert James Purkiss in 2012, has condemned the postponement of his extradition hearing in the United Kingdom until May 2027.

The five-day hearing had been scheduled to begin in mid-November 2026 at Westminster Magistrates' Court in the UK.

Wanjiru's body was found in a septic tank near a British Army training camp in Kenya.

Her family said that the latest delay prolongs their 14-year wait for justice. The family had been fundraising to facilitate the trip and expected to travel to the UK in about three weeks to follow the proceedings.

Purkiss, who was arrested in the UK in November 2025, denied the allegation. He is contesting extradition to Kenya.

The family said it was not properly informed of the postponement and urged authorities to expedite proceedings so he can face trial.

The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

World.title: South Africa: Calls for Calm as Cape Taxi Violence Escalates - South African News Briefs - October 29, 2026
World.content:
press review

Calls for Calm as Cape Taxi Violence Escalates

Calls for calm are growing amid escalating taxi-related shootings in Cape Town, linked to route disputes between rival associations CATA and CODETA, reports EWN. The latest incident at Delft Palm taxi rank left two people injured. Several areas across the province have experienced deadly violence. Cape Town Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis has offered Metro Police support to SAPS. Western Cape Mobility MEC Isaac Sileku has warned the associations to end the violence or face decisive action. A meeting between government and taxi industry representatives is set to seek a lasting solution and protect commuters.

Pastor and Co-Accused Return to Court in Infant Murder Case



Self-proclaimed pastor Caiphus Mkhawane and his co-accused, Ntsako Makhubela and Amanda Mnguni, are set to appear in the Atteridgeville Magistrates’ Court on charges including conspiracy to commit murder and fraud, reports SABC News. Mkhawane and Makhubela also face charges of human trafficking, premeditated murder, rape, kidnapping and robbery with aggravating circumstances. The case stems from allegations that the accused lured a woman and her infant to the Hennops River under the pretext of religious rituals, where the woman was allegedly raped and the child killed. The matter was previously postponed for Makhubela to undergo a mental assessment to determine her fitness to stand trial.

Cat Matlala Back in Court for ID and Bank Fraud Case

Alleged underworld figure Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala is set back in court in connection with an identity document and bank fraud case involving an allegedly fraudulent lease for a luxury property in Waterkloof, reports EWN. The State accused him of using an Eswatini identity document and falsified bank statements to secure the lease. Matlala abandoned his bail application after the State opposed his release, choosing instead to focus on a separate High Court matter. His wife, Tsakane, and co-accused Given Makofane and Claudette Masethe have each been granted R20,000 bail. Matlala also faces separate attempted murder charges in the Johannesburg High Court.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria, Other Countries Demand End to U.S. Blockade of Cuba
World.content:
The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 countries in favour and 17 opposed, including the US and Israel.

Nigeria and the majority of other UN members have voted for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, which is crippling the country.

The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 countries in favour. This included a majority of African countries. Morocco was the only African country that voted in support of the blockade. PREMIUM TIMES previously reported the strong historical and bilateral ties between Cuba and African states.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A total of 17 countries opposed the resolution, including the US and Israel. Also, 25 countries abstained, including Germany and Italy, which had previously voted in favour.

This resolution has been put forward and approved annually since 1992. Last year, more than 160 countries backed the proposal. Although not legally binding, the resolution reflects international opinion of the illegal US blockade of Cuba.

The resolution calls for lifting the economic, trade, and financial embargo against the island nation.

Earlier in the year, the Donald Trump administration introduced additional sanctions that cut off oil shipments to Cuba. It also imposed tariffs on countries that sold oil to the country. The move escalated Cuba's humanitarian and economic crisis.

In his response to Wednesday's vote, the Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said that through the vote, the US was "once again isolated in its attempt to continue strangling the Cuban people."

"Neither its most insane pretexts nor its pressures nor media circus will prevail over the force of facts and truth," he said.

The Cuban embassy in the US celebrated the votes for the resolution.

In a post on X, it wrote, "Victory for Cuba at the UN. Washington was isolated once again. #CubaIsNotAThreat; the blockade is."

Meanwhile, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz celebrated the votes of states that opposed the resolution or abstained.

He told reporters after the vote that he was pleased to see a shift in some countries' stance on US actions against Cuba.

He said, "I'm satisfied that so many countries now, including major economies like Korea, Germany and others, have shifted their position.

"Diplomacy takes time, but now that we've had a tripling of countries that have shifted, we expect that only to continue to grow."

World.title: Africa: Russia-Africa Summit to Test Moscow's Ambitions for Broader Influence
World.content:
A summit with more than 20 African leaders opened in Moscow on Wednesday, in a test of Russia's bid to expand its influence on the continent. The two-day Russia-Africa Summit, the third since 2019, comes as Moscow grapples with heavy sanctions over its Ukraine offensive - and as several African governments turn to it for security assistance.

A total of 48 African countries have sent delegations to the summit, including 22 heads of state, with Russian President Vladimir Putin planning to meet most of them one-on-one.

Africa plays a central role in Russia's strategy to establish itself as the leader of the Global South, said Cécile Marin, a specialist in Russian-African relations and a lecturer at Sciences Po Paris.

"Russia is putting forward a whole narrative denouncing the neocolonialism of the Western powers. Obviously, France is a major target," she told RFI.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Putin is quick to emphasise that Russia, unlike France or the United Kingdom, never colonised African countries, Marin explained. His government has also highlighted the "traditional values" it claims to share with many in Africa, she said.

Moscow has courted ties with Africa since the Soviet era, and has long looked to Africa as a counterweight to what it sees as Western domination over international affairs.

Putin said a world where power is no longer concentrated in the West was quickly becoming a reality.

"The era when the fate of entire continents was determined by a narrow bloc of states is irrevocably gone," he said as he opened an economic forum for business leaders hours before the high-level summit began.

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger launch Tafouk TV channel to push their own narrative

Economic ambitions

The summit is expected to focus on expanding economic cooperation in particular.

Putin told delegates on Wednesday that Russia was "prepared to further expand the geographical reach of our agricultural product shipments". Attacks in the Black Sea linked to the conflict in Ukraine continue to disrupt exports of grain from both Russia and Ukraine, many of which go to Africa.

Putin also announced that Moscow planned to "localise" the production of Russian medicines and vaccines on the African continent, and stressed that Russia was "open to sharing our modern competencies and high-tech digital know-how with our African friends".

The summit is expected to end Thursday with a final declaration on deepening cooperation between Russia and African nations, alongside a separate statement on cooperation in the field of artificial intelligence.

The Kremlin said Russia will also seek to strengthen its diplomatic presence on the continent, where it aims to open a 49th embassy, in Liberia.

Leaked files reveal Russia's blueprint to expand African Sahel alliance

Security dominant

To date, economic ties remain limited. Russia-Africa relations are primarily centred on military and security issues, according to Ivan Klyszcz, a researcher at the International Centre for Defence and Security in Tallinn, Estonia, and a specialist in Russia-Africa relations.

"Most African armies were trained during the Cold War by instructors from either the Soviet Union or the Eastern Bloc," he told RFI. "This means they mainly use Soviet-style equipment, such as Kalashnikovs. These are markets in which Russia enjoys very, very privileged access."

Russian paramilitary forces are also deployed in several countries in Africa, he said, primarily to protect leaders and infrastructure. In some cases, they carry out combat missions - such as in Mali, where the government is using Russian paramilitaries to battle a jihadist offensive.

These forces are not just guns for hire, according to Klyszcz: they are managed by Russian military intelligence and also serve Russian objectives.

Madagascar marks one year since uprising as Russia's influence grows

Shadow of war in Ukraine

Yet Russia's ambitions in Africa may be limited by its war in Ukraine, which is weighing heavily on Moscow's budget.

Paul-Simon Handy, regional director for East Africa at the Institute for Security Studies think tank in Pretoria, said Russia's room for manoeuvre was reduced.

To implement the various policies it has outlined in its Africa strategy, he told RFI, "there would need to be fiscal and budgetary leeway, which does not seem to be available at the moment".

Instead, "the war in Ukraine may mean that Russia can only offer defence assistance and commercial cooperation in the supply of provisions, fertilisers and agricultural equipment".

Close 

The war has already marred Russia's relations with several African countries in another respect, after numerous reports of Africans being forcibly conscripted by Moscow to fight on the frontlines in Ukraine.

The families searching for African recruits lost in the Ukraine war

The French Institute of International Relations estimates that between 3,000 and 4,000 Africans are fighting for Russia in Ukraine, some lured under false pretences and promises of well-paid work.

Countries including Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa have publicly voiced alarm at the fate of their citizens recruited by Moscow.

In an open letter to the African heads of state and other officials attending the Moscow summit, Amnesty International voiced "deep concern regarding Russia's forced and deceptive recruitment" of African nations.

The rights group urged officials to demand that Russia "cease any ongoing and future recruitment of people from Africa and other foreign nationals into its military forces".

This story has been adapted from original reporting by RFI's French service, with additional information from AFP.

World.title: South Africa: Border? What Border? This Is What South Africa's Frontier With Zimbabwe Looks Like
World.content:
A view of the Alfred Beit Road Bridge, which crosses the Limpopo River from South Africa into Zimbabwe. On the right is South Africa, and on the left is Zimbabwe.

Trucks, elephants, donkeys and humans cross the Limpopo River freely

Whatever you want to buy, there's a good chance you'll find it in Musina, Limpopo. The town centre is abuzz from early in the morning with travellers, traders and smugglers. The myriad shops selling electronics, clothes, furniture, washing machines, fridges, toys, toiletries, cigarettes, and alcohol are doing a roaring trade.

Much of it is going across the Beitbridge border, 10km away on a good road, the last stretch of the N1. The bakkies going north are overloaded with goods, marked with the names of the people in Zimbabwe who've ordered them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

At the border some vehicles will cross through the official border checkpoint. But many won't. Instead they'll take a little detour and drive along the dirt road, either west in the direction of Mapungubwe, or east towards where the Sand and Limpopo rivers meet.

We drove west. A few hundred metres along the road, two soldiers, next to their tent, had made a tiny roadblock out of stones. They stopped us. We had a long friendly conversation. The woman was from Potchefstroom and the man from Soweto. Their shift started in April and finishes in November. They told us they frequently turn around Zimbabweans crossing the border. The soldiers used to detain them, but they were just released to cross the border again the same day. So now the soldiers just turn them around and send them back.

We drove on, fully laden trucks passing us in one direction, empty trucks in the other. Not far from the soldiers' roadblock, we found a large hole in the barbed wire fence that runs along the border, with a makeshift road leading down a few hundred metres, to the Limpopo River.

Here goods will be offloaded onto a raft or a boat, or even a human or a donkey if the water level is low enough, and taken across the Limpopo River to Zimbabwe. Our drone showed us a raft and a line going across the river, and activity on the other side.

A man was sitting at another break in the fence. While we were there a few people walked past him across the fence towards the river. He told us he was employed by the game farm he was sitting next to, to prevent poaching. He didn't mind people going past him to cross the border so long as they didn't poach. He told us people pass here carrying all sorts of things, from groceries to blankets, beds and refrigerators, to be sold in Zimbabwe. As we were chatting, one man passed us carrying three 10kg bags of potatoes.

Many of the breaks in the fence are made by humans but some have been made by elephants wandering between the two countries.

One evening as we were driving from Beitbridge to Musina, there was a commotion at a bridge over dense bush just at the entrance to the town. Elephants had been spotted. One person said three. Another six. Several young men energetically tried to find the animals in the thick bush.

We asked one of them what they would do if they found an elephant. Kill it for the meat, was the excited reply.

The next day a traffic official, Ernest Makatu, showed us a video of people chopping up a dead elephant several months ago for its meat. It tastes good, he said.

Makatu wants to end corruption in Musina and South Africa. He is with the Build a Better South Africa political party and in 2029 he intends to stand for president of the country.

Zander Coetzer, who handles security for game farms in the area owned by Hermanus Schoeman, drove us east along the border showing us which breaks in the fence are made by elephants and which by humans, though they are probably used by both species. There are also many donkeys crossing the river, apparently without owners, grazing on both sides. Coetzer told us donkeys are useful for helping to pull stolen cars that sometimes get stuck in the river.

Every day thousands of people cross the border - legally and illegally. Some cross the breaks in the border into South Africa in the morning to work in Musina or on a farm, and return in the evening. This has been going on for decades.

A Zimbabwean man told us he used to often cross the border illegally before getting a work permit.

He said in 2003 he had seen six women drown in the flooded Limpopo at Chivara. "I have crossed that river countless times, got arrested, released, got stripped naked by criminals, but I kept coming to South Africa," he told us. "Crossing a flooded Limpopo River is no joke because the bed shifts when walking on it. Don't worry about crocodiles because they're not found everywhere."

But employment is probably not the main reason people come and go across the border: trade is. There's a huge network of people involved in moving goods from South Africa to Zimbabwe: carriers, people managing the rafts and boats, drivers - all getting a cut of the goods bought in Musina.

Why don't the buyers go through the official border? Because import duties are exorbitant on the Zimbabwean side. Determining what the duties are is hard. This webpage gives an example in which the tax on $610 worth of goods comes to $203. The percentages are laid out in a 1,162-page tariff handbook published by the Zimbabwean government. (Did you know if you import a live whale into Zimbabwe, there's a 10% duty? See page 20.)

In practice the duties appear to be negotiable. "I bought a solar pump for R8,000 in South Africa and was supposed to pay R2,500 at the border officially but negotiated it to R500 which I gave the customs officer. No receipt," one man told us.

So it's often cheaper to pay the various people involved in smuggling goods across the border, including bribing soldiers, than to go through customs.

A woman in Musina connected to cross-border trade explained to us that some shops in the town open as early as 5am. One truck delivering goods to cross the border can make five, or even more, trips a day. "Each load can earn them more than R1,000. There is a good market for chicken, usually braai packs, because it is expensive in Zimbabwe," she said. "All the trucks you see here are headed to the trading point. At the river they use small boats to ferry the loads across. If the water level is low they walk across or use donkeys."

"There are many entrances through the bushes. The one you visited is called Maroyi," she said. "When you leave here you pay a driver's fee for transport, and you also pay the boys you find hiding in the bushes R50 to look out for soldiers."

A smuggler near the border told us: "I carry the goods on my head across the river." He said he generally charges R150 per package. Crossing to the other side takes him 30 minutes. He said he carries all kinds of goods, legal and illegal. He has a Zimbabwean passport. He said he and others do this because they are unemployed and need to make a living.

In Musina we spoke to shopkeepers selling clothes and shoes. Business is not as good as it once was because there are lots of soldier roadblocks on the road to Harare where people have to pay "fees", one told us. So people have switched to other borders, including Zambia. Goods are still cheaper in South Africa, he said, but the cost of paying off soldiers along the way is pushing the cost of importing across Beitbridge too high.

Before meeting him, we were told Hennie Erwee is the lawyer you want if you're ever in trouble. He's a big guy with a big personality. We met him at his office in Musina. He has successfully litigated for Schoeman against the government for infringing his property rights. Now he's running a case, with Schoeman as his client, to get the national government to fix the border.

Close 

Schoeman has had to close his game farm along the border in part because of the uncontrolled animal traffic. "As soon as it's dry, donkeys and cows cross into the farm. If I put out lucerne for my game, the next day there's a hundred donkeys there," he said.

He pointed out that people taking goods to Zimbabwe through the breaks in the border are not breaking South African law; we don't need to worry about that. But the animal traffic is a problem, he explained. "Cattle moving freely across the border, on a daily basis, cross into my farm, mix with local cattle. A big percentage have foot-and-mouth disease."

He is sceptical that South Africa can get the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic under control while this carries on.

The state spends billions of rands protecting the border in a system that is far too bureaucratic. Three years ago the Border Management Authority (BMA) came into existence to co-ordinate the response. But it has already had a troubling audit and serious problems with corruption. And it is clearly failing to control the Beitbridge corridor.

There's a long history of the fence along the Zimbabwean border being built and rebuilt, at large expense and to no avail. Schoeman told us that his security protected the current barbed wire fence while it was put up. But as soon as the fence was built and handed over to the government, his services were no longer used, and holes immediately started appearing.

But if the government did get its act together and managed the Beitbridge border, there would be a different problem. The thriving Musina economy has developed over decades in response to the porous border. Tens of thousands of people probably depend on things being just the way they are to make a living. If every small town in South Africa was as bustling as Musina, our economy would be doing well.

Suddenly fixing the border might just destroy the town's economy.

World.title: Tanzania: No Accountability One Year After Tanzania Election Violence
World.content:
Families of People Killed, Missing Await Justice

One year after Tanzania's contested 2025 elections, authorities have yet to make any arrests for human rights violations committed before and during the vote.

In the months leading up to the elections, the government intensified its repression of the political opposition, government critics, and the media. Authorities also failed to account for a spate of apparent enforced disappearances, including that of former Tanzanian ambassador to Cuba Humphrey Polepole, who was reported missing just weeks before the elections. Polepole had publicly criticized the ruling party, Chama Cha Mapinduzi, for not being "aligned with safeguarding human rights, peace, and respect for people." His whereabouts remain unknown.



On and after election day, police and people in plainclothes killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders in response to widespread protests and while enforcing a five-day nationwide lockdown. A year on, the fate of many remains unknown as families have reported burying their relatives with no body.

Authorities also arrested over 2,000 people they accused of destroying government property and of treason during this period, but later released some. Some, including those interviewed by Human Rights Watch, said police beat them while falsely accusing them of participating in the protests.

In November 2025, President Samia Suluhu Hassan established a commission of inquiry to investigate the violence. It concluded that at least 518 people were killed but failed to meaningfully scrutinize the role of security forces. The president has since established another commission that will reportedly investigate the planning of the unrest and excessive and unlawful use of force during the elections. However it remains unclear whether this includes investigating and ensuring the prosecution of people responsible for security force abuses.

Meanwhile, the authorities have intensified their crackdown on government critics in recent months. The treason trial of Tundu Lissu, the leader of the main opposition party, Chama Cha Demokrasia Na Maendeleo (CHADEMA), continued this year.

On October 21, authorities charged John Pambalu, a CHADEMA official, with treason for allegedly forming an "intention to persuade the public to cause obstruction" of the elections through protests. Treason carries the death penalty in Tanzania.

A year since the election violence, families of those killed or missing are still waiting for answers and justice. President Hassan's government should stop targeting critics and instead ensure credible investigations into disappearances and security force abuses and hold those responsible to account.

Oryem Nyeko, Senior Researcher, Africa Division

World.title: Niger: Prominent Journalist 'Disappeared' for 2 Months
World.content:
Moussa Kaka, a Nigerien journalist, director of the media group Radio TÃ©lÃ©vision Saraounia (RTS) and former correspondent for Reporters Without Borders (RSF), has been missing since 31 August.

Nairobi — Disclose Moussa Kaka's Location; Release Him if Not Charged

Niger's authorities should urgently disclose the whereabouts of the prominent journalist Moussa Kaka, who was forcibly disappeared two months ago, Human Rights Watch said today. They should ensure his safety and release him unless he has been charged with a valid criminal offense.

On August 31, 2026, Kaka, the director-general of Radio Télévision Saraounia and a former correspondent for Radio France Internationale (RFI), left his office in Niamey, the capital, to return home but never arrived, raising immediate concerns. For weeks, his family and colleagues were not able to obtain information about his whereabouts. On September 25, during Niger's Universal Periodic Review at the United Nations in Geneva, Justice Minister Alio Daouda acknowledged that Kaka was being detained. The minister said Kaka was being held for an alleged "offense" and would "answer before the courts," but provided no details about the accusation or his place of detention.

"Two months after Moussa Kaka vanished in Niger, the authorities have yet to provide his location or explain his detention," said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. "Kaka's family will continue to grapple with the uncertainty until the authorities resolve his disappearance."



Kaka is a respected figure in African investigative journalism. For years, he reported for RFI in Niger, until the military junta suspended its broadcasts in 2023. Throughout his career, he has continued his work under successive governments despite the risks and repeated detentions for his journalism.

In September 2007, under then-President Mamadou Tandja, the authorities arrested Kaka and accused him of links to ethnic Tuareg rebels, following his extended coverage of the Tuareg rebellion in northern Niger. He spent 379 days in prison before being released in October 2008 following a sustained national and international campaign for his freedom.

In October 2025, police in Niamey arrested Kaka along with five other journalists after they announced on social media a press briefing about a government-created solidarity fund intended to support the country's security forces. The journalists were charged with "complicity in distributing documents likely to disturb public order" under Niger's broad cybercrime law. All six were subsequently released.

Kaka's recent forced disappearance came amid heightened political tensions following an attempted military coup in Niamey on August 29. After mutinous soldiers attempted to seize power, the junta arrested dozens of suspected soldiers and a former minister. Russian government-controlled Africa Corps forces were called upon to help suppress the mutiny. Kaka's colleagues and friends have expressed concern that his disappearance may be linked to the junta's crackdown after the attempted coup.

Reporters Without Borders has referred Kaka's case to the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances, following an earlier referral to the African Union's special rapporteur on freedom of expression and access to information. African civil society organizations raised his case at the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights in mid-October in Dakar, Senegal. Journalists and human rights activists across Africa have also called for his release.

"Moussa Kaka's place is not in detention," said Alioune Tine, a prominent Senegalese human rights defender and former UN rights expert. "His detention is absolutely unjustified and violates Niger's international human rights obligations, including provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, which Niger has signed and ratified."

Kaka's case highlights growing concerns about media freedom and political repression in Niger, Human Rights Watch said. Since seizing power in a 2023 coup, Niger's military junta has solidified its rule, dismantled democratic institutions, and intensified repression of dissidents. They have dissolved political parties, suspended dozens of civil society organizations, detained journalists under a broad cybercrime law, stripped exiled political opponents of their nationality, announced the country's withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, and extended the political transition without holding elections. The authorities also continue to arbitrarily detain former President Mohamed Bazoum and his wife, and a prominent human rights defender, Moussa Tiangari.

Close 

Under international human rights law, an enforced disappearance occurs when state agents, or people acting with the state's authorization, support, or acquiescence, deprive someone of their liberty and then refuse to acknowledge the detention or conceal the person's fate or whereabouts. Enforced disappearance places victims at heightened risk of torture and extrajudicial execution. It also inflicts profound suffering on families, who are left uncertain whether their loved ones are alive or dead and denied access to justice.

"Niger's authorities should immediately account for Kaka and free him if he hasn't been fairly charged," Allegrozzi said. "Governments and international organizations should press the junta to take immediate action in Kaka's case."

World.title: Angel Studios draws line in sand with Hollywood, bans sex scenes, profanity in bold new pledge
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX — Angel Studios is drawing a line in the sand against Hollywood's approach to entertainment, announcing sweeping new content standards that ban on-screen sex, nudity and certain profanity while promising millions of paying members the power to decide which movies and television shows make the cut.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Angel Studios co-founder and chief content officer Jeff Harmon said the entertainment industry has increasingly lost touch with the families it once served, prompting his company to establish what it calls "The Angel Promise."

"I think Hollywood generally kind of lives in a bubble," Harmon said. "These are excellent craftsmen. They're the best storytellers in the world. Hollywood has built the best storytelling infrastructure in the world."

COMEDIAN LEANNE MORGAN CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD FOR LIVING IN A 'BUBBLE' AND MISJUDGING WHAT AUDIENCES WANT TO SEE

"But at the same time, they've kind of drifted more and more away from the values-based audience that they used to serve," Harmon said. "And with that, in our view, as brothers and as fathers, as a father, Hollywood hasn't been giving me consistently what I need. Once in a while, you get a good one, but you have to sift through all these things to find your good movies and your good stories."

The new initiative, announced Thursday, establishes three core commitments governing Angel's entertainment offerings, namely, audience approval of content, strict standards involving sex and language, and expanded parental controls.

"We promise there's never going to be nudity, and there'll never be sex on screen," Harmon said, explaining that families participating in the Angel Guild will not have to worry about encountering such material when evaluating potential projects.

The company is also drawing a firm boundary around profanity, pledging that Angel's original productions will not misuse God's name.

NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD

"This is a completely unique one," Harmon said. "This has never really happened in Hollywood history."

Harmon described the restriction as part of the company's effort to build trust with religious families.

"What we promise our viewers is that this timeless principle that's thousands of years old, and we're a very faith-friendly studio, is that we're not going to have misuse of God's name on the system on any Angel original content," Harmon said. "So any content we create. Where we are originating, meaning it comes to Angel first, those shows, those TV shows and movies, will not have misuse of God's name, so that families of faith, 'cause we're a faith-friendly studio, can trust that language won't be there."

Under the new standards, the company also prohibits use of the F-word in its stories and profanity in titles submitted for children ages 12 and younger.

HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER BEHIND 'APOLLO 13' REJECTS POLITICS IN HIS MOVIES, SEEKS TO UNITE AUDIENCES

The announcement represents a significant effort to distinguish Angel from traditional Hollywood studios, with the company placing its audience at the center of decisions about what gets produced and distributed.

Harmon said the Angel Guild, which has approximately 3 million paying members, gives viewers an opportunity to approve or reject projects before they enter the company's entertainment ecosystem.

"This is the first time in history that a major Hollywood studio, or top 10 studio in the United States, has come and said, we're going to let the audience have a veto right," Harmon said.

Under Angel's stated policy, films and television series must receive a score of at least 70 out of 100 from Guild members to qualify for inclusion in its entertainment ecosystem.

Harmon said the founders' experiences raising children helped shape the new standards.

"Angel was co-founded by four brothers and a cousin," he said, adding that the founders have 34 children between them.

CREATING THE DEFINITIVE MOUNT RUSHMORE OF PIXAR MOVIES FROM A PARENTS' VIEWING PERSPECTIVE

The goal, he explained, was to create entertainment that parents could trust without having to sift through potentially objectionable content.

"Hollywood hasn't been giving me consistently what I need," Harmon said. "Once in a while you get a good one, but you have to sift through all these things to find your good movies and your good stories."

The third component of the Angel Promise focuses on parental controls. Angel says Guild members will help establish recommended age ratings and plain-language descriptions of potentially sensitive material, while new controls in the Angel app will allow parents to tailor viewing choices to their families.

Harmon said the broader ambition is to reshape the relationship between filmmakers and audiences.

"Our goal was to set out and try to fix this problem of kind of stepping out of the Hollywood bubble and stepping into middle America's shoes," he said.

The company says its Guild has paid out nearly $300 million to filmmakers, while Harmon said more than 100 films were available for members to vote on at the time of the interview.

For Harmon, the new promise is about establishing permanent standards that will outlast any individual film, filmmaker or executive, and give families greater influence over the entertainment they consume.

Some of the studio's prominent recent films include "David" and "The King of Kings."

World.title: Warning signs that your adult child may be quietly cutting you off
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Amid a growing trend of parent-child estrangement, experts say recognizing the early warning signs may help families address problems before they escalate into a no-contact situation.

Nearly four in 10 Americans are currently estranged from at least one close family member, according to a 2025 YouGov poll of 4,395 U.S. adults. That includes 24% who reported estrangement from a sibling, 16% from a parent and 10% from a child.

While estrangement can sometimes seem sudden, experts say subtle changes may signal that a family relationship is beginning to unravel.

CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT

The quiet signs

Mary McLaughlin, a licensed couples and family therapist in Vienna, Virginia, said early signs may include an adult child becoming less willing to share details of their life directly with a parent.

"You might find out about the trip, the new relationship or a promotion at work at the same time everyone else does," she told Fox News Digital.

The parent may still be in contact with the adult child, McLaughlin said, but the child no longer chooses to share parts of their life directly.

ADULT CHILDREN CUTTING OFF PARENTS AS SOME BLAME THERAPY FOR FAMILY ESTRANGEMENTS

Other potential warning signs may include skipping family holidays, birthdays or weddings; leaving texts and calls unanswered; and reducing communication to brief or sporadic exchanges, according to the expert.

The distance may become so noticeable that siblings, grandparents or other relatives comment that they have not seen or heard from the adult child in a long time.

A child who once readily joined family photos but begins stepping out of them may also be signaling that they are starting to see themselves as separate from the family, McLaughlin said.

Blythe Landry, a Pennsylvania-based therapist and founder of Blythe Landry Coaching, said other early signs may include a child becoming involved with a new social group that encourages estrangement over difficult conversations, or "beginning to rewrite history in a way that seems more damaging than what might have happened."

The adult child may also become less willing to let a parent spend time with their grandchildren.

‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT

The most telling sign may be a noticeable shift in the tone of the relationship, Landry said.

"You know your child, and you know when the energy has shifted in a direction that seems dramatically harsher than in previous interactions."

The shift to independence

Laura Wellington, a Connecticut mother who has been estranged from her adult daughter since 2024, said it can be challenging to distinguish early signs of estrangement from typical moves toward independence.

"It’s confusing to the parent because, a lot of times, they look like the general signs of a teenager moving into the young-adult zone — just pulling away and going off and establishing their lives," she told Fox News Digital.

"That’s what I think confuses many parents, because they want to give them the space to start pulling away and showing signs of their own individuality and carving their path."

"They don’t want to fight every battle, because if they fight every battle, then communication breaks down. So they try to pick and choose."

Loss of respect

One warning sign, according to Wellington, is if the child has an "I know everything, you know nothing" mindset.

"What's happening in our society today is … a lot of ‘I know everything, you know nothing’ toward the parent," she said. "There's no respect for what the parents experience. There's no tolerance for them speaking up and saying, ‘No, this is not what you should be doing.’"

"A lot of times, they look like the general signs of a teenager moving into the young-adult zone."

In some cases, the child may begin treating the parent as a subordinate, according to Wellington.

Some parents begin to notice a shift when their adult children start treating them with disrespect, pushing back on their opinions and positioning themselves as the authority in the relationship, she said.

"They become the authority; they flip it. Anytime you say something, you’ll see them bark at the parent and push back on the parent. They really have no respect for the parent."

Different worldviews

Wellington also pointed to major differences in political, religious or lifestyle beliefs as a possible source of growing distance between parents and adult children.

She suggested that some young people who become estranged are "more liberal in thinking," while acknowledging that the dynamic can also work in the opposite direction when a parent holds especially strong ideological views.

"There is extremism sometimes where the parent is extremely something, and then the child … goes the other way," she said.

Richard Blake, Ph.D., a Texas-based psychology researcher who focuses on anxiety and family estrangement, said an adult child’s unwillingness to consider differing views may signal trouble.

He suggested that personality may play a role, with more argumentative adult children who are less willing to consider differing views potentially more prone to family estrangement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Repeated cutoffs

Another possible warning sign, according to Blake, is if the adult child has begun cutting off other people. He said parents should take note if an adult child has repeatedly stops speaking to relatives or openly boasts about ending relationships.

"Chances are, they're going to cut off someone else and it may be the parent," he said. "If you haven’t been cut off yet, you may be in the firing line there."

Communication breakdown

Ongoing communication problems may be an early warning sign, Blake said, particularly when an adult child feels that a parent refuses to listen or acknowledge the child’s point of view.

CLICK HERE TO 

"They may say, ‘My parents just don’t listen. I cannot get through to them. It’s like talking to a brick wall.'"

Parents who consistently dismiss their children’s concerns should not be surprised when conflict develops, he said.

"If you don’t listen to your child, then don’t be surprised if you have conflict with them."

Blake recommends listening actively, avoiding interruptions, repeating back what the other person has said and asking a simple follow-up question: "First, you say, ‘Is there more?'"

No clear warning

While there may be some early signs, Blake emphasized that estrangement can sometimes appear suddenly, with no warning.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"A lot of parents will say, ‘My child never told me the issue. We were best friends. And then I got a letter saying, never contact me ever again.’"

"That is a big problem. It's like people don't even know why they get cut off."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Landry noted that recognizing possible warning signs should prompt honest self-reflection, not just concern about the other person’s behavior.

"If there is an imminent estrangement, dig deep," she advised. "Do you have a part? If so, is there a chance of rectifying it before it occurs?"

World.title: Buckingham Palace 'blindsided' by Thomas Markle allegations as Harry, Meghan face new family turmoil: expert

Buckingham Palace was reportedly "blindsided" by allegations involving Meghan Markle's estranged father, former Hollywood lighting director Thomas Markle Sr.

The Sun reported on Oct. 22 that Thomas Markle Jr. said he found "hundreds, if not thousands" of images depicting child sexual abuse while clearing out boxes at his father's former home in Cebu, Philippines. Markle Jr. told the newspaper that he reported the images to Philippine police and contacted the FBI in the U.S.

The 82-year-old Markle denied the allegations to the Daily Mail, telling the newspaper: "I'm shocked, I'm hurt, and I'm very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I'm being accused of. It's the worst thing anyone could accuse me of."

PRINCE HARRY MAKING 'BIG MISTAKE' THAT COULD DESTROY CHANCE OF ROYAL RECONCILIATION: EXPERT

Fox News Digital reached out to Markle Sr. for comment.

"Following the report, I made more than 40 phone calls to royal sources over the weekend, and nobody I spoke to had heard anything about these allegations before the story broke in The Sun," Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.

"My understanding is that Buckingham Palace was blindsided," she said. "They find themselves dragged into another controversy involving [the Sussexes]. And the allegations are deeply disturbing."

WATCH: BUCKINGHAM PALACE WAS 'BLINDSIDED' BY THOMAS MARKLE SR. ALLEGATIONS: EXPERT

Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace for comment.

In a statement sent to Fox News Digital, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed. In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated."

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she wrote. "I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

WATCH: KING CHARLES MAY PRIVATELY SUPPORT MEGHAN MARKLE AMID CONTROVERSY: EXPERT

The Metropolitan Police said its records show that the letter was received in January 2019, not 2018. Meghan's spokesperson subsequently acknowledged the discrepancy, saying the police's timestamped records should be treated as authoritative.

The letter was written by Markle Sr.'s first wife, Roslyn Markle, also known as Roslyn Loveless, ITV News reported on Oct. 26. The outlet said it had reviewed the letter, which contained allegations of sexual abuse against Markle Sr. He has denied the allegations.

Melvin Matibag, director of the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation, told The Associated Press that the FBI had requested the bureau's assistance in investigating Markle Jr.'s allegations against his father.

Philippine Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla separately told the AP that the Philippine National Police was also investigating Markle Jr.'s allegations against his father. Remulla did not elaborate.

A spokesperson for Remulla told Fox News Digital that the Philippine National Police (PNP) is continuing its investigation.

Schofield said the royal family would likely keep its distance from the Sussexes as its members prioritize their duties while the investigation continues.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"King Charles is in a difficult position," said Schofield. "As a father, I believe he would want to offer Harry emotional support. Let's not forget, it was the king who walked Meghan down the aisle when her own father couldn't. But Harry has repeatedly shared private conversations through interviews, documentaries and his memoir. The king would be reluctant to have a sensitive conversation on this topic with Prince Harry without reassurance that it would remain private."

"As for Prince William, don't expect him to get involved," said Schofield. "This is not his fight. The palace has already established that Harry and Meghan are private citizens who do not represent the crown. This is a matter for the Sussex household. The Metropolitan Police have confirmed that allegations were passed to Sussex's office in 2019, but the police say they did not share those allegations with other law enforcement agencies. My royal sources have given me no indication that the palace was informed."

A spokesperson for London's Metropolitan Police told Fox News Digital: "Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex."

"The letter was reviewed, and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness," the statement said. "The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies. The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach."

The Metropolitan Police's review concerns how the force handled the letter in 2019, rather than a criminal investigation into Markle Sr. British police said they were also considering whether to refer their handling of the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, the police watchdog in England and Wales.

The Times reported that the Metropolitan Police shared the information with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but apparently not with other members of the royal household. Buckingham Palace declined to comment to the newspaper.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

According to the outlet, Scotland Yard said the letter contained several allegations of offenses outside the United Kingdom, but police did not launch an investigation at the time. The force acknowledged that it had not shared the allegations with overseas authorities.

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that although the king might privately offer support to the Sussexes, he is unlikely to comment publicly on the investigation.

"He cannot publicly be seen to be doing anything at all," said Turner. "Neither can any of the members of the royal family because of this potential investigation. According to the prosecutor in Cebu in the Philippines, quick decisions are going to be made."

"What I see is Meghan, again, right in the middle of a controversy that is not of her doing," he said.

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that her sources were not commenting because "this is being treated as a private Sussex matter."

"To date, while there has been no formal comment, needless to say, there's nothing about this the royals would want to be associated with," said Fordwich. "It is extremely unlikely the king, or any royal, comments in any way regarding the gravity of these allegations. Institutional distancing is more than likely."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

People magazine reported that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were receiving updates on the allegations while vacationing with their two children during a school break.

"It's been really difficult," a friend told the outlet. "[Meghan's] really cut up. She has young children, and I think that, alongside the victims, it's just weighing on her mind. It's traumatic."

There is also "a slight sense of relief that this is all coming out," the friend said, adding that Meghan hopes "a proper investigation can take place."

A source close to Meghan told People magazine: "There is a lot to process emotionally. But she's doing okay. She's holding up. She's surrounded by loved ones and is feeling supported right now. She has great people around her getting through this moment."

On Oct. 24, The Sun reported that Meghan sent her father a letter in December 2025 while he was recovering in a Philippine hospital from a leg amputation following a blood clot.

According to the newspaper, Meghan wrote that she was aware of the sexual abuse allegations against Markle Sr. and would never allow him to meet her two children. She also reportedly told him it would be the last time he heard from her.

The outlet reported that Meghan arranged for hospital staff to deliver the letter to her father's bedside, ask him to sign a form acknowledging receipt and record his acceptance of the letter.

Editor's note: This op-ed is part of a series by Eli Steele exploring White guilt in America and the West. Steele is the director of the newly released documentary essay, "White Guilt." See the film at WhiteGuiltFilm.com.

When I was a student at Claremont McKenna College in the 1990s, Morris Dees, the co-founder of the Southern Poverty Law Center, came to speak. Over the years, I have forgotten what he spoke about, but what I do remember is seeing his gun when he adjusted his sports coat. It was the kind of gun that Clint Eastwood carried in "Dirty Harry," only Dees's was burnished silver, with the deep grooves of a six-shooter. Before the speech, he was billed as the man who took on the Ku Klux Klan, and the gun made the legend real. But to those of us in that room, the gun said something more. It told us that racism was alive and thriving, and that Dees needed that gun as a hedge against an evil that might attack at any moment.

Now we have learned that the legend Dees and the SPLC crafted and protected over the years has cost certain Americans their bank accounts.

In August 2024, the SPLC published an article that dismissed complaints from several Christian groups about debanking. The SPLC writer, R.G. Cravens, struck an accusatory tone against the Christian legal group Alliance Defending Freedom and said it "perpetuated a false conspiracy theory that claims big government and big corporations are victimizing conservative Christians."

SPLC SCANDAL UNDERSCORES HOW THE DEMAND FOR RACISM OUTSTRIPS THE SUPPLY | BOBBY BURACK

On Oct. 14, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released a 47-page report on debanking at the nine largest banks it supervises. Regulators reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and approximately 420,000 pages of bank records. The report found that four of those banks, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, PNC and TD Bank, referenced the SPLC while closing accounts or denying loans to conservative and religious customers.

The report's details are far more damning than the summary. WePay, a subsidiary of JPMorgan, screened customers against a list of terms that included "MAGA," "America First" and the names of SPLC-designated "hate groups." In July 2021, WePay closed an account that was raising money for a "devout Christian's" legal challenge to anti-discrimination laws.

In another case, PNC refused a line of credit to a media company because one owner's foundation "has funded several Christian conservative groups, including several identified as hate groups by the Southern Poverty Law Center." A PNC employee explained, "I think it becomes really difficult to justify aligning ourselves with a company whose owners have built very public personas around opinions very contrary to PNC's beliefs/values.:

What struck me was that none of these banks checked whether what the SPLC alleged was true. The regulators found that "mere allegations, negative press or negative reviews contributed to some banks declining to serve average Americans, even in the absence of any validation of the underlying facts or concerns."

It is hard to be shocked these days, but we must recover that ability. Why would a bank let an advocacy group decide who gets an account, without verification of any sort?

It wasn't long before I found the answer in the report: "Fear of being on the wrong side of public opinion led at least one bank to distance itself from certain customer affiliations that could possibly be viewed as partisan." The banks had labeled them a "reputation risk."

My father, Shelby Steele, has a better name for it: white guilt. He has spent forty years on this question. To paraphrase him, white guilt is the eternal drive by many whites, especially those on the Left, to prove their innocence of racism, to show over and over that they are not complicit in America's historical racial sins.

It is this drive that gives white guilt its transactional nature. In order to be able to buy innocence, someone has to have the innocence to sell. And to sell innocence, you need to possess moral authority when it comes to racial matters. The SPLC earned this moral authority in the deep south when it helped integrate the Alabama state troopers and sued the Klan after violent attacks.

But the white guilt machine needs a never-ending supply of hate. If racism begins to fade, then what innocence is there to sell?

MOMS GROUP LABELED ‘EXTREMIST’ FLIPS SCRIPT ON SPLC AFTER FEDERAL INDICTMENT: 'SHUT IT DOWN'

And the Klan ranks had been thinning for years. By the SPLC's own count, the number of Klan groups fell from 130 in 2016 to 72 a year later. The SPLC’s director of its Intelligence Project said they seemed to be "collapsing."

As the Klan shrank, the SPLC knew that it had to manufacture racism, and it did this by widening the definition of what could be counted as hateful and racist. It created the "Hate Map", which put mainstream Christian groups like the Family Research Council and Alliance Defending Freedom alongside the Ku Klux Klan and the Aryan Brotherhood. In 2021, it counted 733 "hate groups." In 2022 it counted 1,225 "hate and antigovernment extremist groups," many of them parents' groups focused on education. Today the list includes Moms for Liberty, PragerU and Turning Point USA.

Every bank knew it was the kiss of death to be seen doing business with the Klan. And when these bankers saw the Christian and conservative groups in the same category as the Klan, they took these accusations on faith. They cut off the customers the SPLC named. In return, they got their innocence. Their banks were cleansed of racists.

JPMorgan may have been the most savvy of them all. It donated to the SPLC and then its own subsidiary used the SPLC’s labels to close accounts it had flagged as racist. It bought innocence and, simultaneously, used it as a weapon.

MIKE DAVIS: SOUTHERN POVERTY LAW CENTER: A TALE OF A RACISM SCAM

The power of white guilt is that it leverages the charge of racism mercilessly. It never has to prove the charge — the charge itself is enough. That has been the power of SPLC all along and it is a most lucrative one. The ones who paid were those who were accused of being Christians who hold the same views as millions of Americans. They were put into the race box and charged accordingly.

The gun that Morris Dees wore to my college turned out to be theater. We believed that it mean that racism was a living threat that might erupt any day now. Decades later, as I have followed the SPLC’s record, I have come to understand that the "Hate Map" is part of the same theater. The banks believed it because it was cheaper than challenging the methodologies of the SPLC and risking their judgement, the racist charge included.

This is the white guilt transaction that my father has long described and warned us against. The gift of this OCC report is that it reveals the truth that many of us have long suspected but could never answer. This report details what happened. But the harder question still remains: what do these banks, the SPLC, and every one who profited from this white guilt machine owe the people that they falsely put on that list?
