World.title: MATT CALKINS: Media keeps calling women's sports advocates 'anti-trans' without a shred of proof
World.content:
I saw it right there in the lede of a Washington Post column Tuesday.

"A transgender girl stretched for a high school race as supporters of a new anti-trans ballot measure chanted 'enough is enough'."

I saw it six days earlier in a Guardian headline about how doctors are fighting an "anti-trans measure" that would separate biological girls from boys in women's sports.

The Portland Mercury got in on it, too, writing in its Monday headline how "anti-trans activists" attempted to overshadow the Thorns' playoff-clinching win.

These aren't columnists offering subjective opinions. These are media outlets writing opinions as fact.

The message? You can't possibly be a women's sports advocate without being transphobic. And that thought is just ... tired.

WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE

I have no doubt there are people who have genuine scorn for members of the trans community. Every group — men, women, Whites, Blacks, gays, Muslims, Jews. etc. — has its haters.

But the voices backing these ballot measures? The figures advocating for girls' and women's spaces? They aren't demonizing trans people. Not in the slightest.

Perhaps the most famous face to speak up on this issue in the past few months is Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham, who said in an ESPN interview: "I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

But she prefaced that very sentence by saying "I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love."

A few days after that interview came out, a high school girl in Seattle named Ahnaleigh Wilson — holding a sign saying "Thank You Sophie For Speaking Up For Girls" — echoed Cunningham's sentiment, saying "I don’t hate trans people and I have nothing against them. I just think that girls should have their own sports."

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM COMMENDS WASHINGTON STATE GIRLS WHO WALKED OFF CROSS COUNTRY RACE OVER MALE TEAMMATE

Fellow Washingtonian Frances Staudt — who says she's been harassed constantly for refusing to play a high school basketball game against a boy — added "There’s only so many times that I can say that what we are standing up for is not anti-trans. This is pro-women’s sports."

Yet the headlines have kept coming.

From Colorado Newsline: "Signatures submitted for anti-trans Colorado ballot measures."

From Politico: "Democrats revamp their midterm playbook for GOP's anti-trans attacks."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

From Ms. Magazine: "This Midterm Season, Five States Are Voting on Anti-Trans Ballot."

If you read these stories, you'll notice that none give examples of someone issuing a slur or insult. They just presume that a bill or person opposing certain demands from members of the trans community is "anti-trans."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

It's pretty glaring when and how the media chooses to use the word "anti."

When Colin Kaepernick wore pig socks and compared cops to modern-day slave patrol, did "anti-police" headlines from legacy media come flooding in? What about when BLM protesters chanted "Pigs in a blanket, fry 'em like bacon!"

That was pure vitriol toward their opponents. You simply don't see that type of rhetoric from the separate-men-and-women-in-sports crowd.

And by the way, that crowd includes Caitlyn Jenner — perhaps the most famous transgender person in the world. It includes Ari Laureano, a detransitioned male who was kicked out of a Portland Thorns game last week for his XX-XY shirt.

The biggest misnomer in this debate is that supporters of biological female-only spaces in sports and locker rooms all have animus toward trans people. But the media keeps repeating the lie that they do.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Makes sense, I suppose. When you don't have the truth, repetition is your best weapon.

World.title: Netanyahu alleges fraud as Arab parties score record gains — emerge as potential kingmakers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

TEL AVIV, Israel: Israel's two Arab parties are in a position to have a say in who the country's next prime minister and government will be — but not if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has anything to do with it, after he alleged serious criminal activities took place during voting in the Arab areas of the nation.

The two parties were projected to win a combined 19 Knesset seats, according to preliminary results. With both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led right-wing bloc and the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist bloc falling short of the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Netanyahu wrote on X that Israel’s election had been "stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," alleging serious criminal offenses, including bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters.

NETANYAHU GAINS OVERNIGHT AS ISRAEL ELECTION HEADS TOWARD POLITICAL DEADLOCK

"The Likud party is transferring to the police, the Shin Bet, and the Central Elections Committee hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence regarding election theft in many Arab polling stations," he wrote.

He cited allegations of thousands of envelopes containing cash and Ra’am ballot slips, threats and violence against polling station staff, multiple votes cast behind the voting curtain, voting under multiple identities, discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and the number of voters, the use of prohibited voter-mobilization software and other offenses.

"We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals. We demand from the Central Elections Committee an immediate response to investigate these criminal offenses that have severely damaged the integrity of the elections in Israel and the election results," he added.

One Arab political alliance, the Joint List, brings together three parties: Hadash, a predominantly Arab-Jewish left-wing party rooted in Israel’s communist movement, and the Arab nationalist parties Ta’al and Balad. With over 90% of ballots counted, the alliance was projected to win 12 seats.

The other Arab party, the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas and affiliated with the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement in Israel, was projected to win seven seats.

Arab citizens make up approximately 21% of Israel’s population. Turnout in this election reached a near record high between 75% to 80%.

"They are a political force to be reckoned with," Dahlia Scheindlin, a former policy fellow at the Mitvim Institute and a senior analyst at Haaretz, told Fox News Digital.

NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE

Scheindlin said that Netanyahu framed his campaign around the claim that the opposition is prepared to form a government dependent on Arab parties’ support, which he argues would lead to the establishment of a Palestinian state that would become a terror state and ultimately bring about Israel’s destruction.

"This is the most consistent message, and he never stopped saying it, including on election day," she said.

Scheindlin said that the issue had become politically sensitive, prompting leading Zionist opposition parties to pledge not to cooperate with the Arab parties.

"They have sworn they would not build a coalition that depends on Arab votes, either from within the coalition or from outside it. If they receive any help, they will have to break that promise," she added.

It is not inconceivable, though highly unlikely, that Netanyahu could reach out to one of the Arab parties to explore the possibility of cooperation, Scheindlin said.

ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW

Dr. Arik Rudnitzky, a researcher in the Israel Democracy Institute’s Arab Society in Israel Program, said that Arab parties had historically remained in the opposition and had not joined governing coalitions.

During the governments of Yitzhak Rabin and, later, Shimon Peres in the 1990s, Arab parties provided a parliamentary safety net from outside the coalition. This enabled the government to remain in office and complete its term even after it effectively became a minority government amid opposition to the Oslo Accords, as the Haredi Shas party left the government.

"Historically, Arab parties were always in the opposition for many reasons. It was quite uncommon to believe Arab parties could [support] the government. It’s a novelty of recent years, plus the fact that their political strength in terms of the number of seats was not as significant as it is today," Rudnitzky said.

Demographic changes alone do not explain the Arab parties’ growing political strength, Rudnitzky said; shifting voting patterns have also played a role.

"In the past, Arab voters supported both Arab and Jewish parties. In the 1980s and 1990s, approximately half voted for Jewish parties," he continued.

Rudnitzky said historical developments, the impact of the Oslo Accords and the entry of new Arab representatives into the Knesset contributed to a gradual shift away from Jewish parties, with more Arab voters turning to Arab parties.

"Today, we can say that between 85% and 90% of Arab voters support Arab parties. This is the main reason for their increased political strength," he added.

Any support Arab parties might provide to a prospective coalition would come in exchange for political concessions, Rudnitzky said. Their demands would likely include a government decision and a plan to combat crime in Arab communities, as well as a new socioeconomic development plan for the Arab sector involving budget allocations.

Ultimately, he said, such arrangements would involve allocating public goods and resources in exchange for political support. "There is no free lunch in politics. Every collaboration, either within a coalition or from the outside, has its political price."

TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE

Scheindlin noted that while the Joint List would not be invited to join a governing coalition — and its members would not want to do so anyway — Mansour Abbas and his United Arab List have pursued a different, more controversial approach. The party has accepted Israel as a Jewish state and seeks to improve the lives of Arab citizens within that framework, she said.

"They are expecting equality as citizens. They accepted Israel’s identity and are willing to work within that framework to improve the lives of their citizens. They are the only ones who have a chance of being invited into a coalition, as they were in 2021," she said.

In September, the Central Elections Committee (CEC) voted to disqualify the Joint List and the United Arab list from competing in the Oct. 27 elections. On Oct. 2, Israel’s Supreme Court overturned the CEC’s decisions against both parties.

Section 7A of the Basic Law: The Knesset bars candidates who deny Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, incite to racism, or support the armed struggle of an enemy state or terrorist organization against Israel from participating in Knesset elections.

Martin Sherman, founder and executive director of the Israel Institute for Strategic Studies, told Fox News Digital that Arab parties in Israel are essentially illegal and should be barred from participating in elections.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They have different social agendas, perhaps, but on the political level, they all oppose Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people. One can only hope that politicians in Israel will realize that and that political ambitions and animosity toward Netanyahu will not prevail," he said.

One former Israeli diplomat noted the irony and said it was a good teaching moment for those who don't understand the country. "Arab Israelis voted in huge numbers and, according to the exit polls, won more Knesset seats than ever before. That is the answer to the ridiculously ignorant accusation that Israel is a supposed ‘apartheid’ state," Shahar Azani, veteran israeli diplomat and former spokesperson of Israel’s consulate in New York, told Fox News Digital.

He added, "Arab citizens are shaping the government and taking part in the Jewish state's democratic celebration, and we welcome it. But with great power comes great responsibility: they must now take the next step and reject the extremist positions some voiced as soon as the results came in, that would alienate them from Israel's Jewish majority."

World.title: ActBlue's woes not over as top Republican predicts potential DOJ charges over foreign cash controversy
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A top House Republican leading the investigation into ActBlue is warning that Democrats' main fundraising platform could potentially face criminal charges.

Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital that the congressional investigation into ActBlue would continue and that he suspected the Department of Justice (DOJ) would act as well if federal prosecutors believed a crime could be proven in court.

"We know that ActBlue did not have the fraud prevention standards in place that were necessary to prevent foreign funds from finding their way, through the ActBlue platform, into Democratic campaigns and Democratic causes. I'm of the belief that we ultimately need to continue this investigation," Steil told Fox News Digital.

ANOTHER ACTBLUE LEADER PLEADS FIFTH AS HOUSE INVESTIGATES ALLEGED FOREIGN DONATIONS

"And then, separate of that, the United States Department of Justice will make a decision as to whether or not they believe that there was a crime committed. And if they can prove that in court, my belief would be that the Department of Justice would move forward."

Steil's committee, along with the House committees on oversight and the judiciary, have for years probed allegations that ActBlue's lax verification standards have allowed foreign cash to seep into American elections. ActBlue has denied any wrongdoing and dismissed the probe as a partisan attack.

DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS

ActBlue has, however, sought to shore up its donor verification standards as the probe has gone on, including most recently rolling out a new passport verification system.

"Our investigation is about getting the facts to the American people, and, in large part, putting ourselves in a position to update our campaign finance laws for the digital era," Steil said. "So many of our campaign finance laws were written for a previous time. It is absolutely essential that we're updating our laws to actually address the fact that we are in a campaign finance digital era."

President Donald Trump directed now-former Attorney General Pam Bondi to open an investigation into ActBlue in April 2025, but the current status of that probe is unknown. Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ with Steil's comments, asking for an update on the investigation.

The platform has long been used by many Democrats to raise money for their political campaigns, including Democratic leaders in the House and Senate, though it said it paused donations from Americans abroad in 2025.

FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT

ActBlue has consistently denied wrongdoing in responses to Fox News Digital and communications to House investigators. Ten top figures within the company, including executives and founders, have pleaded the Fifth Amendment to avoid answering questions in both public and private sit-downs with GOP-led committees.

But a new report released earlier this month, first reported by Fox News Digital, appeared to show employees green-lighting donations despite some questions about where they came from.

Chief among the GOP's concerns was ActBlue's passport number verification. According to the report, the field only required the correct number of characters for a U.S. passport number rather than a valid code for a donation to be accepted.

A letter sent to House investigators by ActBlue's lawyers earlier this month said its new program "adds passport-based identity verification as a further enhancement to ActBlue’s multi-layered approach to fraud and foreign-contribution prevention."

TEXAS AG PAXTON SUES DEM FUNDRAISING PLATFORM ACTBLUE, ALLEGING 'FRAUDULENT AND FOREIGN DONATIONS'

"The new program uses the best available technology to allow eligible donors located abroad to verify their identity using a valid U.S. passport. It reflects substantial engineering investments by ActBlue to ensure that, as it resumes processing contributions from foreign addresses, its compliance systems can withstand scrutiny," the letter said.

Steil said at the time that the update "only confirms what we've been saying: ActBlue failed to verify the citizenship of individuals who made donations from abroad."

Fox News Digital reached out to ActBlue for comment on Steil's most recent remarks.

World.title: Protests erupt in Spain after train crash kills dozens
World.content:
Spain began three days of mourning Thursday after at least 69 people were killed and dozens more injured in the country’s deadliest train crash in decades. But anger is mounting about the alleged incompetence that allowed the accident to happen and protesters clashed with police overnight outside the country’s transport ministry.

Once considered one of the country’s crowning achievements, Spain’s high-speed rail network had not endured a deadly crash since it came into service over 30 years ago.

After the second train accident in less than a year, the tragedy has deepened the feeling among many that there is something broken in Spanish society. The crash follows weeks of protests.

A protest outside Spain's transport ministry where demonstrators demanded accountability following the accident. Ananda Manjon / Europa Press via Getty

Rising costs and a housing shortage that is pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market, have already triggered massive and sometimes deadly protests across the country, and piled the pressure on the Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

On Wednesday, four weeks before the country goes to the polls in a national election, Sanchez visited the site in the central province of Toledo where a quiet stretch of rail lined by olive groves had been turned into a scene of devastation.

Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo after one train crashed into another that was stationary on the line.

Hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police, firefighters and soldiers attended the scene to rescue survivors and recover bodies, before cranes were brought in to move parts of the damaged trains late Wednesday.

World.title: RFK Jr. takes shortcut to make some unapproved peptides available for use
World.content:
The Department of Health and Human Services is giving compounding pharmacies a temporary green light to make six peptides while the agency continues to work on a formal rule change.

In a notice filed Wednesday, the agency said it would exercise “enforcement discretion,” meaning it will not take legal action against compounding pharmacies that make the six unapproved peptides. In practice, that means these pharmacies can start offering them now, even though the peptides aren’t yet on the Food and Drug Administration’s list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make.

The six peptides are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500.

They’ve been promoted online as treatments for everything from faster healing to younger-looking skin and a longer lifespan. None are approved by the FDA, and the agency’s own scientists concluded there is insufficient data to prove they are safe and effective.

The FDA said compounding pharmacies must certify the identity and purity of the compounds. They must also now report side effects, which was not previously mandated.

The move comes as a growing “gray market” has sprung up around peptides, where retailers sell them labeled “for research use only,” a legal workaround that lets them claim they aren’t meant for humans. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others have argued that allowing peptides to be compounded would move people away from this gray market and toward safer products.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, HHS is working to put prevention and patient safety at the center of health care—and that includes confronting the risks of black-market peptides,” Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said in a statement.

Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now leads the Center for Science in the Public Interest watchdog group, said the FDA was essentially “turning a blind eye” to widen access to drugs that have not been proven to work.

Compounding pharmacies generally may use only ingredients the FDA has added to an official list known as the bulk drugs substances list. Adding an ingredient requires the FDA to propose a rule, take public comment and issue a final rule, a process that can take several months.

The agency took a step toward that process in July, when an FDA advisory panel narrowly voted in favor of adding six peptides to the bulk list. The panel included six new appointees with ties to the peptide industry and another who is the son of a U.S. representative who has pushed Kennedy to make peptides more available. (During that meeting, some committee members expressed concerns that the recommendation could make it harder for the FDA to say no to other unapproved drugs in the future.)

On Tuesday and Wednesday, the FDA was scheduled to meet outside groups, including Medivant Healthcare, a compounding pharmacy that offers peptides, according to Reginfo.gov, a federal website that tracks government regulations.

Shabbir Safdar, executive director of the Partnership for Safe Medicines, which researches the dangers of counterfeit medicines, said both the enforcement discretion and upcoming rule change would expose Americans to “untested, dangerous substances.”

“Imagine what it means for the nation’s top drug regulator to announce they won’t enforce the laws on people making completely untested compounds and distributing them to the public,” Safdar said.

World.title: The former youth pastor leading one of the NFL’s best offenses
World.content:
When Nate Scheelhaase was promoted to offensive coordinator of the Los Angeles Rams last winter, he stepped into one of the NFL’s most auspicious jobs, and for a Super Bowl contender, no less.

Not bad for a former youth pastor.

Fresh out of college, Scheelhaase moved to Louisville, Kentucky, in 2014 to work with teenagers at Southeast Christian Church, one of the largest megachurches in the U.S. During that time, he regularly stopped by a few dozen high schools to visit with students. For two high schools’ football teams, he volunteered as a chaplain. The role entailed building trust, finding common ground and helping those he spoke with work for something bigger than themselves.

“An impactful year,” said Scheelhaase, 35.

It wasn’t the typical starting point for a career in coaching — because even though Scheelhaase had been a four-year starting quarterback at Illinois, he wasn’t initially interested in that career path at all.

Without intending to, though, Scheelhaase honed skills while he was a youth pastor that he says helped him rise quickly within the coaching industry.

“I would say that there’s a lot of carryover,” Scheelhaase said in an interview. “From a ministry standpoint, just being around people from all different walks of life, different journeys, being able to meet them where they’re at — that’s also a football locker room. That’s a staff locker room.”

Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase during training camp at Loyola Marymount University this summer. Ric Tapia / Getty

The growth of sports in the U.S. is often a story of their crossover with faith. James Naismith, basketball’s inventor, is said to have believed he could better embody what it meant to be a Christian using sports than the pulpit. Many of football’s conventions, including the huddle, numbered jerseys and padded goalposts, came from Amos Alonzo Stagg, who had gone to Yale to study divinity and began coaching to fulfill a vision of “muscular Christianity.”

Careers in sports have often led to careers in religious roles. Rocky Seto won national championships at the University of Southern California and a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks during 16 years on Pete Carroll’s coaching staffs. In Seattle, Seto’s role eventually evolved to include a weekly address delivered in front of the entire roster and staff. He obsessively prepared his material.

“How am I going to capture the whole room?” Seto said. “It’s basically convincing them that if you learn this, this is going to help us win, help us be better.”

That experience made him feel prepared to give his first sermon. It was 2017, and Seto had just left the Seahawks to become the pastor-in-waiting at Evergreen Baptist Church, in suburban Los Angeles. Standing in front of another packed room of congregants, Seto felt his new job’s mission mirrored that of his last one — to deliver hope.

“You come to church in some ways to take a peek into heaven for a moment, and then we break. It’s like a huddle, and then we break out to basically fulfill the Great Commission outside this building, right?” he said. “And so coaching is no different. The information has to be almost like, ‘This is the greatest thing you need to know.’”

As Scheelhaase’s career was ending in late 2013, all he knew was that he didn’t envision a future in coaching.

He had gotten married a few months earlier, and he had seen enough coaches get fired and hired to question raising a family in an industry with fleeting job security and a nomadic career path. Meetings with Illini alumni in corporate jobs in Chicago also failed to inspire him. Unsure what to do, Scheelhaase called Jason Epperson, a local pastor who served as Illinois football’s team chaplain.

Scheelhaase was a four-year starting quarterback at the University of Illinois. Michael Hickey / Getty

Epperson had just taken a job at Southeast in Louisville, where there was a youth pastor role open. The idea intrigued Scheelhaase, who had grown up outside Kansas City, Missouri, as a devout Christian. When he arrived at Southeast in early 2014, he was trying “to figure out different ways to just connect with people in the area and show them that I was interested in just who they were more than just what they were doing,” Scheelhaase said. “Which I think is always a good spot to start.”

Chris Burke, an ESPN baseball analyst who lived in the area, first noticed Scheelhaase because of his athleticism during pickup games inside Southeast’s gym. Other things about Scheelhaase soon stood out, too.

“He looked perfectly suited for that job,” Burke said. “You can tell he got a kick out of being around young people. He communicated well with them. He had the patience.”

When a local mother told Scheelhaase that her eighth grade son’s father had recently died and that she needed others to be there for her son, Scheelhaase gave him rides and went to practices. The son was Nate Hobbs, the future San Francisco 49ers defensive back whom Scheelhaase still describes as one of his closest friends.

Scheelhaase stopped by Trinity High School, a local powerhouse, with a “confident humility,” said Andrew Coverdale, Trinity’s offensive coordinator at the time, who is now the passing game coordinator at Kentucky. Scheelhaase didn’t expect students to listen to him just because he had been a college quarterback.

“As somebody who taught in high school for a long, long time, I can’t really emphasize enough that kids need every form of mentorship and positive adult presence they can have, because it is brutal to be a teenage kid right now,” Coverdale said. High schoolers are “just dealing with so much and carrying so much. And so I just think having a guy like that around that you can talk to, who has life experience that he’s willing to share in a really winsome way, it was just great.”

Scheelhaase spent a relatively brief year and a half in Louisville, but he said that time shaped him immeasurably. Scheelhaase, who now has three children, said spending time around church leaders and attendees gave him role models for how he wanted to act as a husband and a father. It also changed his career path.

While he was leading a chapel service for football players at Eastern High School in 2014, he gave what he thought was a compelling, relatable speech that pulled in his athletic background and life story. It was received, he said with a smile, by proverbial crickets.

Taking a seat, he was stunned to see the reaction when the school’s head coach stood up to deliver his own pregame speech.

“Everybody was on the edge of their seat,” Scheelhaase said. “And in that moment, I thought, man, there is a cool ability to impact as a coach. And it was probably the thing that triggered the thought of, man, what would it look like to be able to impact in that way and influence in that way.”

Scheelhaase celebrates against the Buffalo Bills at SoFi Stadium near Los Angeles on Oct. 12. Katelyn Mulcahy / Getty

By the start of the 2015 football season, Scheelhaase was at Illinois coaching running backs. Technically, he was new to the profession. Yet recruiting players to campus and developing them once they were on the roster didn’t feel any different, at its core, from how he’d worked to build trust in Louisville.

“You are going to ask people to do really hard things as a coach, things that are counterintuitive to what you want to do,” he said. “Stand in a pocket where you know somebody’s going to hit you in the side of your helmet. To be somebody who loves to catch the football, but you got to go and block. To be somebody that’s willing to do the dirty work, and you’re going to ask them to do it, and the only way I know how to do that is to connect with them on a deep level. They know I not only understand what we’re asking them to do, but I care and I see them in that. And so connection, fortunately for me, it’s how I’m wired. That’s the part I enjoy the most about my job. ...

“And there probably is an element of that’s what I enjoyed even about the job as a high school pastor in Louisville, too, is just connecting with people and seeing there’s oftentimes more common ground than you think.”

In 2023, he became a coordinator at Iowa State. A year later, he left to become an offensive assistant for Sean McVay and the Rams, which to some may have seemed like a backward step; his job revolved around using software to manually draw the plays McVay wanted called each week. In the NFL, however, just being around McVay is a career springboard: The last four Rams offensive coordinators are now head coaches, and Zac Taylor was drawing McVay’s plays before Cincinnati hired him as its head coach. In 2025, a full year before Scheelhaase’s promotion to Rams offensive coordinator, McVay had called him “a special coach” and “a rising star, without a doubt.”

Last winter, as Scheelhaase was interviewing for NFL head coaching jobs, he called interim Stanford coach Frank Reich to ask about the school’s opening. The two had more in common than football. After he retired from a long career as a backup NFL quarterback, Reich attended seminary and worked as a pastor before he became an NFL head coach.

He saw carryover between the two industries, too.

“In coaching or seminary or pastoring, there are a lot of hours,” Reich said in 2019.

The hours Scheelhaase put in in Louisville have paid off in ways he didn’t expect, he said. There, his life revolved around Sundays. In ways he could never have predicted, it still does.

World.title: Trump’s speeches take on darker tone and DHS hack exposes 40,000 workers: Morning Rundown
World.content:
Trump veers into profanity and stereotyping in rally speeches. Contact information of more than 40,000 DHS employees exposed in a hack. And why some consumers are hunting their dinner amid concerns over meat quality.

Here’s what to know today.

Trump’s final campaign swing is taking on a darker tone

President Donald Trump has traveled 22 of 28 days in October, appearing in a total of 19 states. His remarks have averaged 1½ hours. At 80 years old, this frenzied pace is testing his stamina and his ability to deliver a compelling rationale for preserving the Republicans’ slim majority in Congress.

This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.

But between messages about the economy — during which he has touted numbers without substantiation — viewers are getting profanity, physical objectification and ethnic stereotyping.

For example, he emphasized Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s middle name, Mohamed, at a rally in Michigan. Upset that he didn’t win the Nobel Peace Prize, Trump called Norway a “s---house country.” He’s commented on Ohio Senator Jon Husted’s muscular “a--” and said rapper Nicki Minaj’s is “hard to miss.” At a South Carolina event, after punches were thrown at a protester, Trump said, “That was incredible!”

White House communication director, Steven Cheung, insists Trump is “making a significant impact on races.”

While Ronald Reagan popularized “Morning in America,” Trump rallies tell of a gathering darkness. His closing message before the elections leans into the notion that jihadists and communists are hiding in plain sight — and on the ballot.

Subscribe to read the full analysis.

Track early voting tallies by age, gender and more.

Find out how candidates are polling in competitive Senate races.

The races to watch in Ohio? See who’s running and how Republicans and Democrats fared in past elections. Then, scroll to the end of the page to explore data in other states.

Senate What If: Explore different paths to a Republican or Democratic Senate majority, mapped out by NBC News chief data analyst Steve Kornacki and “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker. Then, create your own scenarios.

More politics news:

Trump is calling for criminal charges against Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in Alaska’s Senate race, after the New York Times reported that she and other Democrats worked to recruit a candidate with the same name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. But finding another Dan Sullivan to run doesn’t necessarily run afoul of election laws, legal experts said.

A federal judge refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots in California from alleged noncitizens.

For subscribers: Election prediction markets became less accurate as primaries neared, a new analysis found, challenging the notion that they can predict the likely outcome of a race.

For subscribers: Newly obtained court records reveal Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s estranged mother, who was featured in GOP rival Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad, showed signs of instability in recent years.

40,000 DHS employee names exposed in hack

The seal of the US Department of Homeland Security outside the Nogales-Mariposa port of entry on the US-Mexico border in Nogales, Arizona, US, on Friday, Feb. 21, 2025. Rebecca Noble / Bloomberg via Getty

Anti-fascist activists opposed to the Trump administration said they hacked the Department of Homeland Security and created a database of names and contact information for over 40,000 agency employees. The searchable database is hosted by Distributed Denial of Secrets, a transparency nonprofit that often makes hacked government files available to the public, similar to WikiLeaks.

The group behind the attack calls itself the Department of Peace, and the alleged hackers and DDoSecrets said the release was to protest DHS and its deportation operations.

The 40,000 agency employees whose personal information was shared represent roughly 15% of the more than 260,000 people directly employed by DHS. The data includes work contact information, which can be sensitive because DHS keeps many employees’ identities secret, including those of ICE officers.

What else to know about the hack.

Study estimates three-fourths of NFL players who died in 15-year span had CTE

A new study found that 75% of NFL players who died over a 15 year period had CTE. James Black / Icon Sportswire via Getty

An estimated 75% of football players who died from 2008 to 2023 had signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a new study found, marking the highest estimate to date. “I had to double-check the numbers,” said study leader Yorghos Tripodis, the director of statistics and data management at the Boston University Alzheimer’s Disease and CTE Center, expressing shock at the results.

One huge hurdle in studying CTE, which affects parts of the brain involved with regulating behavior and emotions, is that the condition can only be diagnosed after a person has died. Plus, 99% of the brains donated to research by NFL players had signs of CTE, according to a previous study.

To estimate how many players had CTE more accurately, Tripodis and his team combined data from Boston University’s UNITE Brain Bank with national death records for other former NFL players.

A closer look at the calculations.

Milwaukee Brewers claim their first World Series title

After a 57-season wait, the Milwaukee Brewers are champions. They beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 of the World Series, then poured onto Tropicana Field, in St. Petersburg, Florida, after closer Trevor Megill induced a soft grounder for the final out.

“This is one of the greatest moments of my life,” Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt said on Fox after the game. “Oh my gosh. It doesn’t even feel real. This is surreal.”

Milwaukee is the MLB’s smallest market, and its payroll ranked only 19th out of 30 teams. But the Brewers still completed one of the most dominant postseason runs in MLB history. The team’s 12-2 postseason record is among the best since 1995, when the league expanded the playoffs to include wild-card teams.

Recap the Brewers’ path to their World Series triumph.

Staff Pick: Want cheap, high-quality meat? Hunt your own game

Nicole Schwartz for NBC News

Ground beef prices are near record highs, and concerns about meat quality are mounting. For a growing number of consumers, the solution is to hunt their own dinner.

The National Deer Association, a hunting and conservation advocacy group, says demand for its introductory online hunting course is soaring, particularly among urban and suburban residents in the Northeast corridor.

Meanwhile, local butchers say they are seeing a growing demand from consumers who want beef caught or processed close to their homes.

“There’s a mood in the nation that commercial meat is becoming less and less attractive,” said Kyle Peterson, the owner of Whitleyville Station, a meat and game processing store in Jackson County, Tennessee. “It’s, ‘Where’d this beef come from, where did this pig come from, what’s it been fed?’”

World.title: Their record is strong. Their roster is battered. Can the Thunder still contend for an NBA title?
World.content:
The Oklahoma City Thunder’s win on opening night of the new NBA season was a reminder of everything that makes the league’s 2025 champion a prime contender to win again.

Barely one week later, those aspirations have already been damaged.

Thunder star Jalen Williams, the team’s second-leading scorer and best all-around defender during its title run two seasons ago, fractured a fibula and dislocated his left ankle in a gruesome injury Sunday. The same night, Cason Wallace, a hounding defender and accurate shooter in his own right, tore the labrum in his shoulder.

Thunder general manager Sam Presti didn’t specify how long both will miss, but they are expected to miss months, at a minimum, putting their availability for any playoff run — especially a deep one — in serious doubt. Jeff Stotts, an athletic trainer who runs a site that tracks sports injuries, wrote that since 2005, just one player had sustained a torn labrum like Wallace’s and returned later that season.

“We’ll get them back, we’ll get them healthy, but we got a lot of basketball to play in front of us,” Presti said Monday. “We got to put it together, figure out what the next steps are, because this is part of the business that we’re in.”

Getting Williams back healthy had been central to Oklahoma City’s goal of returning to the NBA Finals. Injuries sidelined Williams for more than half of last season, and he also missed time during last season’s Western Conference finals, which the Thunder lost in seven games to San Antonio.

When San Antonio and Oklahoma City met on opening night, with Oklahoma City winning on the road, it was widely seen as a preview of the spring, when the two teams with loaded rosters featuring superstars still in their 20s were expected again to face off for the right to make the Finals.

“It’s obviously going to be tough without a player” like Williams, Thunder guard and two-time league MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander said. “But he’s not gone forever. He’ll be back better than ever, and we know it. We’ve just got to hold the fort down until he comes back.”

The Thunder aren’t the only team whose season has already been upended by injuries. Minnesota Timberwolves All-Star guard Anthony Edwards is expected to miss around two months after his right knee required an arthroscopic procedure, ESPN reported. A right knee injury will also sideline Utah Jazz star forward Jaren Jackson Jr. for a reported six to eight weeks, while an ankle injury will sideline Orlando Magic star Paolo Banchero at least a month. Indiana Pacers All-Star Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring) and Orlando guard Jalen Suggs (right knee) also will miss time.

Drawing a connection between some of the acute injuries, like Williams’ freak fracture, and cumulative injuries such as the knee that has bothered Edwards for months is difficult, said Dr. Tarek Souryal, a former president of the NBA Physicians Association who was the Dallas Mavericks’ team doctor for more than two decades.

“What you’re witnessing is most likely a statistical aberration, not necessarily evidence of a systemic problem,” Souryal said. “A cluster of injuries, however unusual or alarming, does not by itself establish a causal relationship.”

Wallace and Williams are homegrown talents, drafted and developed by Oklahoma City into centerpieces of the 2025 championship team. The Thunder, under Presti, drafted and traded so well that their depth was often unparalleled around the NBA, with capable emerging contributors backing up more established starters.

The current collective bargaining agreement between the league and the players union, however, makes it financially difficult for a team to keep together a core of players for longer than a few seasons once they get old enough, and perform well enough, to command lucrative long-term extensions.

World.title: Milwaukee Brewers defeat Tampa Bay Rays to claim first World Series title
World.content:
The Milwaukee Brewers’ 57-season wait for a World Series title ended Wednesday as their victory over Tampa Bay completed one of the most dominant postseason runs in MLB history.

Once closer Trevor Megill induced a soft ground ball for the last out and their 4-1 win over the Rays in Game 5 was final, the Brewers rushed up the steps of their dugout and onto the playing field at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida. The celebration had been in the making for more than half a century.

“This is one of the greatest moments of my life,” Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt said on Fox after the game. “Oh my gosh. It doesn’t even feel real. This is surreal.”

After having relocated from Seattle to Milwaukee and played for the first time as the Brewers in 1970, the team didn’t make the World Series until 1982, when it lost in seven games. It then waited 44 years to make its return to the Fall Classic.

Brewers starting pitcher Jacob Misiorowski celebrates after an out during Game 5. Daniel Shirey / MLB Photos via Getty

For a franchise starved for big moments, this year’s team supplied one after another.

The Brewers’ 12-2 postseason record is among the best since the MLB postseason format expanded in 1995 to include wild-card teams. The Brewers’ .857 winning percentage was just off the percentages produced by the 1999 New York Yankees and the 2005 Chicago White Sox, which each went 11-1 en route to their own titles.

“I don’t even have words,” star pitcher Jacob Misiorowski, who threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings of the clinching game, told Fox after the Game 5 win.

Milwaukee is MLB’s smallest market. Its payroll ranked only 19th out of 30 teams. In 12 postseason games, it trailed nine times. But the Brewers won seven of those games by finding ways to prevail in multiple ways. Milwaukee hit seven home runs in a National League Championship Series sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers yet took a 3-0 series lead on Tampa Bay while hitting just one homer. In Game 5, Milwaukee drove in runs using two singles, a sacrifice fly and a double.

Cooper Pratt and Brice Turang embrace after the Brewers defeated the Rays in Game 5. Carmen Mandato / Getty

Down to its final out in the bottom of the ninth inning, Tampa Bay got on the board when Chandler Simpson’s two-out double drove in Liam Hicks to trim the deficit to 4-1. With hard-throwing reliever Aaron Ashby waiting to relieve Megill in case he got into any more trouble, a soft grounder ended the game.

Catcher William Contreras earned Most Valuable Player honors after driving in four runs and hitting .381 during the World Series.

“I don’t have words to say,” Contreras said through a translator.

This was no fluke by a scrappy team that got hot at the right time. Milwaukee had the second-best record in baseball at July’s All-Star break and ultimately won an MLB-high and franchise-record 103 games. After it beat San Diego in the divisional round, it swept two-time reigning champion Los Angeles in the National League Championship Series. Even though the Dodgers’ payroll was more than double the Brewers’, Milwaukee scored 10 more runs over the sweep to secure a World Series berth against Tampa Bay.

William Contreras scores in the sixth inning. Rob Tringali / MLB Photos via Getty

The Rays were in some ways a mirror image of Milwaukee, another light-spending franchise looking to turn its regular-season success — the Rays had won the most games in the American League — into its first World Series victory.

“Best feeling ever,” Christian Yelich, the Brewers’ captain, said on the broadcast.

After one-run wins in the first two games of the World Series — including a Game 2 comeback in which Milwaukee fell behind 4-0 in the first inning — it won Game 3 in a 10-1 rout sparked by Christian Yelich’s stolen base in the fifth inning. When a challenge ruled Yelich safe at second base, Milwaukee proceeded to score eight runs with two outs, blowing the game open without ever hitting a home run.

Milwaukee’s championship run was possible thanks to a dependable core of players who spanned generations. Yelich, 34, and 33-year-old reliever Brandon Woodruff, whose save in Game 3 was his first appearance since July 4 because of injuries, were the only players remaining from a 2018 Brewers roster that was just one win away from that season’s World Series.

The Brewers' Jackson Chourio celebrates from the dugout. Daniel Shirey / MLB Photos via Getty

In the divisional round against San Diego, 20-year-old outfielder Jackson Chourio hit a late two-run homer that saved Milwaukee in its opening game of the postseason. Chourio then delivered a walk-off single to win the following game.

The Milwaukee Brewers celebrate with Trevor Megill #29 after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on October 28, 2026 in St Petersburg, Flo. Mike Stobe / Getty

On the mound, Milwaukee constructed a feared rotation of arms starting with Misiorowski, the 24-year-old with blazing speed who made the All-Star Game as a rookie in 2025 after just five starts. For his encore, Misiorowski in 2026 led a pitching staff that allowed MLB’s second-lowest team ERA during the regular season. When he left games, a bullpen with arms just as nasty and hard-throwing as Misiorowski’s took over.

“This is just incredible,” Megill, on the mound for the final out, said after the win. “Ten-year-old me would be so proud.”

All of the pieces worked, all season. When the regular season ended, Milwaukee stood alone at the top of the standings.

And when the playoffs ended a month later, the Brewers were on top yet again. Their long wait for a title had ended.

World.title: How to watch live 2026 election results on CBS News
World.content:
Control of Congress and the future of President Trump's agenda are on the line in the 2026 midterm elections, as voters cast their ballots for all 435 House seats and 35 Senate races around the country. Candidates for governor are on the ballot in 39 states, along with some high-profile measures like California's proposed billionaire tax.

CBS News will have extensive live coverage of results and analysis on all platforms after the polls close on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

How to watch election coverage with cable

CBS News' "America Decides: Election 2026" live coverage on TV and cable starts Tuesday at 7 p.m. ET. (Find your local CBS station here.)

Anchors Tony Dokoupil and Norah O'Donnell will be joined on the set by"CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King, "Face the Nation" moderator and chief foreign affairs correspondent Margaret Brennan, and CBS News' team of political reporters, including Robert Costa, Major Garrett, Nancy Cordes and Ed O'Keefe.

There will be live updates throughout the evening from CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Anthony Salvanto and reporting from correspondents in Washington and around the country, including Weijia Jiang at the White House, Nikole Killion, Adriana Diaz, Matt Gutman, Skyler Henry, Lana Zak, Kris Van Cleave, Taurean Small, Jan Crawford and Nicole Sganga. Contributors will also include political analysts from both sides of the aisle and experts on election law and security.

How to watch election coverage without cable

Live coverage is streaming on CBS News 24/7 throughout the day Tuesday and all evening long, with election results expected to start coming in Tuesday night.

Watch on the free CBS News app on your connected TV or smartphone, on Paramount+, and all platforms where CBS News 24/7 is available, including CBSNews.com and YouTube.

Beginning at 5 p.m. ET, dive into the latest data on "Election 2026: The Nerd Show," hosted by CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Anthony Salvanto and CBS News congressional correspondent Caitlin Huey-Burns, joined by Democratic and Republican pollsters and other election data experts.

Prime-time coverage anchored by Tony Dokoupil and Norah O'Donnell begins streaming live on all platforms at 7 p.m. ET.

How to watch live streaming local election coverage from CBS Stations

CBS Stations are covering the election live across 15 owned markets. Local streaming channels plan sustained live coverage with a mix of local and network coverage.

Election night live coverage plans include:

CBS News Atlanta is not streaming but local viewers can watch on WUPA Channel 69.

What time will election results come in?

Poll closing times vary from state to state, with the first batch of states closing at 7 p.m. ET, more at 7:30, and large numbers of states at 8 p.m. and 9 p.m. ET. The polls in California and several other Western states don't close until 11 p.m. ET, followed by Hawaii an hour later and finally Alaska — with a closely watched Senate race — at 1 a.m. ET.

Results in some races will take longer to come in than others, depending on various factors including how close the margin is and the state's rules for when mail-in ballots are counted.

CBS News live coverage continues Wednesday on "CBS Mornings" and streaming throughout the day on CBS News 24/7.
