World.title: Trump's increasing support for Russia carries existential danger for Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the six weeks between Prime Minister Mark Carney's trip to the European Parliament and top EU officials arriving for a joint summit in Montreal, the United States has moved considerably closer to Russia.

Just days after Carney returned to Canada, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio invited Russia's Vladimir Putin to December's G20 summit in Miami. Then on Oct. 9, the U.S. lifted sanctions on Russian oil and announced a deal to buy diesel directly from Russia.

Some analysts say Trump's rapprochement with Russia poses a clear danger to Canadians — one not easily solved by closer partnerships with allies an ocean away.

"This is not Trump playing footsie with Putin," said Vincent Rigby, national security and intelligence adviser to the prime minister until 2021. "This is something far, far more serious, and strategically, this can't help but be a concern."

Last week on the White House South Lawn, Trump drew his own parallels between Canada and Ukraine, bragging after a call with Carney: "Just like I told Zelenskyy, we have all the cards."

While Trump has increased his swipes at Canada on the campaign trail, his hostility to Ukraine goes beyond words.

In Trump's one-sided "energy ceasefire," Ukraine was expected to stop hitting Russian refineries but Russia continued to hit Ukrainian electrical plants .

Then came the slowdown in Starlink/Starshield, followed by a round of blame-shifting between the White House and Elon Musk as to who ordered it. The U.S. also appeared to cut off warnings of incoming ballistic missiles , and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump is making it harder to access Patriot missiles .

WATCH | Carney on Ukraine's restricted access to SpaceX technology: Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine | Duration closed caption 3:10 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he is concerned about the reported slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, which created 'real consequences.' He says Canadians likewise 'do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view' and compromise Canadian sovereignty.

"It's been unbelievable," said Rob Huebert, director of the Centre for Military, Security and Strategic Studies at the University of Calgary. "These actions can only be characterized as Trump trying to cause Ukraine to lose the war."

Washington also reportedly leaned on European countries to release billions of Euros in frozen Russian assets, and Trump signed an executive order waiving sanctions against Russia due to take effect two days later.

Maria Popova, an expert on Russia at McGill University and author of Russia and Ukraine: Entangled Histories, Diverging States, says the second Trump administration worked in its first year to make the U.S. more of a neutral party in Russia's war with Ukraine.

She says it now appears Trump is working up to openly allying with Putin.

"We have to start thinking about where this trajectory ends up eventually," she said. "And it ends in the U.S. directly helping Russia's war effort."

Rigby says U.S.-Russian closeness raises immediate fears about Arctic sovereignty, and "could be the end of NORAD in a worst-case scenario," referring to the joint Canada-U.S. partnership to protect sovereign airspace.

Huebert says the lifted oil sanctions and diesel deal could be seen cynically as a temporary move to mollify American voters angry about gas prices.

"For him to try to reduce the price of diesel just before the midterms, you may disagree with it entirely but you can at least understand it," he said.

"But all this other stuff?"

Strongman summit in Shenzhen

A proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month has revived longstanding concerns that Trump is keen to replace America's postwar network of alliances with a new global carve-up between three strongmen.

Trump has expressed openness to the Russian proposal. "Obviously, this is music to Putin's ears," said Popova.

Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said on Sunday that preparations have begun for the three-way summit on the sidelines of the Nov. 18-19 APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.

Huebert says the Russians have long pitched the idea of superpower spheres of influence, in which Washington, Moscow and Beijing would all agree to stay out of each other's backyards. Lesser powers would have to find a modus vivendi with the regional hegemon.

"We really need to be pushing against such a travesty," said Popova, "because the next meeting of the three of them will be to decide the fate of Canada or Taiwan. So we don't want this pattern to even start."

Trump has already made it clear that he sees the entire Western Hemisphere as the domain of the United States .

"We don't want a world that's run by superpowers," said Rigby. "If this is where we're headed — spheres of influence, Russia, China and the United States — this goes back to what Prime Minister Carney said at Davos: that middle powers are effectively going to be marginalized.

"It's very, very concerning."

Living with threats

Canada is pursuing new alliances and rearming, while seeking to keep the U.S.-Canada temperature low and bilateral institutions functioning where possible .

Popova sees parallels in this to Ukraine's past "multi-vector" approach to build connections with other countries, including Canada , that proved invaluable in 2014 when Russia took Crimea.

"In a world that is really becoming a world à trois to a considerable extent, Russia, China, United States, we're going to have to reach out to Europe," said Rigby.

That alliance can strengthen Canadian sovereignty if it leads to deeper integration of defence-industrial bases, greater exchanges of technology, the creation of a payments system less vulnerable to U.S. interference or the launching of new satellites that allow Canadians and Europeans to develop communications and navigational systems that don't depend on Musk or the Pentagon.

WATCH | Trump envoy praises Putin after prisoner release: Trump envoy Witkoff praises 'humanitarian' Putin at meeting in Russia | Duration closed caption 2:02 U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a 'humanitarian' at a meeting in St. Petersburg aimed at ending the Ukraine war, despite no Ukrainian presence at the table. U.S. officials later suggested Putin is open to trilateral meetings with Washington and Kyiv.

But Canada can't alter its geography. It lacks one key advantage of Ukraine, which has land borders with four EU nations, allowing easy resupply. Canada, in the event of real threats or hostilities from the U.S., would be mostly on its own.

Fortunately for Canadians, Trump's hostility toward Canada and fondness for Russia aren't shared by most Americans. For some time, Americans have not trusted Trump to do the right thing on Russia, and that is true also within his own party . Americans, including many Republicans, also don't like Trump's trade war with Canada .

Trump is also unlikely to be as long-lasting as Putin has been. Unless he's able to subvert the U.S. Constitution, he has only 26 months left.

But Rigby says he expects those months to be tumultuous: "You are potentially going to see a president after next week being even more reckless, less restrained and more aggressive."

World.title: More Canadian provinces are ending time changes. What does it mean for your health?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Millions of Canadians will turn their clocks back one hour this weekend, while millions of others will not. This divide is putting Canadians under different time systems — with potentially different consequences for their health.

Most of British Columbia, as well as Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories are no longer changing their clocks twice a year, joining Yukon and most of Saskatchewan. Most of Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces will still turn their clocks back on Nov. 1 for the end of daylight saving time.

For Quebec, this could be the last time. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced Wednesday that his government is moving to end the twice-yearly clock change, but it has not yet decided which time the province will keep. He said that decision will be made after consulting experts.

Research suggests permanent standard time — the time we return to in the fall — is more closely aligned with the body's internal clock than permanent daylight time, which several provinces have chosen.

Here's what winter time would look like across Canada under proposed time-zone changes

Joseph De Koninck, an emeritus professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa, has studied sleep for decades. He said the springtime change is the most problematic because people lose an hour of sleep when they set their clocks forward, creating a mismatch between the body's internal biological clock and solar time.

De Koninck explained that our biological clock uses light to synchronize itself. As daylight changes with the seasons, our circadian rhythms adjust gradually. Making a one-hour adjustment all at once, however, is much more difficult.

"We are able to adapt, but it's not optimal for our health."

The Edmonton skyline at dawn. As one of Canada's northernmost major cities, Edmonton will see winter sunrises as late as 10 a.m. under Alberta's new permanent daylight time. (John Robertson/CBC)

Why morning light matters

Michael Antle, head of the University of Calgary's psychology department and a professor who studies circadian rhythms, said permanent standard time would have been better for Alberta.

Because of the province's northern latitude and position within its time zone, it already has late winter sunrises, Antle said. Permanent daylight time will push them forward another hour.

"It's not the choice I would have made," he said of the province's decision.

Antle said daylight time essentially means society has agreed to get up and go to work or school an hour earlier.

Most people's circadian clocks run slightly slow, making them somewhat "night owlish," he said. Morning light helps speed up that clock.

Michael Antle, a University of Calgary psychology professor, says permanent standard time is healthier because it better aligns with people's body clocks. (Submitted by Michael Antle)

When morning light arrives later, there can be a mismatch between what the body wants to do and what work or school requires.

Antle described this effect as "social jetlag."

Antle pointed to population studies that found people exposed to later sunsets slept less and had higher rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. He also cited Russian research that found winter depression among young people increased while Russia observed permanent daylight time.

WATCH | B.C. scientists warn permanent daylight time could do more harm than good: Why some scientists don't support B.C.'s switch to permanent daylight time | Duration closed caption 2:17

Why researchers say permanent daylight time is a bad idea

Both researchers distinguish between the disruption caused by changing the clocks and the effects of living on daylight time year-round.

Antle said the spring change creates a sudden shift that can leave people feeling as though they're living on the wrong time for several weeks. Permanent daylight time would extend that mismatch through the darkest months of the year.

He would prefer permanent standard time. Continuing to spring forward and fall back would be a compromise, he said, preserving later summer evenings without the longer-term winter mismatch.

Night owls who work regular daytime jobs may struggle the most because they already find it difficult to wake up early, Antle said.

Those darker mornings are also having a real-world impact. Ski hills in Alberta's Bow Valley, for example, are delaying their opening times this winter to give staff more daylight to prepare the slopes before skiers arrive.

But most schools and workplaces have less flexibility to change their hours based on when the sun is up.

WATCH | Why Atlantic Canada should consider permanent standard time: Changing clocks twice a year a question of public health: prof | Duration closed caption 6:43 Rébecca Robillard, an associate professor at the University of Ottawa and co-chair of the Canadian Sleep Research Consortium, explains why Atlantic provinces should consider permanent daylight saving time.

Canada becomes a natural experiment

Canada's emerging patchwork could give researchers an opportunity to study neighbouring populations living under different time systems.

Antle said he would have preferred a year's notice to collect baseline data before Alberta made the change.

He said researchers should examine mental health, vehicle and pedestrian collisions, school performance and attendance, and workplace attendance and tardiness.

De Koninck noted that researchers now have tools to document sleep habits over time and compare how people adapt in different provinces.

But he expects Western Canadians may make their feelings known before researchers have years of data to analyze. People may not fully understand what permanent daylight time means, he said, until they've experienced a winter with much later sunrises.

"Those who've tried it haven't liked it," he said.

For De Koninck, the larger concern is what prolonged sleep disruption can mean for people's health.

"If you feel sleep deprived, then you have a host of issues, psychological and physical," he said.

"You can't play with your sleep."

World.title: EU dropping associate membership title for its closer alliance with Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The words "associate membership" were removed from a joint statement expected to be released at this week's Canada-EU summit, according to a draft seen by CBC News.

But while the statement is now expected to use softer language promising closer ties between the 27-member bloc and Canada, the head of the European Union's executive body continued to use the term in a social media post as she landed in Montreal on Wednesday.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen surprised many last month when she announced the EU would begin the process of making Canada its first associate member — a status that does not exist within the bloc — raising concerns among some members and Canadian politicians about what that would look like.

The draft statement now calls for an "ever closer association." It says this deepening relationship, repeatedly dubbed an "alliance for the future" — language previously used by Prime Minister Mark Carney — will be rooted "in a more active foreign and security policy partnership."

A source speaking to CBC News on the condition they not be named says this statement is now finalized by EU member countries, but Canada could still ask for changes.

Another source said some EU countries opposed the term "associate member," particularly Germany who called it a red line.

News that the summit's joint statement won't mention associate membership was first reported by Politico.

WATCH | 'Names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney: EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney | Duration closed caption 0:42 Prime Minister Mark Carney says what 'matters' at the EU summit set to take place later this week in Montreal is 'Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation so we can live our lives as we choose.'

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday before a cabinet meeting, Carney said the title of Canada's relationship to the EU shouldn't matter as long as it delivers for Canadians.

"The good news is it doesn't matter about specific names or nomenclature," he said.

"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose."

'Associate member' ambitions

Touching down in Montreal ahead of the two-day event, von der Leyen continued to use the term "associate member."

"An ocean separates Europe and Canada. Yet we have never felt closer. We have a new ambition: bringing Canada closer to us than ever before, as associate member of the EU," she posted to social media.

"Montreal, we're about to write a new chapter in our shared history."

The summit comes as the Canadian government is looking to to boost trade, investment and strategic partnerships with the EU bloc as part of a plan to reduce economic reliance on the United States under the unpredictable and volatile leadership of U.S. President Donald Trump.

The version of the EU-Canada statement seen by CBC News commits to reinforcing "a predictable trade environment, deepening collaboration in the Arctic, countering foreign information manipulation and interference and continued support for Ukraine."

It also includes commitments to strengthen co-operation on energy security, build up critical mineral supply chains and advance co-operation on artificial intelligence security and safety.

On Thursday, Carney will host a roundtable with business leaders on the margins of the summit. He will then host a dinner in honour of von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

World.title: He tried to get into Montreal's kosher market. It led to a battle over alleged meat monopoly
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mendy Boyarsky is fed up with the cost of kosher meat in Montreal and he’s on a mission to bring prices down.

But the owner of Aleph Meats is facing an uphill battle.

Trying to get a foothold in the marketplace is now leading to a potential legal showdown at the federal Competition Tribunal.

Boyarsky alleges the Jewish Community Council of Montreal (JCC), which operates Montreal Kosher, known as MK Kosher certification, has used its dominant position in the market to squeeze out competition among meat suppliers — like himself — and pressure local congregations to buy only MK approved kosher products.

The JCC oversees many aspects of life in Montreal’s devout Jewish community including the certification of kosher meat through its non-profit MK Kosher. The JCC denies Boyarsky's allegations.

But Boyarsky thinks the certifier is driving up the cost of food.

“They don't allow competition in the market. So they're able to charge exorbitant prices,” he said.

“There hasn't been another option other than the MK in Montreal for who knows how long,” he says, as he proudly shows off the different cuts of certified kosher meat at Aleph Meats, located in the city of Côte Saint-Luc, in Montreal's west end.

Boyarsky alleges his attempts to break into the commercial side of Montreal’s kosher meat industry are being blocked by the JCC and he can't sell to most synagogues or banquet spaces, for example, because they are exclusively dealing with MK Kosher.

He chose to operate outside of MK Kosher’s certification system and to use a different kosher meat certifier — Kashrut Supervision du Rabbinat (KSR).

“We have to be able to sell it to the synagogues, we have to be able to sell anywhere we want to be able to sell to,” he says.

Without access, even if the retail side of his business goes well, he says he won’t be able to scale his business and survive.

“We have to do it on mass production in order for this thing to work," he said. "We’re kosher certified and we need to have all the gates open for us."

If successful, Boyarsky’s lawsuit could force the JCC to pay millions in damages.

A case that could test the new limits of Canada’s Competition Tribunal

Having a case heard at Canada's Competition Tribunal can be difficult, but Boyarsky’s lawyer says the timing may be right to challenge the JCC’s alleged market dominance.

“There's been a groundswell of support from the Montreal Jewish community that wants to see this case brought to the Competition Tribunal,” said Joshua Krane, a competition law specialist and partner at MLT Aikins in Ottawa.

In response to the rising cost of living and skyrocketing grocery bills, Bill C-56 and Bill C-59, were passed by Parliament in December 2023 and June 2024 — overhauling Canada's Competition Act and expanding private access to the Competition Tribunal.

WATCH | Jewish Community Council of Montreal accused of driving up costs through its kosher certifier: Is there a kosher meat monopoly in Montreal? He’s alleging it's driving up prices | Duration closed caption 5:16 Mendy Boyarsky says he’s fed up with the cost of kosher meat in the city and alleges the Jewish Community Council of Montreal (JCC) is driving up prices through its certifier, Montreal Kosher, known as MK Kosher. The JCC, which runs MK Kosher, denies the allegations.

Krane says the tribunal now has the option to consider a case based on public interest grounds.

Federal Court Judge Jocelyne Gagné will decide whether Boyarsky’s lawsuit has merit and will be heard by the tribunal.

In an affidavit, the JCC denies its certifier enforces any exclusivity agreements with the exception of banquet halls.

In those cases, the JCC argues it’s not practical for synagogues to make sure a kitchen is kosher to MK Kosher’s standards every time a different certifier is used. It added that it does not agree with KSR about what constitutes proper kosher standards.

Rabbi Haim Nataf, who was authorized to speak on behalf of the JCC and MK Kosher, told CBC Boyarsky’s lawsuit is founded on “misconceptions” regarding Montreal’s kosher market.

Nataf said it is a mistake for Boyarsky, a meat seller, to claim he’s in competition with a certifier that doesn’t sell kosher products. He denies that MK Kosher has the capacity to influence pricing.

What is kosher and why is it more expensive?

The term kosher translates to "fit to eat,” and what qualifies comes down to standards set by Jewish community leaders and their interpretation of ancient texts and traditions.

“(Keeping kosher) is one of the definitive characteristics of an observant Jewish home,” says Rabbi Reuben Poupko of the Beth Israel Beth Aaron Congregation, who is not taking sides in the dispute.

In general, Poupko says the method of slaughtering the animal is more humane and pain free. Every step of the process is carefully monitored with inspections.

But “keeping kosher” comes at a cost.

“I've never heard anyone complain it was too inexpensive,” Poupko says. “It is significantly more expensive than regular meat.”

Rabbi Haim Nataf, spokesperson for the JCC and MK Kosher, says setting kosher standards is a religious issue. He says as a certifier, MK Kosher doesn’t have the ability to set prices. (Karol Dahl/CBC)

Nataf told CBC at MK Kosher, the JCC has full-time employees to ensure its strict religious standards are observed throughout the process. This includes drop-in inspections at restaurants and synagogues and 24/7 video surveillance in their prep spaces and kitchens.

MK Kosher is paid a one-time fee for some services, such as attending a slaughter, and recurring fees for others, like maintaining an MK Kosher certificate for restaurants and synagogues.

Nataf rejected the suggestion that MK Kosher brings in a big profit.

“I wouldn't call it a money maker. It definitely has a surplus that is reallocated to other community needs,” Nataf said.

He calculates the MK Kosher certification system only adds about 51 cents per kilogram to the overall cost of meat at retail.

Montrealers travel to New York to buy cheaper food

But Poupko says many community members think Montreal’s prices are higher than other markets.

“The community is divided between those who are agitated and frustrated and those who have quietly surrendered. But not too many people are happy,” Poupko said.

CBC spoke to several of Boyarsky’s customers who said they travel to New York to buy food ahead of holidays or if they are planning to host a large private event.

CBC’s investigation found that at certain locations in New York — such as Bingo Wholesale, a well-known grocer — there are significant savings on beef. Even after factoring in currency conversion, ground beef was on average 40 per cent to 50 per cent cheaper at Bingo Wholesale than at some of Montreal’s MK Kosher certified butchers and grocery stores.

Frustrated with local prices, kosher meat customers in Montreal told CBC it's common to travel to New York in search of deals. (Louis-Marie Philidor/CBC)

Between Oct. 16 and 19, CBC visited four major grocery chains that had kosher counters and two kosher butcher shops in Montreal to check prices.

Nataf, with the JCC and MK Kosher, says Bingo Wholesale is an outlier in New York.

He doesn’t believe beef prices are higher in Montreal and argues consumers need to shop around.

“I’m convinced there are very reasonable deals out there,” he said.

Boyarsky and the JCC dispute the overall size of the kosher meat market in Montreal. According to documents provided by the JCC as part of its affidavit, Montreal's top three MK-certified kosher meat distributors totaled $37.5 million in gross sales for 2025.

An old practice persists

One of the challenges is there may be a perception that JCC is freezing out competitors because it subscribes to a religious law called Sh’chutei Chutz.

Sh'chutei Chutz is grounded in Jewish law where a community maintains a closed market. Poupko says it's a relic from small villages in Eastern Europe when meat from outside the community was banned to protect local butchers, who played multiple roles in the community such as prayer leaders and mohalim .

While other Jewish communities have dropped the law as a guiding principle, the JCC has held on to what critics now call an outdated standard.

“The fact that there is not significant competition in Montreal is a significant contributing factor to the cost. There's no question,” Poupko says.

But Nataf argues the law is used to make sure traditions and standards are maintained in Montreal.

“I'm not saying it's very popular, but it's still around,” he said.

He argues that the JCC’s interpretation of Sh'chutei Chutz is quite lenient, in part because MK Kosher does certify beef from overseas.

Aleph Meats, owned by Mendy Boyarsky, gets KSR beef from South America, often making it more affordable.

CBC’s investigation found ground beef, for example, was between 18 per cent to 37 per cent cheaper at Aleph Meats than MK Kosher certified products at the locations that were price checked.

Montreal’s Jewish Community divided over the case

Krane, Boyarsky's lawyer, says he’s confident the Competition Tribunal will agree to hear the case. Then the real work will begin.

“We have to show there's been a practice of exclusivity. And then we have to show that that practice has resulted in higher prices or less choice for consumers,” Krane says.

Nataf, the JCC spokesperson, doesn't think the lawsuit should move forward.

Typically issues within the Jewish community are handled internally by the Rabbinical Tribunal of Montreal (Beth Din) — which operates under the JCC — rather than being fought out in court.

“I don't think it's the place of tribunals to interfere in kosher certification and generally religious beliefs and discussions,” said Nataf.

But since the Beth Din is also part of the JCC, Boyarsky says he had no choice but to take this route.

“They’re the prosecutor, they’re the judge and they’re the jury. They get to decide who can sell what, who can bring it in, they control everything across the board,” he said.

Bovarsky added that he's personally putting a lot on the line.

“There's a possibility that I won't be able to go into the synagogue, or I'll be thrown out of the community," he said.

“But if we win … the community will be the major beneficiary.”

World.title: U.S. midterms could be the country's most expensive elections yet. To what end?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The 2026 U.S. midterm elections are shaping up to be the most expensive elections in the country's history.

This election cycle will reach $11.6 billion US in spending, according to AdImpact, an advertising intelligence company that analyzes political advertising.

That would surpass the midterm record set in 2022 at $8.9 billion US and the $11.2 billion US spent during the 2024 presidential cycle.

To put things in a Canadian context, Liberal and Conservative parties in total raised $95 million US in 2024 and 2025, per Elections Canada. Meanwhile, Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico alone is projected to have raised $146 million U.S.

Indeed, combined ad spending in the Senate race between Talarico and Ken Paxton, the state's Republican attorney general, has topped $500 million US, according to ad-tracking data — on pace to become the most expensive U.S. ​Senate contest ever.

Just how much will campaign money play a role in determinin g who wins?

Here's a closer look.

Why are these elections so expensive?

As with everything, costs have gone up, making election-related expenses, primarily advertising, higher than in previous campaigns.

But since the 2010 U.S. Supreme Court's Citizens United decision opened the door to unlimited independent spending in federal elections, spending has increased exponentially.

WATCH | Trump accused of mounting intimidation campaign ahead of midterms: Trump accused of mounting fear-based intimidation campaign ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:47 Critics accuse U.S. President Donald Trump of mounting a fear-based campaign designed to intimidate voters ahead of next week's midterm elections. Trump has offered a $1-million US reward for election fraud tips, while administration officials have repeatedly refused to rule out sending federal officers to the polls.

Jen Heerwig, an associate professor of sociology at Stony Brook University who researches the political contributions of American corporate elites, said there are a number of highly competitive midterm races in which outside groups have stepped in to supplement candidate spending.

That means groups like super PACs (political action committees) have become increasingly important vehicles for election spending, she said.

Super PACs, unlike traditional candidate committees or regular PACs, can accept donations of unlimited size, Heerwig said, such as the hundreds of millions Elon Musk is pouring intoRepublican-aligned super PACs.

"And now we're seeing these groups spend alongside candidate campaigns in record-shattering amounts."

The "relentless rise of the mega donor" is one of the main stories of these midterm elections, said Henrik Schatzinger, a political science professor and director of the t he Center for Politics and the People at Wisconsin-based Ripon College.

In 2014, to be one of the Top 40 donors, one would have to have contributed at least $2.3 million US as an individual, Schatzinger said,

In this election, he said, one would have to spend at least $25 million US. "It's a pretty wild situation."

Which party is raising the most money?

When it comes to money raised by individual candidates in the House and Senate races, Democratic candidates are far outraising their Republican political opponents. That's money that goes specifically to the candidate that they can control.

According to the U.S. Federal Election Commission, Democratic candidates have raised more than $906 million US for these midterms. Republican candidates lag behind with more than $420 million US raised.

Of the money raised by Senate candidates, the Top 10 were all Democratic contenders. And across the 10 battleground Senate races, the Democratic campaigns raised more than five times as much as the Republican ones, according to Politico.

Meanwhile, for House races, eight of the Top 10 fundraisers were also Democrats.

While Republicans lag in candidate donations, they have a significant advantage when it come to money from outside groups like super PACs.

Republican-leaning donors gave $1.7 billion US, compared with $832 million US from Democratic-leaning givers, per Washington Post calculations.

In Texas, for example, groups backing Paxton have spent about $239 million US, more than five times the money spent by the largest Democratic-aligned groups, Reuters reported.

Four of the five top donors were Republican, the Post found, with the largest individual political donor being Musk, pouring in $446 million US of his own money.

The largest individual political donor has been Elon Musk, pouring $446 million US of his own money into the 2026 midterms. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

"The Republicans are kind of the party of billionaires and the Democrats are the party of millionaires," said Alex Keena, associate professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, in Richmond, Va., who researches campaign financing.

"That's the state of American politics right now."

Does that give Republicans an advantage?

Even though outside groups are giving Republicans the fundraising edge, that won't necessarily translate to votes, say some observers.

Heerwig said she's skeptical that super PAC spending will be as effective as candidate spending. And the amount Democratic candidates are raising from individual donors, compared to Republicans suggests far more grassroots enthusiasm for the Democrats.

"At the end of the day, there are only a handful of billionaires who will cast ballots but millions of small-dollar don ors," Heerwig said.

Schatzinger echoed that this election shows there's more energy among the small donor Democrat base than the re is among the Republican base.

"I think that's probably a better indicator of where this election is headed as opposed to just looking at a couple of mega donors who are putting in hundreds of millions of dollars."

Is this money well spent?

According to AdImpact, broadcast television remains the dominant force in political advertising, with an estimated $5.6 billion US being spent by the campaigns.

Digital spending across Facebook, Google, Snapchat and X is estimated to be around $1.6 billion US.

B ut Keena, the academic who researches campaign financing, q uestioned how much any of this spending will make a difference.

"My read of the evidence is that it's not really going to affect the outcome of the race."

In Texas, Republicans have poured millions into negative ads against Talarico. Yet polls suggest the race remains extremely tight — Talarico possibly has a small lead in a state that hasn't had a Democratic senator in more than 30 years.

Keena questioned how many voters are being reached by broadcast TV commercials.

"A lot of the political science research that looks at the effectiveness of ads relies on experiments from the 90s and early aughts when people did watch TV."

Keena said it's also very difficult to measure the effect of ads on social media.

'Money can buy you the megaphone'

Schatzinger said that many studies show ad effects dissipate often within a week, meaning a lot of this money is being spent on ads that may not be all that effective.

He suggested that the political mood of the country — where cost of living issues remain a priority issue, and where President Donald Trump is saddled with record low approval ratings — may be too much of a hur dle for cam paign ads.

"Money can buy you the megaphone, but you can't really buy the national mood, " Schatzinger said.

Todd Belt, professor of political management a t D.C-based Ge orge Washington University, said there seems to be a panic setting in among Republicans.

"They don't have the message. They don't have the policies. They have the money," he said.

"What we have set up here is an amazing natural experiment where we're going to find out: Can you outspend the economy and people's policy interests?"

World.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk to conduct his 1st spacewalk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The International Space Station is roughly 400 kilometres above Earth, moving at roughly 7.66 kilometres per second, and on Thursday, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk will be whizzing around Earth while working outside of it.

Kutryk, along with NASA astronaut Anil Menon, will conduct one of two spacewalks where they will install eight solar arrays. After the scheduled second walk on Nov. 5, these new arrays will increase the station's power capacity from 160 kilowatts to 215 kilowatts.

Canada is playing a prominent role in this spacewalk.

CSA astronaut Jenni Gibbons will serve as capcom, or capsule communicator, from the Johnson Space Center in Houston.

She has served as capcom a few times already, including during the Artemis II mission where Canadian Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon with three NASA astronauts.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut and backup Artemis II crew member Jenni Gibbons served as capsule communicator (capcom) during an Orion manual piloting demonstration on the fourth day of the mission. (Bill Stafford/NASA)

Then there's Canadarm2, the robotic arm that was crucial in the construction of the ISS, and which is used to move supplies and catch cargo spacecraft.

It already removed the arrays, called the International Space Station Roll Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs), from a SpaceX Dragon cargo earlier last week. It later moved them into position on the station's mobile base.

And finally, the CSA will also be involved at its Robotics Mission Control Centre in Longueuil, Que.

During Thursday's spacewalk, Canadarm2 will help Kutryk and Menon pick up and move each solar array from the mobile base to its final destination. Kutryk won't be riding the arm. Instead it will be Menon.

NASA astronauts perform a spacewalk to install an International Space Station Roll Out Solar Array with the assistance of the Canadarm2 robotic arm in 2022. (NASA)

The whole spacewalk is a demonstration of Canada's capabilities in space, said Mathieu Caron, director of CSA's astronaut office.

"I think what it means for Canada is an acknowledgement of the important role that we've been playing as part of this international collaboration," he said, noting spacewalks and capcom shifts are important roles that wouldn't be assigned to just anybody.

"There would be no way to accomplish this spacewalk without the help of Canadian robotics."

No walk in the park

"It's ridiculously dangerous, but we're well-prepared," said CSA astronaut David Saint-Jaques, who was the last Canadian to conduct a spacewalk in 2019.

"It is a shocking feat of teamwork. But it's an amazing experience to be basically your own little satellite of the Earth."

And he notes that the spacesuit is more than just something you wear.

"A spacesuit is not a piece of clothing. It's not like some, you know, winter suit," he said. "It's a miniature spacecraft in the shape of a human body that you have to fly."

CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk takes part in a spacewalk training session at Johnson Space Center in Houston. (NASA)

There was a close call with European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano during a 2013 spacewalk, when his helmet began filling with water. He was able to return to the safety of the ISS shortly after.

But Kutryk has trained long and hard for this spacewalk, and the crew prepared the suit checks over the past week.

While the hours' long spacewalk will no doubt be daunting, Kutryk will be able to see the world — the universe — as few on Earth have.

"A spacewalk is, for many astronauts, it's the peak of their career," Saint-Jacques said, noting that even thinking about his spacewalk sends shivers down his spine.

He also offered a message to Kutryk: "Josh, I know you're gonna do a good job. You've got this."

Saint-Jacques says Kutryk is a "stellar guy" who knows the procedure by heart, having practised it several times. He says the biggest challenge will be "to take a moment to look around, look at Earth, just let it all sink in."

World.title: N.S. premier doubles down on complaint to professor over AI data centre comments
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sibo Chen has been writing critically about the environmental impacts of resource extraction and AI growth. Houston says Chen was lacking in information, but speaking as an expert.

A staffer from Premier Tim Houston's office emailed a complaint last week to a Toronto Metropolitan University professor and included a CBC News reporter and the chair of the professor's department on the email.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is doubling down on a complaint his office sent to a university professor in Toronto who commented on a proposed artificial intelligence data centre.

A staffer from Houston's office sent the complaint last week, emailing a copy of the message to a CBC News reporter and the chair of the professor's department.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Premier Tim Houston said he's glad his communications adviser sent the critical email.

"I'm happy he sent that message to provide some additional information to somebody who was clearly lacking in information but yet speaking as an expert," Houston said.

The feedback came after Sibo Chen, an associate professor of communication at Toronto Metropolitan University, gave a media interview to CBC saying that public concerns about the data centre project over water usage and electricity rate hikes were valid.

William Burns, a communications adviser with the premier's office, said Chen's "slanted comments" were irresponsible and not backed by research on the local community.

Sibo Chen, an associate professor in the Toronto Metropolitan University's school of professional communication, is shown in this undated handout photo. (Sibo Chen/Handout/The Canadian Press)

"Nova Scotians deserve facts, not speculation presented in a way that creates unnecessary anxiety," said Burns' email, which Chen shared with The Canadian Press.

Members of the public and opposition parties in the province have expressed concerns about Everwind Fuels' proposed multi-billion dollar data centre, which would be leased to U.S. AI company Anthropic for 20 years.

A petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org had over 24,000 signatures as of Wednesday afternoon.

'I'm becoming the subject of my own study,' Chen says

Chen suggested that copying the department chair implies the government was trying to intimidate him.

"I actually study how scholars get harassed when they go to do knowledge mobilization ... I'm becoming the subject of my own study," he said.

Chen says he has studied environmental controversies in Canada for 10 years and this is the first time he has received a complaint from a premier's office.

Comments 'should send a chill down peoples' spines, Chender says

"I'm very critical about the oilsands, but I never received a complaint from the premier's office in Alberta," he said in a video interview Wednesday. His comments, he said, were about the general implications of AI data centre development and backed by peer-reviewed research.

The premier said he doesn't know how often his team reaches out to academics to criticize the comments they make to the media.

"I'm not sure how often we are communicating with people who are presenting in the media, but I hope it's a lot," Houston said.

"If somebody is presenting themselves as an expert and speaking definitively on something that they're wrong on, I think it's incumbent on all of us … [to] say there's some information you're missing," he added.

Nova Scotia NDP Leader Claudia Chender called Houston's comments disturbing.

"The comments that we heard just now from the premier, that he hopes that his staff are reaching out to people in the media regularly to correct them on their professional point of view, that should actually send a chill down peoples' spines," Chender told reporters Wednesday.

Data centre criticism

Chender said the premier's comments lead her to believe that his staff are "bullying" independent experts who criticize his government's projects.

The 18,600-square-metre data centre would draw 95 megawatts of electricity in its first phase and 420 megawatts after an expected expansion in mid-2028. Everwind says it will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure so that project will not increase power rates.

Everwind estimates that the facility will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in its first phase and 500,000 litres per day after the expansion is completed.

In his email to Chen, Burns said the government will not support a project that increases power rates to customers.

He also highlighted another CBC interview, where Lois Landry, the warden of Richmond County explained there are provisions in place to protect residents and limit the amount of water the data centre would draw from nearby Lake Landrie.

Burns also suggested that as a professor from a Toronto university, Chen could not understand the impact of data centre in Nova Scotia.

EverWind's data centre will be in Point Tupper, just outside Port Hawkesbury, N.S. (Taryn Grant/CBC)

Chen said the response from Burns suggests the government is sending the message that citizens don't need to be concerned about the project.

However, he said the province hasn't provided enough information to the public about the proposed data centre and he understands why Nova Scotians are worried.

Chen said local university professors may not feel comfortable expressing their concerns about the data centre after seeing the pushback he received from the Nova Scotia government.

"I think that's precisely why people don't want to comment on this," he said.

World.title: Higher mortgage costs set to depress already ‘bleak’ housing market
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Bank of Canada just hiked its trendsetting policy rate for the first time in three years, and that means mortgage rates are on the move for some Canadians.

The central bank raised its benchmark rate by a quarter of a point to 2.5 per cent on Wednesday. Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem says more hikes could be coming if inflation — which is largely linked to rising fuel costs — persists in the months ahead.

Canada's major banks are already responding by raising their prime interest rates in step with Wednesday's decision. All five of Canada's major banks raised their prime rates by a quarter point to 4.70 per cent. That's the rate they offer their most credit-worthy customers.

Variable rate mortgages will increase first, as they are directly linked to the issuing bank's prime rate.

Rates for new fixed mortgages are linked to the bond market. When a central bank raises interest rates, newly issued bonds offer higher payouts. As investors demand higher yields, lenders increase mortgage rates to maintain their profit margin.

"In a rising rate environment, choosing whether to go fixed or variable can be really challenging. Variables are lower, and provide flexibility, but future rate increases need to be budgeted for," Clay Jarvis, a mortgage expert at Ratehub.ca, stated in a press release after Wednesday's rate announcement.

"Fixed rates are elevated, but once you qualify your mortgage costs are set. That kind of stability can be worth paying a premium for," he added.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem speaks during a news conference on Wednesday in Ottawa, where the central bank's governing council decided to hike interest rates by a quarter per cent. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Speaking to reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday, Macklem acknowledged that rising interest rates could be uncomfortable for many Canadians and businesses.

"Look, we get it," he said. "It's not going to feel good immediately, but that's how you get inflation back down, and that will feel good for Canadians and Canadian businesses."

Variable rate mortgage holders will feel it most

The Bank of Canada's first rate hike since July 2023 will be immediately felt by variable rate mortgage holders. Toronto-based broker Marcus Tzaferis says that change could be significant.

On a $500,000 mortgage, a rate hike of 25 basis points would add about $70 per month on average to a holder's monthly payments. It might not sound like a lot, but, Tzaferis said, "to a consumer that's already stretched, these 25 basis point incremental increases are going to have an impact."

The central bank also signalled that more rate hikes could be on the horizon — and if the bank hiked rates by another 50 or 75 basis points, Tzaferis said, "you can see how that will affect people's monthly budgets."

Because rate hikes were expected, Tzaferis says he's already been fielding calls from Canadians trying to assess their options.

Barbara Best stands in the kitchen of her Toronto condo on Wednesday. She recently switched from a variable to a fixed rate mortgage and says the price increase is worth it for the peace of mind. (Laura MacNaughton/CBC)

Like Barbara Best. She's had a variable rate mortgage on her Toronto condo since 2022 — the same year the Bank of Canada began a long cycle of rate hikes — but recently renegotiated to a fixed rate months in advance of when her mortgage was up for renewal.

Because fixed rates are currently much higher than variable ones, that means she's paying a lot more each month, but Best says it's worth it.

"It was a jump in payment but it gives me that certainty. It gives me that peace of mind," Best said.

Tzaferis says "now is the time" to shop around for a fixed rate mortgage if holders want to get out of a variable one, or if their mortgage is coming up for renewal soon.

"The kind of most critical thing is for Canadians to start their renewal process early," Tzaferis said. Being aware of what the best rates on the market are and getting the conversation started with an adviser could help consumers make a choice that's right for them, according to Tzaferis.

Hike could pour more cold water on housing market

The hike also stands to worsen the already soft housing market.

Deputy governor Carolyn Rogers said Canada's housing market is already struggling, particularly in Ontario and British Columbia, and the rate increase will add to those pressures.

WATCH | Bank of Canada's housing outlook 'pretty subdued': Bank of Canada's housing outlook 'pretty subdued' — but not just because of rates, official says | Duration closed caption 1:23 Bank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers, speaking after the central bank hiked a key interest rate, said the organization's outlook for housing is 'pretty subdued' for a few reasons, including overall economic uncertainty.

Wednesday's rate hike shrinks the pool of eligible buyers, shifting power from sellers to those who can qualify for the financing needed to make a purchase. Home prices could dip lower.

Earlier this month, the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) cut its forecast for 2026 home sales for the third time this year.

Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Toronto-based real estate law platform Ownright, agrees that Wednesday's rate hike will add to the dour mood in the housing market.

"A rate hike likely locks us into year-over-year declines in housing activity for the rest of this year and into next, and I don't see things turning until there's a rate drop," he said in a statement after Wednesday's rate decision.

"The market was already as bleak as we've seen in a long time. The only saving grace is that it's hard to imagine it dropping much further."
