World.title: WATCH: Holness hits back at Beenie Man after Hurricane Melissa relief comments
World.content:
This file photo shows Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness addressing a special press briefing at Jamaica House on Tuesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

ST ELIZABETH, Jamaica — Against the backdrop of criticism from dancehall veteran Beenie Man over the Government’s hurricane relief efforts, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness on Wednesday took a swipe at the artiste.

He said over $300 million of the Government’s $3.8 billion allocation to the health sector post Hurricane Melissa was spent to rebuild the Black River Hospital.

“[With] all the dignitaries… who are here, I thought to myself the Minister [of Health Dr Christopher Tufton] neglected to invite Beenie Man, because then he would see first-hand how the Government has been spending on the recovery,” Holness said on Wednesday during the reopening of the Black River Hospital.

Beenie Man criticised the Holness administration’s handling of millions of dollars in donations it received to assist Jamaicans devastated by the storm.

World.title: Holness points to sabotage
World.content:
A woman walks past these Hurricane Melissa-wrecked buildings in Black River, St Elizabeth, last Friday. Today marks the first anniversary of the Category 5 storm that inflicted heavy damage on sections of the island. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that changes are coming to the public sector as there are individuals deliberately delaying or derailing government programmes. As such, he said the country should prepare for a shake-up in how the public service operates.

Holness said he was increasingly concerned that some public officers were obstructing the Government’s plans, warning that it could no longer be “business as usual” as Jamaica continues to recover from Hurricane Melissa.

“I don’t usually speak in extreme terms, and there are some subjects that it is better not to speak about them. But more and more I’m coming to the conclusion that there are persons in the public sector who are determined to, again, to use the very harsh word, sabotage. And I don’t say it lightly, they delay, derail policies, programmes, and initiatives of the Government. I see you, [and] I’m preparing the country to expect these changes, as it cannot be business as usual,” he said.

The prime minister was speaking at a special press briefing at Jamaica House on Tuesday during which he outlined plans to reduce government spending and improve the delivery of public services as the country faces the continuing cost of hurricane recovery.

While announcing further spending restrictions, Holness said the Government would also examine how ministries, departments, agencies, and public bodies operate, with the aim of removing duplication, improving coordination, and speeding up decisions.

He indicated that personnel changes would form part of that process, particularly where leadership, capacity, or performance needed to be strengthened.

Holness said the changes were necessary to ensure that the public service could respond more effectively to the country’s needs, especially as the Government tries to move recovery projects forward while controlling expenditure.

“Government must be reset and reorganised to meet the needs of our country. Government must be frugal and disciplined in its use of public resources, agile in its decisions, and responsive to the people it serves,” he said.

The warning comes as the Government intensifies its efforts to redirect funds towards hurricane recovery, including an additional $9.65 billion for the Restoration of Owner and Occupant Family Shelter (ROOFS) programme.

Holness said the Government could not meet every demand without making difficult choices, and that savings would have to be found in some areas to finance higher-priority needs.

“If I have to find $9.65 billion for the ROOFS programme, some things will have to be cut elsewhere,” he said.

Among the measures announced on Tuesday was an immediate pause on the purchase of motor vehicles for public officials until March 31, 2027, alongside a review of Government property leases and restrictions on hotel retreats and end-of-year celebrations.

The measures build on a moratorium on non-essential official overseas travel announced last week, scheduled to remain in effect until March 31, 2027.

Holness said greater financial restraint must be matched by improvements in how public institutions work, arguing that Government leaders and senior officials must make priorities rather than attempt to satisfy every demand at once.

He said the Government would be expected to make changes to its systems and procedures, while warning that officials who delay or derail its programmes could not expect the existing arrangements to continue unchanged.

World.title: Sagicor delivers double boost to Melissa-hit schools
World.content:
Little London High School grade 11 student Alyssa Hinds (second right) presents a plaque of appreciation to Christopher Zacca (second left) — president and CEO of Sagicor Group Jamaica Limited, and chairman, Sagicor Foundation Jamaica — in recognition of the organisation’s support. Sharing in the moment are Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director, National Education Trust; and Garfield James, principal, Little London High School.

SAGICOR Foundation Jamaica on Monday handed over restored facilities at two schools damaged by Hurricane Melissa last October and announced the allocation of an additional $30 million to support further school restoration.

The $30 million, the foundation explained, will build on the record $152 million raised through the 2026 Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run, which surpassed its $150-million fund-raising target.

“Last year, following the hurricane, Sagicor allocated $200 million to national recovery efforts, separate from and in addition to the funds raised through the Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run. I am pleased to share that $30 million of that allocation will support additional school projects, helping to fast-track restoration and return more children to safe, welcoming spaces,” Sagicor Group Jamaica President and CEO Christopher Zacca said during the handover at Little London High School in Westmoreland.

The foundation said that restoration works, at a combined value of approximately $50.4 million, have been completed at Little London High and Mayfield Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth.

Approximately $22.2 million was invested at Mayfield Primary and Infant School while approximately $28.2 million funded restoration and infrastructure works at Little London High School. The projects addressed priority sections damaged by the hurricane rather than complete school-wide refurbishments.

The two schools are among five selected to benefit from the 2026 run. Work at the remaining beneficiaries — Hopewell High, Green Pond High, and Salt Marsh Primary and Infant — is nearing completion, the foundation said in a news release.

The foundation also said it will work with the Ministry of Education and the National Education Trust (NET) to identify additional schools with the greatest need for restoration support.

On Monday, Zacca credited the public’s support for helping turn the fund-raising effort into completed improvements.

“The real value is a student focusing on a lesson instead of a leaking roof, a teacher working in a safe space, and parents sending their children to school with greater peace of mind. After the year these communities have endured, that stability means everything,” the release quoted Zacca.

“When we asked Jamaica to ‘Run for the West’, people answered the call. They registered, donated, volunteered and supported because they understood that getting our children back into safe and functional schools had to be part of the recovery of western Jamaica. Today, we can actually see what that generosity has accomplished. These improved spaces mean students and teachers can focus again on what matters most — teaching, learning and building a better future,” Zacca added.

Sagicor Foundation board member Brigette Azan said restoring schools is ultimately about protecting opportunity for Jamaica’s children.

“Education remains one of the greatest tools we have for creating opportunity. Not every child starts life with the same advantages or resources, but every child deserves the opportunity to learn, discover their talents, and fulfil their potential. That is why getting our students back into safe, welcoming schools matters so much,” Azan said.

Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director of NET, said the completion of the projects demonstrates what can be achieved through purposeful partnerships centred on students and their education.

“When we first began this process, the priority was clear: identify the schools where the need was greatest and help get our children back into safe spaces where they could learn and thrive. NET was pleased to work with the Sagicor Foundation from those early stages, supporting the process of identifying the beneficiary schools and the areas requiring attention. Seeing the work completed at Mayfield Primary and Infant School and Little London High School is especially meaningful because, ultimately, this is about ensuring that the disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa does not become a lasting barrier to our children’s education,” Harris Ghartey said.

World.title: Kranium: A ‘glitch in the dancehall matrix’
World.content:
Kranium recently returned to New York for a performance at Sony Hall after a four-year absence.

“I am a glitch in the matrix.”

For Kranium, the statement is more than a catchphrase. It is his unapologetic assessment of a career that has challenged conventional thoughts about what it takes to establish oneself in dancehall, particularly the long-held assumption that an artiste must be physically based in Jamaica to remain connected to the culture and build a successful career.

Born in Jamaica, but based in New York, USA, for much of his professional journey, the Nobody Has to Know hitmaker has established an international presence while operating outside the island’s borders.

And while he is not seeking recognition for changing the game, he believes the evidence of his impact is already there.

“I don’t just feel that way; I know it for a fact,” Kranium told the Jamaica Observer when asked whether he considers himself among the artistes who helped change perceptions about where a dancehall career can be built.

“The facts and the history are there: I took dancehall music and cemented myself as a household name while living outside Jamaica. Unfortunately for those who withhold that information it is already written: Kranium is a glitch in the matrix,” he added.

It is a confident position, but one Kranium believes his body of work supports. Attributing his success to more than just overcoming geographical barriers, the entertainer shared that he has had to tap into his creativity while ensuring he remained authentically himself.

“I didn’t feel like I had to work twice as hard. What I had to do was create authentic, quality music and be real with myself,” he said.

That commitment to authenticity has helped Kranium to cultivate a catalogue that includes songs that have received gold and platinum certifications across three major markets.

For him, those milestones are both a measure of achievement and an incentive to keep pushing.

“Seeing them gives me more motivation to take things to the highest level at my own pace,” he said. “Most importantly, seeing them on my wall reminds me that I am a very talented artiste. It gives me all the validation I need.”

He also sees room for Jamaican music to compete more forcefully on the international stage, provided the ambition extends beyond simply being successful within the genre.

“Yes, I think we can compete at the highest level once we understand that we need to be the best in the school, not just the class,” he said, indicating that geography is not the defining factor in whether a song travels. He explained that the quality of the music and the way it is introduced to audiences matter more than an artiste’s physical location.

“I know how to make authentic music. Even if I were under a rock, if the song is a hit, it will take off with the right juggling,” he said. “I think you can still stay connected as long as you remain true to the culture and understand the importance of paying attention to the current state of dancehall.”

His comments take on added significance against the backdrop of his recent return to New York for a performance after a four-year absence.

The city has played a significant role in his development as an artiste, making the occasion more than another date on an international schedule. The timing also coincided with the anniversary of his first album, We Can, achieving gold certification, creating what he described as the right moment to reconnect with the market.

“Now was the right time to return because everything aligned — the anniversary of my first album, We Can, going gold and, most importantly, the fact that I hadn’t done a show there in four years,” he said.

For Kranium, the performance felt like a homecoming, and he approached it with the intention of making the night memorable for the audience. From the energy of the show to his choices of fellow performers, he was deliberate about how the experience unfolded.

“It felt like a homecoming. That’s why I worked so hard to make sure the show stayed active all night, right down to who I wanted to share the stage with,” he said.

The return also signals that he intends to maintain that connection without over-saturating the market. While he recognises the value of appearing regularly before an audience, he is mindful of the balance between being present and overdoing it.

“There’s a fine line between being in the market frequently and overdoing it. But, for sure, it won’t take that long for me to hold another event there,” he said.

World.title: Christine Lagarde quittera ses fonctions de présidente de la BCE en février
World.content:
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde poses as she leaves a sideline event during the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok on October 14, 2026. | Anthony Wallace/AFP via Getty Images

Cette décision permet au président français Emmanuel Macron d’avoir son mot à dire dans le choix de son successeur avant les élections de l’année prochaine.

FRANCFORT — Christine Lagarde a annoncé jeudi qu'elle quitterait ses fonctions de présidente de la Banque centrale européenne le 7 février, mettant ainsi fin à des mois de spéculations sur son avenir et laissant vacant le poste à la tête de l'une des institutions les plus puissantes d'Europe.

La BCE a confirmé son départ dans un communiqué, mais n'a donné aucun détail dans l'immédiat sur ses projets après son départ.

Cette annonce ouvre la voie à un accord global entre les capitales de l’UE concernant les nominations au sein du directoire de la BCE, composé de six membres.

World.title: Christine Lagarde to step down as ECB president in February
World.content:
This article is also available in: French

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde poses as she leaves a sideline event during the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok on October 14, 2026. | Anthony Wallace/AFP via Getty Images

The moves gives French leader Emmanuel Macron a say in choosing her successor before the election next year.

FRANKFURT — Christine Lagarde said she will step down as president of the European Central Bank on Feb. 7, ending months of speculation about her future and creating a vacancy at the top of one of Europe’s most powerful institutions.

"It has been a source of great pride to serve this institution," Lagarde said on Thursday morning. "I thank all of those who have supported me on this journey over the past seven years."

The ECB gave no immediate details about her plans after leaving.

World.title: Quebec premier boycotts Mark Carney’s EU summit
World.content:
In the letter, St-Pierre Plamondon says Ottawa has “decided to sideline Quebec” from the talks. He says this leaves his government with “neither a chair at the negotiating table nor the opportunity to speak,” even though the summit is on Quebec soil.

Under Canada’s federal system, he argued, the provinces implement international agreements that fall within their powers. Without Quebec’s consent, a deal that runs against its interests “will simply not be implemented,” he wrote. He also accused Ottawa of withholding “critical information” on the negotiations.

He offered to meet European leaders “in the near future, in a more opportune context.” He will send Quebec’s chief diplomat, Pascal Paradis, to the summit in his place.

Carney said Wednesday his office had offered the premier the honor of welcoming the Commission president to Montreal, and a seat at the head table. “I hope he will reconsider,” he said. On Tuesday, the prime minister had accused St-Pierre Plamondon of choosing to “leave an empty chair again.”

The row has soured the upbeat mood around the summit, which Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have billed as a milestone. Leaders will launch an “Alliance for the Future,” a framework for shared prosperity and economic security.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s letter says many of its topics fall under Quebec’s responsibility, including health, education and natural resources.

World.title: UK social media ban likely to require photo ID checks
World.content:
It will inform regulations to implement the ban which ministers have said they aim to introduce to parliament this year.

Three of the methods identified by Ofcom — photo ID matching, using a digital ID service, or banking-based checks — require a passport or driving license at some stage, while the fourth, facial age estimation, may in some cases need to be followed by a supplementary check using one of the other methods because of a high margin of error at younger ages.

“This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right,” Ofcom CEO Melanie Dawes said.

While the age checks would involve processing of personal data, “available methods can be delivered in a way that protects users’ privacy and complies with data protection law,” Ofcom said.

It also said social media platforms should take steps to mitigate circumvention, like enabling users to report suspected underage accounts, and using age inference technology to spot activity from users who may be underage.

The regulator said it will consult on further guidance for platforms once regulations to implement the social media ban are laid.

World.title: In the Middle East, the next front line is the narrative
World.content:
We live in an era where wars are fought not just on battlefields, but also on our screens, in our minds and through the narratives we are led to believe. Narratives are influencing perception while missiles destroy infrastructure. What happens when the war for truth becomes more dangerous than the actual battle itself? Who’s controlling the narrative?

Najla Al Midfa, researcher, TRENDS Research & Advisory

When wars end, the fighting over what they meant begins: who won, who was to blame and who can be trusted to keep the peace. These questions are settled less on the battlefield than on screens, in feeds and in group chats. For a Middle East emerging from the war that began on February 28, that contest may decide whether any new security order holds.

The region is now asking what comes after deterrence. That question brought policymakers, military leaders and researchers from the United States, Europe, Asia and the Gulf to the TRENDS 6th Annual Conference, held in Abu Dhabi and organized by TRENDS Global, in collaboration with its global offices. The answer cannot be measured only in missiles and alliances. Information resilience should be treated as security infrastructure, planned and funded like air defense, not managed as public relations.

What happens when the war for truth becomes more dangerous than the actual battle itself?

The struggle over perception can now matter as much as events on the ground. That is no longer hyperbole. In any crisis today, governments, media outlets, political movements and non-state groups compete in real time to define what is happening. Disinformation, coordinated propaganda and now content generated by artificial intelligence (AI) mean a false account can reach millions before an official one is drafted.

As former BBC correspondent Karen Allen put it at the conference, “Now in an instant, I’m able to influence millions of people,” and algorithm manipulation is what we are increasingly seeing.

This year’s war showed how real that is. Within days of the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, an AI-generated video of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa on fire, with crowds fleeing, was viewed tens of millions of times, according to BBC Verify. Fabricated images of damaged U.S. facilities in the Gulf spread just as fast, some posted by Iranian state-linked outlets. UAE Minister of State Noura Al Kaabi later described the attacks on the country as coming “from the sky and behind our screens.” Her government’s answer was to treat “fake news and misinformation as a security threat.”

A more damaging false story was not a single video. It was the idea that the Gulf was a party to the war. The UAE did not want this war and said so. On March 3, Minister of State Reem Al Hashimy said the UAE did not “seek to expand the circle of confrontation,” that it had “repeatedly confirmed” its territory could not be used for any military operation against Iran, and that “returning to the negotiating table is the only rational way forward.” The attacks continued anyway. Reuters reported, citing UAE defense figures, that 186 ballistic missiles and 812 drones were fired at the country in the first days of the conflict.

Information resilience should be treated as security infrastructure, planned and funded like air defense, not managed as public relations.

Tehran sought to blur that record, framing strikes on Gulf cities as retaliation against American aggression. Its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, told NBC News that Iran had “not attacked our neighbors,” only “American bases,” and called the hotels hit in Dubai “collateral damage.” Countering that narrative does not require propaganda of our own. It requires putting the record in front of the world quickly and repeatedly: the UAE’s public calls for restraint before the war, its refusal to let its territory be used against Iran, and the hundreds of missiles and drones fired at it, most of which it shot down. Facts published fast, through verified channels, in Arabic, English and Farsi, are harder to bury than corrections issued too late.

Even after a war ends, the threats do not disappear; they simply take different forms. Ceasefires and reconstruction depend on public trust. If populations come to believe that the peace is a betrayal, or that a neighbor cannot be trusted, no deterrence framework or security pact will survive contact with domestic politics. Spoilers understand this. Their cheapest weapon is a story.

Seen from the Gulf, the lesson of recent years is that speed and credibility beat silence. Crisis communication is not a side function of security. When official channels inform the public quickly, consistently and honestly, rumors have less room to grow. When they hesitate, someone else fills the gap.

None of this is simple. Governments everywhere are still working out where countering disinformation ends and controlling speech begins, and that debate should stay open. But the common ground is wider than it looks: a society cannot be secure if it cannot tell what is true.

The harder test comes now. After a war, influence campaigns shift from shock to slow erosion: relitigating who was to blame, questioning whether Gulf governments can protect their people, and setting neighbors and communities against each other. Young connected audiences are the main target. They are also the best defense.

Protecting our societies from that influence does not mean closing them. It means official channels fast and credible enough that people turn to them first. It means platforms held to clear rules on labeling AI-generated conflict content, as X began to do in March. And it means a generation of young Emiratis and Gulf citizens equipped to verify what they see and able to tell the region’s story themselves rather than leaving it to others.

The harder test comes now. After a war, influence campaigns shift from shock to slow erosion.

This is not only a Gulf problem. The campaigns aimed at audiences in the Gulf also shape how Washington and Brussels understand the region. The UAE and its partners already work closely on defense and intelligence. Detecting and exposing cross-border influence operations belongs on that shared agenda as a joint effort between governments, platforms and researchers.

Diplomacy, investment, and deterrence will rebuild the region’s security. Whether that security holds will depend on something harder to measure: what people across the region believe about each other, and about who protects them. For the UAE, winning that argument with facts is not public relations. It is part of keeping the country safe.

Najla Al Midfa is an Emirati researcher at TRENDS Research & Advisory, a company under TRENDS Group. Her research focuses on geopolitics, international relations, economic diplomacy and regional security, with a particular interest in the UAE’s foreign policy and strategic partnerships. She holds a master’s degree in Global Affairs and Diplomatic Leadership from the Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy, where her thesis examined the UAE’s economic diplomacy through its Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement strategy.

World.title: Don’t turn a methane pause into a retreat
World.content:
Sixty investors, representing over €9.5 trillion in assets under management, have called for the EU Methane Regulation to be maintained and implemented as adopted. That statement pre-dated the Commission’s proposed one-year delay. Its central concern, however, is more relevant now: investors need a stable framework against which companies can plan, manage risk and allocate capital with confidence.

The regulation was designed with phased implementation. It gave companies, importers and national authorities time to prepare for stronger measurement, reporting and verification of methane emissions. It has helped bring methane from the margins into boardroom discussions, where it belongs.

Why methane matters to investors

For investors, methane performance can offer a useful view of how a company is run. It is an indicator of operational discipline, process safety and the quality of management oversight. By setting requirements for measurement, reporting and verification, the regulation can also improve the availability, consistency and reliability of methane data. That gives investors a stronger basis to compare companies and assess whether they are managing risks that could affect long-term value. Maintaining the regulation’s core provisions and avoiding any further delay would protect the progress already under way.

The EU’s position as a major oil and gas importer gives the Methane Regulation particular weight. Clear import requirements can improve the quality and comparability of emissions information across global supply chains. They can help create a more level playing field for companies supplying the European market, rather than allowing weak data or weaker controls to become a commercial advantage.

The choice is not between competitiveness, affordability and effective methane management. Europe can support all three.

This matters for competitiveness as well as climate-related financial risk. Energy affordability is a legitimate concern, particularly for businesses and households facing continued market volatility. But well-designed, practical rules can reward operational excellence, support informed investment decisions and give companies a clearer basis on which to plan, while implementation can be managed in ways that preserve market flexibility and limit unnecessary costs for consumers.

World.title: Spain: cranes clear twisted train wreckage as rescuers work through the night
World.content:
Personnel from Spain's Military Emergency Unit (UME) remained at the scene, working among derailed carriages and scattered debris while heavy cranes lifted sections of wreckage from the tracks. Images released on Thursday show emergency workers examining the damaged trains and coordinating operations at the crash site in the Castilla-La Mancha region.

 

The disaster occurred when a high-speed service operated by state-owned Renfe struck the rear of a stationary train belonging to private operator Iryo. The collision left carriages derailed and badly damaged, with rescue teams continuing their work into the following day.

Meanwhile, authorities established a temporary morgue at the Institute of Forensic Medicine in Toledo to identify those killed in the disaster. Military vehicles and police patrols were stationed outside the facility as forensic identification procedures got under way.

The two operations continued in parallel on Thursday, with emergency teams clearing the wreckage near Urda while forensic specialists worked to establish the identities of the victims. The crash is Spain's second major deadly railway accident of 2026, following a collision in January that killed 45 people.

World.title: ECB President Christine Lagarde to step down next February, months before her mandate ends
World.content:
Christine Lagarde will step down as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) on 7 February 2027, the bank announced on Thursday, about nine months before her eight-year term was due to end.

 

The announcement came as the ECB prepared to unveil its latest interest rate decision.

Lagarde informed the ECB’s Governing Council, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, and European Council President António Costa of her decision, the bank said in a statement.

The ECB gave no reason for her departure.

“The Governing Council thanked President Lagarde warmly and gave her a long standing ovation,” the statement said.

European Council President António Costa has thanked Lagarde for her service, praising her “dedication as President of the European Central Bank since November 2019”.

“To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay,” Costa said.

Her successor will be appointed by the European Council, which brings together EU leaders.

Under EU rules, the president is appointed by a qualified majority vote, following a recommendation from EU finance ministers and consultations with the European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council.

Lagarde, a former French finance minister and managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), took office in November 2019. Speculation about an early departure had been building for months.

The ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday. Lagarde is due to face reporters after the decision.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated

World.title: In Pompeii, a woman's wardrobe resurfaces with beauty items and jewels
World.content:
The wardrobe of a woman from ancient Pompeii has come to light again. Thanks to the work of archaeologists it has been possible to recover the interior of a cabinet that held everyday items in house IX 11, 7, or the house of Cornelius Maximus, in the central area of the city buried by Vesuvius.

 

Looking at these objects, it is almost as if we can conjure up the life of a woman of Pompeii before the site was destroyed in AD 79. Among the finds are make-up tools (tweezers, a spatula for mixing pigments), a glass balsamarium, a perfume burner to fill the home with pleasant fragrances, a bronze lamp, alongside lead weights, probably used for a commercial activity and kept in a small wooden box of which only faint traces remain.

Marble pilaster - Pompeii Archaeological Park Parco Archeologico di Pompei

What was in the Pompeian woman's wardrobe

Vases and pots in bronze, glass and ceramic were also found: everyday household objects, but perhaps also heavy with memories, as in the case of an elegant little jug decorated with pine-scale motifs. There is also a necklace composed of at least twenty-four miniature objects in faïence, bone, glass paste and rock crystal, all pierced for suspension and representing deities (Bes and Mercury can be identified), feet and hands, pine cones and bunches of grapes.

Objects found in the wardrobe - Pompeii Archaeological Park Parco Archeologico di Pompei

According to experts, such necklaces were sometimes regarded as "magical" objects used in spells and potions; in reality they are what are known as crepundia, literally 'rattles': necklaces with amulets that were given to children to protect them, but also so that they could be heard when they moved.

It was not unusual for adults to keep them too, often in small boxes or, as in this case, in cloth bags inside wardrobes, apparently as keepsakes of a childhood of which little else remained. The Roman world was characterised by a high degree of geographic mobility at all levels, from slaves to wealthy merchants, so that many people found themselves living far from relatives and parents and from the places of their childhood.

The small treasure hidden in the wardrobe

Another secret kept in the wardrobe unearthed in the excavation is a small hoard of coins: there are 38 of them, all bronze, preserved in a "cistella", a small container made of plant material using basketry techniques, the remains of which were analysed after being recovered during the dig. The presence of the coins in particular suggests that the owner or owners did not have time to recover the objects of value, whether economic or emotional.

Coins found in the wardrobe - Pompeii Archaeological Park Parco Archeologico di Pompei

If they were in the city at the time of the catastrophe, they will have tried to flee. If they managed to escape, they would not have returned to dig under the floors for their possessions, unlike others whose efforts have left traces revealed by recent excavations. But perhaps they did not succeed and may be among those who, as the historian Tacitus recalls, died without heirs and whose property would have been used for the refounding of Pompeii, which ultimately never took place. These are questions destined to remain open.

The human dimension of Pompeii's past pieced back together

"Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art; it is also somewhere where the most ordinary objects restore the human dimension of the past. The value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces of a life: personal habits, work, memories," says the director of the Archaeological Park, Gabriel Zuchtriegel.

"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of the person who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their everyday life," the director adds.

Objects found in the wardrobe - Parco Archeologico di Pompei

What we know about the House of Cornelius Maximus

The excavation has helped clarify some aspects of the house in which the wardrobe was found. The facade of the dwelling, tentatively attributed to a figure named Cornelius Maximus on the basis of inscriptions now no longer visible, had already been excavated in 1912. Only now, however, has part of the rooms behind it been investigated, as part of the major restoration and accessibility project for the adjacent Insula dei Casti Amanti.

Although our knowledge of the house remains partial, some highly interesting data have emerged: on the one hand, the refined Fourth Style wall paintings in the room with the wardrobe, attributable to the workshop on Via di Castricio, indicate a certain standard of living, in line with the central position of the house, which overlooks one of the main arteries of the ancient city.

On the other hand, at the time of the eruption various works were nevertheless in progress that must have affected liveability considerably. Added to this is the discovery of at least two mouse skeletons, found inside an amphora on a mezzanine. According to analyses carried out in the park's laboratory, they probably belonged to the species Apodemus sylvaticus, also known as the "wood mouse".

Vases and urns - Pompeii Archaeological Park Parco Archeologico di Pompei

Mice of this kind normally live in natural environments and gardens, from where they often invade attics and storage areas in human dwellings in search of food. The two specimens found at Pompeii were not fully mature, as indicated by the degree of development of their skeletons (117 tiny fragments). The discovery adds to evidence of the presence of rodents in other Vesuvian contexts, such as the service quarters of the suburban villa at Civita Giuliana or the sewers of Herculaneum, and offers the image of an urban society that also had to contend with unwelcome guests.

World.title: US measles surge reminds of Europe’s vaccination gaps
World.content:
The United States is at risk of losing its measles-free status as cases surge, raising fresh concerns about the vulnerability of European communities where vaccination coverage remains below the level needed to prevent sustained transmission.

 

More than 4,500 cases have been reported in the US this year — roughly twice the total reported last year. A forecast published in JAMA suggests that measles could become endemic again in the US if vaccination rates fail to improve, potentially resulting in 851,300 cases, more than 170,000 hospitalisations and 2,550 deaths over 25 years.

The outbreak across the Atlantic could also signal a wider risk, Kitty Mohan, vice-president of the Standing Committee of European Doctors (CPME) and its rapporteur on vaccination, told Euronews.

“Due to international travel routes and the ease and speed at which people move across borders, combined the infectiousness of measles before the rash starts, people can travel quite far whilst infectious and so the disease can spread rapidly,” Mohan said.

Measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases. People can transmit the virus for around four days before the characteristic rash appears, meaning they may travel across borders before realising they are ill.

“15 mins face to face with someone who is infectious will mean you are likely to get measles,” Mohan said.

The US is not the only country where measles continues to circulate. The biggest outbreaks currently are in Bangladesh, with cases surpassing 65,430, Indonesia with 46,578 and Guatemala with 31,222 cases.

“Whether an imported case leads to further transmission in Europe depends primarily on immunity levels in the affected community in Europe and whether the virus reaches groups with low vaccination coverage,” the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews.

Vaccination coverage was 92% for the first dose and 88% for the second dose — a “strong population protection,” ECDC said.

But that remains below the recommended 95% two-dose coverage needed at national and local levels to prevent sustained transmission and achieve measles elimination. National averages can also conceal areas or communities with lower vaccination coverage.

“Most measles cases occur in unvaccinated people,” the ECDC said, recommending that countries close immunity gaps, ensure both vaccine doses are administered on time, offer catch-up vaccination to eligible adolescents and adults, and maintain strong surveillance and outbreak-response systems.

The consequences extend beyond those who can choose to get vaccinated. Infants who are too young to receive the vaccine, as well as people who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons or whose immune systems cannot mount an adequate response, depend on high levels of immunity in the wider population.

“Herd immunity or maintaining vaccination rates above a threshold would protect these groups - so lower rates make them more susceptible to disease,” Mohan said.

Pockets of low coverage

The problem is not confined to countries with low national vaccination rates. Clusters of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people can emerge within otherwise well-protected populations, creating local conditions in which outbreaks can take hold.

Coverage gaps can reflect a range of factors, including difficulties accessing vaccination services, limited information or awareness, and concerns about vaccines.

“There are traditional risk groups - such as traveller communities and some religious groups who historically have been reluctant to vaccinate,” said Mohan.

However, ECDC underlined that “the presence of a group of unvaccinated people does not automatically mean that a large outbreak will spread across the wider population,” using the Urkult festival in northern Sweden as an example. The outbreak at the festival occurred between 30 July and 2 August this year, mainly affecting unvaccinated children and adolescents. It involved 28 cases, including 12 secondary cases, but did not lead to sustained transmission in the wider population.

"The fact that there were relatively few secondary cases among those exposed at the festival is due to the high level of immunity within the population, a result of strong participation in the childhood vaccination program," said Johanna Rubin, Acting Head of the Vaccination Unit at Sweden’s public health agency.

“This once again highlights the importance of high community-level protection,” ECDC said.

For now, the risk for Europeans remains the same, ECDC said, as per its latest assessment, with the overall risk set as moderate for infants under 12 months, children aged one to five and immunocompromised people. For older unvaccinated children and adults, the risk is estimated to range from low to moderate. People with immunity from vaccination or previous infection are considered to have a low risk of measles.

ECDC surveillance data indicate fewer reported measles cases in 2026 than in 2025, although 2026 figures remain preliminary and should be interpreted with caution.

Measles is endemic in twelve European countries: Bosnia and Herzegovina, France, Georgia, Germany, Italy, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Poland, Romania, Russia, Türkiye, and Ukraine.

Romania reported most of the cases, with numbers reaching 30,692 in 2024, up from 3,371 in 2023.

Six European countries: Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan have re-established endemic measles transmission based on the number of cases in 2024 earlier this year.

World.title: What worker guarantees do unions and lawmakers demand to unblock EU Inc?
World.content:
The EU’s plan for a single, digital company form is stuck on a question that has split lawmakers for weeks. Whose workers’ rights apply when a company incorporates in one country but employs people in another?

 

The Council adopted its negotiating position on 23 October. In Parliament, the Legal Affairs Committee’s votes on EU Inc. were cancelled twice this month because political groups could not agree on employee participation. A new committee vote is scheduled for 5 November, with a plenary vote set for 12 November.

The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) argues that the Commission’s reassurance that employment law is unaffected only answers part of the problem.

Individual rights versus collective rights

Labour lawyers broadly accept that ordinary employment rights survive. Under EU conflict-of-law rules, choosing another country’s law generally cannot strip a worker of the mandatory protections of the country where they habitually work.

The gap, unions say, is in rights tied to the company itself, especially board-level worker representation. Under the Commission’s proposal, participation rights for an EU Inc. follow its registered office. Because the company can register in one country without locating its headquarters or workforce there, founders could effectively choose the participation regime when they incorporate.

“We do see that risk,” ETUC Deputy General Secretary Isabelle Schömann told Euronews, pointing to evidence from existing European companies. She says the practice is established: “We already have evidence that businesses are looking for a letterbox company.”

She cited data from the European Trade Union Institute showing that 63% of existing European Companies (SEs) are empty “shelf” entities.

What unions want

ETUC wants the safeguards written into binding articles rather than recitals, which guide interpretation but are not enforceable. Its main demands are:

A workplace rule. Collective and participation rights should apply where employees habitually work. “European legislation is not there to downgrade existing protection for workers,” Schömann said.

Non-regression. Where several national regimes apply, the highest level of participation should prevail.

Workforce aggregation. Employees in branches, subsidiaries and controlled group companies should count towards national co-determination thresholds, so companies cannot split their headcount to stay below them.

An anti-circumvention clause. This would cover artificial structures, not just “wholly artificial” arrangements.

Data and enforcement. Labour inspectors and unions would get access to workforce data. Workers and unions could sue in the country of work, and serious abuse could lead to loss of EU Inc. status.

The loopholes unions see

The Council’s mandate adds an optional safeguard for branches. Host countries with participation rules can opt in. A foreign company whose branch workforce passes their threshold must either create a local subsidiary or grant equivalent rights. Unions say this falls short because it is optional, covers branches rather than every group structure, and could keep workers away from the parent board.

Its anti-abuse provision, allowing national authorities to act against “wholly artificial” arrangements, is case-by-case and reactive. A firm with some genuine activity in its country of registration might escape it even if it chose that country partly to avoid co-determination.

Other concerns include the speed of the process. Schömann said “48 hours is too short to allow for the preventive checks that any business has to undertake,” and warned that fast closures could leave workers unable to trace unpaid wages and social contributions.

Stock options are the other flashpoint. ETUC says they must not substitute for pay: “you can’t pay your electricity bill with it,” Schömann said. “If you want to retain talent, you have to pay those talents.” Parliament’s draft would make option plans voluntary and bar them from replacing wages or cutting social-security contributions.

Startups: ‘getting it right’

Startup groups reject the idea that they want to weaken labour protection. Simon Schaefer, CEO of the startup network Factory, signed a 15 October letter warning EU leaders that negotiations were hollowing out the proposal. His priority is preserving free choice of administrative headquarters, which he sees as what makes EU Inc. a true alternative to Delaware.

On fraud, he was direct. “We agree with every try and effort to prevent fraud,” he said. “We’re in unison with the trade unions that we do not want to abuse workers’ rights,” he added.

He argues that targeted rules, such as barring stock options from pushing pay below the minimum wage, are better than excluding entire industries. Schaefer said he is prepared to see the file delayed if it worsens. “For us, getting it right is almost more important right now than the actual speed,” he said.

What's next?

The sticking point is the fallback if management and workers cannot agree on participation. Social Democrats and Greens treat a protective default as a red line, while Renew and business-friendly lawmakers object to exporting one country’s co-determination model across borders. A compromise reported in Parliament would require companies to create a local subsidiary once they pass a host-country threshold, but that could leave the parent board untouched. If the 5 November vote goes ahead, it will show if the gap can be bridged.

World.title: More refineries 'spread across the globe' needed to avoid disruptions during wars, says expert
World.content:
Energy expert and analyst Osama Rizvi believes high fuel prices have become a “structural feature” of the market, warning that it could take months for supplies to recover and prices to fall.

 

The European Commission is treating the loss of refining capacity as a vulnerability that Europe can no longer afford to ignore.

Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen warned that the prolonged war in the Middle East should serve as a "wake-up call". The EU should ensure that there is an adequate refining capacity at home, he said. Rizvi thinks the world needs a "refinery revolution" and have more refineries spread "across the globe" so they don't become "vulnerable" during geopolitical crisis.

World.title: Putin calls Elon Musk a 'genius' as Russia builds its own Starlink rival
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has praised US tech billionaire Elon Musk as a “genius” for deploying thousands of satellites into orbit, as Moscow works to develop its own satellite internet network.

 

During an exhibition in Moscow on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit, Putin was told that Musk had more than 5,000 satellites in orbit.

“Elon Musk is a genius, truly a genius,” Putin said, adding that Russia was proud to have started developing its own system.

Putin also said Moscow was in close contact with American partners, including Musk, despite political tensions. “Because in orbit, it is very important not to get in each other's way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” he said.

Russia is seeking to build its own alternative to Starlink, Musk’s satellite internet service.

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy, and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere, any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora. Special thanks to Elisa Schouten for her contribution.

Skip next section 8-year-old girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German zoo

10/29/2026 October 29, 2026 8-year-old girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German zoo

The park has both grey and arctic, or polar, wolves Image: STAR-MEDIA/IMAGO

An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by a wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.

The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.

Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.

Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.

The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.

The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.

"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.

The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.

The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.

Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.

The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.

"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.

The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.

A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year, in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.

World.title: European Central Bank (ECB) head Christine Lagarde to step down in February, before her term ends
World.content:
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde is to resign nine months ahead of the end of her 8-year term. European Council President Antonio Costa has said the process to find a successor is underway.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the European Central Bank for seven years, has announced that she is stepping down prematurely from the position.

"European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the president of the European Council Antonio Costa that she will step down from her position on 7 February 2027," the ECB said in a statement.

European Council President Antonio Costa said a process to find her successor would start immediately.

The announcement comes ahead of a key meeting of the bank this week that is likely to focus on France's deteriorating public finances.

No reason has so far been given for Lagarde's premature departure, but there has been speculation that she would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose her successor before French elections that could see a far-right victory and influence the choice.

This is a developing story. More to follow.

World.title: Ship reported on fire off Oman as Iran escalation fears mount
World.content:
A ship in the Strait of Hormuz is reported to be on fire, a British maritime agency says. Iran has meanwhile said it has shot down another US drone as military tensions with Washington continue.

A ship on fire has been reported in the Strait of Hormuz, British maritime agency UKMTO said on Thursday.

The agency, which is run by the British Royal Navy, did not give details on the cause of the blaze or any casualties.

Iran has, however, recently stepped up its attacks on ships that it sees as using the waterway without proper authorization.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting sea mines while using an "unauthorized" route, but it is not known if the case reported to the UKMTO is one of them.

This comes as Iran has reported shooting down another US drone east of the waterway as fears grow of a new escalation in the US-Iran war.

Iran steps up attacks in Strait of Hormuz

The UKMTO said the captain of another ship had reported the blaze onboard a vessel spotted 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) north of the town of Khasab in Oman, which is located just off the strait.

The status of ⁠the ​crew is ​unknown, and so far ​no information has emerged pertaining to ⁠damage or environmental ⁠impact.

Since the Middle East war was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Tehran has sought to control the strait, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, and has attacked ships it considers to be unauthorized users of the waterway.

Oil exports through the waterway fell again last week, according to shipping data provider Kpler.

Attacks on ships in the strait are at the highest level since the war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where the burning ship was reportedly sighted.

The Strait of Hormuz is a vital chokepoint for oil and gas transport Image: REUTERS

US drone downed

The reported ship fire comes as Iran says its forces have downed a drone near the strait, with the Tasnim news agency citing the IRGC as saying a new, advanced air defense system was used.

The report said that Iran's armed forces have destroyed 14 drones of this type and more than 50 MQ-9 Reaper drones since the war broke out.

The claims have not been independently verified, though the US Congressional Research Service says dozens of US aircraft and drones have been reported lost or damaged since the war began.

The MQ-1 Predator can be used both for surveillance and attack Image: Col. Leslie Pratt/epa/picture alliance

Fears of new US strikes

The latest incidents come as US President Donald Trump is widely seen to be considering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.

Last week, Trump said, "we may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war. He did not, however, give any timeframe.

A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are currently heading to the region.

As reports of a possible renewed escalation swirl, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly nonetheless fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia.

If confirmed, the ouster would be the latest in a series of such high-level departures under the Trump administration, with Sylvia's predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee being forced to retire last October.

According to a report in The Atlantic, no reason was given for Sylvia's departure and no replacement has been named.

World.title: Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches
World.content:
Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis.

"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.

"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

Vincent Kompany's illness has seen a large amount of support from the coaching community Image: Markus Ulmer/Ulmer/Teamfoto/IMAGO

The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.

"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.

"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."

Eberl, though, shut down the suggestion that this was related to pressure or stress.

"It's an illness. Any one of us can get it. It has nothing to do with the pressure we face in the Bundesliga," Eberl said.

Why do coaches push themselves so hard?

Nevertheless, with Kompany admitting he hadn't listened to his body and his assistant coach Aaron Danks saying that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge", it is clear that the Belgian had been working very hard of late.

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face in elite sport.

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that," coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."

Coaches in need of more support

It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?

"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.

"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.

"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

Frank Wormuth (left) also had moments where he realized football had taken over Image: Pro Shots/IMAGO

A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.

"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.

"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."

German football identity: Frank Wormuth To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.

"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.

"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."

Will change come to coaching?

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.

"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.

"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.

World.title: India news: 'Cockroaches' back Gandhi's rally against election chief
World.content:
10/29/2026 October 29, 2026 Opposition bloc promises 'public impeachment' process against election chief

Several leaders from India's opposition alliance, the INDIA bloc, have finalized the "public impeachment" proceedings they intend to carry out against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the controversial revision of voter lists.

They did this in a meeting on Thursday at Indian National Congress (INC) President Mallikarjun Kharge's residence while he himself was in Bengaluru, local media reported.

They now plan to hold a mock Parliament sitting at Kharge's residence on Friday to conduct the "public impeachment" which is purely symbolic.

It will include speeches by opposition leaders, accounts by victims of the electoral roll revision, a motion passed by Kharge and a concluding speech by INC leader Rahul Gandhi. That's ahead of a planned November 1 rally to demand Kumar's removal.

The Election Commission of India began the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in 2025 to remove redundancies from India's electoral rolls including dead voters and those appearing more than once. Since then over 13 crore (130 Million) voter names have been deleted. There have also been reported irregularities allegedly on Kumar's part to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party.

The BJP has denied allegations that the SIR exercise has benefited them, arguing it helped weed out "infiltrators" from the voter list.

On Tuesday, the INC claimed it was denied permission to hold the "public impeachment" of CEC Kumar at various venues, the Hindustan Times reported, and accused the government of trying to "silence" the voice of common people after "destroying" the electoral system.

Under law, the CEC can be removed by the Indian parliament through a process similar to the impeachment of a Supreme Court judge. He or she may also resign by submitting a written resignation to the president of India.

World.title: Spain train crash: PM Sanchez calls for investigation as 3 days of mourning begins
World.content:
Emergency crews worked through the night after a high-speed train collision killed 68 people. PM Pedro Sanchez has pledged a full investigation into Spain's second major train accident this year.

Spain began three days of national mourning on Thursday in remembrance of the 68 people killed in one of Europe's deadliest train disasters in recent memory.

On Wednesday morning, a high-speed train run by state operator RENFE slammed into the back of a stationary train operated by private Italian-Spanish company Iryo in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid.

A British tourist who was rescued from the RENFE train told the Associated Press that "suddenly, everything started falling apart."

"We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over," the man said.

Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was on holiday in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the RENFE train when "I woke up and I was in the air."

Pablo Mejia, 42, escaped with injuries to his head, telling the AFP news agency that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.

He recounted "a very strong hit ... a lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos," while wearing a bloodstained jumper and holding a tattered suitcase. "I think I've been born again," he said.

Workers started to use cranes to move parts of the damaged trains late on Wednesday Image: Oscar Del Pozo/AFP

Emergency crews work through the night

Emergency crews continued searching through the wreckage overnight for survivors and bodies, using cranes to move mangled metal.

Relatives of passengers gathered at nearby facilities seeking information about missing loved ones.

Residents of the nearby town of Urda joined emergency workers in helping survivors, providing first aid supplies, water and blankets.

Protesters gather outside the Ministry of Transportation to demand accountability Image: Ananda Manjón/Europa Press/IMAGO

Teams of Red Cross workers offered support.

Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia told AFP news agency that many people are in shock and "haven't taken on board what has happened."

"The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.

Crash survivors wait to board buses outside a municipal center Image: Susana Vera/REUTERS

Authorities are collecting DNA samples from relatives in Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to help identify the missing.

Spain's rail network safety in question

Wednesday's crash was Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year and has raised fresh questions about rail safety.

Transport Minister Oscar Puente blamed the crash on an "inexplicable" decision to allow one train to continue after an automatic control system failed along a stretch of track.

He said the RENFE high-speed train had travelled about 25 kilometers before hitting the stationary Iryo train.

Audio recordings reveal pre-crash exchanges

On Wednesday evening, Spanish media published audio recordings revealing confused conversations between the train drivers and the railways control center in the 30 minutes before the crash.

In one recording pubblished by the El Pais newspaper, among others, a control center operator appears to instruct the driver of the RENFE train to resume his journey at normal speed after some technical issues.

"Continue your journey and then proceed ... at normal speed [and] with normal operation," the operator tells the driver.

"At normal speed?" queries the driver, to which the controller confirms: "Yes."

A few minutes later, in another recording, the driver of the Iryo train then informs the control center that she is "stationary in front of the entry signal at [the town of] Urda" — about 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) ahead of the RENFE train.

When she is still told to "resume the journey" normally, she says she cannot because of the security system error, reiterating that this is why she is stationary.

The second recording suggests therefore that the control center was aware of the stationary Iryo train having already instructed the RENFE train to travel towards it — but no further action appears to have been taken.

Spanish PM pledges full investigation

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who visited the crash site, pledged a full investigation and measures to strengthen rail safety.

"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sanchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."

In January, 46 people died when a high-speed train derailed and collided with another in the southern Andalusia region.

The latest disaster comes just weeks before Spain's November 29 general election which Prime Minister Sanchez had called hoping to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents — and distract from right-wing attacks on his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which they both deny.

About an hour before Wednesday's crash spread, Sanchez had posted a campaign message on social media reading: "There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country."

Within 24 hours, Transport Minister Puente was facing calls to resign while Sanchez's main rival, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, demanded a full investigation of the crash and canceled campaign events for the day.

"This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families," Nunez Feijoo said. "But that does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers."

There was noticeably less restraint on show from Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, who will be hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives.

"More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring," he said, refusing to join Nunez Feijoo's campaign pause.

"I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.
