World.title: Estonia to call all women aged 40 for breast cancer risk analysis screening
World.content:
Estonia is set to become the first country in the world where people are invited to screening programs based on genetic data. Next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation for genetic testing to determine their individual breast cancer risk, regardless of whether or not they have health insurance.

Until now, women have been invited to breast cancer screening after their 50th birthday, but starting next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation so that each woman's risk of developing breast cancer can be calculated based on genetic data.

"If this risk is higher than usual – if the risk for these 40-year-old women is the same as it is for other women at the age of 50 – then including these women in screening earlier is justified. Starting mammography already at the age of 40," said Steven Smit, head of the biobank laboratory at the Estonian Genome Center.

Around 3,000 genetic variants are taken into account when calculating the risk. However, the study does not include BRCA gene mutations, which led actress Angelina Jolie to decide to have her breasts removed 13 years ago to prevent developing the disease.

"These are hereditary forms of cancer, which are assessed through separate tests as needed if there has been breast cancer in the family," Smit said.

There are almost 10,000 40-year-old women in Estonia, and invitations will be sent both to those who have already donated their genes to the Estonian Genome Center and to those who have not.

"The gene donors' data will not be checked automatically. The first step is still to go to the Health Portal and submit a declaration of consent there so that the data can be used in the healthcare system," said Krista Kruuv-Käo, head of preventive services at the Estonian Health Insurance Fund.

The same declaration of consent must also be completed by women whose data is not in the Estonian Genome Center. They will receive a referral to a laboratory to provide a blood sample.

It is also possible to put this service in place for other serious diseases, but the Health Insurance Fund does not consider this reasonable, as the state would not have the capacity to follow up on them.

"We are also analyzing how we could use genetic risk in the case of cardiovascular diseases to more precisely involve those people whose risks are higher in preventive measures," Kruuv-Käo said.

Currently, the Estonian Genome Center holds data on approximately one-fifth of Estonia's population, and no new gene donors are being accepted.

"The Genome Center would certainly be fully prepared for this, but at the moment there is simply no funding available for it. The Genome Center's general funding has also been reduced in recent years," Smit said.

World.title: Flora U-19s draw 2-2 with 9-man Chelsea in UEFA Youth League
World.content:
The game was the first leg of the UEFA Youth League second qualifying round, played at the A. Le Coq Arena in Tallinn.

After a sending-off, the visitors were down to 10 men early on in the second half, falling to nine players shortly before full-time after a second sending-off, but held on for the draw

Midfielder Sander Alamaa put Flora ahead in the fourth minute, but Chelsea striker Jashayde Greenwood equalized a quarter of an hour later and then Chizaram Ezenwata put the visitors in front shortly before half-time. Flora's equalizer came on 60 minutes, when Alamaa converted a penalty won by left-back Karel Isok.

"Before the game we said Chelsea are vulnerable on the counter-attack. For the first goal I got a good run at the center-back and took my chance. It was a good start to the game. For the second goal I'm not sure it was a penalty, but at least it was given our way. I saw the goalkeeper dive one way and just put the ball calmly in the other corner," Alamaa told ERR after the match.

Chelsea finished with nine men: center-back Dante Waite was sent off on 55 minutes and midfielder Isaac Silva collected a second yellow on 89.

"In some ways you could feel the difference in level with players from a Premier League club's academy. They were technically very high-quality players. In midfield their players played some unbelievable passes. But if you go into duels the way we did today, we can take down anyone," Alamaa added.

World.title: New apps challenge Tallinn's official public transport website
World.content:
Public transport apps enterprising developers have come up with are growing in popularity and offer an alternative to Tallinn's official public transport website.

Unlike many European capitals, Tallinn still has no official public transport mobile app, while critics say the official site at transport.tallinn.ee is getting outdated and is not very user-friendly.

"The people who should know how best to do these things haven't done anything. This is the kind of thing that was being done in 2010, and in 2026 we really shouldn't still be dealing with something like this," said Kaspar Sanglepp, creator of the Go Now app, one of the competing products.

"To quickly see bus times, you have to go to different websites and click through a lot of things. I wanted to be able to get that information with one click," Sanglepp said.

"The visual design is 10–15 or more years old. It takes so much time just to get to the route planner," said Sander Pukk, creator of another app, called Mis? Kuhu? ("What? Where to?").

All public transport vehicles in Tallinn and Tartu send their location to the system every 10 seconds. Using this publicly available data, developers have created three different free apps. Despite not being advertised, between them they have amassed over 2,000 daily users.

The newest app on the scene, Tallinn Live, garnered 4,000 views in four days.

One of the newly created Tallinn public transport apps. Source: ERR

"Tallinn Live project, it's very simple: you just are going to the app, you are just using it. That's why it's basic, and that's why people love it," Taha Yasin Erel, creator of Tallinn Live, told "Aktuaalne kaamera".

"I got lots of, hundreds of comments, hundreds of new ideas, and I started with these ideas, and people started to like it more," Erel went on.

Most public transport stops in Tallinn are still old school in that they lack display boards and have only printed timetables. At peak times and with all the ongoing roadworks in Tallinn, there is often a difference between when a bus, trolleybus or tram is scheduled and when it actually arrives, something which apps can help with.

"Real-time information has definitely been the main thing. Many stops still don't have those display boards, so being able to see whether a bus is running late or not has been the subject of the most positive feedback," Pukk went on.

According to Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse, however, surveys show that people are satisfied with Tallinn Transport's website. The city nevertheless plans to update it.

"The Transport Department (TLT) is currently carrying out the relevant analyses, and we certainly plan to update it in the coming years to make it more user-friendly, with an app or a mobile view," Jesse said.

World.title: Israel piles pressure on Arab parties as Netanyahu seeks government
World.content:
Jerusalem – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc on Thursday piled pressure on Israeli Arab leaders over unproven accusations of foreign funding, in a push to neuter parties that made strong gains after an otherwise indecisive election.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, a far-right firebrand with a history of attacks on Palestinians, went so far as to encourage Israel “immediately” to order the arrests of Arab party leaders.

Israel was nearing the completion of ballot-counting from Tuesday’s election in which neither Netanyahu nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot looked able to secure a majority in the parliament known as the Knesset.

A looming threat on the horizon, meanwhile, was the prospect of a return to war with Iran, alongside Israel’s ally the United States, which is holding its own crucial midterms next week.

Israel’s election saw a soaring performance by Israeli Arabs, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after the country’s creation in 1948, as outrage boiled at calls by ministers such as Ben Gvir to treat the Israeli minority group much as Israel has dealt with Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

The Arab parties together have enough votes to take the opposition bloc over the finish line, but Eisenkot has baulked, after relentless attacks by Netanyahu who warned his right-wing Jewish base that voting for the opposition would put Arabs in power.

Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, a conservative who heads the Central Election Commission, requested an investigation by the Shin Bet security service into allegations that key Arab party Raam received money from Qatar, the energy-rich Gulf powerbroker that has channels for Hamas.

“The Raamgate scandal is a political earthquake. Israel’s elections have been stolen!” Netanyahu’s Likud party said.

Government officials did not offer evidence to back the allegations.

Netanyahu himself has long been under the cloud of allegations related to Qatar after the arrests last year of two of his aides for allegedly receiving payments from the Gulf power.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, for years tacitly supported Qatar funding to Hamas-ruled Gaza, hoping to preserve stability.

That paradigm collapsed on October 7, 2023 when Hamas carried out the deadliest single attack ever on Israel, under Netanyahu’s watch.

– Kingmakers under pressure –

With nearly 93 percent of the vote counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was at 53 seats and the opposition forces led by Eisenkot had 48 — both well under the 61 needed to form a government.

The two main Arab formations were on track for an unprecedented 19 seats.

Some observers quickly said that the allegations would help Netanyahu by making the Arab lawmakers even more toxic to Eisenkot.

Yousef Jabareen, the head of one of them, the leftist Arab-majority Joint List, told AFP on Wednesday that he was willing to cooperate with the opposition to bring down Netanyahu but without joining it in a government.

He said the priority was to end “Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government” but noted that the Arab lawmakers disagreed on plenty with Eisenkot, who has largely backed the destruction of Gaza ordered by Netanyahu after the October 7 attack.

In response to the new allegations, Eisenkot said he was receiving updates and promised “utmost vigilance” against election interference.

“On the other hand, we cannot allow political actors to exploit the situation and influence the timing of the inauguration of the 26th Knesset,” he said.

One of Eisenkot’s right-leaning allies, Avigdor Lieberman, called the allegations “dramatic and unprecedented” and urged a swift investigation.

An Israeli police statement said that they would investigate every complaint about election integrity.

– The great survivor –

Netanyahu, who has led Israel on and off for more than 19 years, is known as a wily political operator.

He also tried on Tuesday to raise allegations of fraud, saying that Arab parties were caught with envelopes of cash and encouraging his base to come out in response.

Police said they arrested three suspects but the election commission called it an isolated local case.

Another factor that could play into the formation is an attack on Iran.

Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened to strike Iran, with his ally, US President Donald Trump, signalling he is ready to attack after next Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is forecast to lose ground.

Eisenkot has warned the military that Netanyahu has no mandate and that officers must not respond to his “political needs”.

But an attack could raise pressure on Eisenkot to join an emergency unity government, an option he has publicly ruled out, or keep the clock running until Israel can call new elections.

President Isaac Herzog will decide after the publication of the official results which person to task with a first chance of forming a government.

World.title: TotalEnergies profit hits record on high oil prices
World.content:
Paris – French oil and gas giant TotalEnergies said Thursday that its net profit hit a new record in the third quarter as the war in the Middle East pushed up hydrocarbon prices.

Net profit reached $8.3 billion in the period from July to September, up from $5.4 billion in the preceding three months.

“In a high-price environment characterised by historic refining margin levels and a bull gas market, TotalEnergies is once again fully leveraging its integrated business model and its geographic diversification,” chief executive Patrick Pouyanne said in a statement.

The company had already reported a strong rise in its bottom line in the preceding two quarters, similarly driven by soaring oil and gas prices as well as its trading activities.

TotalEnergies said the surge in profits would be reflected in a higher dividend for shareholders.

“The board of directors commended the very good operational performance of all business segments which enabled the company to capture higher market prices,” the company said in its earnings statement.

The group will undertake a new capital increase reserved for employees, “who will benefit from a 20 percent discount on the share price”.

The board confirmed a third interim dividend of 0.90 euros per share for 2026, up 5.9 percent compared to 2025.

TotalEnergies will also proceed with share buybacks for cancellation of $2.5 billion “for the fourth quarter as well as for the first quarter 2027”.

World.title: Taiwan says Pakistan briefly closed airspace to Taiwanese flights
World.content:
Taipei – Pakistan briefly closed its airspace to Taiwanese cargo and passenger flights, Taiwan said on Thursday, suspecting China of being behind the unprecedented move.

“We suspect definitely China was behind this,” Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi told AFP after confirming that Pakistan had closed and reopened its airspace to Taiwanese airlines.

China Airlines and EVA Air, which are both based in Taiwan, normally fly over Pakistan on their Asia-Europe route.

Last weekend, however, they began rerouting their Europe-bound flights further south over the Gulf or further north over Russia, AFP analysis of flight tracking data shows.

Some Taiwanese flights have resumed flying over Pakistan, according to the latest data.

“China Airlines and EVA received a notice from the Pakistan authorities that they will lift the ban, but only temporarily… till the end of the winter,” Chen said.

Neither airline would confirm that Pakistan had closed or reopened its airspace when contacted by AFP.

“We condemn Pakistan, and if China is behind this, I think that is a very bad practice to use its leverage over the countries in the Global South to do that,” Chen said.

“I think that gets in the way of the safety of the passengers and the smooth operation of the global supply chain.”

Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told Bloomberg News on Wednesday that the airspace was closed in adherence with Beijing’s “One China policy”.

China’s foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters on Thursday that “as far as we are aware, there are no obstacles for residents of the Taiwan region to travel internationally”.

– ‘Isolate Taiwan’ –

China claims Taiwan as part of its territory and opposes the self-governed island’s participation in international organisations and exchanges with other countries.

Chen said it was the first time a country had closed its airspace to Taiwanese commercial flights.

In April, the Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar revoked overflight permits for Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te’s flight to Eswatini, Taipei’s only African ally, forcing him to postpone the trip.

At the time, Taiwan blamed “intense pressure” from China for the revocation.

“China now learned that this could be an effective way to block our airspace access and therefore sort of further isolate Taiwan,” Chen said.

“We see this is the discovery that they can weaponise the airspace assets.”

Taiwan does not have formal diplomatic ties with Pakistan, which has close relations with China.

Chen said “many like-minded” countries had assisted Taiwan over the airspace closure.

“We are afraid that this might be a practice that spreads to other Global South countries,” Chen said.

“I think that is a major concern for not only for Taiwan, but also for other countries in the region and beyond.”

Pakistan and China have maintained close diplomatic and strategic relations for decades, often describing their partnership as an “all-weather friendship” that is “higher than the Himalayas, deeper than the oceans, sweeter than honey and stronger than steel”.

China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a major investor, particularly through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and has poured tens of billions of dollars into funding massive transport, energy and infrastructure projects.

World.title: US fires top army general in latest ouster: media
World.content:
Washington – The United States has fired its top military planner, The Atlantic reported Wednesday, in a surprise shake-up as President Donald Trump appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran.

Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed this week from his role as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the magazine reported, citing unidentified defense department officials.

Sylvia’s ouster would be the latest in a series of high-profile departures from the military since Trump returned to power a year ago.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said last month that the United States has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20 percent, in a move he said is aimed at “accountability.”

He suggested the cuts targeted officers who failed to get on board with his efforts to ensure the military is focused on war-fighting rather than the “woke” policies of previous administrations, describing the reductions as an “accomplishment.”

No reason was given for Sylvia’s departure and no replacement has been named, The Atlantic said.

AFP has contacted the Pentagon for comment.

The reported sacking comes as Trump is widely considered to be weighing fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.

“We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump said last week, referring to US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war.

He did not give any indication on timing.

Neither the United States nor Iran has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, settling instead into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships.

Sylvia’s previous roles included leading the 101st Airborne Division — the US army’s air assault division — and heading a unit in Iraq.

World.title: Iraq clinches three medals on Day 1 of Asian Judo Championships in Amman
World.content:
Amman (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s national judo team captured three medals on the opening day of the Senior Asian Judo Championships, currently taking place in the Jordanian capital, Amman, featuring top-tier competitors from across the continent.

The Iraqi delegation concluded Day 1 with one silver medal and two bronze medals, marking a competitive start to their continental campaign.

In the men’s 73 kg category, Mohammed Sattar claimed the silver medal after advancing through the preliminary and semifinal brackets, while teammate Hussein Raad secured the bronze medal in the same weight division.

In the women’s competitions, Maryam Hamid took home Iraq’s third medal of the day, earning a bronze in the 52 kg division.

The early podium sweep reflects ongoing development efforts by the Iraqi Judo Federation, the national coaching staff, and continuous administrative backing from the Iraqi National Olympic Committee to elevate combat sports on the international stage.

World.title: Miami Heat earn first win of NBA season with Antetokounmpo
World.content:
Los Angeles – The Miami Heat finally earned their first win since the start of the season and the arrival of superstar Giannis Antetokounmpo, defeating the Atlanta Hawks 129-117 on Wednesday.

The Greek two-time NBA Most Valuable Player had been expected to immediately propel Miami into the ranks of Eastern Conference contenders, but his first victory in a Heat uniform came at the fifth time of asking.

Antetokounmpo, who had a triple-double in defeat to the Dallas Mavericks two nights earlier, again racked up impressive numbers, with 24 points and 18 rebounds.

This time he was backed up by teammates Bam Adebayo, who scored 24 with nine rebounds, and Andrew Wiggins who added 18 points.

Former Milwaukee Bucks star Antetokounmpo reached 1,000 career steals, while Adebayo became the Heat’s all-time leading rebounder, surpassing the record of 5,791 previously held by Udonis Haslem.

“I can’t really put it into words, man. I just wish I could have did it at the crib,” Adebayo said at Atlanta’s State Farm Arena.

The star-packed Philadelphia 76ers bounced back from Sunday’s disappointing loss against Detroit to move to 4-1 with a 114-109 victory in a back-and-forth clash with the Indiana Pacers.

LeBron James and the Sixers struggled to see off Indiana, which this week announced it would be without star Tyrese Haliburton for around two weeks due to a hamstring injury.

The Sixers fell behind in a lop-sided third quarter, but rallied down the final stretch to seal the road victory.

Tyrese Maxey scored 17 of his 27 points in a blistering fourth quarter showing to spare his team’s blushes.

James managed just 13 points but added 10 assists, while Joel Embiid had 21 points and 11 rebounds, and Jaylen Brown provided 20 points.

“JB and (Embiid) and Bron kind of got on me not being aggressive the first three quarters. When JB checked back in the game in the 4th quarter he said ‘you owe us, take us home,'” said Maxey.

“I just gotta do what my vets tell me to do.”

The Oklahoma City Thunder suffered their first loss of the season, falling 120-96 to the Dallas Mavericks.

A victory would have made the Thunder the only team in NBA history to start three straight seasons 5-0, but they were denied as Cooper Flagg scored 26 points with eight assists for Dallas.

“I think we just got guys that are bought into a winning culture,” said 19-year-old star Flagg.

– Dybantsa debut –

AJ Dybantsa, the top overall pick of the NBA Draft, played his first NBA minutes during the Washington Wizards’ 121-111 loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Nineteen-year-old Dybantsa had missed the Wizards’ first four games with an ankle sprain but started Wednesday, scoring 19 points.

The Cavaliers clinched victory in the final quarter. Donovan Mitchell scored 19 points with seven assists.

French superstar Victor Wembanyama poured in 36 points with 14 rebounds as his San Antonio Spurs won a third straight game with a 117-111 triumph over the Utah Jazz.

The Houston Rockets, one of three remaining undefeated teams, became the first to improve to 5-0, with a 132-100 win against the Bucks.

Fred VanVleet top-scored with 24 while Amen Thompson added 23.

World.title: Asian stock markets fluctuate after mixed tech results
World.content:
Hong Kong – Tech firms diverged Thursday with a mixed bag of results for some of the AI sector’s big beasts tempering the recent spurt of optimism amid growing anxiety about companies’ investment and debt.

Markets enjoyed a healthy run-up in the previous two days as traders welcomed strong reports from South Korean chip titan SK hynix and a highly impressive IPO filing from Claude-creator Anthropic.

That helped steady nerves among investors who have started to question the vast sums pumped into the AI build-out and when they will see returns, with the spike in borrowing costs compounding concerns.

But uncertainty crept back in Asia on Thursday after Samsung Electronics’ 107.4 trillion won ($80.5 billion) third-quarter operating profit fell short of estimates, even as it represented a breathtaking 783 percent year-on-year jump.

The reading was also the first time any tech company had recorded quarterly operating profit of more than 100 trillion won, Samsung said.

That came after Wall Street titan Alphabet reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business.

Alphabet dived 10 percent in after-hours trade, while Samsung lost more than five percent in Asian trade — showing that traders have set a high bar for firms’ earnings.

Still, Microsoft posted forecast-topping revenue and profit, fuelled by its Azure cloud computing division, and Oracle issued a healthy revenue forecast.

And Moody’s Ratings warned that the elevated interest rate environment could pose problems.

“With interest rates much higher in many global regions than they were in 2021, refinancing risk will become more visible as loans originated in 2020-22 approach maturity,” it said in its latest Private Credit Quarterly.

“These vintages were underwritten when rates were low and competition was intense, often with higher leverage and more aggressive terms.

“Even in the absence of additional rate hikes, refinancing pressures are likely to challenge weaker borrowers with 2020-22 vintage loans, with not all emerging unscathed.”

Among tech firms in Asia, SK hynix rose more than one percent to build on its strong showing this week, while Japan’s Kioxia and Advantest were also well up, but Tokyo Electron and SoftBank retreated along with Taipei-listed TSMC.

Broader markets fluctuated, with Japan’s Nikkei up along with Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila.

But Seoul sank nearly three percent, with Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei and Jakarta also down.

There appeared little major reaction to the Federal Reserve’s widely expected decision to hold interest rates, as it cited the need for more data in the fight against inflation, which has held stubbornly above officials’ two-percent target for five years.

Two dissenting members of the panel voted for an immediate interest rate increase.

Bank chief Kevin Warsh said policymakers needed more information in the coming weeks to “determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the two-percent goal”.

Oil prices dipped after Wednesday’s rally, though they remain above $100 as reports say the United States is planning to mount a new military attack in Iran after the US midterm elections.

Investors are keeping track of efforts in Israel to form a new government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the opposition were tied in this week’s general election.

The outcome of negotiations could play a major role in the future of the Iran war.

World.title: It only takes one rumour: How a small trigger can lead to a deadly stampede
World.content:
Stampede at Kolkata pandal during Durga Puja claimed 19 lives.

The anatomy of a stampede

Psychology of the crowd

How should police act and react?

Preparing for the unexpected

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: It begins with a rumour, feeds on panic and ends in tragedy. A stampede can turn a celebration into chaos within minutes, leaving thousands gathered in joy struggling to find a way out. In a tightly packed crowd, even a small disturbance can have deadly consequences.A similar script played out in Kolkata on October 17. On the night of Maha Saptami during Durga Puja, pandal-hoppers gathered in large numbers at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin pandal. The crowd swelled further after a sudden spell of rain prompted people waiting outside to seek shelter, while visitors near the exit stopped moving.An announcement over the public address system warning that the pandal was about to collapse added to the panic. Investigators believe several factors contributed to the stampede, including overcrowding, narrow entry and exit points, inadequate crowd management and the misleading announcement.The crowd crush, which police said lasted around three minutes, claimed 19 lives and left at least 25 people injured.India is a country of festivals, and its massive religious gatherings also make it prone to stampedes. This year, it was Kolkata.Last year, it was Karur in Tamil Nadu and the Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj. The locations change, the crowds differ, but the tragedy keeps repeating itself.This raises an important question: despite elaborate planning and dedicated crowd management teams, why do stampedes keep happening? And what can authorities do to prevent a small disturbance from turning into a disaster?Public excitement soars during religious gatherings. Actual turnout often exceeds what authorities anticipate, resulting in more people entering an area than it can safely accommodate.As the crowd swells, even a small disturbance, a rumour, someone tripping and falling, a sudden power outage or even a broken barricade can lead to a situation in which people lose control of their movement.According to a 2014 report by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), titled Managing Crowd at Events and Venues of Mass Gathering: A Guide for State Government, Local Authorities, Administrators and Organizers, crowd disasters can be triggered by several factors.Structural problems such as weak temporary structures, collapsed barricades, poorly lit stairways, slippery roads and narrow entrances and exits can lead to a crowd crush.Fires, electrical failures and security scares can also turn an otherwise manageable gathering into a dangerous crush.The report explains the causes of stampedes through the "FIST" model which is an acronym for Force, Information, Space and Time. According to the model, the four factors that can contribute to a crowd disaster are the force exerted by the crowd, the information that triggers its reaction, the physical space available and the duration of the incident."The FIST circumstances namely crowd force, the information upon which the crowd acts, the physical space involved, and the time duration of the incident play a very important role resulting in either overcrowding or high desired velocity," the report says.In simple terms, when too many people are packed into a limited space, pressure builds as those behind continue moving forward while those in front are unable to move. At extreme crowd densities, people can be pushed against one another with such force that they lose control of their movements. Even those who remain standing can struggle to breathe.Deaths in such situations do not necessarily occur because someone has literally been "trampled" under the feet of others. The NDMA says compressive asphyxia, which occurs when pressure on the chest prevents a person from breathing, has historically been the most common cause of death in crowd disasters."On occasions, this has led to deaths because of crushing, suffocation, and trampling. Historically, compressive asphyxia has been the most common reason for deaths in crowd disasters," the report says.Crowd psychology is also a factor that can contribute to a stampede-like situation. According to the NDMA report, individuals often conform their thoughts and behaviour to those of a larger group rather than acting independently."Individual behaviour in a crowd is sometimes influenced by the behaviour of others. The individuals within a crowd may act differently than if they were on their own," it says."The unlawful actions of a few people can result in larger numbers following them. Research has shown that understanding of crowd behaviour has led to community based approach to crowd control instead of force based control," the report adds.For instance, long queues at places of worship may lead some devotees to climb over fences, prompting others to follow and causing overcrowding in another area.However, crowd behaviour is not always irrational. People react to incomplete information, the movement of others and the fear of danger. In dense crowds, they may also lose the ability to control their own movement.This is why rumours and misleading announcements can be particularly dangerous. People may begin moving towards an exit without knowing what is happening elsewhere in the venue. If the exit is already congested, the sudden movement can increase pressure on those trapped in the crowd.Talking to The Times of India, former Bihar director general of police Abhayanand, who handled several such gatherings during his long service, said police should refrain from using force when a crowd is already panicked during a stampede-like situation."There is always a trigger, however small. It is followed immediately thereafter by a rumour which spreads like wildfire," Abhayanand said."I haven't followed any SOP in my days. I followed two basics: The crowd has panicked. Don't increase the panic by lathi charge. If there is an individual in whom the crowd has trust and if he can be made to communicate with the crowd, its effect is magical," he added."Crowds where there is some common binding force experience stampede. Such stampedes are easier to manage," he further said.Abhayanand also recalled handling a similar situation during the funeral procession of Ranvir Sena chief Brahmeshwar Mukhiya in Patna in 2012. He said police refrained from using force against a particularly unruly gathering of supporters."The crowd was itching for a trigger, and a police lathi charge could have set things off. We restrained ourselves because the repercussions would not have been limited to the capital but could have spread across the entire state," he told TOI."Those indulging in arson wanted the police to react and resort to a lathi charge. That was precisely what they were trying to provoke, but we did not allow that trigger to be pulled," he added.His account points to the importance of police response when a crowd is already on edge. An attempt to disperse people by force can worsen the situation if it causes them to rush towards a narrow exit or move against an incoming crowd.The NDMA has also laid down guidelines on how authorities should manage crowds and respond when a stampede-like situation develops.According to the agency, the guiding principle should be to bridge the gap between demand and supply. This requires controlling the number of people entering a venue, regulating the crowd within it and managing the outflow when necessary.The NDMA recommends designated staging points through which visitors should pass, along with effective systems to count and monitor people moving through them. Multiple routes should be encouraged to prevent bottlenecks and facilitate the movement of vulnerable groups.Crowd management also requires authorities to anticipate disturbances without allowing their response to trigger a larger crisis."Such miscreants should be immediately quarantined and removed. Action should be taken immediately with tact and firmness, without inviting undue attention from the general public, which may be there if force is used," it says."Inappropriate or poorly managed control procedures may precipitate crowd incidents rather than preventing them. For example, police reacting to a group of unruly people may chase them in a direction opposite to the incoming crowd, which may create a collision, and hence a disaster. Special attention should also be given to the border of the venue and the floating crowd moving there because the mischief is usually caused at such places," it adds.The agency also recommends "input control" by restricting or staggering entry to prevent overcrowding. Authorities must be able to regulate, slow or temporarily stop the inflow when a venue reaches its safe capacity.This also means keeping entry and exit routes clear, ensuring that people leaving a venue do not collide with those entering, and monitoring areas where crowds tend to gather or stop moving.Communication is another important part of crowd management. The NDMA says a lack of reliable information can cause people to panic or change direction, leading to dangerous crowd movements."Communicating with visitors and providing them with the correct information is a very critical factor in all situations," the report says, stressing that communication is essential during normal operations, emergencies and recovery.The Kolkata tragedy showed how quickly things can go wrong when these safeguards fail. Police said the crowd had become congested near the exit during the rain, even as the entry point remained open. The misleading announcement about the pandal collapsing is believed to have added to the pressure, although investigators are still examining the exact sequence of events.Ultimately, effective crowd management lies in anticipating pressure, regulating movement and ensuring that a small trigger does not turn into an uncontrollable chain of events. The challenge is not just to prepare for the thousands expected to attend an event, but also to recognise when a gathering is becoming unsafe and act before it is too late.

World.title: 'Act as protective umbrella': SC says banks must compensate digital fraud victims
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday said banks must be held accountable for compensating victims of digital fraud, stressing that they should act as a âprotective umbrellaâ for customers vulnerable to digital arrest scams.

A bench headed by CJI Surya Kant questioned why unusually large withdrawals from a retired person's bank account could not trigger timely intervention to prevent the loss, Bar and Bench reported.

During the court's suo motu hearing, attorney general R Venkataramani said banks are getting better at identifying suspicious transactions and that preventive measures were being put in place.

The amicus curiae sought reports and suggestions from state police forces, noting that digital arrest scams continued despite awareness campaigns.

World.title: SC disposes of Mahua Moitra's plea seeking public disclosure of AIF, FPI beneficiaries
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday disposed of Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra's plea seeking public disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners and portfolio holdings of alternative investment funds (AIFs), foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) and their intermediaries, saying it could not issue directions in the absence of a legal framework mandating such disclosures.

A bench of Justices BV Nagarathna, R Mahadevan and DK Upadhyaya said there was no existing legal regime requiring full public disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners of these funds. It said the court could direct the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to ensure compliance if such a framework existed, but could not issue a mandamus without one.

"Had there been any legal regime and the SEBI was not following it, the court can direct for compliance but in the absence of any framework or legal regime, the court cannot issue any mandamus," it observed.

The bench also questioned Moitra's decision to approach the court, suggesting that she could have raised the issue in Parliament and sought a discussion on it.

Advocate Prashant Bhushan, appearing for Moitra, argued that the court could direct SEBI to ensure full disclosure of the actual beneficiaries of these funds even in the absence of a specific regulatory framework. He contended that innocent investors were being "manipulated" by investors who artificially boosted the share prices of companies.

World.title: From Hitler’s rise to farmers’ misery in India: How the Great Depression changed lives far beyond America
World.content:
In October 1929, billions of dollars in wealth evaporated from the American stock market, setting off an economic catastrophe that would reach far beyond Wall Street.

Years of speculative buying, easy credit and inflated share prices had created a market built on the expectation that stocks would keep rising.

When confidence collapsed, investors rushed to sell.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged nearly 13 per cent on October 28 and another 12 per cent the following day, in what became known as Black Monday and Black Tuesday.

But the crash was only the beginning. Bank failures, collapsing demand and business closures deepened the American downturn, while the withdrawal of US loans, falling international trade and the constraints of the gold standard carried the crisis across borders.

The result was the Great Depression, a global disaster that would help propel Adolf Hitler towards power in Germany, devastate farmers in colonial India, push millions of Britons into unemployment, and expose the fragility of economies around the world.

What followed was not merely a financial collapse, but a decade of economic hardship and political upheaval that changed the course of the twentieth century.

Germanyâs economic collapse turned Hitler into a political force

The Great Depression hit Germany at a time when its economy was already vulnerable, turning a global financial crisis into a national catastrophe.





The country was still struggling with the consequences of the First World War, including reparations, political instability and the devastating hyperinflation of 1923.

Its recovery during the second half of the 1920s depended heavily on foreign credit, particularly loans from the United States.

Under the Dawes Plan of 1924, American lending helped stabilise German finances and supported economic recovery.

But this dependence became a major weakness when the Wall Street crash struck in October 1929.

As American banks and investors came under pressure, new lending dried up and foreign creditors recalled short-term loans. German banks and businesses struggled to obtain credit, investment declined and companies began cutting production and jobs.

The consequences were severe. Industrial output contracted, businesses failed and unemployment soared.

By 1932, around 5.6 million Germans were registered as unemployed, while industrial production had fallen by approximately 40 per cent from its 1928 level.

The crisis also paralysed political decision-making. Chancellor Hermann MÃ¼llerâs coalition government collapsed in March 1930 amid disagreements over unemployment insurance, paving the way for increasingly unstable governments that relied on presidential emergency powers.

This economic desperation created an opening for Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party. They portrayed the Weimar Republic as weak and incapable of protecting ordinary Germans, promising jobs, national revival and decisive leadership. Their message appealed to sections of the middle class, struggling farmers, small business owners and workers disillusioned with the political establishment.

The electoral shift was dramatic. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Nazis won just 2.6 per cent of the vote in the 1928 parliamentary election.

Their share rose to 18 per cent in September 1930 and 37 per cent in July 1932, making them the largest party in the Reichstag.

Nazi campaigning deliberately exploited the hardship. A 1932 election poster preserved by the US Holocaust Memorial Museum carried the slogan âOur Last Hope - Hitlerâ, presenting the Nazi leader as an answer to national despair.

The party used mass rallies, newspapers, posters and speeches to promise economic recovery and political order.

At the same time, it spread antisemitic conspiracy theories, blamed Jews and communists for Germanyâs problems, and attacked democratic institutions.

Hitler did not win an outright majority in a free national election. On January 30, 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg appointed him chancellor following negotiations with conservative political leaders who believed they could control him. The Nazis subsequently dismantled democracy and established a dictatorship.

The Great Depression did not, by itself, cause Hitlerâs rise. But the collapse of American lending, mass unemployment and the failure of Germanyâs political leadership to restore confidence created conditions that the Nazis exploited with devastating consequences.

Indiaâs farmers were crushed as crop prices collapsed

In British-ruled India, the Great Depression turned a global economic crisis into a rural emergency, exposing the financial vulnerability of millions of cultivators and deepening resentment against colonial rule.

As international demand weakened and agricultural prices plunged, farmers earned less from their crops but continued to face debts, rent and land revenue obligations. For many, the crisis meant selling produce at a loss, struggling to repay moneylenders and risking the loss of their land.

A 2022 research paper by historian Alok Oak, published in Studies in Indian Politics, documents the scale of the collapse. Indiaâs agricultural price index fell from 203 in 1929 to 127 in 1931, using 1873 as the base year.

The price index for raw cotton dropped from 133 to 70 over the same period. The decline was particularly damaging for cultivators who depended on commercial crops to generate cash for household expenses, rent and taxes.

The crisis was compounded by the structure of the colonial economy. According to Oak, the British government refused to devalue the rupee amid concerns about meeting its foreign financial obligations.

Meanwhile, Britainâs exports to India fell from Â£90.6 million in 1924 to Â£52.9 million in 1930, a decline of about 41 per cent. Falling trade and agricultural prices squeezed rural incomes and weakened economic activity.

The timing was significant for Indiaâs independence movement. At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress declared Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, as its goal.

On January 26, 1930, Congress observed Independence Day, building momentum for a new phase of resistance.

The Depression did not create the struggle against British rule, which had much deeper roots, but worsening economic conditions made questions of taxation, rural livelihoods and control over Indiaâs economy more urgent.

Mahatma Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930, beginning with the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi.

By challenging the British monopoly on salt and the tax imposed on a basic necessity, Gandhi chose an issue that affected Indians across social and economic divisions. The campaign transformed an everyday grievance into an act of mass resistance and helped bring the nationalist movement into the lives of ordinary people.

Gandhi also urged Indians to boycott foreign goods, particularly British-made cloth, and promoted khadi and domestic production. These campaigns had a political and economic purpose. Reducing dependence on imported goods could challenge British commercial interests while encouraging Indians to support local producers. At a time when the global crisis had exposed the vulnerability of export-dependent economies, the message of economic self-reliance gained added significance

Research by Stanford University political scientists Rikhil Bhavnani and Saumitra Jha has also identified a link between economic shocks and nationalist mobilisation.

Their working paper found that districts producing export crops and affected by interwar trade shocks, including the Depression, were more likely to support the independence movement in the 1937 and 1946 elections.

The researchers argue that these shocks helped bring agricultural exporters into a broader coalition demanding political change. The findings suggest that the Depressionâs political consequences extended beyond immediate protests and influenced support for nationalism in subsequent years.

The crisis also reinforced Gandhiâs emphasis on village industries and economic self-reliance. He argued that political freedom would mean little if rural India remained trapped in poverty and dependent on external markets. Gandhi promoted khadi and cottage industries as ways to create employment, strengthen village economies and reduce dependence on imported goods.

In 1934, the All-India Village Industries Association was established to advance this wider effort.

Historian Alok Oak argues that the Depression and the limits of colonial economic policy helped strengthen Gandhiâs focus on rural production and economic autonomy.

Britainâs industrial decline pushed millions out of work

Britain entered the Great Depression with its traditional industries already struggling to compete in international markets. Coal mining, shipbuilding, iron and textiles faced declining demand and growing competition, leaving industrial communities vulnerable when the Wall Street crash of 1929 further restricted global trade.

As exports weakened and businesses cut production, unemployment soared. According to the UK National Archives, the number of unemployed people climbed to almost 3.5 million by 1932, with the North East of England, Scotlandâs industrial lowlands and the mining valleys of Wales among the hardest-hit regions.

Families faced prolonged hardship, while the governmentâs introduction of a means test in 1931 intensified resentment among people seeking unemployment assistance.

The crisis also exposed the limits of Britainâs monetary policy. The country had returned to the gold standard in 1925, tying sterling to a fixed gold value. As economic activity contracted, deflation deepened and unemployment rose, the government faced growing pressure to defend the pound while supporting the domestic economy.

The situation became critical in 1931 as investors withdrew funds from London and the Bank of England lost gold reserves.

The National Archivesâ record of the governmentâs September 20 announcement says more than Â£200 million had been withdrawn from the London market since mid-July. Britain suspended the gold standard the following day.

The political consequences were immediate. The Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald split over how to address the financial emergency and public spending. MacDonald subsequently formed a National Government with Conservative and Liberal support, while Labour suffered a major defeat in the October 1931 election.

The departure from gold eventually gave Britain greater freedom to lower interest rates and allowed sterling to depreciate, helping exporters and supporting the early stages of recovery.

A research paper by economists Jason Lennard and Meredith M Paker found that leaving the gold standard reduced unemployment by 2.7 percentage points in export-intensive industries relative to less export-dependent industries.

Yet recovery was uneven. Traditional industrial regions continued to experience hardship, and hunger marches brought the plight of unemployed workers into public view.

Britainâs experience demonstrated how the Great Depression could undermine established industries, destabilise governments and force a major economic power to abandon a monetary system it had once considered essential to financial stability.

From Wall Street to the World

The Great Depression proved that an economic crisis does not stop at a countryâs borders. A stock market collapse in America helped fuel the rise of Hitler in Germany, deepened the misery of farmers in colonial India, pushed millions of Britons out of work, and devastated economies around the world.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Yet the damage went far beyond lost jobs, failed banks and falling crop prices. Across continents, the Depression changed not only how people earned a living, but also how they viewed their governments and their future.

Its legacy helped reshape the global economic order. The failure of protectionism, the instability of international finance and the inability of countries to contain the crisis through isolated national responses influenced the push for greater economic cooperation after the Second World War, including the Bretton Woods system.

But the Depressionâs most enduring warning is political as much as economic: when livelihoods collapse and governments appear powerless, public anger can become an opening for extremism.

The crash began on Wall Street in 1929; its consequences reached farms, factories, homes and parliaments around the world, changing the course of the twentieth century.

World.title: MLC election results: BJP wins big, but Congress and Samajwadi Party send a message from Nagpur, Varanasi
World.content:
The MLC elections across four states brought both shock and cheer for the BJP and Congress. While the Congress suffered a humiliating defeat in Karnataka, where it is in power but failed to win a single seat, the BJP faltered in two constituencies which mattered the most.

One being Nagpur, which is home to the RSS headquarters, and Varanasi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's parliamentary constituency.

The BJP nevertheless emerged as the largest party, winning 13 of the 28 seats contested, while its allies took the NDA's tally to 16. The alliance swept all four seats in Karnataka, won six of the 11 seats in Uttar Pradesh and secured four of the eight seats in Bihar. In Maharashtra, the ruling Mahayuti won two of the five seats, while the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi secured three.

The Congress's only victory came from Nagpur, a political stronghold of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and Union minister Nitin Gadkari. In Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party retained the Varanasi Teachers' constituency and was heading towards victory in the Graduates' seat, both of which it had won in 2020.

BJP-led NDA secured 16 of the 28 MLC seats across four states, while the SP won five seats in Uttar Pradesh and Congress retained Nagpur in Maharashtra.

What began as celebrations and sharp jibes at the Congress on Wednesday turned into a war of words on Thursday, as the results in Nagpur and Varanasi gave the opposition grounds to question the BJP's claims of electoral dominance.





BJP mocks Congress over 'zero' seats

As the early results came in on Wednesday, BJP leaders targeted the Congress over its poor performance, particularly in Karnataka, where the party is in power but failed to win a single seat.

PM Modi took a swipe at the opposition party on X, pointing out that voting in the four states had taken place using ballot papers.

"Guess how many seats Congress won?" he asked.

The remark came amid the Congress's repeated allegations over electronic voting machines and its demand for a return to ballot-paper voting.

BJP president Nitin Nabin also targeted the Congress, saying the party had failed to win public support despite voting being conducted using ballot papers.

"The people are repeatedly rejecting Congress' anarchist politics," Nabin said, adding that public trust remained with PM Modi irrespective of whether elections were conducted using EVMs or ballot papers.

BJP president Nitin Nabin targeted Congress over its poor performance in the MLC elections, pointing out that voting had taken place using ballot papers.

BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi also attacked Rahul Gandhi over his allegations of vote theft

"Kamchori ki aadat chhodiye. Vote chori ka shabd apke muh se khud chhoot jayega," he said, asking the Congress leader to give up what he described as a habit of avoiding hard work.

Nagpur win gives Congress a chance to respond

Congress candidate and sitting MLC Abhijeet Wanjari defeated BJP's Sudhakar Kohale to retain the Nagpur Division Graduates' constituency after more than 40 hours of counting.

Kohale had initially taken the lead before Wanjari overtook him through preferential votes.

Nagpur is important for the BJP. Besides housing the RSS headquarters, it is associated with Fadnavis and Gadkari, both of whom campaigned for Kohale.

The Congress had wrested the seat from the BJP in 2020, when Wanjari defeated Sandip Joshi. By retaining it in 2026, the party prevented the BJP from reclaiming a constituency it had dominated for decades.

The Maharashtra Congress also targeted Fadnavis over a social media post in which he had claimed that the party had failed to win a single seat.

Congress leader Jairam Ramesh questioned the BJP's setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi after PM Modi mocked the party's performance in the MLC elections.

Sharing a screenshot of what it said was a deleted post by Fadnavis, the party accused him of celebrating before counting was complete.

The post had described the Congress's performance as a "big fat zero".

The Congress said Fadnavis had been forced to delete the post after the Nagpur result and warned that the outcome was only a trailer of future political battles.

Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh also responded to PM Modi's remarks, questioning the BJP's losses in Nagpur and Varanasi.

"The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he's lecturing others! Before counting Congress's seats, I wish he'd also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS's stronghold of Nagpur?" Ramesh said.

"Mr. Modi, stop the trolling," he added, accusing the government of failing to address inflation, unemployment and weak private investment.

Ramesh claimed that voters in Varanasi, Nagpur, Lucknow, Prayagraj and Patna had expressed dissatisfaction with the Centre's policies.

Varanasi setback gives SP a boost ahead of 2027

The BJP's biggest setback in Uttar Pradesh came from Varanasi, where the Samajwadi Party retained the Teachers' seat and established an unassailable lead in the Graduates' constituency.

The BJP retained six of the 11 seats contested in the state, while the SP won four and was heading towards a fifth.

The SP had won both Varanasi seats in 2020 as well. Six years later, the BJP has failed to dislodge the party from either constituency despite its strong presence in the region.

Although the two MLC constituencies cover a wider geographical area than PM Modi's Lok Sabha seat, the results carry political significance given Varanasi's association with the Prime Minister since 2014.

They also come after PM Modi's victory margin in Varanasi declined from nearly 4.8 lakh votes in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections to around 1.5 lakh in 2024.

Across Uttar Pradesh, the SP's tally is set to rise from three seats in 2020 to five, while the BJP has retained its tally of six.

The SP had also emerged as the largest party in Uttar Pradesh in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning 37 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats against the BJP's 33.

BJP deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya acknowledged that the party had expected a better performance.

"These elections are decided by highly educated and qualified voters. The BJP has repeated its previous performance, but we expected to win more seats. We will examine why we fell short," Maurya said.

The SP, meanwhile, has repeatedly accused the BJP of electoral irregularities, allegations the ruling party has rejected.

On polling day, Akhilesh Yadav had claimed that the BJP was attempting to influence even the MLC elections, which have a limited electorate.

"If the BJP can do this in MLC polls for teachers and graduate constituencies where a limited number of people cast votes, one can imagine their preparation for the assembly polls," he had said.

What do the results mean for 2027?

The NDA's overall tally shows that the BJP and its allies remain ahead in these Legislative Council contests.

But the results in Nagpur and Varanasi also show that the party has struggled to regain certain seats despite its strong presence in both regions.

In Uttar Pradesh, the SP and Congress are preparing to contest the 2027 assembly elections together, hoping to build on their performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The alliance won 43 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats in 2024, reducing the BJP's tally from 62 in 2019 to 33.

Akhilesh Yadav has said the alliance will continue in 2027, although the two parties still need to settle their seat-sharing arrangement.

The MLC results, however, cannot be treated as an indication of how the state will vote in the assembly elections. These contests involve a limited electorate of registered graduates and teachers, unlike assembly polls, which are decided by a much wider voter base.

For the BJP, which is seeking a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, the challenge will be to counter the opposition's gains. For the SP-Congress alliance, the question is whether it can repeat its 2024 Lok Sabha performance when the state's 403 assembly seats go to the polls in 2027.

World.title: 'Vote chori' row: INDIA bloc to hold 'mock Parliament' to 'impeach' CEC Gyanesh Kumar; mega rally on Nov 1
World.content:
Earlier, bloc had sought permission from Delhi Police for Ashoka Hotel

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

We are protesting against this and will continue our fight,â Kharge said in a statement shared by the Congress on X.âThere is a Mock Parliament tomorrow, and on November 1, we are holding a rally where people are coming from across the country. World.title: A vitamin clue to stroke in the young? Bengaluru study finds low B6 levels
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A vitamin that helps the body process proteins and regulate important chemical reactions may offer a new clue to why young adults suffer strokes. A study by researchers in Bengaluru has found significantly lower levels of vitamin B6 in young adults who had an ischaemic stroke than in healthy people of a similar age.

Ahead of World Stroke Day on October 29, the findings draw attention to a possible factor associated with stroke in young adults. The study compared 171 young adults who had suffered an ischaemic stroke, caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain, with 249 healthy controls.

Median vitamin B6 levels in stroke patients were 40.9 nmol/L, compared with 65.6 nmol/L in the control group. Vitamin B6 insufficiency, defined by the researchers as levels below 30 nmol/L, was found in 12.3% of stroke patients, compared with just 0.7% of healthy controls.

Vitamin B6 is found in liver, fish such as tuna and salmon, chicken, chickpeas, sunflower seeds, pistachios, potatoes, bananas and spinach.

Prof Manjari Tripathi, head of the department of neurology at AIIMS, said vitamin B6 is essential for homocysteine metabolism. âLow vitamin B6 levels can impair this process, allowing homocysteine to rise. Elevated homocysteine can damage blood vessels, promote inflammation and contribute to clot formation, increasing stroke risk.





Maintaining adequate vitamin B6 levels through a balanced diet is important,â she said.

The Bengaluru study adds to evidence linking vitamin B6 levels with stroke risk, but whether improving these levels can prevent strokes remains unclear. Dr Pravin Gupta, chairman, Marengo Asia international institute of neuro and spine, said the study was significant because vitamin B6 levels can be measured through a blood test.

âHowever, this study shows an association, not proof that vitamin B6 supplements can prevent stroke.

Further research is needed,â he said.

The researchers, led by scientists from the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, found that lower vitamin B6 levels were independently associated with higher odds of ischaemic stroke even after accounting for other factors. Among stroke patients, vitamin B6 levels were strongly inversely correlated with homocysteine, an amino acid associated with blood vessel health.

in 2026, the case-control study adds to research into factors associated with stroke among younger adults. However, it cannot establish whether low vitamin B6 contributes to stroke, results from other health or dietary factors, or reflects an underlying process. Further studies are needed to validate the findings.

The results do not establish that vitamin B6 supplements can prevent stroke or that routine testing for the vitamin should be recommended for young adults.

World.title: Jamia student protest: Why is the Lyngdoh Committee report significant? | Explained
World.content:
The story so far: Jamia Millia Islamia recently set up a five-member committee to draft the constitution of its students’ union, which was dissolved in 2006. This came amid ongoing protests which began on October 12 to demand restoration of elected representation.

The committee, chaired by Dean of the Faculty of Social Sciences Zubair Meenai, is meant to look at why the students’ union was dissolved, the relevant court rulings, and the recommendations of the Lyngdoh Committee, dated 2006.
