World.title: ECB President Lagarde resigns at time of mounting challenges for Europe
World.content:
FILE PHOTO: European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde gestures as she addresses the press following the ECB's Governing Council meeting, at the ECB headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany, on February 5, 2026.

A source with direct knowledge of the matter says Christine Lagarde resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally

FRANKFURT, Germany – European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation on Thursday, October 29, ending months of speculation about her future just as Europe enters a period of rising economic volatility and divisive electoral politics.

Lagarde will step down on February 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick a successor well before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favored to win.

The move comes as the ECB battles inflation risks from an Iran-driven oil shock while a sharp rise in bond yields, especially in France, threatens to dampen growth.

“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde said in a short video shared on social media.

A source with direct knowledge of the matter said Lagarde had resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally. As ECB president, she was expected to remain neutral to safeguard the institution’s independence.

European Council President Antonio Costa said in a statement the process to find a successor for Lagarde would begin immediately. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely seen as frontrunners.

“The rumored successors are both very competent, well-established central bankers, so for markets, it won’t matter too much,” Piet Haines Christiansen, an economist at Danske Bank, said.

Financial markets did not move much after the announcement, with some analysts noting the ECB had by now built a reputation that outlived any of its leaders.

“The ECB is now quite well-established, the market is familiar with the way it operates,” Goldman Sachs’ head of Fixed Income Macro Investing Simon Dangoor said. “Our view is that institutional behavior is likely to outlast Lagarde, and be quite similar, whoever takes over.”

Lagarde’s term was scheduled to run until the end of October 2027, but speculation about an early departure had been mounting for months, with the World Economic Forum seen as a likely destination.

Rate hikes and bond turmoil

The ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle aimed at preventing an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages.

But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields — especially in debt-laden France — that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation.

Caught between persistent inflation fueled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday while signaling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely.

“There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB’s inflation forecast due to higher energy prices,” Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said.

The ECB is due to announce its interest rate decision at 1315 GMT on Thursday, followed by Lagarde’s regular press conference at 1345 GMT.

Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of next year, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.

French turmoil in focus but no action

The more immediate challenge for policymakers may be turmoil in bond markets.

A global rise in yields, fueled by stronger growth expectations, higher debt issuance and massive investment linked to artificial intelligence, is pushing up borrowing costs for governments, households and businesses alike.

In France, investors have become increasingly uneasy about the country’s growing debt burden and uncertain fiscal outlook following this year’s elections. Concerns have been amplified by suggestions from parts of the political left that debt held by the ECB could be written off.

The result has been a sharp increase in French borrowing costs. France is now paying some of the highest yields in a quarter-century to raise money on bond markets, while the premium investors demand to hold French debt over benchmark German bonds is larger than for any other euro zone country.

That has fueled speculation that the ECB might be forced to respond, if only verbally for now.

“They’ve typically come up with a new tool that’s customised for that specific set of circumstances,” said Dangoor at Goldman Sachs.

The ECB’s first line of defence would probably be flexible reinvestment of proceeds from bonds acquired during its vast asset-purchase programs of the previous decade.

Beyond that, it could activate its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, a scheme designed to counter what policymakers deem unjustified market pressure. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No report of Indonesian President confronting, scolding Marcos
World.content:
The video contains no footage, audio, or documentation of the alleged confrontation. Instead, the content features an unidentified male commentator reacting to a third-party social media post unrelated to the claim.

Claim: Indonesia’s president publicly confronted and scolded President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., telling him to “fix yourself and your country.”

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The YouTube channel “PINAS BALITA TV” with 175,000 subscribers published a video bearing the title: “GRABE NA! NAKAKAH1YA TO! IND0NESIAN PRESIDENT HARAPANG SINUP4L-P4L at NA-REALTALK si BEBE EM?” (This is too much! How embarrassing! Indonesian President confronted and engaged BBM in real talk?)

The video’s thumbnail, posted on October 17, 2026, shows an enraged Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto pointing directly at the President’s face before press microphones and cameras.

In the video’s original thumbnail, the uploader claimed that the Indonesian leader told Marcos to “fix your country and yourself,” though this line has since been edited out as of writing.



As of writing, the video has garnered 3,100 views and 234 likes.

The facts: No credible news reports or official footage confirm that Indonesia’s Subianto confronted or publicly engaged Marcos in real talk before the press.



AI image detectors IsThisAI reveal that the thumbnail of the video is 99% likely to be AI-generated. Meanwhile, SightEngine flagged it as 87% likely to have used generative AI, and TruthScan estimated an 85% edit probability with high confidence.



“The background crowd appears to be cloned or manipulated, showing unnatural repetition patterns. Shadows on the subjects’ faces and clothing are inconsistent, further suggesting digital editing,” the TruthScan findings said.

Lack of evidence: The video contains no footage, audio, or documentation of any confrontation. Instead, the content features an unidentified male commentator reacting to a third-party social media post.

The commentator compares how both governments address climate challenges — particularly El Niño — contrasting Indonesia’s reported distribution of water pumps with the Philippine government’s recommendation to collect rainwater using buckets. The commentator heavily criticized the administration’s suggested solution.



Existing ties: Diplomatic ties between the Philippines and Indonesia remain stable as of writing. Both countries held bilateral meetings in 2024, and Marcos, along with First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, formally welcomed President Subianto during the opening ceremony of the 48th ASEAN Summit held in Cebu in May 2026.

Marcos also traveled to Jakarta to attend Subianto’s presidential inauguration in 2024.

Debunked: Marcos has been a frequent subject of false claims, particularly controversies:

– Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is a Metro Manila-based journalist who primarily covers Bicol and Baguio. She is also an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: LIST: Evidence submitted by prosecution to impeach court vs Sara Duterte
World.content:
PROSEC. Members of the prosecution listen to a ruling during Day 22 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 7, 2026.

Rappler obtained a copy of the prosecution's formal offer of evidence. Here are key documents that are part of the submission.

After the prosecution wrapped up the presentation of its case in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, it submitted its formal offer of evidence to the court.

It’s a mandatory submission that allows the prosecution to state the specific purpose of each piece of evidence, although the defense may still contest it.

Rappler obtained a copy of the formal offer of evidence. Below are key documents that are part of the submission.

1. Her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs) from 2007 to 2025, from the Office of the Ombudsman

Her SALNs show her or her husband’s continued stake with Gencorp, Metro City Chow Foods Corporation, and Cale88 Foods Corporation, while she is already a sitting vice president, apparently in violation of Article VII, Section 13 of the Constitution.

Her SALNs supposedly prove she did not declare her 51 firearms, her properties in Matina and Kembali, her cash on hand and in bank from 2019 to 2025, and various insurance policies and investments.

Prosecutors say her ending bank balances from 2022 to 2025 do not match her declared total personal assets for those years.

2. Corporate records of companies tied to her and her husband Mans Carpio

The prosecutors submitted SEC records of the following entities to prove that she and/or her husband are either an incorporator, shareholder, or member of the board of directors. City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation Metro City Chow Foods Corporation Gencorp Industries Cale88 Foods Corporation Mati City Ice Plant and Cold Storage Geometry Security and Investigation Agency Great Jolly Times Food Corp Timesquare Bee Foods Corp Davao New Royal Taipan Foods Corporation Davao Emerging Taipans Corporation 3Kids Trucking Services CYK&T Davao Corporation SGT Fortune Horse Corporation Davao Bounty Times Foods Corporation Madayaw Fisheries Amianan Shores Cabletow 88 Shipping and Marine Services Carpio Lawyers Pikimong Pikimong Philippines Corporation JTC Group of Companies Philippines

The general information sheets and/or audited financial statements of many of these companies supposedly prove Duterte and/or her husband did not receive dividend income from the firms.

The SEC records of some of these companies also show that Duterte and/or her husband subscribed a paid-up capital to the firms, yet the shareholdings were not declared in the SALN.

3. Philippine Statistics Authority records

Their marriage certificate establishes that there is no prenuptial agreement between them.

4. Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilgGEPS) records of contracts won by their supposed companies

The procurement records between Gencorp and either Davao City LGU, PhilHealth Region 10, and the Overseas Workers Welfre Administration Region 11 supposedly prove she violated the constitutional prohibition on government officials being financially interested in government contracts. Most notably, Gencorp bagged 19 contracts worth at least P34 million with the Davao City LGU led by her brother Mayor Sebastian Duterte from 2022 to 2026.



Play Video

5. Records of her firearms with the Philippine National Police

The certifications issued by the PNP Firearms and Explosives Office (FEO) to Duterte and her husband document their combined total of 51 guns worth P7.2 million, assets not declared in her SALN.

6. Land Registration Authority (LRA) records of relevant properties

The transfer certificates of title, among other LRA documents, detail Duterte and her husband’s properties in Kembali and Matina, which are absent from her SALNs.

7. Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) reports

AMLC records detail covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs) involving Duterte and her husband worth P4.4 billion from 2007 to 2025. The amount includes P424 million during her stint as vice president.

.The AMLC reports cover large US dollar cash withdrawals, time deposit renewals, single-day multi-million peso transfers, and significant over-the-counter cash withdrawals/check encashments.

One of their companies, Cale88, supposedly received P368.8 million in foreign remittances, including P319.3 million from senders in China.

8. Bank records

Prosecutors submitted records from the following banks: BDO Unibank (seven accounts) BPI (six accounts) Landbank (one account) Metrobank (three accounts) Philippine Savings Bank (two accounts) Security Bank (one account) PNB (four accounts) Unionbank (one account) Asia United Bank (two accounts)

Prosecutors say the 27 bank accounts show total year-end balances of P207.6 million from 2022 to 2025, which were not declared in her SALNs for those years.

9. Insurance and investment company records

Duterte and her husband have active insurance policies across seven companies from 2022 to 2025, none of which were declared in her SALN.

These companies are: BDO Life (two insurance investments) BDO Securities (seven securities/ other investments) BPI AIA (one insurance investment) FWD Life (one insurance investment) Manulife (six insurance investments) Allianz (two insurance investments) Prulife (five insurance investments)



10. Tax records with the Bureau and Internal Revenue (BIR)

The BIR records of the couple show their combined income of P85.3 million from 2027 to 2025, which prosecutors assert is vastly disproportionate to their declared net worth and calculated unexplained wealth.

Some of the documents also show that Duterte earned income from practicing law and received funds from Davao City Hall while she is vice president.

11. Forensic examination report

The forensic report of veteran Certified Public Accountant or CPA lawyer Alexander Cabrera found that Duterte and her husband have an unexplained wealth of at least P817.8 million from 2022 to 2025.

Play Video

– Rappler.com

World.title: [READOUT] How can businesses win back customers amid a weak peso and high inflation?
World.content:
Businesses must balance rising costs against the dwindling purchasing power and growing frustration of cash-strapped consumers

What can businesses do to win over customers already struggling with high prices? An October study by Organic Intelligence suggests a concrete response some brands could consider.

Asked what would make a brand feel genuinely on their side, the top response was a price freeze (27%), ahead of smaller tingi sizes (16%), free shipping (14%), and promotional bundles (12%). The study’s researchers later told Rappler that a price freeze campaign would be highly effective in building customer loyalty with value-conscious customers.

The findings reflect how financially stretched consumers have become. The survey of 800 urban Filipinos, conducted in May, also found that 42% had borrowed for essentials such as food and transportation, while 45% said inflation had drained their motivation to get ahead.

And the pressure is unlikely to ease in the near-term. September inflation reached 7.2%, with further acceleration expected when October figures come out on November 5.

READ: The urban Filipino is tired, cash-strapped, and sick of the ‘resilience’ excuse

Meanwhile, businesses must weigh consumer sentiment against how much of their rising costs they can realistically pass on to consumers.

The peso closed at another historic low of P64.17 to the dollar on Tuesday, October 27, despite the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) delivering a larger-than-expected 50 basis point rate hike just five days earlier. That brought its policy rate to 5.50%, following four consecutive increases this year.

After the same Monetary Board meeting, the BSP raised its 2027 inflation forecast from 5.4% to 6%, signaling that businesses may have to contend with higher costs and weaker consumer purchasing power for longer.

The BSP, however, is in no hurry to defend the peso at any particular exchange rate. Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said the central bank would largely let the currency find its own level, intervening only to cushion excessive movements that could worsen inflation.

Former BSP deputy governor Diwa Guinigundo pointed to deeper problems behind the peso’s slide, including weak capital flows, the country’s balance of payments deficit, low foreign investment, and investor uncertainty surrounding corruption allegations and the ongoing messy impeachment trial.

Consider the numbers:

The Philippines recorded a $9.1-billion balance of payments deficit in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $5.3 billion a year earlier. Foreign portfolio investments registered $4.25 billion in net outflows from January to August, reversing $4.58 billion in inflows a year earlier.

The country’s hefty import bill also creates enormous demand for dollars. Consider that imports of mineral fuels and related products alone increased by $2.56 billion year on year in the first half of 2026.

And the pressure could persist. The BSP forecasts another $8.5-billion balance of payments deficit in 2027, alongside a $19.4-billion current account deficit.

Foreign exchange reserves, meanwhile, fell from $104.8 billion in August to $99.5 billion in September, partly due to BSP foreign exchange operations, valuation adjustments, and government withdrawals. Still, those reserves are enough to cover 6.2 months of import.

READ: [READOUT] What a stickier inflation wave could mean for businesses

How this affects businesses depends on which side of the dollar they sit.

Import-dependent manufacturers, retailers, airlines, and companies with unhedged dollar debt face higher costs. Exporters and business process outsourcing firms earning dollars while paying expenses in pesos could benefit from the exchange rate. Higher interest rates, meanwhile, make new borrowing and refinancing costlier, adding pressure to firms already struggling with input costs.

Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. says prolonged inflation may pose a greater threat to economic growth than higher interest rates, especially with household consumption accounting for around 70% of the economy.

Looking ahead, the November 9 third quarter 2026 GDP release will be the next measure to watch after economic growth slowed to a disappointing 2.3% in the second quarter of 2026.

Yet difficult economic conditions have not stopped companies from raising capital.

GCash parent Mynt completed the largest IPO in Philippine history on October 20, with the Philippine Stock Exchange reporting a P60.9-billion offering, including the overallotment. Meanwhile, Cebu-based Aznar Shipping is set to launch a smaller IPO of up to P737 million, targeting a December 18 listing to finance fleet and shipyard expansion.

We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters.

World.title: Who are the candidates short-listed for SC associate justice?
World.content:
Marcos will pick his next SC associate justice appointee in place of retiring Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier

MANILA, Philippines – A total of 11 candidates have been short-listed by the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for the position of Supreme Court (SC) associate justice vice Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier, who will retire on November 16.

Here are the short-listed candidates in alphabetical order:

Court of Appeals (CA) Associate Justice Ramon M. Bato Jr.

Solicitor General Darlene Marie B. Berberabe

Commission on Audit Chairperson Gamaliel A. Cordoba

CA Associate Justice Ramon A. Cruz

CA Associate Justice Maria Elisa Sempio Diy

CA Associate Justice Myra V. Garcia-Fernandez

CA Presiding Justice Fernanda Lampas Peralta

Commission on Elections Commissioner Ernesto P. Maceda, Jr.

CA Associate Justice Ronaldo Roberto B. Martin

CA Associate Justice Walter S. Ong

Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice Maria Rowena M. San Pedro

Under the 1987 Constitution, the JBC is mandated to screen applicants for the judiciary and the Office of the Ombudsman. After the screening, the JBC will conduct public interviews of the qualified candidates. A deliberation will follow, then the council will submit a short list to the president who will then make the appointment.

In this case, the JBC held the public interviews for the new candidates on October 13 and 15. It no longer interviewed bets who already went through the process since their interviews were still valid.

The judiciary is independent, but it is the president who is constitutionally mandated to make appointments to the courts. In this case, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will appoint his next justice to the High Court after Lazaro Javier reaches the mandatory age of 70 next month.

According to the SC, the short list has already been transmitted to Malacañang.

An SC justice must be a natural-born citizen, at least 40 years old, and have been a judge or law practitioner in the Philippines for at least 15 years or more. This is found under Section 7(1), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.

On top of this, a JBC 2020 rule states that an SC justice must serve a minimum of 2.5 years. This means that the eldest age of a candidate should be 67.5 years old, since the mandatory retirement age for justices is 70 years old.

On Thursday, the JBC also published the short list of chief justice nominees. These are the five candidates seeking to succeed Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo:

Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen

Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa

Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda

Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao

Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez

The chief justice and associate justice posts will be Marcos’ second and third appointee to the SC, which is currently dominated by appointees of former president Rodrigo Duterte. – Rappler.com

World.title: SM Active welcomes every Filipino to an active lifestyle at SM Supermalls
World.content:
Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by SM Supermalls and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

For years, SM Supermalls has brought sports and wellness closer to every Filipino through its facilities, tournaments, and community events. As more Filipinos embrace an active lifestyle, SM Supermalls is broadening its quest of providing more opportunities and spaces to stay fit. SM Supermalls is opening a new chapter by bringing its efforts together under one brand: SM Active.

Evolving from SM Active Hub, SM Active is SM Supermalls’ broader vision to make active living part of everyday life for more Filipinos. Through SM Active, individuals and communities will experience a more integrated active ecosystem, making their experiences more meaningful and memorable.

Operating within the SM Ecosystem, SM Active brings together its facilities, sports and wellness offerings, and corporate partners. By leveraging SM Supermalls’ vast network, SM Active creates more opportunities to keep active and build stronger connections.

IMMERSIVE EXPERIENCE. SM Active’s quality facilities set the stage for play and wellness



“For over 30 years, SM has invested in spaces and experiences that encourage Filipinos to move, play, and connect. Through SM Active, we are bringing these strengths together under one brand with a simple goal: to make active living more accessible, inclusive, and part of everyday life for communities across the country. As we continue to grow our ecosystem of facilities, partners, and programs, SM Active aims to become every Filipino’s gateway to a healthier and more active lifestyle,” said Steven Tan, SM Supermalls president.

A GROWING COMMUNITY. SM Active connects sports and wellness enthusiasts through one integrated network



Through SM Active, SM Supermalls is looking to bring more communities together by leveraging its nationwide footprint, deep partnerships, and quality facilities nationwide. SM Active is more than just a wellness initiative. It is SM Supermalls’ long-term pledge to empower more Filipinos to stay active and healthy.

AN INSPIRING SPACE. SM Active is home to professional athletes and fitness enthusiasts



Whether you’re just starting an active lifestyle or looking to level up, SM Active offers a wide range of facilities and events to keep you moving. With the country’s largest network of mall-based sports and active living facilities, SM Active features 108 pickleball courts, 176 bowling lanes, three ice skating rinks, expanding jogging paths, and more developments underway. Beyond providing spaces to play, SM Active brings communities together through regular events, and transforms open areas into vibrant spaces for sports, fitness and wellness.

Together, these offerings have made it easier for newbies, enthusiasts, and experienced athletes to find activities that match their interests. SM Active elevates this experience by uniting the country’s most comprehensive network under one unified brand.

VALUED PARTICIPATION. From weekend workouts to friendly tournaments, SM Active brings people together through movement



“SM Supermalls believes that active living should be accessible to everyone. This has been part of our core mission ever since. With SM Active, we are unifying all our programs, experiences, and facilities to reaffirm our commitment to making active living a part of everyday life,” said Tan.

GET MOVING. SM Active is the place to play, compete, and connect with a thriving active community



– Rappler.com

World.title: All 5 chief justice candidates make it to JBC shortlist
World.content:
JBC. The Judicial and Bar Council commences the public panel interviews for the position of chief justice of the Republic of the Philippines, in view of the compulsory retirement of Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo on November 6, 2026.

Marcos will pick his chief justice from the list that includes Leonen, Caguioa, Zalameda, Dimaampao, and Marquez

MANILA, Philippines – All five Supreme Court (SC) associate justices aspiring to become the country’s next chief justice have made it to the Judicial and Bar Council’s (JBC) shortlist, SC spokesperson Camille Sue Mae Ting confirmed to Rappler on Thursday, October 29.

Multiple sources also confirmed to Rappler the said information.

This means that the following are eligible to be chosen as the country’s 28th chief justice and successor of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo who is retiring on November 6:

Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen

Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa

Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda

Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao

Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez

The judiciary is a co-equal and independent branch of the government but under the rules, it’s the President who appoints people to the judiciary. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will pick his appointee from this shortlist provided by the JBC.

Under Article VIII, Sections 4 and 9 of the 1987 Constitution, the SC vacancy must be filled by Marcos within 90 days. So, he has until February 2027 to pick the next chief magistrate.

Leonen will serve as acting chief justice once Gesmundo retires until the President names his appointee.

After screening applicants, the JBC held the public interviews for the five qualified candidates on October 22 and 26. After this, it held deliberations and determined the shortlist.

The next chief justice would be Marcos’ second or third appointee to the SC, which is currently dominated by Duterte appointees. Marcos’ other pending appointment is the replacement for Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, who retires on November 16. Either appointment could come first.

Once these appointments are made, there will now be three Marcos appointees to the High Court. Only Leonen and Caguioa were appointed by former president Benigno Aquino III.

World.title: China’s Monroe Doctrine and Its Strategic Blunder in Myanmar
World.content:
The United States has its Monroe Doctrine, which asserts American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere, placing Latin America within its sphere of influence. Over the past three decades, China’s rapid economic growth and military expansion have transformed it from a regional power into a global superpower. It is therefore unsurprising that Beijing would seek to establish a similar sphere of influence over neighboring Southeast Asian countries.

Myanmar holds particular strategic importance for China. Through Rakhine State, Beijing can access the Indian Ocean, bypassing the strategically vulnerable Strait of Malacca during a crisis. Myanmar also possesses substantial deposits of rare earth elements essential to modern technologies. Furthermore, the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) is one of the six major economic corridors under China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

Yet in pursuing these geopolitical objectives, China appears to be missing the forest for the trees. Its decision to prop up Myanmar’s military junta at the expense of democratic forces represents a serious strategic miscalculation—a bet on the wrong horse. Following a widely discredited sham election, the junta has attempted to rebrand itself as a civilian government under former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing, with a ruling party dominated by military officers and loyalists. Such a regime is ill-equipped to deliver what China needs: a stable, secure and predictable neighbor capable of supporting its long-term economic ambitions through the BRI and its broader maritime strategy.

The culprit behind an unstable neighbor

Since the 2021 military coup, Myanmar has become increasingly unstable, while ethnic resistance organizations (EROs) have expanded their territorial control. Ironically, many resources and infrastructure projects China hopes to develop now lie in territories controlled by EROs and People’s Defense Forces (PDFs). Rare earth deposits are concentrated in Kachin State, where the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) exercises substantial control. The Chinese-backed Kyaukphyu deep-sea port, a strategic gateway to the Indian Ocean, lies in Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army (AA) has established extensive territorial control. Significant stretches of the China-Myanmar gas pipeline also pass through areas where resistance forces operate in Magway and Mandalay regions.

So far, PDFs and EROs have shown considerable restraint in refraining from attacking these strategic assets. This reflects, in part, their desire to earn Beijing’s goodwill and demonstrate their ability to safeguard Chinese investments.

An unreliable partner turning to criminality

Myanmar’s economy has deteriorated sharply under the weight of military expenditure, corruption, nepotism and mismanagement. The junta is in no position to fulfill its commitments under numerous bilateral economic agreements with China, particularly because it cannot guarantee security in project areas. Worse, the regime has allowed scam centers to proliferate, with some military officers reportedly maintaining close ties to the warlords operating them. Many centers, particularly in northern Shan State, have targeted Chinese citizens. Despite repeated requests from Beijing, the military failed to take effective action.

Operation 1027, launched by an alliance of ethnic armed organizations, proceeded with Beijing’s tacit approval after the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) framed it partly as a campaign against scam operations. Among those subsequently handed over to China was Bai Suocheng, a former lawmaker from the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party.

Beyond its inability to provide stability and security, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime is hardly a trustworthy ally. He has repeatedly sought to balance competing powers against one another and could readily turn against China if doing so served his interests. His efforts to court Western goodwill were evident in a recent TIME magazine interview, a low-profile U.S. delegation visit to Naypyitaw in September and the expensive hiring of Washington-based lobbying firms to advocate on its behalf.

Previously, Min Aung Hlaing courted Russia to counterbalance China’s influence, only to turn back toward Beijing when Moscow could not meet his needs. Beijing should think twice before entrusting its long-term strategic interests to a regime whose loyalty is conditional and whose survival is increasingly uncertain.

Why the opposition is a more reliable partner

Many EROs have concluded that genuine autonomy, security, and prosperity are unattainable under military-dominated rule. They increasingly see their future in a federal democratic union. For decades, these organizations understood that none could defeat the military alone. They also recognize that their battlefield successes since 2021 would have been far more difficult without the nationwide Spring Revolution, which fundamentally transformed the country’s political landscape.

This convergence of ethnic resistance and the broader pro-democracy movement has created an unprecedented opportunity. In March 2026, the movement took a significant step forward with the formation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF). It brings together influential resistance actors, including the KIO, KNU, CNF, Karenni National Progressive Party (KNPP), Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), and National Unity Government (NUG). A few months later, the federal units of Sagaing, Mandalay, and Magway joined the initiative.

The SCEF combines political leadership and military coordination within a common framework. It seeks not merely to defeat the junta but also to lay the institutional foundations for a future federal state. For China, this emerging coalition offers an alternative to continued dependence on a weakening military regime.

The assumption that China cannot tolerate a flourishing democracy in its neighborhood oversimplifies Beijing’s strategic interests and Southeast Asia’s political realities. China already maintains important economic and diplomatic relationships with democracies such as Japan, South Korea and India. Myanmar is comparatively small, and any government emerging from the current conflict will have compelling geographic and economic reasons to maintain constructive relations with its powerful neighbor. A federal democratic Myanmar has no inherent reason to be antagonistic toward Beijing.

Myanmar’s democratic forces are also learning that the West is unlikely to sustain its strategic attention. The Trump administration included Myanmar among the countries subject to a full travel ban, while its dismantling of USAID disrupted American assistance. Washington’s reported attempts to reengage clandestinely with the junta have further frustrated the democratic movement.

In contrast, the NUG has adopted a pragmatic approach toward Beijing. Its 10-point Position on China, released on January 1, 2024, explicitly commits to safeguarding Chinese investments and cooperating with China against online scams and human trafficking. Democratic forces thus recognize the importance of maintaining a workable relationship with their powerful neighbor.

A strategic opening for Beijing

China’s ambition to achieve national rejuvenation and modernization by the centenary of the People’s Republic of China in 2049 requires long-term strategic thinking rather than short-term political expediency.

By recalibrating its Myanmar policy, Beijing has a rare opportunity to earn the goodwill of the Myanmar people at a pivotal moment. Supporting a political settlement that recognizes the aspirations of ethnic nationalities and democratic forces would not undermine China’s interests. On the contrary, it could help establish the stability, security, and predictability Beijing has long sought.

China should therefore engage constructively with the SCEF and other credible democratic stakeholders rather than continue to prop up a failing junta. Such engagement could protect Chinese investments, improve regional stability and strengthen Beijing’s international standing.

The underlying principle of a Chinese Monroe Doctrine—a regional sphere of influence shaped by strategic interests—is understandable as a geopolitical ambition. But achieving that ambition requires choosing partners wisely. If China wants to secure its long-term interests in Myanmar, supporting the forces capable of building a stable federal democratic union would be a far more prudent investment than backing a military regime marked by declining territorial control, economic mismanagement and uncertain loyalty.

Than N. Oo is a co-founder of advocacy group Free Myanmar and writes frequently about Myanmar’s political developments.

World.title: Nationalist Regime Supporters Turn Against China Over Northern Shan
World.content:
Staunchly nationalist supporters of the Myanmar military are growing wary of the regime’s increasing dependency on China on all fronts, voicing rare criticism of the way Chinese money and influence are being allowed to shape their country.

It was the question of northern Shan State that finally galvanized this resentment among the pro-military crowd.

Many nationalists believe that China enabled Operation 1027, the offensive by an alliance of three ethnic armed groups that dealt a serious blow to the Myanmar military in 2023-24. They staged protests at the time accusing Beijing of interference, and the sentiment has recently resurfaced over what they see as the “Sinicization” of borderlands that the regime has lost in northern Shan.

“We accept them making investment in our country. But supplying arms and funds to ethnic armed groups to capture towns and interfering in our government is unacceptable,” a nationalist told The Irrawaddy. “Public opinion must be voiced openly.”

The renewed criticism comes after the Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—an ethnic coalition comprising the Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD), and a Shan militia group—issued a statement on Oct. 23 accusing Kokang’s Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) of imposing Chinese language in schools, granting land rights to foreigners, and erasing local traditions in territories it seized during Operation 1027. The MNDAA swiftly rejected the allegations as unfounded.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and the stability of the China–Myanmar border.

Ta’ang civil society groups similarly condemned the MNDAA in April after it seized Kutkai Township, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

At the peak of Operation 1027, China pressured armed groups to agree ceasefires with the regime in northern Shan, but since then has allowed them to consolidate their quasi-autonomous administrations there rather than handing back all the territory they had gained to the regime.

No other armed group has been able to consolidate administrative control as rapidly as the MNDAA, which analysts say would be impossible without Beijing’s backing.

Regime supporters were initially silent about this perceived Sinicization, but started to voice concerns when exiled independent media widely covered Chinese border encroachment in northern Shan areas controlled by the MNDAA. The regime warned domestic outlets not to publish stories that could damage bilateral ties, but the concerns persisted.

The pot seems to have boiled over when Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun in mid-October recommended “high-level autonomy” for ethnic monitories. His remark was interpreted in different ways across Myanmar’s political circles, stirring debate over China’s intentions.

Along Myanmar’s eastern frontier, three armed groups are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, the others being the United Wa State Army (UWSA) and the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA). The latter two have upheld ceasefires with the Myanmar military for nearly four decades, and in return they exercise de-facto autonomy in their fiefdoms, serving as effective buffers that insulate China from Myanmar’s instability.

Under the 2008 Constitution, the MNDAA’s Kokang—with a population of fewer than 200,000—is a self‑administered zone, but that covers only Laukkai and Kongyan townships east of the Salween River. But after Operation 1027, the MNDAA reorganized both that original enclave and newly captured areas into four districts: Laukkai, Kutkai, Hsenwi, and Monekoe. Governance in these territories increasingly mirrors administrative practices seen in Beijing, raising alarm not only among staunch nationalists but also among some lawmakers.

“We don’t like it when a powerful neighbor interferes in our sovereignty,” one MP remarked. But he admitted, “The Myanmar government is not in a position to shut out China. We don’t have that strength, and we are deteriorating in every aspect.”

Democracy activists, for their part, accuse Beijing of propping up the military since the coup, reaping political and economic benefits. The exiled leader of the Democratic Party for a New Society, Hnin Hnin Hmwe, said the regime itself is starting to worry about its over-reliance on China.

“China has pushed its interests so far that even the regime is beginning to feel constrained,” she said. “At the same time, China maintains ties with revolutionary forces. China is shrewd to keep the balance.”

World.title: Resistance Forces Inflict Heavy Losses on Regime Troops in Indaw
World.content:
A Myanmar junta offensive to reclaim territory in Sagaing Region’s Indaw Township near the Kachin State border has suffered heavy losses in resistance ambushes, resistance sources said.

Dozens of junta troops were killed and many, including a tactical commander, were reportedly captured by pro-democracy forces.

Troops from two regime Tactical Commands advancing south from Indaw town toward Wuntho and Tigyaing were ambushed by resistance forces on October 4. According to reports, the regime units buried the bodies of dead soldiers in local villages, and one Tactical Command lost contact with its base.

The regime retook control of Indaw town and the Mandalay-Myitkyina road from resistance forces at the end of April. However, it is still conducting clearance operations in the area.

On October 4, roughly 700 troops from Indaw, led by Colonel Kyaw Win Tun, deputy commander of the 33rd Light Infantry Division (LID), advanced south and split into two Tactical Commands: Tactical Command 331, led by Col. Myo Thein, and Tactical Command 332, led by Col. Kyaw San Win.

Both were ambushed by resistance forces, sparking fierce clashes and prompting the regime to bomb the area from the air, Indaw Revolution (IR), a local news information page, reported on Monday.

IR reported that locals found the bodies of 50 regime soldiers near Nanthe Village and cremated them on October 23. Other soldiers’ bodies were spotted near villages on the Indaw-Tigyaing road, it said.

“Eyewitnesses reported over 50 dead bodies. More than 20 [regime soldiers] surrendered, and it is initially understood that a tactical commander was among them,” a source close to the resistance forces told The Irrawaddy.

Intense clashes were reported between regime troops and resistance groups—including the civilian National Unity Government’s People’s Defense Force (PDF), the Kachin Independence Army, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front and allied groups—on October 25 and 26.

Zin Yaw, a military defector and military analyst, told The Irrawaddy that both Tactical Commands had suffered heavy losses.

“Tactical Command 332 led by Col. Kyaw San Win lost communication with the base for 48 hours,” Zin Yaw said.

The troops led by Col. Kyaw San Win advanced along the Indaw-Tigyaing road and ended up near Ma Au Kone Village, which is 23 km south of Indaw town.

According to the reports, some regime soldiers were captured by or voluntarily surrendered to resistance forces.

However, The Irrawaddy couldn’t independently verify the situation, and there has been no official statement from resistance forces or the regime yet.

Madaya Myohman force, which is under the command of the Mandalay PDF and is believed to have taken part in the ambushes, stated that the regime’s 33rd LID faced heavy losses on Monday.

The clashes and bombing in the area forced residents of at least 35 villages in Indaw and Wuntho townships to flee their homes, according to a source close to the resistance.

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Applications Plunge at Thai CI Centers Amid Boycott
World.content:
The number of Myanmar migrant workers applying for Certificates of Identity (CI) in Thailand has dropped sharply in the past few days following the launch of a social media campaign against the CI process, according to migrant groups and agents.

The Myanmar regime opened five Thai hubs on October 14, offering migrant workers CI required for residency and work. In exchange, workers must comply with a new Labor Ministry mandate to remit 25 percent of their wages through official channels and pay 2 percent annual tax.

The number of registered Myanmar workers in Thailand rose to nearly 3 million as of November 2025, but a significant population remains undocumented.

Many migrants say that as low-wage workers they can barely afford CI application fees, while the regime’s mandatory 6,000-baht remittance rule adds an extra layer of cost.

Labor activists say the boycott is also being driven by reluctance to legitimize the regime or help fund its ongoing military attacks on civilians.

Migrants launched the online campaign on Oct. 18, calling on the Thai government to grant them residency-work permits without CI documents.

Regime Labour Minister Maung Myint slammed the campaign on Oct. 20, insisting the new process was meant to ease CI registration for workers in Thailand. He claimed that around 1,500 workers had used the new centres in the first few days. However, migrant workers groups and agents said applications have plunged as the campaign gains momentum.

“Very few workers are applying for the CI,” Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee, which assists migrants, told The Irrawaddy on Tuesday.

“Normally, the CI centre in Samut Sakhon alone receives over 1,000 CI applications daily,” he said, adding that the hub has gone quiet in the past few days.

He estimated that at least 500,000 workers are due to apply for their CI, but few are showing up at centers.

Labor activists said workers were also delaying CI renewal because of the cost.

“Migrants’ income levels vary,” Naing Aung Aung of the Arkan Worker Organization in Thailand told The Irrawaddy. “Some took loans to pay for passport and visa issuance. They don’t have extra savings.”

He said the regime’s remittance scheme is unviable given it can easily be bypassed by bribing corrupt officials. Applicants can secure a CI without evidence of remittance for a fee of 1,500 baht, according to labor activists and agents.

Experts note the new policy benefits the cash-strapped regime while piling financial burdens on low-paid workers and cutting remittance lifelines for their families at home. They argue that instead of restrictions and punishment, workers should be offered incentives to remit money through official channels.

Under the current scheme, Myanmar workers lose at least 5,000 kyats for every 100 baht they remit via regime-endorsed channels. While official channels offer 125 kyat per baht, informal markets offer upwards of 130.

The Labour Ministry continues to push the new scheme, projecting that 2026 inflows will match last year’s total of US$ 5.6 billion. Annual remittances have more than doubled since 2019, driven by the mass emigration of workers escaping the turmoil and economic collapse that followed the 2021 coup.

World.title: Hostage Diplomacy: How the Myanmar Junta Is Weaponizing Jailed Aung San Suu Kyi
World.content:
As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s November summit approaches, the Myanmar junta—desperate for international recognition—has made a series of minor concessions regarding access to jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Highlighting the regime’s ongoing atrocities against civilians, observers and anti-regime groups have warned that the regime’s moves are merely a ploy to win resumption of full participation in ASEAN and ease international pressure.

Since the 2021 coup, the Myanmar regime has been barred from attending high-level ASEAN summits for failing to comply with the bloc’s peace plan, which calls for the immediate cessation of violence against civilians and the opening of a dialogue among all concerned groups, among other things.

Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to meet with ICRC representatives in Naypyitaw on August 3, and to receive books and a diplomatic letter from King Charles on October 19. The jailed Nobel Peace Prize laureate was also permitted to talk with her youngest son, Kim Aris, on October 22, for the first time in the five years since her arrest.

Domestic and regional observers warn that the regime has started using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to gain access to the bloc’s upcoming summit.

“The regime led by the sham president Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to scam the world by using hostage diplomacy,” said Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma.

She cited another recent instance of hostage diplomacy, in which the junta jailed 78 Filipino trafficking victims who had escaped from scam centers. Instead of repatriating them, the regime used the victims as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Maria Teresa Lazaro, the Philippine foreign secretary, who was forced to request the release of her compatriots during a visit to Naypyitaw in January, then thank the internationally-isolated regime for freeing the jailed Philippine nationals.

An ASEAN humanitarian delegation led by the bloc’s special envoy Maria Teresa Lazaro is scheduled to visit Myanmar for two days starting Wednesday.

The tactic was used again with the detention of U.S. citizen Adam Castillo, which allowed the regime to secure engagement with the U.S, Stothard said. A delegation of U.S. officials visited Naypyitaw to secure Castillo’s release.

“The regime continues to use its hostage diplomacy by … dangling Aung San Suu Kyi to secure normalization of relations with ASEAN,” she said. “ASEAN and the international community shouldn’t be easily scammed this way. They shouldn’t be normalizing relations with a gangster who is the architect of genocide and war crimes.”

Thailand welcomed the U.S. engagement with the regime and expected discussions to be held at the upcoming ASEAN summit in Manila on how to proceed with the Myanmar issue, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told media on Friday.

The minister, who is working to improve relations between ASEAN and the military regime, commented that the regime’s granting of permission for Aung San Suu Kyi and her son to speak represented a positive development.

Further evidence of the regime’s concerted effort to secure ASEAN’s recognition and support can be seen in Naypyitaw’s recent decision to form an ASEAN Affairs Committee to communicate and cooperate with the bloc.

Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, who chairs the committee, said it was formed to foster additional channels of engagement with ASEAN. The regime is currently engaging regional neighbors on a country-by-country basis according to priority levels, he added.

Coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been engaging with the U.S., and in recent months has visited ASEAN members Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

David Gum Awng, deputy foreign affairs minister of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), told The Irrawaddy he shares the view that the regime is using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to secure Min Aung Hlaing’s attendance at the upcoming ASEAN summit.

“Civilian leader Daw Aung San Suu Kyi is entirely innocent and is merely a political hostage unjustly detained by the regime for political reasons. Allowing her to receive books and gifts sent by King Charles and permitting a 20-minute phone call with her son is purely a political transaction by the regime,” he said.

He said the regime’s recent moves are a political ploy, despite some ASEAN member countries’ characterization of them as a positive development, and warned that “ASEAN needs to see this reality.”

Mon Mon Myat, lecturer at the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, remarked that the junta’s apparent relaxation regarding access to the jailed civilian leader “might include hopes of being allowed to attend the ASEAN summit. It appears they urgently need both international recognition and assistance. On the other hand, they might be pushing for this out of fear of becoming more isolated on the international stage if the ICJ ruling comes out later this year.” The International Court of Justice is considering a genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya minority in Rakhine State.

The regime’s charm offensive may be having some effect. Former Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in an exclusive interview with Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should assist in Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN. For the time being, however, ASEAN as a bloc is upholding its summit ban, citing the failure to honor its peace plan. Known as the Five-Point Consensus, the plan established over five years ago in Jakarta includes calls for an immediate end to violence and the holding of dialogues. Both coup president Min Aung Hlaing and his rubber-stamp parliament have formally rejected the plan. Meanwhile, the regime continues its five-year campaign of airstrikes, shelling and village burnings.

The NUG’s David Gum Awng said ASEAN must clearly and decisively call out the regime’s total failure to implement the peace plan. He warned that bilateral engagement with the junta by individual member states is emboldening the regime’s war crimes against civilians, rather than applying necessary pressure.

“While ASEAN member states may have different views on the country’s crisis, there must be definite consequences if the junta fails to comply with the agreements. Without clear repercussions for their defiance, the regime has absolutely no incentive to cooperate,” he added.

Citing the junta’s ongoing attacks on civilian targets, Stothard noted that hostage diplomacy is a smokescreen for the regime’s continued brutality against its own people.

“ASEAN and the international community should not be engaging or dancing with a regime that has turned Burma into a transnational crime hub, created the worst humanitarian crisis in the region, and will negatively impact ASEAN for years to come,” Stothard said.

World.title: The Fatal Flaw in China’s Myanmar Policy is Economic Collapse
World.content:
While Beijing’s military‑centric approach — backed by its “three bottom lines” — defines China’s Myanmar policy, the ground reality shows that civil war is not the only source of instability. Alongside the widening conflict, Myanmar’s foundations are being shaken by a deepening economic crisis with historical echoes. The collapse of General Ne Win’s Burma Socialist Programme Party regime four decades ago was not triggered by battlefield defeat, but by economic breakdown — a reminder that today’s regime faces the same danger.

Deepening economic crisis

When Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited in August 2024, the junta was facing not only military setbacks but also severe inflation marked by surging commodity prices. Thanks to Chinese financial assistance, inflation eased after his trip and the kyat stabilized at around 4,000 per US dollar. But it plunged again after military-staged elections early this year and now hovers near 4,600 per dollar.

Starved of hard currency, the junta restricted imports and choked off border trade. The cost of fuel and cooking oil surged, followed by staples such as rice, eggs, and onions, as well as household electronics and medicines. Vehicle prices soared, and black markets reemerged. Domestic manufacturing, agriculture, and livestock industries — reliant on imported technology, seeds, feed, fertilizers, and medicines — were hit hard, while foreign investment also dwindled.

As the kyat weakens, commodity prices are surging again and shortages are widespread. This is not merely a policy miscalculation: the junta channels all foreign currency into military spending, compounding the economic crisis. Without an end to war, the economic crisis cannot be fixed.

Corrupt state apparatus

Another major issue is systemic corruption in the bureaucracy. Graft grew steadily under military rule from 1988 to 2010 but was restrained somewhat by public oversight during the 2010–2020 reform period. But since the 2021 coup, the entire machinery of government — from Min Aung Hlaing and the top brass down to the lowest ranks — have exploited power for personal gain.

Legal restrictions and licensing requirements have become tollbooths for bribery. Payment is required for import permits, ID cards, passports and the right to travel at home or abroad. Importers routinely pay bribes, while ordinary people face extortion by soldiers and police on the streets. This endemic corruption has also facilitated the boom in narcotics production and online fraud gangs.

Narcotics and online scams

Myanmar is among the world’s largest producers of heroin, methamphetamine, and synthetic drugs, with output now rising annually as officials, soldiers and police turn a blind eye in exchange for bribes.

Online scam syndicates previously confined to borderlands are now spreading inland. Evidence from Karen State and northern Shan’s Kokang shows that gangs are relocating under the protection of military‑linked MPs, administrators, border guards, police, and senior officials. Even as criminal syndicates elsewhere in northern Shan are dismantled, Muse—the only border town Naypyitaw still controls thanks to China—remains an online scam hub, highlighting the regime’s complicity in cyber-fraud.

In other words, the economic crisis is not a standalone problem, but deeply intertwined with systemic corruption, narcotics production, and scams.

Poverty and social collapse

Illicit revenues from narcotics and scam syndicates have flooded Myanmar, fueling inflation and driving property values to unsustainable heights. Ordinary citizens are bearing the brunt as the country’s economic crisis deepens. Chinese loans cannot solve this problem.

The persistent civil war, combined with entrenched corruption and criminality, rampant inflation, and worsening shortages, has created a dire situation. While a handful of elites hoard wealth, most of the population struggles to afford basic food, leaving Myanmar society fractured and unstable.

A UNDP report released on October 8 revealed that one in three Myanmar citizens — over 17 million people — are already experiencing multidimensional poverty, with another 19 million at risk. In total, about 37 million people, or 68 percent of the population, are either poor or vulnerable to poverty.

Years of conflict, displacement, economic collapse, and climate shocks have devastated housing, healthcare, education, and livelihoods, worsening deprivation.

China’s other Myanmar headaches

Beyond these crises, China must also reckon with four other problems.

First is anti‑China sentiment — which is rising not only among resistance forces but also within the regime itself. Resistance anger is fueled by Beijing’s support for a failing military regime, not hostility toward Chinese people.

For the regime, however, anti‑China sentiment remains a core worldview. In times of political, economic, or military crisis, the Myanmar military often resorts to Burman nationalism, routinely stoking anti‑China and anti‑Muslim prejudice. In this way, it diverted public anger over rice shortages in 1967 by orchestrating anti‑Chinese riots. Today, the regime sponsors ultranationalist groups such as Ma Ba Tha to sustain this narrative.

Propping up the regime offers China no protection from Naypyitaw’s deep-seated disdain. This hostility is not incidental but fundamental; Beijing will be forced to confront it again and again no matter how much support it provides.

Second, the regime’s corrupt apparatus continues to protect online scam syndicates, undermining China’s efforts to suppress them.

Third, the regime has closed key border trade gates including Muse and Chinshwehaw once worth billions annually to China. At a time when Chinese goods are cheaper than Japanese or Western equivalents, the border-trade shutdown is a major loss. Meanwhile, talk of opening trade routes with India has alarm bells ringing in Beijing.

Fourth, the regime is seeking to reestablish relations with the United States. While China might accept restoration of normal diplomatic ties, anything deeper would be difficult for Beijing to tolerate given its red line over Western engagement with ethnic armed groups.

‘Three bottom lines’ collapse

China’s policy goal is stability in Myanmar. But by betting on the Myanmar military to deliver it, Beijing has tethered itself to failure. The regime’s reliance on force over negotiations, corruption over the rule of law, entanglement with narcotics and scams—coupled with economic breakdown—guarantee perpetual instability.

Despite Beijing’s support, Myanmar remains mired in conflict and crisis. The “three bottom lines” have not been upheld: civil strife is intensifying, ASEAN engagement is faltering, and international powers are finding new entry points.

China’s core objective — stability in Myanmar — remains unfulfilled.

World.title: Malaysia to Seek Clarification Over Reports of Detained Myanmar Returnees
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR—Malaysia will seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country are being held in military detention, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Monday.

Malaysia in late September sent back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.

Kuala Lumpur said the group agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centers amid an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

Myanmar pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.

Mohamad told parliament on Monday that Malaysia’s charge d’affaires in Myanmar would investigate the allegations and learn the condition of those reportedly detained.

“If there is news that the 300 people are still being detained, we will ask the Myanmar government to explain to us,” he told parliament in response to a lawmaker’s question.

“We will ask the Myanmar government to ensure that the assurances it gave us are honored,” he added.

Myanmar news outlet the Democratic Voice of Burma reported on Thursday that more than 400 ethnic Rakhine residents who returned from Malaysia earlier this month “remain in military custody” after arriving in Yangon.

They were among a group of 1,476 returnees who arrived by ship outside Yangon, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says Myanmar agreed to take back amid the anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

An additional 3,524 people are expected to be repatriated in a second phase.

The UN has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.

Myanmar’s coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since the putsch, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants earlier this month.

During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing said migrants from his country held in Malaysian detention centers will be returned home “as soon as possible”.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” he told a joint news conference with Anwar.

The opaque repatriation scheme has been criticized by rights monitors, some fearing ethnic Rohingya may be sent back to a country where they have experienced persecution that rights experts say amounted to genocide.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks 41st Worldwide for Public Order and Security, Global Index Shows
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 41st out of 143 countries and jurisdictions in the Order and Security factor of the 2026 World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index, improving one position from last year, according to the organization’s latest report.

The ranking measures one of eight areas the index assesses, evaluating how the rule of law functions worldwide. The Order and Security factor covers the absence of crime, civil conflict and violent methods of resolving disputes.

Kazakhstan ranked 42nd in this category in the previous edition of the index. However, the improvement in the security-related measure contrasts with Kazakhstan’s overall performance. The country ranked 67th out of 143 jurisdictions in the 2026 index, down from 66th in 2025. Its overall score declined 1.4% to 0.53.

The index assesses eight areas: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice.

In the 2026 edition, Kazakhstan ranked 102nd in constraints on government powers, 67th in absence of corruption, 80th in open government, 98th in fundamental rights, 58th in regulatory enforcement, 40th in civil justice and 69th in criminal justice. Denmark topped the overall ranking, followed by Norway, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg.

The WJP Rule of Law Index draws on household surveys and surveys of legal practitioners and experts. The 2026 edition covers 143 countries and jurisdictions, representing approximately 95% of the world’s population.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Georgia Work to Expand Cross-Border Access to Financial Markets
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Georgia are working to make it easier for financial institutions to access each other’s capital markets, with regulators exploring mutual market recognition mechanisms to support cross-border investment and financial services. The initiative was a key focus of AIFC Connect: Tbilisi 2026, an event hosted by the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), the National Bank of Georgia, GFTN and ITS on Oct. 28 as part of the Tbilisi Finance Summit 2026.

The initiative builds on a memorandum of understanding signed on Sept. 9 by the Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA), the AIFC’s financial regulator, and the National Bank of Georgia. The agreement provides a framework for regulatory cooperation, information exchange and developing mechanisms to facilitate access to the two markets, particularly in capital markets and asset management. Under the memorandum, the regulators will develop practical arrangements that account for the legal and regulatory requirements of both jurisdictions.

“Our shared priority now is to translate these commitments into practical measures,” said Evgeniya Bogdanova, AFSA chief executive officer.

She said the goal was to expand opportunities for financial institutions, facilitate entry into new markets and support cross-border services while maintaining investor protection standards.

The Tbilisi event brought together regulators, banks, investment firms, stock exchanges and financial and technology companies from both countries to discuss economic trends, capital markets and opportunities for closer cooperation.

Bakhtiyar Tleubekov, chairman of the AIFC Authority’s management board, said the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route added another dimension to Kazakhstan-Georgia cooperation by improving connectivity between Asia and Europe and creating opportunities for trade and infrastructure investment.

“The AIFC is well positioned to contribute to these efforts through its internationally recognized legal and regulatory framework and capital market infrastructure,” he said.

The event also featured an overview of Georgia’s economic outlook and capital markets by Irakli Gabriadze, head of the Economic Development Corporation of Georgia, and a presentation on Kazakhstan’s capital market by Birzhan Astayev, chief markets and products officer of the Astana International Exchange.

A panel discussion brought together representatives of financial and investment institutions to examine opportunities for cross-border transactions, investment and business cooperation. Participants included representatives of Kazakhstan’s National Investment Holding Baiterek, Halyk Bank Georgia, ITS, TBC Capital and Galt & Taggart.

Trade and investment ties

Economic ties between Kazakhstan and Georgia provide a foundation for deeper financial cooperation. Bilateral trade reached $184.5 million in 2025, while trade turnover totaled $53 million in January-April 2026, according to the AIFC. Kazakhstan has invested more than $500 million in Georgia’s economy, while more than 600 companies with Georgian participation operate in Kazakhstan.

The AIFC also serves as a platform for Georgian businesses seeking access to Kazakhstan’s market and international financial services. Twenty companies from Georgia are registered in the center, representing sectors including finance and insurance, information and communications, manufacturing and agriculture. The center offers a legal and regulatory framework based on English common law principles. AFSA supervises financial and market activities, while the Astana International Exchange provides infrastructure for raising capital and trading securities. The AIFC Court and International Arbitration Centre handle legal matters and commercial dispute resolution.

The Middle Corridor connection

Financial cooperation is part of a broader partnership spanning transport, logistics and infrastructure. Kazakhstan and Georgia are among the countries working to improve transport links along the Middle Corridor, which connects Asia and Europe. Their efforts include expanding container transportation, coordinating tariffs and advancing digitalization along the route, creating potential investment opportunities in transport infrastructure and related sectors.

One example is Middle Corridor Multimodal Ltd., an AIFC-registered company established by railway companies from Kazakhstan, Georgia, Azerbaijan and China. The company aims to coordinate rail and maritime transport along the corridor and improve transit operations.

The AIFC said its platform has attracted more than $28 billion in investment to Kazakhstan’s economy since its launch. More than 6,800 companies from over 90 countries are registered in the center. The Tbilisi event concluded with business networking and business-to-business meetings focused on potential cross-border investments and joint initiatives.

World.title: Kazakhstan Calls for Stronger Cooperation Among Turkic States Ahead of OTS Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi called for stronger political dialogue and closer trade and transport ties among Turkic states at an Oct. 29 meeting ahead of the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), the ministry’s press service reported.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived in Ankara on Oct. 28 for an official visit to Türkiye and is scheduled to attend the summit, Akorda reported.

The ministerial meeting focused on cooperation within the organization and current international and regional issues.

Tileuberdi emphasized the importance of strengthening unity and solidarity among Turkic states, deepening political dialogue and expanding trade, economic, transport and logistics links across the organization. He also highlighted the outcomes of the informal OTS summit held on May 15 in Turkistan under the theme Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development.

According to the ministry, Tileuberdi said the meeting had given new impetus to the organization’s digital agenda and laid the groundwork for deeper cooperation in artificial intelligence, innovation and advanced technologies.

At the end of the ministerial meeting, participants adopted documents to develop and expand the activities of Turkic organizations. They also reviewed and approved draft final documents for the 13th OTS summit.

World.title: Kazakh Government Outlines Budget and Tax Measures After Tokayev’s Address
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan plans to expand AI in budget management, overhaul investment coordination, consider higher taxes on wealthy citizens, and raise the minimum monthly wage to 110,000 tenge ($242) in 2027 as the government moves to implement President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state-of-the-nation address.

The measures were discussed at an Oct. 29 meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, who called for coordinated action by the government and regional administrations to carry out the president’s priorities.

Tokayev has designated 2027 as the Year of Nationwide Construction, with the People’s Construction program expected to drive infrastructure development across the economy. In his address to the nation, he said Kazakhstan should become “one large construction site,” with large-scale construction taking place across all regions.

“The president’s address to the people of Kazakhstan sets a historic task before us to build and pass on to future generations a qualitatively new country with a strong and dynamic economy,” Bektenov said.

He called on the government and regional administrations to mobilize available resources to build and modernize socially and economically significant facilities, as well as housing and utility infrastructure.

Bektenov also stressed the need to align investment policy, small and medium-sized business development, budget and tax reforms, digitalization and social support with the country’s long-term economic goals.

AI to be used more widely in budget process

Bektenov instructed the Ministries of Finance, National Economy, and AI and Digital Development to expand the use of digital tools and AI in budget procedures. Tokayev identified this priority in his address, saying, “To prevent unjustified and inefficient spending, it is advisable to use the capabilities of artificial intelligence technologies.” He also called for completing the digitalization of the treasury system and establishing a unified approach to managing budget flows.

The government aims to introduce automated checks throughout the budget process, including systems to identify risks of misusing public funds or spending them inefficiently. Digital solutions should also enable real-time monitoring and auditing of budget data and transactions.

The Finance Ministry was tasked with creating a treasury information system and integrating government systems for managing budget revenues and expenditures. Bektenov said all public spending must be clearly prioritized, with an emphasis on delivering tangible economic returns.

Government to review investment policy and taxation of wealthy citizens

Tokayev called for investment policy management to be concentrated in a single center, saying in his address that investment efficiency should be assessed by the number and quality of production facilities launched and their actual contribution to the economy.

The government plans to revise investment management mechanisms, strengthen investment projects’ contribution to the economy, and expand small and medium-sized businesses’ participation in public procurement.

Bektenov instructed the Ministries of National Economy and Foreign Affairs, together with the Baiterek holding, to submit coordinated proposals within 10 days for establishing an integrated investment management system. The proposals should identify a central decision-making body, clarify participants’ responsibilities, and improve coordination with investors.

The government also aims to prioritize projects involving deeper processing and higher labor productivity. Relevant ministries, the Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund and Baiterek Holding have one month to prepare a list of such projects, identifying potential investors, implementation timelines, localization levels and expected economic benefits.

Separately, several ministries, Samruk Kazyna, Baiterek and the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs were instructed to submit proposals within a week to expand small and medium-sized businesses’ access to procurement by government agencies and quasi-public companies.

The National Economy Ministry must also refine targeted amendments to the new Tax Code and coordinate them with government agencies.

On taxation, Tokayev said it was time to discuss introducing a higher tax rate for people with large fortunes. In his address, he framed the initiative as a matter of fairness and called for proposals from the government and Kurultai.

Bektenov instructed the Ministries of National Economy and Finance to study international practices and submit proposals on taxing particularly wealthy citizens within one month.

The Finance Ministry was also tasked with improving local tax collection, reducing the shadow economy and completing the digitalization of tax and customs administration, including through AI tools.

Plans for 2027: higher minimum wage and support for small businesses

Kazakhstan plans to increase the minimum monthly wage to 110,000 tenge (US$242) from Jan. 1, 2027, First Vice Minister of National Economy Azamat Amrin said at the meeting. The government aims to increase real household incomes through sustained, high-quality economic growth and lower inflation. Measures to monitor pricing will be strengthened alongside tariff policy.

In his address, Tokayev said the country’s main goal was to raise household incomes, stressing that this required systematic efforts to combat inflation.
