To support entrepreneurship, the government plans to develop a medium-sized business development plan that will include long-term financing mechanisms, technological modernization and reduced administrative pressure.

The government is also considering a three-year moratorium on inspections and preventive controls for micro and small businesses from Jan. 1, 2027, in consultation with members of the Kurultai, Amrin said. The proposal has not yet been presented as a finalized measure.

In his address, Tokayev proposed that the Kurultai and government discuss another three-year moratorium, describing it as an opportunity to overhaul the inspection system and move toward digital regulation.

The government has also prepared a package of targeted Tax Code amendments based on proposals from the business community. The government will examine the possibility of a higher tax rate for wealthy citizens in light of international practices.

To support Tokayev’s infrastructure agenda, the government has established an Infrastructure Development Fund, Amrin added.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans 21 Logistics Centers, 20% Power Surplus Under Tokayev’s Nation Address
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan plans to build 21 new logistics centers by 2030, add 13.3 gigawatts of power generation capacity by 2029 and accelerate the digitalization of water resources, agriculture and geological data as the government works to implement President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state-of-the-nation address.

The government outlined the measures at an Oct. 29 meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov. The plans span transport infrastructure, access to energy, mineral exploration and the use of digital technologies to improve economic productivity.

Tokayev has called for Kazakhstan to strengthen its position as a logistics hub in Eurasia, modernize agriculture and geological exploration, and secure a sustainable energy surplus to meet rising domestic demand.

Kazakhstan to digitalize water resources and introduce AI in agriculture

Kazakhstan has developed a National Digital Water Resources System, and five reservoirs already have digital twins. The government plans to digitize all reservoirs by the end of 2027. Tokayev emphasized the importance of digital tools in water management, saying in his address that “for full and accurate accounting of water resources, it is critically important to make full use of digital tools.”

In agriculture, the government plans to introduce three platforms in stages: Smart Data Agro, Smart Farm and Smart Agro Platform.

The initiatives align with Tokayev’s call to modernize agriculture through technology and expand the use of AI. In his address, he described introducing AI in agriculture as a timely proposal that should be implemented without delay, linking modernization to higher agricultural productivity and Kazakhstan’s potential role in addressing future global food shortages.

Digital economy to expand income opportunities

More than 20 digital platforms already provide earning opportunities for more than 500,000 people in Kazakhstan, Minister of AI and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said. The government plans to expand rural access to e-commerce, improve logistics infrastructure and provide digital skills training. It also intends to introduce a retraining platform integrated with employment systems.

The work will include connecting rural entrepreneurs to existing online marketplaces, expanding networks of parcel collection and delivery points, and organizing deliveries to remote settlements. In his address, Tokayev called for a people-centered digital economy, saying that “opportunities must not depend on where people live.” The government also plans to train people to use e-commerce platforms, digital tools and AI, Madiyev said.

Kazakhstan to launch 20 geological exploration projects

Kazakhstan has launched a state geological survey at a 1:50,000 scale for the first time as part of efforts to study the country’s mineral resources, Vice Minister of Industry and Construction Iran Sharkhan said.

Tokayev called Kazakhstan’s mineral resource base a strategic advantage and urged a fundamental change in geological exploration. “We must turn geology into a high-tech industry,” he said in his address, calling for advanced technologies to study the country’s subsoil and improve access to geological data.

Over the next three years, the government plans to implement 20 geological exploration projects covering about 100,000 square kilometers. Alongside traditional methods, the projects will use Ionic Leach technology, satellite data, unmanned aerial vehicles and AI to identify hidden mineral deposits. Preliminary indications of potential have already been obtained at seven sites. Areas with confirmed prospects are expected to be prepared for auction next year, Sharkhan said.

Tokayev also called for a national system to manage critical metal reserves, drawing on international experience and providing long-term financing mechanisms for projects in the mining and metallurgical sector.

The sector is undergoing extensive digitalization. The Unified Subsoil Use Platform contains more than 70,000 geological reports and 109,000 exploration coverage maps. All primary geological information has been digitized, representing about 4.8 million records.

Separately, Kazakhstan has approved a methodology for assessing the balance of industrial production capacity. The framework is intended to help evaluate new projects in light of market demand, existing industrial facilities and resource availability. Its findings will be considered when granting investment incentives.

Kazakhstan plans 21 new logistics centers by 2030

Kazakhstan will continue developing transport and logistics infrastructure, expanding international freight routes and digitalizing the sector as it seeks to strengthen its position as a leading logistics hub in Eurasia. In his address, Tokayev stressed the importance of logistics, calling it a key factor in the country’s progress. He warned that without developed transport logistics, even countries that currently hold leading positions would fall behind. Bektenov said international and domestic logistics, transport digitalization and electricity supply must be addressed in the context of major global transformations.

Kazakhstan currently has 46 logistics centers. Another 21 are planned by 2030, Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev said. The country is also expanding its overseas terminal network to attract transit cargo. Three terminals are already operating, while seven projects are under development. Road and border checkpoint construction and modernization are continuing. Work on the Aral-Caspian highway began in August and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028. Preparatory work is underway this year for the Kokshetau-Petropavlovsk section, with construction scheduled to begin in 2027. The modernization of 37 road checkpoints is also underway, with completion planned by the end of 2027.

Kazakhstan also plans to strengthen its air cargo transit capacity. The country plans to modernize airport infrastructure, including runways and terminals, as well as refueling facilities and cargo terminals, over the next three years. The country has also begun upgrading its air navigation system. National cargo carrier Air Cargo has signed an aircraft supply agreement. Its first Airbus A340 is expected to arrive in November, followed by a second aircraft in March. The carrier’s fleet is expected to reach 10 aircraft in the longer term.

Transport digitalization is proceeding through the integration of information systems on the unified E-Kolik (E-vehicle) intelligent platform. The government is also working to eliminate paper-based consignment notes for domestic and international freight, with electronic permits and consignment notes being tested in several countries. The initiatives are expected to shorten processing times and improve transparency across entire cargo routes.

Kazakhstan targets 20% electricity capacity surplus by 2029

Kazakhstan plans to add 13.3 gigawatts of new power generation capacity by the end of 2029, including 7.4 gigawatts from conventional sources and 5.9 gigawatts from renewable energy, Vice Minister of Energy Bakytzhan Ilyas said. Tokayev identified energy shortages as a strategic challenge in his address, noting that rising industrial activity, construction, agriculture, digitalization and data center development would require substantially more electricity. He called for Kazakhstan to achieve a “sustainable energy surplus” by 2029.

The planned capacity additions are expected to cover electricity demand from households and the economy, including future energy-intensive AI infrastructure and large data centers, while creating a 20% surplus in generation capacity.

Coal-fired power plants currently account for 13.7 gigawatts of installed capacity, gas-fired plants for 7.1 gigawatts and large hydropower plants for 2.5 gigawatts. Renewable energy facilities account for 3.8 gigawatts.

Renewables generated 8.5% of Kazakhstan’s electricity in the first nine months of 2026, exceeding the planned 7% share, according to the Energy Ministry.

By the end of 2035, the country expects to commission at least 8.4 gigawatts of additional renewable energy capacity, including approximately 1.8 gigawatts of solar generation.

World.title: Tokayev’s Vision of Strong Cities and Regions Requires Nationwide Development, Analyst Says
World.content:
ASTANA — Improving cities, modernizing infrastructure and raising living standards have been recurring priorities in President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state-of-the-nation addresses. His latest address brought these themes together with a renewed push for AI, energy security and technological development, reinforcing priorities he has emphasized throughout his presidency.

In a comment to The Astana Times, political analyst Rasul Kuspanov of the National Analytical Center at Nazarbayev University said Kazakhstan’s priority at this stage should not necessarily be announcing new projects, but ensuring that existing plans are implemented and translate into tangible improvements in people’s lives across the country.

Kuspanov said the emphasis on digitalization and AI reflected a direction Kazakhstan had pursued for several years. However, he noted that the country’s technological ambitions would depend on whether it could build the infrastructure needed to support them and improve the capacity of its public administration to deliver results.

AI ambitions require energy and infrastructure

Tokayev called for Kazakhstan to move beyond consuming digital technologies and develop its own technological capabilities.

“Our goal is to build a truly people-centered digital economy,” he said in his Oct. 28 address.

He also acknowledged that digitalization has not always delivered meaningful results, sometimes amounting to the automation of existing procedures or the purchase of expensive software without a clear understanding of its practical benefits.

“We must be realistic in assessing our capabilities and use the best that new technologies can offer for the well-being of our people,” Tokayev said.

For Kuspanov, one of the central questions is whether Kazakhstan can provide the energy and computing infrastructure required for this transition. The country continues to face electricity shortages, while the expansion of data centers and wider adoption of AI will increase demand for reliable power.

Tokayev set a strategic target of achieving a sustainable electricity surplus by 2029 and said it may be possible to begin construction of the Balkhash nuclear power plant as early as next year. He also called for accelerating the development of additional generating capacity.

The proposed data center valley in Ekibastuz is another part of Kazakhstan’s digital ambitions. But Kuspanov said the success of such initiatives would depend on implementation rather than the announcement of new plans. He also highlighted the importance of applying AI in public administration. He said Kazakhstan has already introduced digital tools for government employees and public feedback, but further integration of technology into the civil service will require institutional changes alongside technical solutions.

Alatau and the challenge of implementation

Another major initiative is Alatau, which Tokayev has presented as a center of accelerated development and an environment conducive to investment and entrepreneurship. The president announced plans for an investment court based on English common law to hear commercial cases. A separate civil court would handle other matters under the city’s special legal regime. The initiative builds on Kazakhstan’s experience with the Astana International Financial Centre, which operates under its own legal framework.

For Kuspanov, Alatau represents an opportunity to develop a new technological and investment hub, but its long-term success will depend on the institutions established to support it. That brings the discussion back to public administration.

“The civil service as the backbone of the state and even well-designed policies depend on the quality of the people responsible for carrying them out,” Kuspanov said.

He welcomed Tokayev’s emphasis on reforming the state apparatus, saying that Kazakhstan needs capable officials who can turn ambitious plans into practical outcomes.

The same principle applies to infrastructure investment. Tokayev said Kazakhstan would allocate 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) from the National Fund by the end of 2029 to modernize infrastructure nationwide.

Kuspanov said using National Fund resources could bring visible benefits if the money goes to necessary projects and is spent efficiently.

“If transfers from the fund are spent efficiently and on worthwhile projects, such as modernizing the Petropavlovsk-Kokshetau highway, I think citizens of Kazakhstan will be pleased to see the results of this work for themselves,” he said.

He also stressed the need for close oversight of public spending to ensure that allocated funds are used for their intended purpose.

Better cities, stronger regions

Urban development has also been a recurring priority for Tokayev. In his latest address, he called for government-approved medium- and long-term development plans for major cities, with safety, comfort and attractiveness treated as state priorities.

“Strong cities are the foundation of strong regions, and strong regions are the foundation of a strong state,” Tokayev said.

The president also linked quality of life to access to adequate social infrastructure. He called for large-scale construction across the country, emphasizing that the initiative should extend beyond individual projects to cover all regions.

According to Kuspanov, the challenge is to ensure that development reaches beyond the largest urban centers. Roads, utilities, public facilities and other infrastructure shape not only the appearance of cities but also the economic opportunities available to their residents.

Kuspanov said Kazakhstan’s regions differ considerably in their level of economic activity and infrastructure. He pointed to the East Kazakhstan Region as an example of active economic and industrial development, praising the work of the local administration.

His assessment of the North Kazakhstan Region, where he grew up and regularly visits family, was more critical. In some districts, he said, infrastructure remains underdeveloped.

“People in smaller towns and rural areas should also have access to the basic conditions necessary for a decent quality of life. Regional policy should therefore be systematic rather than concentrated on a handful of pilot territories or the country’s largest cities,” he said.

Kuspanov said the goal should be to create conditions in which every region can develop in a modern and sustainable way.

From announcements to measurable outcomes

Tokayev’s address also included measures with a more immediate social impact. Kuspanov said many Kazakh citizens would pay attention to the announced minimum wage increase, describing it as an important measure for public-sector workers.

“While the increase may not transform their financial circumstances, it remains significant for those affected,” he said.

Tokayev’s broader economic agenda includes efforts to curb inflation, improve public spending and channel more financing into the real economy, with commercial banks urged to expand investment lending. However, Kuspanov said the address contained few fundamentally new ideas. After years of reform, he noted, the priority is now to deliver on existing commitments and extend their benefits nationwide.

World.title: Kazakhstan Leads Central Asia in Wages but Records Decline in Purchasing Power
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranks third among six Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries with available data for monthly employer labor costs, behind Belarus and Moldova, according to the CIS Statistical Committee. In 2024, labor costs in Kazakhstan reached 878 euros (US$1,015) per employee per month, significantly exceeding the figures recorded in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

The figures highlight differences in how employers across the region compensate workers and cover the broader costs of maintaining a workforce, including wages, bonuses, social protection, professional training and other employee-related expenses.

Kazakhstan’s average nominal monthly wage reached $988 in the first half of 2026, according to the Eurasian Economic Commission. This was nearly 61% higher than in the Kyrgyz Republic, where the average stood at $615, and 67.3% higher than in Uzbekistan, at $591. Kazakhstan’s figure was 2.8 times Tajikistan’s $358.

Among CIS countries, only Russia and Belarus reported higher average nominal wages during the January–June period, at nearly $1,400 and more than $1,000, respectively.

However, wage growth varied considerably across the region. The Kyrgyz Republic recorded the highest nominal wage index, at 127.5%, followed by Tajikistan at 119.6%. Kazakhstan’s index was 110.3% compared with the same period a year earlier.

In real terms, Kazakhstan recorded the weakest performance. Its real wage index fell to 99.4%, indicating a 0.6% decline in purchasing power. Kazakhstan was the only CIS country in the comparison with a real wage index below 100%.

By contrast, the real wage index reached 115.3% in the Kyrgyz Republic and 114.9% in Tajikistan, indicating stronger growth in purchasing power.

Employer labor costs vary across the CIS

Wages are only one component of the cost of employing workers. Employer labor costs also include paid leave, bonuses, social protection contributions, housing, professional training and cultural or household services provided to employees.

According to the CIS Statistical Committee, comparable data for 2024 were available for six countries. Belarus recorded the highest monthly labor costs per employee, at 949 euros (US$1,097), followed by Moldova at 903 euros (US$1,044). Kazakhstan ranked third at 878 euros (US$1,015). Uzbekistan reported the lowest figures, at 475 euros (US$549), and the Kyrgyz Republic at 542 euros (US$627).

Labor cost composition also differed across countries, reflecting different approaches to employee compensation and social protection.

In Azerbaijan and Moldova, payment for hours worked accounted for the largest shares of total labor costs, at 74.4% and 70.3%, respectively. The proportions were lower in the Kyrgyz Republic, at 57.3%, and Uzbekistan, at 58.3%, where social protection and other employee-related expenses accounted for comparatively larger shares.

Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan also recorded relatively high shares of monetary incentives, suggesting that bonuses and other financial rewards play an important role in employee compensation. Incentives accounted for 13.1% of total labor costs in Kazakhstan and 17.9% in Uzbekistan.

Social protection contributions represented another major difference between countries. Belarus recorded the highest share, at 24.7%, followed by Moldova at 19%. Kazakhstan had the lowest proportion among the countries compared, at 6.3%.

Labor costs in Kazakhstan continue to rise

Kazakhstan’s Bureau of National Statistics publishes labor cost data annually. In 2025, employer labor costs reached nearly 6 million tenge (US$13,158) per employee per year, or 499,100 tenge (US$1,095) per month.

The labor cost index indicates that employers’ expenses have increased every year in recent years. The highest annual increase was recorded in 2022, when the index reached 121.9%. The lowest was reported in 2024, at 113.3%.

The index’s gradual decline between 2022 and 2025 may indicate a shift toward more moderate increases in employee-related costs.

Significant regional differences

Labor costs varied substantially across Kazakhstan in 2025, reflecting differences in regional economic structures and wage levels. These differences are partly tied to regional economic specialization. Oil-producing western regions generally have higher wages, while agriculture plays a more prominent role in the Turkistan and Zhambyl regions, where wage levels are comparatively lower.

Overall, the figures show that Kazakhstan has higher employer labor costs and nominal wages than its Central Asian neighbors, while still trailing Belarus and Moldova in total monthly labor costs per employee. At the same time, the decline in real wages highlights the gap between rising nominal earnings and the purchasing power they provide.

World.title: Tokayev Arrives in Ankara for Official Visit, Set to Attend Turkic States Summit
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived in Ankara on Oct. 28 for an official visit to Türkiye, where he is scheduled to attend the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan welcomed Tokayev at the Presidential Palace in Ankara. A guard of honor was lined up for the ceremony, and a mounted guard escorted the Kazakh president’s motorcade to the palace. The national anthems of Kazakhstan and Türkiye were played, accompanied by a 21-gun salute, reported Akorda.

The presidents continued the meeting with members of their official delegations. Tokayev congratulated Erdoğan and the Turkish people on the eve of Türkiye’s Republic Day, celebrated on Oct. 29, and highlighted the importance of expanding bilateral cooperation.

He said Kazakhstan and Türkiye share historical and linguistic ties, as well as similar traditions, and described their political relations as founded on mutual trust and friendship.

“Türkiye is one of Kazakhstan’s five largest trading partners. In addition, the Turkish side ranks among the top 10 investors that have invested significant funds in our country’s economy,” Tokayev said.

He also pointed to Erdoğan’s state visit to Kazakhstan in May, which he described as productive. The visit resulted in agreements and the launch of projects in trade, investment, and cultural and humanitarian cooperation. The two countries also held the sixth meeting of their High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council.

According to Tokayev, bilateral relations have reached the level of eternal friendship and expanded strategic partnership.

“Developing our bilateral partnership serves our common interests,” he said, adding that his participation in the Turkic States summit and the upcoming COP31 climate conference in Antalya would provide further momentum for bilateral and multilateral ties.

Erdoğan, in turn, congratulated Tokayev and the Kazakh people on Kazakhstan’s Republic Day, celebrated on Oct. 25.

He noted that a book titled The Phenomenon of the Kurultai, dedicated to the history of Kazakh statehood, had recently been presented in Ankara. He also mentioned the Kazakh translation of Nauryz – Common Heritage of the Turkic World, a book examining the holiday’s history and significance.

Erdoğan said the two countries intend to follow up on agreements signed during his May visit to Astana, including the Declaration on Eternal Friendship and Expanded Strategic Partnership.

“We intend to increase trade turnover to $15 billion and intensify the investment dimension of bilateral relations,” he said.

The presidents also discussed cooperation in transport and logistics, energy, artificial intelligence, agriculture and the defense industry, as well as closer cultural and humanitarian ties.

World.title: Political analyst: ‘If Aliyev has to choose between Russia and Turkey, he will choose Russia’
World.content:
Tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey

Political analyst Arastun Orujlu has discussed the reasons for the recent tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey, as well as their possible consequences, in an interview with Meydan TV.

In his view, one of the main reasons for the disagreement between Baku and Ankara is Azerbaijan’s growing closeness to Israel.

– Mr Orujlu, what do you think is the main reason for the tensions that have emerged between Turkey and Azerbaijan in recent days?

– The tensions between Turkey and Azerbaijan have nothing to do with Islam or religious values. These factors serve merely as a pretext, primarily for official Baku, which uses them to provoke conflict. However, I do not rule out personal motives either. Experience shows that personal considerations often lie behind the Azerbaijani authorities’ strong reactions to the actions of other countries.

Ilham Aliyev views every issue through the prism of his personal interests. Nevertheless, I believe the current tensions are primarily political. They reflect Azerbaijan’s desire to distance itself from neighbouring countries and pursue a foreign policy oriented towards Tel Aviv and Washington. This trend is now clearly visible.

– You link these tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy. In Turkey, however, people have criticised the Azerbaijani authorities both over their policies on the hijab and over their relations with Israel. To what extent does this criticism reflect political considerations? Are there genuine disagreements between Ankara and Baku on these issues?

– These are separate issues, so let me address them one by one. The hijab has always been a matter of principle for Turkey’s Justice and Development Party (AKP). For a long time, it sparked heated political debates in Turkey. The country experienced serious upheaval and a painful period over this issue. Therefore, if the current Turkish government, led by the AKP, had failed to respond to what was happening, it would undoubtedly have damaged its standing among its own voters.

In fact, the first reaction did not come from the AKP leadership. It began on Turkish social media, where journalists and individual users started protesting. Only later did the AKP leadership respond, and not at government level. The response came from Oktay Saral, an adviser to Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on party affairs.

As for Israel, the problems here are genuinely serious and entirely political. Turkey and Israel are engaged in an intense struggle for influence in the South Caucasus, the Middle East and the eastern Mediterranean. Israel is effectively seeking regional dominance. Turkey, meanwhile, believes it should take the leading role because it has stronger moral and historical claims to it, as well as greater military capabilities than Israel. Turkey’s strong reaction to the genocide unfolding in Gaza also plays an important role.

We know these problems have existed for quite some time. There is no doubt that Israel is trying to expand its influence in Central Asia through Azerbaijan and the South Caucasus. Central Asia is one of Turkey’s key foreign policy priorities, and Israel has already begun strengthening its position there. The two sides have very sharp disagreements over this issue.

It is also well known that the Azerbaijani authorities maintain exceptionally close relations with Israel. After the United States, Azerbaijan may well be Israel’s closest partner.

– In this context, how do you assess Azerbaijan’s decision to declare 31 Turkish citizens persona non grata? How might this decision affect relations between the two countries?

– As far as I can tell, Ilham Aliyev is trying to weaken Turkey’s influence in Azerbaijan. I do not mean its influence over the government, but rather Turkey’s role in Azerbaijani society. Although no opinion polls have been conducted, the situation clearly suggests that Turkey became the most popular country among Azerbaijanis after the 44-day war. Deep historical, cultural and ethnic ties explain this. Perhaps this is precisely what worries Ilham Aliyev.

He effectively signalled that a conflict was brewing at the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) congress. For some reason, many observers overlooked his remarks. In his speech, Ilham Aliyev addressed not only economic and social problems but also put forward three political arguments with an underlying message.

First, he stated directly that nobody had provided Azerbaijan with free support, and that even weapons and ammunition had been sold at global market prices. Azerbaijanis immediately thought of Turkey when they heard these words. Yet Ilham Aliyev himself has repeatedly said that Azerbaijan would have found itself in a difficult position without Turkish support. At the Victory Parade following the 44-day war, he stood alongside Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on the main podium. Now, suddenly, he has made this statement. It is quite clear that he directed it specifically at Turkey.

Second, in the same speech, he stressed the need to improve the quality of education. But if Ilham Aliyev genuinely wants to improve education, he should appoint professionals to senior positions in the sector. Today, Azerbaijan’s education system is run entirely by brokers, shopkeepers and traders who have nothing to do with education.

The third point concerned strengthening patriotic sentiment. Aliyev was effectively saying: “I will fight against Turkey, and your first homeland is Azerbaijan.” That was the message behind his words.

Look at who took part in all the disputes and conflicts that followed. They included media outlets linked to the Azerbaijani authorities, individuals, influencers, media platforms, experts and even people who call themselves opposition party leaders. They all joined the campaign. It was carefully planned.

Let me repeat: it appears that Ilham Aliyev has set himself the task of weakening Turkey’s standing and influence in Azerbaijani society. Alternatively, someone may have assigned him that task.

– We have previously seen the Azerbaijani authorities use similar rhetoric and pressure tactics when relations with other countries deteriorated. For example, when relations with Europe worsened, independent NGOs and media representatives became targets. When tensions with Russia escalated, authorities targeted the Sputnik news agency and several politicians. During tensions with Iran, they put pressure on religious believers. Now we see a similar approach towards Turkey. Which specific issue, in your view, lies at the heart of the disagreement between Azerbaijan and Turkey?

– I believe the issue concerns foreign policy alone. As I have already said, Azerbaijan is moving closer to Israel, and this process is advancing very rapidly. Moreover, Azerbaijani media have featured not merely people who support Israel, but individuals with direct links to Israeli organisations. They have accused Turkey of wrongdoing while defending the Azerbaijani authorities’ position.

For example, the English-language Azerbaijani website News.Az published an article by a certain Roman Gurevich. After reading it, I noticed that subsequent events in Azerbaijan unfolded according to the scenario described in that article. This shows that Israel has considerable influence over Azerbaijani media.

All the websites and media outlets that belong to Global Media Group also have links to Israel. People in Turkey can see this and understand that Azerbaijan is moving away from them. Relations between Israel and Turkey have deteriorated to such an extent that Azerbaijan has effectively found itself having to choose a side. Ankara can clearly see that Azerbaijan — or, more precisely, Ilham Aliyev and his family — are choosing Israel. I believe this is the main reason for the current conflict.

But what measures can they take against Turkey? Turkey has no levers of influence within Azerbaijan. Western countries, for example, once had some influence over certain NGOs and media outlets. The authorities arrested their representatives on fabricated charges. When relations with Iran deteriorated, they arrested religious believers. During tensions with Russia, they detained IT specialists whom the Azerbaijani authorities themselves had invited into the country.

Turkey has no comparable resources in Azerbaijan. Taking such steps against Turkey would also carry serious risks. Azerbaijan itself has considerable leverage in Turkey, including a network of lobbyists it funds and media resources. In addition, Azerbaijani investments in Turkey amount to around $20 billion.

Nevertheless, I do not think relations will deteriorate to the point of a complete break. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s phone call was more than an invitation. It was also a warning with a clear message: “Stop this process.” The Azerbaijani authorities had been orchestrating an extremely dirty campaign against Turkey, including at the military leadership level. Perhaps even Russia and Iran have not faced attacks this harsh.

– How might the current tensions affect the future of relations between the two countries?

– These tensions have already affected relations. The relationship between Azerbaijan and Turkey rests on several distinct foundations, unlike Azerbaijan’s ties with other countries.

The first is the relationship between the two states. The second is the personal relationship between Ilham Aliyev and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, which brings together various interests. For example, companies close to the AKP operate in Azerbaijan. The third foundation is the connection between the two societies. This is the most reliable pillar of their relationship.

The concept of “One nation, two states” is more than a slogan. The relationship between the two peoples has deep historical roots stretching back at least 120 to 130 years. This third pillar has suffered the damage.

Various groups hostile to Turkey have become more active in Azerbaijan and taken advantage of the situation. They have effectively received a signal that they can now criticise, insult and accuse Turkey. As a result, they have dealt a significant blow to the most important foundation of relations between the two countries.

– At what level will the two countries maintain their political and strategic alliance after this?

– That will depend on many external factors. The results of elections in Israel and the political situation in the United States will play an important role, for example. Recently, an American researcher published a book alleging that large sums of money had been transferred to Donald Trump’s son-in-law through Azerbaijan. This should not surprise us, because Azerbaijan conducts much of its foreign policy through lobbying and financial mechanisms.

Future developments will depend on these factors. For example, if the Republican Party loses the US midterm elections and Trump’s influence weakens, Ilham Aliyev will have to realign himself with either Russia or Turkey.

I say this with full responsibility: if Aliyev has to choose between Russia and Turkey, he will choose Russia. Around 70% of people in Azerbaijan’s current leadership have ties to Russia, while 30% have ties to Israel. There are virtually no people in the Azerbaijani leadership who look to Turkey.

Tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey

World.title: Georgia’s new gambling tournament law raises ombudsman concerns, draws Patriarchate response
World.content:
International gambling tournaments in Georgia

Georgia‘s parliament has passed a bill in its second reading that would allow casinos to organise international gambling tournaments. The initiative provides for permits to hold such tournaments, the introduction of relevant fees and fines for violating permit conditions.

Under the bill, an “international gambling tournament” is defined as a competition organised by a casino in which the prize fund is guaranteed in advance by the organiser and at least 80% of participants are foreign nationals.

Georgian government representatives have justified the move by citing its potential to boost tourism and economic activity. However, the country’s ombudsman has criticised the fast-tracked legislative process and the lack of a proper assessment of potential social harm.

Metropolitan Anton of Vani and Baghdati said the Georgian Patriarchate would discuss the issue on 30 October and present its unified position to the public following the meeting.

What will change?

Under the bill, organisers will be exempt from paying fees for the use of gaming tables used exclusively for international gambling tournaments if the prize fund exceeds 3 million lari. Organisers will also be allowed to generate revenue from holding such tournaments.

International gambling tournaments may be held both at licensed casino premises and at other venues.

The annual permit fee for organising such tournaments will be 100,000 lari (approximately $39,000). Violating permit conditions will carry a fine of 50,000 lari, while organising or holding an international gambling tournament without the required permit will result in a fine of 150,000 lari.

According to the bill’s authors, the amendments aim to improve the legal framework governing gambling and establish clear regulations for organising international gambling tournaments.

The bill’s sponsors note that existing legislation neither defines the term “international tournament” nor contains provisions regulating such events. They argue that this creates uncertainty for businesses and regulatory authorities.

What does the ombudsman say?

Following the bill’s first reading, Georgia’s ombudsman called on parliament to halt its further consideration and adoption.

According to the ombudsman, the fast-tracked consideration of an issue affecting the public interest is particularly problematic, especially without a proper expert assessment or comprehensive analysis of potential human rights risks.

The ombudsman argues that the bill lacks an assessment of its impact on public health and a proper analysis of potential social harm and the costs of preventing it. Furthermore, relevant experts and organisations were not involved in drafting the legislation, while international experience was not taken into account.

The ombudsman also notes that the bill’s explanatory memorandum claims the proposed changes will not affect children’s rights but provides no justification for this conclusion.

“When considering bills of this kind, it is crucial to conduct a comprehensive and thorough examination of the issue, including by ensuring broad participation of experts in the relevant field,” the ombudsman stressed.

The ombudsman emphasises that discussions of the proposed amendments should not focus solely on potential economic benefits. Instead, their impact on public health and social well-being, as well as the associated risks, must be given due consideration.

What does the Patriarchate say?

According to Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze, head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s public relations department, no prior discussions were held on the issue, and the Patriarchate itself has not yet examined the bill in detail.

Jaghmaidze noted that the Patriarchate has been actively involved in developing regulations governing gambling since 2017. He also said that the Patriarchate had reviewed the ombudsman’s position and largely shared the arguments presented.

“The Patriarchate cannot remain on the sidelines of such a process. We hope that dialogue with the bill’s sponsors will lead to a positive outcome,” Jaghmaidze said.

Metropolitan Anton of Vani and Baghdati said the Georgian Patriarchate was examining the legislative initiative concerning international gambling tournaments and preparing its official position on the matter.

According to the metropolitan, the Patriarchate will hold a discussion on 30 October to examine potential risks associated with the bill, after which it will formulate and publicly announce its unified position.

“Judging by what is apparent so far, I see certain risks. We have not yet fully examined the details — I have only heard some discussions about the issue on television. Of course, we will study the details and express our opinion. Frankly, much remains unclear, although we may still receive further explanations,” Metropolitan Anton said in an interview with InterPressNews.

He added that the Patriarchate intended to discuss the issue with government representatives and formulate its position on the bill in consultation with other senior clergy.

“Of course, we cannot remain indifferent,” the metropolitan said.

How has government policy on gambling changed?

In recent years, the Georgian Dream party’s gambling policy has primarily focused on tightening restrictions and limiting the number of people allowed to gamble.

During the early years of Georgian Dream’s rule, parliament twice rejected legislative initiatives aimed at banning gambling s and tightening regulations, in 2013 and 2019. In 2013, one of the arguments against such measures was the potential damage to the advertising industry, while Bidzina Ivanishvili warned of the risk of creating an unfavourable investment climate.

The situation changed significantly in late 2021, when parliament adopted a comprehensive package of gambling regulations. According to the government, the measures were intended to restrict access to gambling and limit its advertising.

Major restrictions came into force in March 2022:

The minimum gambling age for Georgian citizens was raised to 25.

Socially vulnerable individuals, public officials and people included in a designated register were banned from gambling.

Gambling s were banned on television, outdoors and on Georgian websites, with limited exceptions for certain forms of sponsorship.

Taxation and regulatory oversight were tightened.

The minimum gambling age for foreign nationals remained 18.

Subsequent changes revealed a distinct approach: maintaining strict restrictions for the local population while encouraging the development of the gambling industry targeting foreign customers.

According to an industry review published in June 2026, the government introduced a bill to establish preferential licensing and tax arrangements for online gambling companies targeting overseas customers.

The initiative proposed incentives for operators serving foreign markets, while maintaining a higher tax burden on the segment of the industry catering to Georgian citizens.

World.title: Armenian parliament ratifies framework agreement on Trump Route (TRIPP) project
World.content:
Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

The parliament of Armenia has ratified a framework agreement on strategic co-operation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project. The parties initialled the document during Marco Rubio’s visit to Yerevan on 26 May 2026 and signed the final version remotely just a few days later.

TRIPP (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) is a road that will connect Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory. The project also aims to reopen regional transport links. As a result, Armenia will gain access to third countries via Azerbaijan. For several years, Yerevan and Baku could not agree on this issue. Azerbaijan demanded a road that it called the “Zangezur corridor”. Armenia’s authorities said they were ready to reopen all transport routes but rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied a loss of Armenian control and sovereign rights over the territory. The two sides reached an agreement only on 8 August in Washington. Under the deal, the road will remain under Armenia’s sovereign control, while the US will join the project as a business partner. The initiative took the name “Trump Route” after the US president, who mediated the agreement.

Parliament ratified the agreement with 63 votes in favour and 32 against. Only MPs from the ruling faction supported it.

The parliamentary opposition had announced in advance that it would vote against ratification of the framework agreement. Opposition MPs argued that the document took US and Azerbaijani interests into account but failed to protect Armenia’s interests.

MPs from the ruling faction, by contrast, believe the project will reopen regional transport links on the basis of reciprocity. In their view, this would benefit Armenia economically. The opposition disagrees, pointing to the lack of any financial assessments.

Debates on ratifying the TRIPP project began in parliament the previous day. MPs had only two hours for the discussion. However, opposition lawmakers managed to raise all their concerns and put forward several proposals.

Opposition MP on the interests of the US, Armenia and Azerbaijan

Anna Grigoryan, head of the opposition Armenia faction, noted that Armenia and the United States had signed a bilateral document concerning the implementation of TRIPP. However, she said, the document also refers to a third party — Azerbaijan.

“Azerbaijan’s interests are actually reflected in this document more directly and clearly than the interests of the Republic of Armenia.”

Grigoryan also outlined what she believes each side stands to gain from the project.

“The US gains a direct presence in the region, particularly along the border with Iran, in a strategically crucial area. Azerbaijan secures a link between Nakhchivan and the rest of the country — a goal that both Azerbaijan and Turkey have long pursued.”

When asked what Armenia stands to gain, she said the question was harder to answer.

“When the political majority tries to answer this question, the first word they use is ‘unblocking’. But on the ground, no transport links are being reopened and no borders are opening. So that part of the answer does not reflect reality.”

Should the launch of TRIPP be linked to the signing of a peace treaty?

Narek Karapetyan, leader of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, is concerned that Azerbaijan may lose its incentive to sign a peace treaty once the Trump Route begins operating.

“Azerbaijan gets what it set out to achieve, while what we are supposed to get — peace — could be postponed for five to ten years. Why would they sign a peace treaty with Armenia if they are already getting a link to Nakhchivan?”

Official Yerevan has not ruled out the possibility that the Trump Route could begin operating before Armenia and Azerbaijan sign a peace treaty.

The MP argues that the two important issues should not be treated separately. He proposes linking the implementation of the Trump Route to the signing of a peace treaty.

Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Ruben Rubinyan disagreed. In his view, it is a positive development that TRIPP can proceed without depending on the signing of a peace treaty.

“If you argue that we should not implement this project in order to secure the signing of a peace treaty, you are saying that TRIPP is a bad initiative for Armenia. But TRIPP is by no means a bad initiative for Armenia.”

The ruling party representative welcomed the prospect of “elements of peace taking shape on the ground” independently of the peace treaty. By “elements of peace”, Rubinyan means both the launch of the Trump Route and the ongoing process of delimiting and demarcating the border between the two countries.

Background to the Trump Route project

The Trump Route offers Armenia a real opportunity to reopen regional transport links. For Azerbaijan, it provides the shortest route connecting the country with Nakhchivan.

The project envisages using the railway along a stretch of about 43km through Armenian territory. A motorway, energy infrastructure and digital communications links will also run through the area.

All infrastructure located on Armenian territory will remain under Armenia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction.

The ratified framework agreement provides for the establishment of TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the project’s development and implementation.

Initially, the US will own 74% of the company’s shares and Armenia will hold 26%. After 49 years, if the parties extend their co-operation for a further 50 years, Armenia’s stake will rise to 49%. Armenia will grant TRIPP Development Company exclusive rights to use and develop land, along with other necessary powers within the areas allocated to the project, for 49 years.

Armenia and the US still need to agree on and adopt the company’s charter and shareholder agreement.

It also remains unclear what border-crossing arrangements will apply to Armenian citizens travelling through Nakhchivan.

Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said the two sides had yet to agree on the technical details of travel through Azerbaijani territory.

“We still need to discuss these issues with Azerbaijan. They fall within the framework of Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.” Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.”

Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

World.title: ‘Like a black cat in a dark room’: Georgia’s opposition ban case enters sixth day of hearings
World.content:
What happened at Georgia’s opposition ban hearing

On 28 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the sixth day of hearings on a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties. The court is currently hearing submissions from the parties involved. On Tuesday, it heard arguments from representatives of the Coalition for Change.

The lawsuit names the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties whose aims include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The United National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining Georgia’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The lawsuit holds the party responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the accusations. Hearings are scheduled to continue through 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the claim, meaning at least four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

The Coalition for Change is represented in court by Nika Gvaramia, Tengo Tevzadze, Maia Kopaleishvili, Giga Lemonjava and Marika Arevadze. None of their motions was granted.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia clashed twice with the coalition’s representatives, over their citation of a European Parliament resolution and their reference to the “Russian doctrine”.

The hearings will resume on 29 October at 11 a.m.

Judge Nadaraia: “European Parliament resolution is irrelevant to this case”

Giga Lemonjava presented an 8 October 2026 European Parliament resolution at the hearing. The resolution compared the Georgian ruling party’s bid to ban opposition parties with the Russian and Belarusian models, describing it as part of a strategy to eliminate political pluralism and turn Georgia into a one-party state.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia interrupted the presentation and asked how the resolution was relevant to the proceedings. Lemonjava replied that it was not directly relevant to the case but that the public should be informed about it.

Nika Gvaramia commented: “Public hearings mean that participants are speaking not only to the court but also to the public.”

Nadarაიa responded: “Public hearings mean that everyone can follow the proceedings, not that someone can make political statements here.” He also reprimanded Gvaramia, saying: “You are interrupting me and disrupting the proceedings.”

Judge Nadaraia says comparison with Russia’s new doctrine is irrelevant to court proceedings

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia raised a similar objection for a second time during Giga Lemonjava’s address.

The opposition representative drew attention to two claims in the lawsuit against the opposition: that the previous government, when the United National Movement was in power, artificially restored the borders of the former South Ossetian Autonomous Region in 2007 and started the war with Russia in 2008.

Lemonjava argued that these claims closely matched Russia’s new foreign policy and security doctrine. If the court accepted them, he said, a Georgian state institution would be giving legal legitimacy to Russia’s version of events for the first time. “You need to be aware of this danger,” he told the judges.

Lemonjava also argued that giving legal force to these claims would contradict Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution, which obliges state institutions to take all measures to ensure the country’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Nadaraia did not allow Lemonjava to continue with this line of argument, describing his remarks as “demagoguery” and saying he had gone beyond the scope of the proceedings. The judge again told him not to interrupt.

Judge Gotsiridze: “Do not look for a black cat where there is none”

Maia Kopaleishvili, representing the Coalition for Change, and Constitutional Court judge Eva Gotsiridze previously served together on the court’s panel. At the hearing, they clashed over a section of the lawsuit concerning an alleged attempt to enter parliament.

Kopaleishvili questioned whether Gotsiridze had studied the ruling party’s lawsuit thoroughly enough. The judge called the remark inappropriate.

“Perhaps this issue simply needs clarification. Do not look for a black cat where there is none,” Gotsiridze replied.

Opposition representative Kopaleishvili tells ruling party lawyers: “You were my students”

Maia Kopaleishvili addressed Archil Gorduladze and Tornike Cheishvili, who are representing the ruling party in court.

“You said opposition parties should be banned to protect future generations from a threat. You were my students. What threat do my colleagues and I pose to the country’s future?” Kopaleishvili asked.

Gvaramia warns of return to Soviet-style one-party elections

Nika Gvaramia noted that 28 October marked 36 years since Georgia held its first multiparty elections in 1990, as the Soviet Union was breaking apart.

“And now we are going back to where we started,” he said.

Gvaramia also described as a “distorted reality” the attempt to remove Lelo opposition party leader Badri Japaridze from politics, despite his being one of the signatories of Georgia’s 1991 Act of Restoration of State Independence.

Opposition assesses court hearing

Tornike Artkmeladze, a member of Lelo, said after the hearing that banning opposition parties in a single move would destroy what had been painstakingly built over the past 35 years.

“This is preparation for the first stage of clearing the political field — first of parties, and then they will move on to banning any active political activity. Georgian Dream wants to be the only force on the political scene. But they fail to understand that there are at least a million people in this country who will not give up their freedom,” Artkmeladze said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan’s former powerbroker sentenced to 14 years, suspended, for treason
World.content:
Mehdiyev, former powerbroker, sentenced in Azerbaijan

Ramiz Mehdiyev was a man who could influence who became a member of Azerbaijan’s parliament, which newspaper was shut down and who received a pardon. He headed the presidential administration for 24 years, first under Heydar Aliyev and then under Ilham Aliyev, chaired the pardons commission and was widely regarded as the country’s unofficial second-in-command.

He has now been found guilty of treason.

A Baku court sentenced Mehdiyev, 88, to 14 years in prison.

However, the sentence was suspended due to his age and health.

Despite being found guilty of attempting a coup, Mehdiyev will not go to prison.

Mehdiyev was convicted on four charges:

Actions aimed at the violent seizure of power;

Treason;

Money laundering;

Accepting a bribe on an especially large scale.

The court also ordered his property confiscated by the state and recommended that he be stripped of his state awards.

The verdict was delivered on 22 October, but became public only five days later, on 27 October. The trial was held behind closed doors, and the verdict has not been published. The list of confiscated assets and their value have also not been officially disclosed.

The verdict brings the criminal case to a close, but leaves unanswered the main question that has fuelled debate for the past year: why did Mehdiyev come under scrutiny, and why now?

In recent months, government officials, pro-government media, independent commentators and the opposition have offered different, sometimes contradictory, explanations.

Official version shifts from hints of Kremlin involvement to accusations against opposition

In the early days of the investigation, pro-government news agency APA presented its own account of events.

According to the agency, in early 2025, amid rising tensions between Baku and Moscow, Mehdiyev proposed a plan to Russia to overthrow Azerbaijan’s government and establish an interim State Council, which he intended to lead.

The agency claimed that Russian President Vladimir Putin informed Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev of the plan during a meeting in Dushanbe on 9 October.

However, a detailed statement issued by Azerbaijan’s State Security Service on 12 February 2026, followed by the indictment, presented a different timeline.

According to investigators, in August and September 2025, Mehdiyev drafted a document in a foreign language entitled “Proposals for Reorganising the System of Public Administration” and passed it through his aide, Eldar Amirov, to Ali Karimli, chairman of the opposition Azerbaijan Popular Front Party (APFP).

The final version of the document was sent on 3 October.

The indictment also refers to the Union of Russian Azerbaijani Organisations, a group registered abroad and known as the “Union of Billionaires”.

The State Security Service claims the organisation was established by foreign intelligence services and was led by Abbas Abbasov, a former first deputy prime minister, and screenwriter Rustam Ibragimbekov.

According to the investigators’ account, Mehdiyev, Abbasov and the APFP leadership were part of a group that conspired to seize power by force.

The focus of the case has therefore shifted significantly over the past year.

While the Kremlin was initially portrayed as the main player behind the alleged plot, the opposition took centre stage by the time the investigation concluded.

In February, the State Security Service released an audio recording in which Mehdiyev can be heard speaking in Russian with a woman believed to be a foreign intelligence officer. He tells her that he has proposals for reorganising the system of public administration.

The woman replies: “That is your own business.”

Judging by the published excerpt, the woman believed to be an intelligence officer appears to distance herself from Mehdiyev’s proposals rather than show interest in them.

In September, a bribery charge was added to the case. However, authorities did not disclose who allegedly paid Mehdiyev, what the payment was for or how much money was involved.

The official statement on the verdict also refers to a “foreign state” but does not identify the country.

Official rhetoric casts Mehdiyev as traitor, oligarch and schemer

The day after the verdict was announced, the presidium of Azerbaijan’s National Academy of Sciences decided to expel Mehdiyev from its membership. The decision must now be approved by the academy’s general assembly.

Academy president Isa Habibbayli described Mehdiyev’s actions as “a betrayal unworthy of a scholar”.

The central message at the meeting was that betrayal was unforgivable from someone who had enjoyed every privilege the state could offer for many years.

Meanwhile, pro-government websites focused on Mehdiyev’s assets.

They published lists of villas, plots of land, stakes in shopping centres and bank shares allegedly belonging to him, as well as information about the Sharq-Gharb publishing house.

Lawyer Chingiz Ganizade told Modern.az that once the verdict comes into force, the confiscated property could be sold at auction, rented out or partly transferred to war veterans and families of fallen servicemen.

He noted, however, that the verdict had not yet taken legal effect and that there was a 20-day period for appealing it.

Another aspect of the case involves personal grievances.

After the verdict, television presenter Khoshgadam Hidayatgizi published a lengthy post on social media. She alleged that Mehdiyev had pressured the authorities to close her newspaper in 1999–2000 and blocked her candidacy in the 2005 elections.

She also said she had learned of an alleged plot to kill her by staging a car accident.

These claims could not be independently verified. Hidayatgizi also highlighted what she described as a striking change in attitudes towards Mehdiyev: people who once called him “father” and “aksakal” – a respected elder – were now among his fiercest critics.

Eldar Namazov, a political analyst and former head of the presidential administration’s secretariat, testified as a witness in the case. He recalled warning in 2020 that the network Mehdiyev had built posed a threat to the state.

Namazov told Oxu.az that Mehdiyev attended all court hearings remotely, was fully conscious and did not object to Namazov’s testimony.

A common thread running through this rhetoric is the attempt to portray Mehdiyev as an outsider to the political system.

Yet official discourse has largely avoided a central question: why was a man who shaped personnel policy, the ideological course of the country and the system of media control for 25 years allowed to remain untouchable throughout that period?

Critics question verdict delivered behind closed doors

Independent sources have focused less on the substance of the charges against Mehdiyev than on the lack of transparency surrounding the trial.

The Turan news agency says the closed-door proceedings make it impossible to independently assess the prosecution’s evidence or the defence’s arguments. It is also unclear why the verdict was announced only five days after it was delivered, or whether Mehdiyev intends to appeal.

According to the agency, political interpretations of the case in the context of Azerbaijan’s relations with Russia also remain speculation rather than established fact.

Turan columnist Tapdig Farhadoglu highlights another contradiction:

The first official document to reveal the income and assets of a man who headed the presidential administration for 24 years was not a declaration of assets, but a criminal verdict.

Even the information released about the verdict does not disclose the scale of the asset confiscations.

Lawyer Akram Hasanov offered a brief and pointed reaction on social media: “If Mehdiyev had died a few years earlier, he would have been buried in the First Alley of Honour.”

For the opposition, the most sensitive aspect of the case concerns Ali Karimli.

Karimli, chairman of the opposition Azerbaijan Popular Front Party (APFP), and Mammad Ibrahim, a member of the party’s leadership, are being held in connection with the same criminal case, although the charges against them are being handled in separate proceedings.

Both are accused of attempting to seize power by force. The relevant article of the Criminal Code carries a sentence of 12 to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment. A preliminary court hearing is scheduled for 3 November.

The APFP rejects the charges as politically motivated. In a statement issued in September, the party said Karimli had refused to testify from the outset of the investigation and denied claims that he had co-operated with Mehdiyev.

Against this backdrop, it is significant that Mehdiyev was convicted before proceedings against Karimli had begun.

Legally, the conviction of one defendant does not predetermine the outcome of proceedings against others in the case.

Politically, however, the situation looks different: the alleged central figure in the plot has already been found guilty, casting a shadow over the forthcoming trial of Karimli.

Why was the sentence suspended?

The court cited Article 70 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code, which allows a suspended sentence if the court concludes that the convicted person can be rehabilitated without serving time in prison.

Lawyer Ramil Suleymanov explained that a suspended sentence is not the same as house arrest. If the convicted person breaches the conditions imposed by the court, the suspended sentence can be revoked and the person sent to prison to serve the term.

The Turan news agency notes that the probation period under the law ranges from six months to five years. The length of the period imposed on Mehdiyev has not been disclosed.

The political significance of the verdict, however, appears to be independent of the form of punishment. Mehdiyev has been officially found guilty of treason, his assets are to be confiscated, and he could lose his state awards and membership of the National Academy of Sciences.

The authorities have secured this outcome without exposing the 88-year-old to the risk of dying in prison.

A suspended sentence also leaves open the possibility of tougher punishment in future. Any breach of the court-imposed conditions during the probation period could lead to the suspension being revoked and Mehdiyev being sent to prison.

This means the sentence could still be enforced through actual imprisonment at a later date.

At the same time, the verdict presents an obvious contradiction.

The state portrays Mehdiyev as a man who attempted to overthrow the constitutional order by force, yet considers it acceptable to leave him at liberty.

This leaves two possible explanations: either the threat was not as serious as the charges suggest, or the main purpose of the verdict was not so much to neutralise a threat as to send a political message.

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Abkhaz businesses to be required to install solar panels amid energy crisis
World.content:
Businesses in Abkhazia will be required to install solar panels. The government sees the measure as one way to tackle an energy shortage that has affected the region for years during the autumn and winter.

The initiative aims to reduce peak demand on the power grid and give commercial properties a more independent electricity supply. Under the proposal, newly built commercial premises and businesses would have to meet part of their electricity needs through alternative sources, such as solar panels.

The authorities are currently discussing the electricity consumption threshold above which businesses would have to use alternative, self-contained power sources.

Some businesses in Abkhazia have been using solar panels for several years. For them, installing the panels was a necessity, as they had no other way to secure an uninterrupted electricity supply. However, they received no assistance or incentives from the authorities for doing so.

It remains unclear whether the government will help businesses install solar panels now that the measure is set to become mandatory. This issue is also still under discussion.

Abkhazia relies on the Inguri hydropower plant as its sole source of electricity. Under an agreement with the Georgian side, with which Abkhazia jointly operates the plant, the region receives 40% of the electricity it generates. However, this has not been enough for the past decade, particularly in autumn and winter, when water levels at the plant fall.

Abkhazia’s budget has recently begun to include funding for electricity imports from Russia, but this money is also insufficient to cover the shortfall fully.

As a result, the region faces scheduled power cuts every year from November to March.

The main, though not the only, cause of the shortage is uncontrolled cryptocurrency mining, which consumes huge amounts of electricity. Authorities have managed to reduce the scale of mining significantly in recent years, helping to ease the problem. However, they have yet to resolve it completely.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Six-fingered ‘trolls’ working for Georgia’s authorities: Myth Detector identifies 445 fake accounts
World.content:
Fake pro-government accounts in Georgia

The organisation Myth Detector has identified a new network of so-called “trolls” comprising 445 fake accounts. The findings follow monitoring of the Facebook pages of TV channels Imedi and Rustavi 2, whose editorial policies align with the government’s agenda.

The accounts operate in a co-ordinated manner, liking posts by Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze and pro-government philosopher Zaza Shatirishvili.

The posts cover topics including bans on opposition parties, Western interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and threats to the country’s sovereignty. Myth Detector believes the aim is to create the impression of widespread public support for the government’s rhetoric.

In an earlier investigation, the same organisation identified 434 similar profiles. Myth Detector concludes that the emergence of new accounts indicates that the practice is continuing.

Monitoring revealed several common characteristics across the network of fake accounts: identical profile pictures; anatomical and geographical inconsistencies typical of AI-generated images; recurring first and last names; and similar patterns of behaviour on social media.

According to Myth Detector, most of these accounts were created within a two-day period. A total of 329 profiles were registered on 25 August 2026 and another 109 on 26 August.

Of the 445 accounts identified, 316 use AI-generated profile pictures. The remaining 129 feature images of public figures, landscapes, posters or photographs belonging to other social media users.

The organisation says some of the newly discovered accounts overlap with profiles identified in October by the non-governmental organisation ISFED.

What do the fake accounts like?

According to Myth Detector’s analysis, the suspicious Facebook accounts were mobilised around posts published by TV channels Imedi and Rustavi 2. Their activity focused primarily on political statements by Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze.

Co-ordinated likes were particularly noticeable under posts about a possible ban on opposition parties, Western interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and alleged threats to the country’s sovereignty from Western institutions.

The fake accounts actively liked posts by Irakli Kobakhidze and Kakha Kaladze concerning a lawsuit against opposition parties filed with the Constitutional Court. Co-ordinated activity was particularly evident under a Rustavi 2 post in which Georgia’s Foreign Ministry described critical comments by EU representatives about a possible ban on opposition parties as interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and an attempt to put pressure on the Constitutional Court.

Accounts mobilised around statements by Shalva Papuashvili supported the argument that foreign interference threatens freedom and democracy in Georgia.

Co-ordinated likes were also recorded under posts criticising the methods used to disperse protests in France and other European cities, drawing parallels with the situation in Georgia.

The accounts’ activity is not limited to engaging with posts by senior officials.

According to Myth Detector, co-ordinated likes also appeared under posts by pro-government philosopher Zaza Shatirishvili. He is one of the leading ideologues of the ruling team and the anti-Western platforms associated with it. His rhetoric closely echoes the narratives of the ruling party and its affiliated People’s Power movement.

Co-ordinated likes were also recorded under a post showing Bidzina Ivanishvili attending a party event, as well as under material covering a statement by Georgia’s Foreign Ministry.

AI-generated images and identity theft

According to the investigation, a significant proportion of the fake accounts attempt to imitate real people’s profiles.

They use photographs and biographical details of people with different ages, professions and interests, creating the impression of a diverse group of government supporters.

The profiles list a wide range of employers, including municipal and government institutions, banks, insurance companies, microfinance organisations and major media outlets such as Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and even the Pirveli TV channel.

In some cases, the stated place of employment does not match other information in the profile. For example, an account registered under the name Levan Kavtaradze features a photograph of a man standing beside a car during the grape harvest, yet lists the perfume and cosmetics retailer Voulez-Vous as his employer.

Keti Giorgadze’s profile lists Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty as her employer, while the accounts of Temo Khitarishvili and Nutsa Simonia name the news service of Pirveli TV.

According to Hive Moderation, there is more than a 90% probability that the photographs found in the 445 accounts were generated using artificial intelligence. In some cases, the probability reaches 100%.

The images contain anatomical defects, inconsistencies in the surrounding environment and distorted text — all characteristic signs of AI-generated content. In some pictures, the number or shape of fingers looks unnatural, while others show altered architectural details, logos and national symbols.

A photograph posted by an account under the name Simoniko Janashia shows a person holding a cup with their left hand, which has six fingers instead of five. A mark associated with images generated by the Gemini AI model is also visible in the bottom-right corner of the picture.

In other examples, a hand holding a wine glass is missing its little finger, while hands appear unnaturally fused together or blended into clothing.

A photograph shared by Tako Dvalishvili shows a person holding a book. However, the text on its cover is distorted: instead of the words “History of Georgia”, it displays something illegible.

The organisation also identified geographical inconsistencies. Comparisons with genuine images of well-known locations in Georgia show that AI alters architectural details and surrounding landscapes, sometimes even adding structures that do not actually exist.

Reproducing the visual appearance of old profiles

The investigation found that some of the newly identified accounts use profile pictures that had previously appeared on accounts uncovered by Myth Detector and later removed by Facebook.

In some cases, these visual similarities include identical anatomical flaws characteristic of AI-generated images. For example, photographs used in personal profiles under the names Tako Chagelia and Nia Gamkrelidze show the same finger defect previously observed in the profile picture of an account attributed to Maiko Vibliani.

The investigation also identified other common patterns in the behaviour of some accounts. A total of 196 profiles had liked the Tbilisinews.ge page, 14 had liked Ai Politika and three had liked Rustavi 2. Fake accounts identified by the organisation in previous investigations had also liked the Ai Politika page.

Most of the suspicious profiles have no friends at all, while some have only one or two. The investigation also uncovered accounts created in 2024 with friend lists ranging from 169 to 4,800.

Fake pro-government accounts in Georgia

World.title: Five baobab trees destined for Georgia seized in South Africa
World.content:
South Africa blocks shipment of baobabs to Georgia

Authorities in the South African city of Durban have blocked the shipment of at least five baobab trees. The trees were reportedly destined for a landscaping project in Georgia. A criminal investigation into the case is now under way.

According to Daily Maverick, officials discovered the baobabs at a warehouse in Durban owned by Africa Global Logistics (AGL), a subsidiary of Paris-based transport giant MSC Group.

Bidzina Ivanishvili, Georgia’s informal ruler, is known for his passion for collecting rare trees and plants. His name has featured in several cases involving the import of exotic trees into the country. In 2022, an attempt to bring eight baobabs from Kenya to Georgia attracted international attention. However, all eight trees eventually dried up and died.

What happened

According to South Africa’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE), those involved in exporting the trees failed to produce valid permits authorising their possession and removal from the country.

The baobab is one of Africa’s most recognisable tree species and can live for up to 2,000 years. In South Africa, it is among 50 endemic tree species that receive special protection. Without the appropriate official permits, it is illegal to cut down, damage, move, possess, sell, transport or export these trees.

The identities of the Georgian buyers and their representatives have not yet been disclosed.

Candy Botha, AGL’s regional marketing manager, told Daily Maverick that the company had provided logistics services only. It was neither the owner of the cargo nor the exporter, and it did not hold the required permits.

After learning that the trees were in Durban, Daily Maverick visited the AGL warehouse and photographed at least five baobabs. The trees lay on their sides on a paved surface. They appeared to have been left there in direct sunlight for two to three months.

Asked about the trees’ legal status, the company said such matters fell outside its responsibilities as a logistics provider. AGL also refused to disclose the client’s identity or contact details, citing confidentiality.

After Daily Maverick sent further questions to the DFFE, it emerged that no valid export licence had been issued for the trees. There was also no permit authorising their removal and relocation. According to available information, the baobabs came from the Waterberg District in Limpopo province.

Based on photographs, Jeff Nichols, a specialist in endemic plants, suggested that the trees could be more than 50 years old if they had been taken from the wild. If they had instead been grown under artificial conditions with irrigation, he estimated their age at 20 to 30 years.
