World.title: The inner Sydney school where the gates are opened to everyone
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The inner Sydney school where the gates are opened to everyone Julie Power October 29, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was a moment when old knees felt young again. A bit like the ABC’s Old People’s Home for 4 Year Olds, Green Square Public School and Community Spaces’ new multi-generational choir began on Monday when seniors sang with the school’s junior choir and executed a few knee-bending dance moves. Green Square resident Kathleen Hii with Green Square Public School librarian Yvette Lewington, who lives locally, with her daughter in the large multi-purpose play area. Wolter Peeters The school, in one of the most densely populated neighbourhoods in Australia, is for children by day. But its grounds, basketball court and meeting rooms, managed by Sydney City Council, are for everyone on weekends, holidays and after 6.30pm on school days. That’s prompted many in the community – neither grandparents nor parents of students – to volunteer at the school, too.



Principal Nicole Molloy said it was the first authentic community shared facility that she’d experienced. “We don’t close our gates at 3pm every day and keep people out. They’re welcomed in,” Molloy said. Now celebrating its first birthday, the project by architects BVN, developed with advice from Molloy and other teachers, has won the Daryl Jackson Award for Educational Architecture from the 2026 Australian Institute of Architects. Green Square Public School and Community Spaces designed by BVN Architects has just won the most important award in Australia for educational architecture. Wolter Peeters AIA jury chair Adam Haddow said in “a time of societal paranoia and public distrust, good architecture is about trusting people”. Green Square was designed to include people, not exclude them. Haddow hailed projects that are left open for public use where “occupants assume that someone is not going to come and tag a building or burn it down”.



It was architecture that assumed most people were good, wanted to live in great places, connected to their friends, family and the people around them. Local Kathleen Hii, 75, a member of the new choir and who started a playgroup for the community, said they hadn’t realised the Beatles’ song Here Comes the Sun had moves the children knew. “Sun sun sun, full squat, then rising,” Hii said. BVN co-chief executive Ali Bounds and Green Square Public School and Community Spaces foundation principal Nicole Molloy in the award-winning campus. Wolter Peeters They were a bit hard on the seniors’ knees. But something magical happened, some intergenerational transmission of knee oil, and Hii said they had young knees again. “We walked out of there [on Monday] after singing feeling two inches taller,” she said. BVN co-chief executive and architect Ali Bounds said they had turned the original brief upside down. Initially, the multipurpose play area with a full-size basketball court was planned for the top floor. But they moved it to the ground floor next to the community spaces – where it was easily accessible – to avoid the public traipsing through the classrooms destined for 600 students when full.



Bounds said there were often teenagers waiting outside after 6pm asking, “‘When’s the gate opening?’ And that happens most days.” Hii said the school and its shared facilities had given the community a sense of belonging. “It is the magnet, it is the conduit.” Related Article Architecture ‘Looks like the Opera House’: Why Ray Hadley’s new apartment is a winner Many seniors now read to the young students. “I joke about rent a grandma,” said Hii, adding many of the children she read to were born overseas. “One child was from Mongolia, another from mainland China … None had a grandparent here.” The NSW government announced in September that every new public school will share facilities with the community outside school hours, and more than 200 have already undertaken to do so.



Premier Chris Minns said, “I’ve never been a fan of locking up school grounds to the public. I want kids and families to be able to use the grounds outside of school hours.” Many schools fear vandalism, and about 1200 schools have large security fences to keep people out. Molloy said some people had feared the school would be damaged or graffitied. “I’ve not had a single issue because it’s special to everybody.” EA House designed by Bokey Grant won the national award for residential housing in 2026. Clinton Weaver The community had developed a real ownership of the space. “Because it’s theirs seven days a week. We’ve been here a year, and the place is well looked after and loved, and not just by us.”



Green Square’s walls are covered in a fine tensile mesh designed to make children feel safe without feeling imprisoned. It is also covered in a web of brick slips that provide privacy from the apartments that surround the school in every direction. Just as the ground floor spaces and rooms can be used in different ways, Molloy and other teachers wanted the school’s classrooms to adapt. Furniture was designed to be moved, rooms have large dividers, small spaces for groups, outdoor meeting areas and large wet spaces for art. New Sydney Fish Market | 3XN GXN in association with BVN Architecture and Aspect Studios Rasmus Hjortshøj Other national winners include: Sydney Fish Market by 3XN in association with BVN and ASPECT Studios, which won for commercial architecture

Lacebark apartments by Smart Design Studio won the Frederick Romberg Award for Residential Architecture for multi-residential architecture apartment design

World.title: McReight joins back-row greats with first John Eales Medal
World.content:
Breaking SportRugby UnionWallabies McReight joins back-row greats with first John Eales Medal Jonathan Drennan October 29, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Fraser McReight has won the John Eales Medal as Australian rugby’s best player of the year after his international teammates recognised his consistently excellent performances for his country this season. McReight received the game’s highest honour at the Rugby Australia awards in Sydney on Thursday night, while 21-year-old inside centre Faitala Moleka was crowned Wallaroos Player of the Year and Reds star Treyvon Pritchard named rookie of the year. Fraser McReight has been recognised by his peers for Rugby Australia’s highest honour Getty Images The John Eales medal is based on votes submitted by Wallabies players after every Test match. McReight joins a long list of outstanding back-rowers to have won the award since it was established in 2002, including David Lyons, Phil Waugh, George Smith (twice), Rob Valetini (twice), David Pocock (twice) and former captain Michael Hooper, who won the award a record four times. Like Hooper, McReight has played some of his best rugby when the Wallabies are under the greatest pressure. A ferocious competitor at the breakdown, McReight has also developed an accomplished all-around game, establishing himself as one of the best openside breakaways in world rugby.



McReight was also recognised for his outstanding defensive performances – particularly in the 16-point defeat to France in Brisbane in July, in which he scored two tries as well as making 19 tackles, with the award for Defender of the Year. McReight has also become the first Queensland Reds player to claim a John Eales medal since former Wallabies fullback Chris Latham 20 years ago. The late Peter Meagher who has been recognised by Rugby Australia for his outstanding service to the game. Meagher family Brisbane Junior Rugby Union Western Region chair Paula Watkins was honoured with the inaugural Peter Meagher Spirit of Rugby Award, in recognition of her dedication and tireless support for the community game. Meagher, a much-loved figure in the Randwick rugby community, was one of 15 people tragically killed in the terrorist attack at Bondi Beach last year while taking photographs of the Hanukkah festival as a volunteer.



“Rugby Australia decided to honour Marzo”, who held a longtime association with Randwick rugby club, by rebranding the award previously named after Nick Farr-Jones in his honour. National team captains Isabella Nasser and Henry Hutchison took home the Shawn Mackay Awards for the Women’s and Men’s Sevens Player of the Year, respectively. 2026 Rugby Australia Awards - winners list John Eales Medal - Fraser McReight

Wallaroos Player of the Year - Faitala Moleka

Shawn Mackay Award for Men’s Sevens Player of the Year - Henry Hutchison

Shawn Mackay Award for Women’s Sevens Player of the Year - Isabella Nasser

Swyftx Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year - Jock Campbell

Swyftx Super Rugby Women’s Player of the Year - Siokapesi Palu Sekona

Santos Men’s Rookie of the Year Award - Treyvon Pritchard, Queensland Reds

Santos Women’s Rookie of the Year Award - Amelia Whitaker, Wallaroos

Junior Men’s Player of the Year - Edwin Langi, Australia U20 and NSW Waratahs

Junior Women’s Player of the Year - Waiaria Ellis, Wallaroos and NSW Waratahs

Cadbury Try of the Year - Siokapesi Palu Sekona, Wallaroos vs. Scotland, Canberra

Defender of the Year - Fraser McReight, Wallabies vs. France, Brisbane

Fedex Referee of the Year - Nic Berry

Peter Meagher Spirit of Rugby Award - Paula Watkins, Queensland Rugby Union

Joe French Award for Outstanding Contribution to Rugby - Craig Robberds, ACT Rugby

Geoff ‘Bunter’ Shaw Community Coach of the Year Award - Kieran Smith, NSW Rugby

Andrew Cole Community Match Official of the Year - Julius Ambat, NSW Rugby First-time winner Nasser led the Australian Women’s team to the World Championship title while Hutchison, who last achieved this accolade in 2021, guided the Men’s side to their first tournament win since 2023 when they claimed gold in Valladolid. Japan-bound fullback Jock Campbell won the Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year title after an outstanding year for the Reds, while ACT Brumbies and Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona was named Super Rugby Women’s Player of the Year. Amelia Whitaker was also named women’s rookie of the year after her first season for the Wallaroos.



Australian U20 and NSW Waratahs prop Edwin Langi won Junior Men’s Player of the Year for his performances across the year in both programs, while 19-year-old Waiaria Ellis picked up Junior Women’s Player of the Year after shining on the international stage. Referee of the Year Award was awarded to the experienced Nic Berry, who has taken charge of 41 Tests over the last ten years since retiring from playing professional rugby. A uniquely designed coastal home inspired by an iconic West Australian hiking track took out one of the top prizes at the National Architecture Awards on Thursday. Officer Woods Architects claimed the Robin Boyd Award – the best new residential architecture house – for their Eric Street dual residence in Cottesloe. The Cottesloe house is a maisonette design which looks like a big house but contains multiple dwellings. Robert Frith/Acorn Photo Owners Donna Dransfield and Tony York said the design of their home focused more on outside living than indoor floorspace and was inspired by the Bibbulmun Track – one of the world’s great long-distance walk trails, stretching 1000 kilometres from Kalamunda in the Perth Hills, to Albany on the south coast. “We really wanted a house where you don’t walk in the front door, and you’re in a house,” Dransfield said.



“We wanted a house where the outdoor area was part of the house and the living space, so you’re always in and out, and you can live out there, but you can come in to access something.” Dransfield walked the Bibbulmun Track with her daughter and then again with her son, and said the six weeks spent trekking the trail and sleeping in huts made them want to design their house with the bedrooms separate from the main residence. The kitchen in the upstairs dwelling of the Eric Street house. Robert Frith/Acorn Photo “You’re always outside, and you do it for so long that then you get used to that, and it’s such a beautiful way of living, and sleeping at night, smelling the trees,” she said. “So I think for me, that was a big part of how I’d like to live. Wouldn’t it be nice if you could live like that?”



A walk through of the property reveals its balance between public engagement and privacy. The kitchen and dining zones face the street and ocean, while the living and sleeping areas retreat around a sheltered, north-facing courtyard. Upstairs, two pavilions – the living quarters and bedrooms – and a post-swim sauna frame a pair of protected outdoor spaces, including a breezy entertaining deck and a terrace, buffered by deep planters. Overhead, intersecting skillion roofs provide deep solar shading while channelling rainwater into on-site soakwells to recharge the local aquifer. Officer Woods describes the Eric Street property as “a useful residential model”. “A single house with a broad range of possible occupations, set up for future horizontal subdivision – an adaptable hybrid which allows for long-term flexibility,” they say.



“Its design embraces the idea of the ebb and flow of life, accommodating multiple mutable lives, comings and goings, changes in circumstances and the varying spatial requirements related to each.” In between the bedroom and living areas is a patio area that can be completely enclosed or open depending on the weather. Robert Frith/Acorn Photo The property is split into two separate dwellings – the top is the couple’s main residence and the bottom is frequently used as an Airbnb and has generated $150,000 in income so far – but they have completely different designs. Architect Trent Woods describes the bottom house as “more conventional” in design while the upstairs is “two separate pavilions in a garden”. “It’s what you might see in a semi-detached, it’s got a shotgun plan of bedroom, bedroom, loungeroom, like a terrace house,” Woods said.



“The internal square metreage for the house upstairs, is 137 square meters, which is extremely modest in this day and age. “And to get two houses at that level, it’s unusual to privilege the garden over the internal space, which is something Tony and Donna really wanted to do, to make those gardens and make all those connections.” York said the project came in at $2.2 million and replaced their former 1930s single-storey house they had lived in since 2001. “The house was really dark and really cold, and we were completely overshadowed by the building to the west of us, and we were below everything around us,” he said. “Part of the brief for this place was definitely we want a lot of sunlight. We want to be able to see the sky.”



The couple now have ocean views. Jury members said the simple planning of the house was a “great model for future housing” and one of the reasons for its win. The bedrooms in the upstairs dwelling are completely separate from the living areas. Robert Frith/Acorn Photo “At Eric Street in Cottesloe, Officer Woods Architects has created a dual residence on the site of a single-family home,” they said. “A series of indoor and outdoor spaces is woven together to provide the perfect balance of outlook and privacy, with distant views to the beach and carefully mediated connections to the neighbourhood.



“Eric Street provides a great model for future housing, with a modest but assured architectural approach balanced with skilful planning that allows for dual occupancy for extended family or to sublet as a secondary residence.” Officer Woods also took out the Marshall Clifton Award at the WA Architecture Awards for new residential architecture earlier this year.

World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

“Those who’ve been traumatised by the bogong moth invasion (C8), should spare a thought for some of us up here on the Sunshine Coast tackling a far creepier calamity: lawn prawns,” claims Mary Carde of Parrearra (Qld). “We’ve had so much rain that these land-dwelling crustaceans are fleeing the saturated garden and slinking under doorways onto a much drier surface, then die within a couple of hours due to lack of moisture, leaving a sea of husks to be vacuumed up.”

“Apropos of Michael Britt’s item re price per-unit (C8), my mother taught me to do that, using mental arithmetic, 65 years ago,” claims Sally Deves of Kingston (ACT). “Nothing new!”

On the advice of Rev Dr John Bunyan of Campbelltown, there will be no further talk of an alternative Halloween (C8): “C8 is no place for religious controversy but the idea of honouring Martin Luther is appalling. Luther called for the expulsion of Jewish people and the destruction of their homes and synagogues, with centuries-long consequences. His proposals were implemented by the Nazis to whom he was a hero. Kristallnacht in Germany (and the neo-Nazi demonstration outside State Parliament) coincided with Luther’s birthday. The Lutheran Churches, I think unhappily, retain his name but have repudiated this aspect of his writings.”

VoVogate continues, and Daniel Low of Pymble thinks Ted Richards (C8) “may be right. The company is putting fewer and smaller VoVos in the packs and increasing the plastic spacers to make it seem the same size. However, I’d say he’s lucky if there are less because the flavour has also diminished. I was bought a packet for my 19th Birthday (I’m a leaper) two years ago, and it wasn’t the taste of my childhood.”

Tony Tucker of Leichhardt digresses, but not without credence: “Of course Iced Volvos, er, VoVos, have gotten smaller. Remember what happened to Waggon Wheels? Speaking of wheels, that’s something that has gotten larger. Look at how the size of Raptors, Renegades, Rangers, Rebels, Rams, Ringos and Rongos has grown in the testosterone-infected world of the AWD ute!”

World.title: A little philanthropy goes a long way
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters A little philanthropy goes a long way October 29, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. They say philanthropy begins at home. I’m wondering what Victoria’s rich list (say those with $5 billion or more) are doing to support those in need in our state and what they pay in tax. That people fleeing domestic violence are being asked whether they can sleep in their cars and homeless people are being offered tents (″⁣People in need of housing offered tents amid crisis″⁣, 29/10) is an indictment of our social contract. Obscene wealth is an indicator that our capitalist system is broken. Philanthropy is a Band-Aid, but one that has the potential to alleviate much suffering. Will our billionaires stand up like Warren Buffett and Melinda Gates have done and show the way to others?

Lynn Frankes, Kew Being homeless is not their fault

Homelessness Australia chief executive Kate Colvin’s assertion that “there are now so many points of vulnerability in our housing and homelessness system that the cracks are starting to join” is a dire assessment of the respective systems that have fallen by the wayside due to protracted neglect by state and territory governments – a long time in the making of the “cracks joining up”.

Crucially, one of the primary reasons that women can’t leave a violent relationship is because of a dearth of alternate safe and available housing is tantamount to a choice between homelessness and violence as previously identified and documented by Dr Anne Summers report (2022) “The Choice: Violence or Poverty”.

Needless to say that “years of policy failure that has created the crisis we are now seeing is “feeding on itself” (ie vicious cycle) with catastrophic human consequences to an expanding number of people experiencing homelessness in our country through no fault of their own.

Jelena Rosic, Mornington This is not the education state

With disgraceful decisions like this, how can we call ourselves the education state (″⁣Schools left shocked by disability support cuts″⁣, 29/10)? I am a retired grandmother who does partial homeschooling for her grandson because schools are already underfunded and struggling to provide the additional support to many students need as it is.

This underfunding has now been enshrined until 2034 in the new bilateral funding agreement with the federal government. With disability inclusion funding now also cut, how on earth can teachers, education support staff and principals, teach and support children how they want/need to?

The government is reducing student-level funding rates by 2.5 per cent, and for mainstream schools only, a reduction of $850 per term for eligible students from 2027. Our children are the future, they are our culture bearers, our decision-makers, our future business owners, teachers, nurses, and trades people. How can we step into the future when our Victorian government can’t even fully fund and take care of our schools now.

Premier Ben Carroll’s decision is shameful and a disgrace, and does not reflect the values that an education state should demonstrate. I urge the premier to immediately reverse this decision and ensure every student in public schools has the funding they need and deserve.

Rosemary Charleston, Yarraville



Think outside the box

Petrol up, food up, and there is speculation the Reserve Bank wants to raise interest rates again that will hit home loan borrowers with yet another increase. Where some of those extra payments are coming from defeats me. Young people with a mortgage do have to eat and commute. Can the ″⁣economic experts” not think outside the box and suggest another tactic that doesn’t penalise the already struggling?

Wendy Hinson, Wantirna THE FORUM Invite more to debate

The Age reports (29/10) that the premier and the leader of One Nation in Victoria are ready for the first debate, while Jess Wilson will not be attending. Given Warren Pickering is not even in the Victorian parliament and was chosen by a Queenslander, not the Victorian members of One Nation, then it seems appropriate that the leader of the Australian Democrats who will be contesting this election as a party, the leader of the Greens, and the leader of the Socialist Party should also be included in the debate. Seems only right that there is a bigger representation than the narrow view of those already attending.

Bruce McMillan, Grovedale More balance, please

Jess Wilson is quite correct in arguing that the leaders’ debate be only between the premier and the leader of the opposition. They are the only likely leaders of the state after the election.

Insisting that the One Nation leader be included is a continuing ploy by Ben Carroll inferring that an alternate government can only be a coalition of Liberal, Nationals and One Nation. I note, however, that the Greens are not included in the debate as a possible partner in a potential Labor government. Some balance in this discussion is needed.

Peter Norman, Glen Iris



More than one debate

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson appears reluctant to attend a televised debate. Residents of Jess Wilson’s electorate of Kew may be wondering if they witnessed a warm-up for this when Wilson chose to not attend a recent ″⁣Candidates Community Forum″⁣ about climate and energy policies.

A state government needs to be capable of managing many issues beyond headline grabbers of potholes and crime rates. Our safe futures depend on sound, evidence-based plans on managing climate impacts and the transition to clean energy.

These policies need to be presented and debated. Surely communities deserve a better level of respect.

Greg Davies, Glen Waverley Different visions

For a young person, Jess Wilson is surprisingly mired in the past. Her youth is not per se an impediment to being a good premier (Lara Giddings was 39 when elected premier of Tasmania) but I would have expected that Wilson’s policies would reflect that we live in the 2020s, facing existential threats from climate change, environmental degradation, cataclysmic political change with right-wing populism, and the knowledge that the country has failed its First Nations Peoples in many ways.

Instead, Wilson is going back to last century policies to dig for gas to keep the lights on. How long will it take to find gas, build infrastructure, build new electricity plants and new transmission lines? How much environmental damage will this cause? I abhor One Nation, but it exists, and ignoring the party won’t make it go away. Wilson must engage with its leader in debate even while rejecting any suggestion of power sharing. Tearing up Treaty and replacing it with a government department has failed countless times at state and federal level – so many departments of Aboriginal Affairs, so much money, so few positive outcomes. Labour is a tired government, but it has had a vision for the future; the Liberals have a vision for the past.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Not egalitarian

So let me get this straight, at the top end, people are buying homes for between $5 million and $150 million, while at the other end women fleeing domestic violence are offered tents because there is no room for them elsewhere. How has it come to this where the richest live in a bubble, while those in need are discarded.

Australia likes to say it’s egalitarian but the above proves otherwise and it breaks my heart.

Samantha Keir, East Brighton Renewable benefits

Renewed calls for nuclear power ignore economic reality, even if you ignore the long-term environmental impact. It may have made some sense in 2012, but since then, thanks to the EV revolution, even the previous prohibitive cost of battery backed renewables is now competitive. The wholesale cost of electricity has recently dropped due to continued adoption of renewables and battery storage. Checking my household electricity bills from before the current government was elected, I see my rates have hardly changed at all. So, talking of higher prices leaves me personally baffled.

Daryl Budgeon, Hadfield Dazed and confused

In these difficult days with costs rising in everything from food, petrol, mortgage repayments and a third of the population living with food insecurity, it is forecast that the public are about to spend millions to celebrate Halloween. Strange days indeed.

Peter Roche, Carlton



Mind the birds

We manage to spend an estimated $500 million on Halloween in a country where some can’t put food on the table and all face rising bills and inflation. Halloween is fallout from the US and results in more plastic landfill and rubbish – gone in a few days – not to mention the risk of the “fake spider webs” to bird life.

Christine Barnett, Highton Cut military spending

It was refreshing to read Ross Gittins (Comment, 28/10) point out the need for the government to tax the export of our minerals and fossil fuels and avoid wasteful spending in order to avoid inflation and balance the economy.

One area of spending he did not highlight was the waste in government spending on the military and in particular the billions of dollars being spent to support US military strategy in our region as part of the AUKUS alliance. The use of our bases by the US military is not in Australia’s best interests.

The military is one important possible area for cuts in government spending, and it would help balance the budget.

Bruce Henry, Moonee Ponds How to help

The charity Foodbank reports that around one-third of Australian households are experiencing food insecurity, defined as irregular access to sufficient nourishing food (“For millions, Australia is the hungry country″⁣ , 26/10). This is a disturbing finding.

What can be done to ameliorate the suffering? The federal and state governments could increase their funding of Foodbank in each jurisdiction. The Commonwealth could raise more taxes from our energy exporters, and use this revenue to reduce taxes for low income earners and improve the JobSeeker and pensioner allowances. The Commonwealth also needs to find ways to create more competition in the energy and insurance sectors, whose charges these days account for big hits on family budgets. Assisting households to become less dependent on the energy grids by going solar is a good start.

Cutting migration significantly is not an answer, as it would cause labour shortages in key industries, including agriculture and food-processing, and hence increase inflationary pressures.

Andrew Trembath, Blackburn The Trump effect

Further to your correspondent’s contribution (Letters, 29/10), I agree with their premise that social media has provided a “safe” opportunity to voice hatred that has in fact always simmered below the waterline. I would, however, add that the rise of Donald Trump in US politics from 2016 has given, first Americans and then the world, the licence to be abusive, to mock people for their looks or disabilities or even gender and to be disrespectful just because others hold alternative views.

Furthermore, Trump has legitimised rejecting anything when it does not go your way and that truth in communication has virtually become an irrelevance. Unfortunately, his influence in this sphere seems to have increased exponentially since he was first granted “legitimacy” in US politics by US voters and his sycophantic Republican acolytes.

This decline in our social fabric is now clear to see in Australia.

Mark Thomson, Beaumaris More things change

Recent letters have lamented the standard of behaviour of our representatives in parliament. I’m re-reading David Copperfield by Charles Dickens, first published in 1850.

In one scene, when young David is in school and the class is seriously ″⁣mucking up″⁣ he observes the hapless schoolmaster ″⁣endeavouring to get on with his tiresome work, amid an uproar that might have made the Speaker of the House of Commons giddy″⁣.

It seems not much has changed in 176 years.

David Smith, Cheltenham



Just turn off, 1

Columnist Kylie Moore-Gilbert is spot on in holding the online domain largely responsible for the current popular addiction to hatred and violence (Comment, 28/10), but her solution to redesign internet regulation and legislate, is too tepid, and by her own description, politically implausible.

A simple, cost-effective way, which avoids politics altogether and is available to every individual and business, is just turn it off.

I can’t hear the protests because I’ve turned it off, but everyone I talk to agrees with me.

John Laurie, Riddells Creek Just turn off, 2

I’m an old lady but I remember my mother saying, “Never write down on paper anything you wouldn’t want read out in court.”

If she were alive now, I’m sure she would say the same about computers. Many people today would do well to heed that advice.

Pamela Pilgrim, Highett Money or your life?

People who say we should keep on using gas, coal or even nuclear energy because we can’t afford “unreliable” alternative energy reminds me of a question I ask my students: Would you rather have $1000 or your life?

They understand the answer.

Suzanne Palmer-Holton, Seaford Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING



Politics

If Pauline Hanson has a vision for the country she hopes to lead, it must be hidden in her Bluey colouring book.

Annie Wilson, Inverloch Among Jess Wilson’s promises, will she promise to slow down and stop when shaking anyone’s hand in the future?

David West, Essendon Columnist Shaun Carney (Comment, 29/10) should be compulsory reading for all Coalition, One Nation and fearful Labor voters. We are no different, and in many cases better off, than the rest of the world.

Randall Bradshaw, Fitzroy Furthermore

OK America, this is your chance to save yourselves and the free world. Make Donald Trump impotent for the next two years.

Graham Fetherstonhaugh, Fitzroy North I almost reported a truck driver going down South Road in Moorabbin for bad driving until I realised he was just avoiding the potholes.

Peter Venn, East Bentleigh



My late father used to say there would always be wars as wars make money but only for the arms manufacturers.

Susan Munday, Bentleigh East Have doubts about everything should be foremost in everyone’s thoughts in this social media, AI era.

Richard Crago, Burwood East The mind boggles – women fleeing domestic violence will receive a tent (″⁣Services offer the homeless tents″⁣, 29/10). It is to hoped they receive a bucket and spade as well.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove Why are the lower-income members of Australia the ones who pay the penalty of increased interest rises, while the wealthy benefit from the extra earnings? When will this be changed?

Bruce Dudon, Woodend Finally

Israeli election ″⁣on edge″⁣. Seems to me, the whole world is on edge, and it’s putting my nerves and teeth on edge.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East

World.title: Your fast guide to the US midterms and how they work
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms Your fast guide to the US midterms and how they work Madeleine Heffernan October 29, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

On November 3, Americans will head to the polls for midterm elections that could have big ramifications for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency. All seats in the US House of Representatives and a third of those in the Senate come up for grabs. The results will determine whether the Democrats can neuter Trump’s agenda or if he will maintain his grip on America until the presidential election in November 2028. Donald Trump’s approval rating has slumped from 47 per cent to 32 per cent. AP Photo/Alex Brandon The elections, which are on track to be America’s most expensive ever, are being fought on everything from the cost of living to the war on Iran, artificial intelligence and data centres, abortion rights, the immigration crackdown, and, of course, the president himself.



How do the midterms work? The US midterms take place on the Tuesday after the first Monday of November, as stipulated in a law passed 181 years ago. They are held midway between presidential elections to determine the make-up of Congress, which comprises both the House of Representatives (which has two-year terms) and the Senate (six-year terms). For a majority, Republicans and Democrats need to win 218 House seats and 51 Senate seats. Fairfax Media The Trump administration narrowly controls Congress. In the House of Representatives, the Republicans hold a five-seat majority, with 219 seats (including an independent who votes Republican) against the Democrats’ 214. In the Senate, Republicans have 53 seats versus the Democrats’ 47 (including two independents who vote Democrat). Come November, all 435 seats in the House (the lower chamber of Congress) are up for grabs. In addition, a total of 35 Senate seats (the upper chamber) are in play, which comprises a third of all Senate seats, plus two seats vacated by prominent Republicans JD Vance (who became vice president) and Marco Rubio (who became secretary of state). In addition to Congress, 36 out of 50 states will have gubernatorial elections on the same day.



Who’s expected to win? To take control of the House, the Democrats need to pick up at least six more seats (218 seats in total); in the Senate, they need to win a net four seats (51). Polling suggests Democrats are on track to win the House easily, and possibly the Senate. Senator Jon Ossoff is expected to win Georgia for the Democrats. AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite That’s largely because the unpopular war on Iran and high inflation have pushed Trump’s popularity to the lowest point in his political career. Trump started his second term with an approval rating of 47 per cent, but the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll found his approval rating had slumped to 32 per cent. The same poll found 43 per cent of registered voters planned to vote for the Democrats in these midterms, and 35 per cent for the Republicans – the biggest lead for the Democrats this year.



The Democrats winning control of both houses would frustrate Trump’s agenda for the final two years of his presidency, plus revive the party ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign. “A win is now measured based on how many seats Democrats pick up rather than getting to a balance or status quo,” says Cory Alpert, who worked in the Biden-Harris administration. Related Article US midterms On the road in Ohio: Why Trump is on the defensive in this crucial state Alpert expects young Democrat senator Jon Ossoff to beat Republican Mike Collins in the battleground state of Georgia, and Democratic nominee Roy Cooper to defeat Michael Whatley in North Carolina. “I think races in Texas, Ohio, Alaska, and Michigan are all toss-ups, which in this environment probably favour the Democrat in the race. Florida, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska are on my watch list for potential flips. “If we see any of those flip on the night, it’s a Democratic wave election.”



Which seats matter the most? Texas is a key battlefield, with former teacher and seminarian James Talarico hoping to become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from the conservative state since 1988. Talarico, dubbed “Talafreako” by Trump, is up against the president-endorsed state Attorney-General Ken Paxton. “If Talarico wins, it’s a banner year for Democrats,” Alpert says. “If Paxton wins, the margin will tell us a lot.” In the swing state of Michigan, epidemiologist and Democrat progressive Abdul El-Sayed – nicknamed “Mohamed” by Trump – is up against Republican Mike Rogers for a Senate seat. Emma Shortis, a senior researcher at The Australia Institute think tank, says former president Joe Biden’s support of the Netanyahu government in Israel is “one of the key fault lines of the Democratic Party. The result in Michigan will tell us a lot about the ideological make-up and political momentum of the party ahead of the next presidential election.” Democrat James Talarico would make history by winning Texas these midterms. Bloomberg It’s lawyers at 10 paces in Alaska, a state Trump won in 2024. This time around, Democrat Mary Peltola is up against incumbent Republican senator Dan S. Sullivan and a similarly named unaffiliated candidate called Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. There is also another long-shot candidate named Gerald Heikes.



Last week, the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit requesting Alaska not to certify its Senate results if Peltola wins, arguing that having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot threatened the “integrity” of the vote count. Peltola’s team responded by asking a federal court to dismiss the Trump administration’s lawsuit, describing it as baseless and raising “profound constitutional concerns”. Ohio is home to a hotly contested Senate race, with incumbent Republican Jon Husted neck and neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown. But it’s the battle for the Ohio governorship that has produced international headlines. In an attack ad, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy featured the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton, who was allegedly molested by her stepfather as a child. (The mother called her daughter a liar). The New York Times called it the “most ruthless ad of the midterms”. Then there’s Maine, which has something of a maverick streak when it comes to politics. The Democrats initially picked oyster farmer Graham Platner to take on veteran Republican senator Susan Collins, until an allegation of sexual assault (which Platner denies) killed his candidacy. Former Maine Senate president Troy Jackson is trying to snatch the Senate seat from his five-term Republican rival Collins. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: These films blew up the box office. Now you can finally watch them at home
World.content:
From Obsession to Hokum, these horror box office hits are perfect for a cosy, spooky night in this Halloween.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the words of Mean Girls’ Gretchen Wieners, horror is so fetch right now. From YouTuber breakouts like Obsession and Backrooms to nostalgic blockbuster hits like Scream 7, the genre is firing on all cylinders, especially among Gen Z. It has massively boosted the box office, contributing more than $1.82 billion in the US alone, just shy of last year’s record of $2.02 billion. And the year’s not over yet. With Halloween just around the corner, it’s the perfect time to catch up on the buzziest horror offerings – many of which are now available to stream at home. Grab the popcorn and prepare to be spooked. One thing is clear after watching Obsession: Be careful what you wish for. Focus Features via AP Obsession (HBO Max) This year delivered several stellar horror titles, but Obsession arguably led the pack. Directed by 27-year-old YouTuber Curry Barker, the film follows Bear (Michael Johnston), a typical “nice guy” who can’t get over a crush on his co-worker Nikki (Inde Navarrette). So, naturally, he wishes on a cheap novelty toy, asking it to make her love him more than anything in the world. This, of course, goes horribly wrong. The once self-assured Nikki turns into what can only be described as a psychotic love monster – one who will go to any lengths, even inflicting violence upon herself and others, to make Bear happy. Related Article YouTube How this 20-year-old went from building worlds in Minecraft to making Hollywood movies After making waves at last year’s Toronto International Film Festival, the movie quickly picked up steam at the box office, grossing more than $739 million globally off a tiny $1.06 million production budget. Critics gushed over the film’s timely take on gender relations, and suggested Barker (along with Backrooms′ Kane Parsons) heralded a YouTuber horror revolution. It did so well, in fact, that Barker already has three upcoming features in line, including Anything But Ghosts starring Breaking Bad’s Aaron Paul and a Texas Chainsaw Massacre remake for A24. It also made Navarrette an overnight star, one potentially worthy of Academy attention.



Chiwetel Ejiofor is caught in the Backrooms, a film that came from internet mythology. A24 Backrooms (Stan*) Just over a week after Obsession came Backrooms, another horror from a former YouTuber that left audiences both stunned and energised. Directed by 21-year-old Kane Parsons, the film adapts the director’s popular online series, which in itself was inspired by a viral creepypasta about an infinite, yellow liminal space. A down-and-out furniture store owner (Chiwetel Ejiofor) stumbles into this mysterious realm, leading his therapist to follow in an attempt to save him. Unnerving, claustrophobic and anxiety-inducing, the film developed solid word-of-mouth, especially among younger audiences, eventually becoming A24’s highest-grossing release of all time. Welcome to the Great Hall of Scream Queens, Rachel McAdams. AP Send Help (Disney+) Finally, Sam Raimi (The Evil Dead) has returned to his unhinged comedy-horror roots. Send Help takes a genuinely terrifying premise – crash-landing on a remote jungle island with your pompous nepo baby boss – and turns it into a darkly hilarious tale that eventually has you begging the characters to just eat each other. Starring Rachel McAdams (The Notebook) and Dylan O’Brien (Teen Wolf), this film may not have blown the box office away, but it still delivered some of the best dark comedy performances of the year, especially from McAdams who proved herself a surprisingly solid scream queen. Exit 8 is simple, yet deeply unnerving.



Exit 8 (Amazon Prime Video) Horror films based on popular video games can be hit-and-miss, but Exit 8 was definitely a hit. Its simple premise follows a man who becomes trapped in an endless underground station and must use any anomalies in the environment to help guide him out. Beyond its respect for the source material, audiences praised the film for its use of eerie liminal space and its deeper exploration of personal guilt. Despite only receiving a limited release, the Japanese film’s average earnings per-theatre became the third-highest of any movie in the US top 10, even surpassing the buzzy Zendaya and Robert Pattinson film The Drama. Once again, it was Gen Z who flocked to cinemas to see it. Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is mind-boggling in the best possible way. Madman Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (Mubi) After her 2024 film I Saw the TV Glow, anyone with an interest in surrealist horror had their eye on Jane Schoenbrun. The director’s latest release somehow got even weirder, placing Hannah Einbinder (Hacks) and Gillian Anderson (Sex Education) in an abandoned summer camp where their characters, both actors, attempt to reboot an indie slasher. It’s bloody, dreamlike and slightly meta, paired with pertinent underlying messages around desire and queer identity. In other words, it’s peak Schoenbrun. The dumb writer climbs into the dumb waiter. What could possibly go wrong? Roadshow Hokum (Rent or buy on YouTube, Apple TV or Amazon Prime Video)



A supernatural folk-horror starring Adam Scott and a creepy bunny man? It’s a recipe for success. Damian McCarthy’s tale sends a jaded horror writer (Scott) on a journey to Ireland where he plans to scatter his parents’ ashes. However, his hotel is haunted by a 400-year-old witch who he eventually confronts while searching for a missing hotel employee. Somehow both cosy and terrifying, this film creates slow burn dread like few others, building to some of the most frightening jump scares I’ve seen in a while. It also helps that Scott (Severance) is a master at playing a grumbling anti-hero. Ralph Fiennes returns as a scientist conducting weird experiments. Sony Pictures 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (Amazon Prime Video) No horror list would be complete without a zombie flick – and this one just happens to be utterly brilliant. Following last year’s 28 Years Later, Nia DaCosta’s instalment of the acclaimed franchise focuses on a cult led by the megalomaniacal psychopath Jimmy (Jack O’Connell), who’s intent on offering uninfected people as satanic sacrifices. It’s incredibly grisly, crushes your faith in humanity (as all good zombie movies should) and offers one of the most twisted villains in contemporary horror history. It also contains a scene in which Ralph Fiennes rocks out to an Iron Maiden song while pretending to be the devil. Cinematic gold. Loading Leviticus (HBO Max from October 30) One of the best horrors of the year was made on our own doorstep. Leviticus is Australian director Adrian Chiarella’s debut feature about a closeted country boy who outs his love interest in a jealous rage, resulting in a sick form of conversion therapy that inadvertently summons an evil entity that mimics those you desire most. The film quickly became a breakout hit, developing major word-of-mouth buzz for its handling of queer trauma and religious repression. But unlike other recent films critiquing religious dogma, this one has much more heart.



Related Article Australian film ‘Did homophobia become OK again?’ Backlash inspires breakthrough horror film Scream 7 (Paramount+) Nostalgia is still alive and kicking. Scream 7 brings Ghostface back to terrorise the residents of Pine Grove, including original scream queen Sidney Prescott (Neve Campbell) and her teenage daughter. To keep it fresh, the killer uses AI deepfakes to manipulate its victims. How timely. Though far from a critical hit, the film smashed the box office, grossing nearly $309 million worldwide – the highest earnings in the franchise’s 30-year history. Undertone may well be the scariest movie ever heard. AP Undertone (Amazon Prime Video) This eerie debut film from director Ian Tuason offers a horrific spin on the current deluge of podcasts. Undertone follows a pregnant paranormal podcaster who discovers 10 anonymous audio recordings which piece together a disturbing story involving a folklore demon that preys on infants. Having originally been conceived as an immersive 250-page audio-cue script, some critics claimed this was the scariest movie they’d ever heard. Audiences clearly agreed, with the film grossing 43 times its production cost globally. *Stan is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead.

World.title: Winston Peters: No deals, no separatism and the ‘trough of Waitangi’
World.content:
Winston Peters told New Zealand First supporters to vote for National's Chris Bishop but insisted it was not a political deal.

In a wide-ranging interview with Mata with Mihingarangi, the New Zealand First leader described the endorsement as a "statement of respect".

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tarso3ET1As

Peters also defended his opposition to race-based funding, arguing government resources should be allocated according to need, not race, and describing race-based funding as separatist thinking.

Asked what was separatist about Te Aka Whaiora, the now-defunct Māori Health Authority established by the previous government to address disparities between Māori and non-Māori health outcomes, Peters responded, "because your plan does not close the gaps".

He continued: "It just has a whole lot of elitist Māori at the trough in which the mass Māori, the majority of Māori in whose name they make these demands, get absolutely nothing".

He pointed to funding allocated to the Waipareira Trust and an investigation into Manurewa Marae as examples of what he called "electoral corruption".

Peters also declared that the Treaty of Waitangi had become the "trough of Waitangi".

Challenged on whether needs-based funding had succeeded in closing the gaps between Māori and non-Māori in health, education and justice, Peters insisted it had.

On education, he argued that improving Māori achievement began with getting children to attend school but rejected the suggestion that poverty and a lack of transport were contributing factors in truancy.

However, when asked whether funding for the Māori wardens and the Māori Women's Welfare League was itself race-based, Peters argued it was needs-based.

He said the work of Māori wardens was a matter of commonsense, not separatism, and that a Māori warden telling a young person, "look son, I don't think that's the right thing to do", had a better chance of success than a police officer delivering the same message.

In a quick-fire round, Peters chose Whananaki over Whirinaki and crayfish over oysters. He named the late Labour MP Kerry Burke, who served in Parliament from 1972 to 1990, as the best Speaker of the House.

World.title: Waiouru fire remains at 3700ha as containment efforts continue
World.content:
Strong winds challenged firefighters tackling a blaze at the Waiouru Military Training Area on Thursday.

More than 90 people from Fire and Emergency, the Defence Force and the Department of Conservation have been targeting hotspots to try and secure the perimetre of the vegetation fire, which was sparked by gunshots during military training on Sunday.

Fire and Emergency incident controller Ben Cozens said drones, used to identify hotspots, would be used overnight if conditions allowed.

The weather forecast for Friday showed stronger winds, but some rain, which could both help and hinder firefighters' efforts.

Cozens said it would likely take several more days to bring the blaze completely under control.

Thursday morning Operations Briefing at the Waiouru Fire Station. Fire and Emergency New Zealand

Earlier, on Thursday morning, he told RNZ drone crews conducting thermal mapping overnight had confirmed the fire remained at approximately 3700 hectares.

"While containment efforts continue, several hotspots have been identified within areas of mature timber inside the Waiouru Military Training Area," he said.

"Fire crews have been deployed to these locations today to suppress remaining areas of heat and strengthen containment lines."

Cozens said forecast rain and strengthening winds were expected to make conditions more challenging and increase demands on ground crews.

World.title: 21 schools found with elevated drinking water nitrate levels
World.content:
More than 20 schools have had drinking water with elevated nitrate levels above half the legal limit which has been linked to serious health outcomes.

A New Zealand study found an increased risk of premature birth at levels well below that, the College of Midwives recommends pregnant women avoid anything over five milligrams per litre, while international research links colorectal cancer to levels as low as one milligram per litre.

Audio player for " Drinking water nitrate levels linked to serious health outcomes " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2226772%2F21-schools-found-with-elevated-drinking-water-nitrate-levels

Drinking water nitrate levels linked to serious health outcomes Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The 21 schools are mostly in Canterbury and Waikato.

In recent years five schools have breached the legal limit for nitrate of 11.3mg/L - Five Forks School in North Otago, Ashburton Borough School's rural Laghnor site, Te Kowhai, Harrisville and Te Wharekura o Te Rau Aroha in Waikato - with two topping 17 mg/L.

Upgrades to three of the schools' water supplies have been completed and work is underway at Ashburton's Laghnor site.

The Ministry of Education said it did not hold information on upgrades at Harrisville or Te Wharekura o Te Rau Aroha because the projects had been funded and managed by the schools themselves.

The ministry said upgrades at Five Forks School cost $47,900 and $36,000 at Te Kowhai School.

Green MP Lan Pham said it was unacceptable the costs were borne by schools, towns and taxpayers.

"What this data shows us is that it's not just Canterbury. We've got schools in the Bay of Plenty, Waikato, Hawke's Bay, Manawatu, Otago. This is an increasingly a New Zealand national issue."

Pham said politicians should explore some form of levy or polluter pays scheme, citing the millions of dollars the Ashburton District Council had allocated to manage rising nitrates in Tinwald, the $5m budgeted by Selwyn District Council in its search for a lower nitrate water source, and the estimated $400m Selwyn said it would cost for a long term solution.

"I think it's a really basic thing that people should be able to trust the quality of the water that comes out their taps, especially for our children in their most core place, at their school," she said.

Green MP Lan Pham. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The Ministry of Education would not confirm how many schools it was working with nationwide to address nitrate levels that were below the legal limit but still elevated.

A spokesperson said the ministry did not have data on school drinking water results with nitrate concentrations above half of the Maximum Acceptable Value (MAV) and was "unable to provide a verified national count of results at this time".

However, in response to a written parliamentary question from the Green Party in September, Education Minister Erica Stanford said 21 schools were known to have nitrate concentrations of 5.65mg/L or more:

Ashburton Borough School (Laghmor site), Canterbury

Carew Peel Forest School, Canterbury

Galatea School, Bay of Plenty

Harrisville School, Waikato

Koputaroa School, Horowhenua

Kōrakonui School, Waikato

Lake Rerewhakaaitu School, Bay of Plenty

Longbeach School, Canterbury

Macraes Moonlight School, Waitaki

Marotiri School, Waikato

Pukehāmoamoa School, Hastings

Pukehina School, Bay of Plenty

Puketapu School, Hawke's Bay

Riversdale School, Southland

Tasman School, Tasman

Te Kowhai School, Waikato

Turakina School, Taranaki

Waianiwa School, Southland

Wainuioru School, Wairarapa

Wairere School, Waikato

Weedons School, Canterbury

Stanford responded to written questions stating she had not received any advice or briefings about schools that had upgraded their supplies because of high nitrate.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Critics of the official nitrate limit of 11.3mg/L, which is based on 1958 World Health Organisation guidelines, argue it is too high for human and waterway health.

Some scientific evidence suggests far lower levels pose an increased risk of pre-term birth and other reproductive risks. The New Zealand College of Midwives advises women to consider an alternative water source if nitrate is higher than 5mg/L.

In June RNZ revealed the Ministry of Health had quietly launched a review into the health effects of nitrate in drinking water after the Danish government reduced its nitrate drinking water limit by almost 90 percent.

Lincoln University adjunct professor Karyne Rogers co-authored the country's first nationwide survey of rural schools' drinking water, commissioned by the education and the environment ministries and published in 2024.

The study, which examined water at 245 rural schools, found more than a quarter had water that exceeded at least one of the drinking water standards.

Three schools had illegal levels of arsenic and another five had lead above the limit.

"We were seeing E coli popping up in more than 20 schools and things like lead and arsenic, which are heavy metals and highly insidious for young people to ingest," she said.

Results that did not breach legal limits were still concerning, Rodgers said.

"We're seeing more and more studies coming out of Europe that are recommending a tenth lower than the actual [nitrate] Maximum Acceptable Value," she said.

Rogers also co-authored a 2025 GNS Science study that tested 3800 rural drinking water supplies.

Researchers found five percent were over the legal limit, and another 31 percent were over half the limit.

The study used isotope testing to track the source of the nitrate pollution and identified dairy effluent as a primary cause.

Rogers said she wanted to see councils using the same tools to investigate the source of nitrate contamination.

"One of the few tools that can be done to understand and provide evidence - conclusive evidence - about the source is through the nitrate isotopes which will fingerprint the nitrate source, whether it's synthetic chemicals or animal waste or human waste or other causes," she said.

New Zealand Rural Schools Leadership Association president Andrew King. Supplied / Oropi School

New Zealand Rural Schools Leadership Association president Andrew King said there had been positive moves to reduce the burden on schools that supplied their own drinking water and he hoped to see more.

"I think the biggest thing is making sure as many schools as possible are upgraded as quickly as possible and that schools are supported when things are not right," he said.

"For the moment it's the responsibility of someone in the school community to get that information to the lab monthly. There is a new self-testing kit available for schools, which the cost is covered, and is a much easier process to undertake rather than having to drive from a country school into town.

"It's just another thing to worry about and the irony is rural schools don't have the resourcing and the time to address it as easily as a larger school that would have a full-time caretaker or groundsperson who can do all the liaising that needs to happen with the experts."

Gus Gilmore, chief executive of the new School Property Agency, said 98 school and kura would receive full upgrades this financial year as part of the $30m Drinking Water in Schools programme.

The cost could "vary significantly" and depended on treatment requirements, existing infrastructure, school capacity and other factors.

He could not confirm whether the agency had plans to conduct further nationwide surveys.

Environment Minister Nicola Grigg. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Environment Minister Nicola Grigg said drinking water suppliers - in this case schools - were responsible for ensuring water was tested and met standards, and for providing safe and sufficient water to the communities they served.

She said regional councils managed land use and activities that could affect water quality at its source, subject to central government direction.

"Protecting drinking water sources is an important public health issue. Nitrate concentrations have increased in some parts of the country due to past decisions and practices and I am keeping a watching brief on this," she said.

World.title: Why the seven Māori electorates have taken on special importance
World.content:
In a campaign where electorate seats and overhangs may play an unusually significant part in who gets to form the next government, the seven Māori electorates have taken on special importance.

They've got it all - strategic voting calculations, rebel MPs, a Labour MP standing as an independent, and what RNZ's deputy political editor Craig McCulloch calls "the least predictable electorate in the whole country".

Te Pati Māori is doing better than expected across the seats, Māpuna host and political commentator Julian Wilcox says on this week's episode of RNZ's politics podcast, Caucus. While the party started this term with six of the seven electorates, its high-profile internal ructions meant two of its MPs walked away and are standing as incumbents under different banners. It's now actively campaigning for the electorate vote alone, telling its supporters to vote for the Greens or Labour.

Audio player for " Overhangs, gangs, rogue-ish polls, & the most unpredictable electorate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2226513%2Fwhy-the-seven-maori-electorates-have-taken-on-special-importance

Overhangs, gangs, rogue-ish polls, & the most unpredictable electorate Caucus Download MP3 56m

It's arguably a way of making reality look like strategy, given how much support TPM lost through its civil wars. But it seems to be paying off, Wilcox says. It's allowed TPM to push the line that most of the leading candidates from other parties will likely get in on the list. According to the Whakaata Māori polls over recent weeks, Te Pati Māori candidates are leading in four seats, Labour in two, and the Greens in one.

In Hauraki-Waikato, TPM's Hana Maipi-Clarke looks to be well ahead with 45 percent of the candidate vote. When pushed in the Whakaata Māori electorate debate as to how close she came to leaving the party, she was evasive. "Her lack of an answer gives you an answer," says Wilcox. "But she's with the party now. A lot of us thought that electorate would be quite tight. Kingi Kiriona is a fantastic, strong candidate. Really, really well known in the community. Got a good ground campaign. But it's not close".

That's not to say the in-fighting has been without consequence. The ex-Te Pati Māori MPs in Te Tai Tokerau and Te Tai Tonga - Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris respectively, are both a distant last in the polls. And in both seats the TPM candidates are also being well beaten. "So it's almost as if voters were punishing both of those candidates for the turmoil that we've seen this term," says McCulloch.

Tākuta Ferris (L) and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi. RNZ

The split Te Pati Māori vote is "playing out big time in those two electorates", says Wilcox, "which is why we're seeing Labour candidates coming back because lots of voters are going, who do we know? Labour".

In the other seats, though, Te Pati Māori is defying predictions of its demise. And Wilcox says you only have to look at the Labour Party to see why. "It's called Māori retrenchment. [Chris Hipkins] has given up on Māori aspiration and policy. They won't say this in the Labour Party but that's the feeling on the ground from Māori voters. You are leaving us because that's the way you think you will become prime minister."

It was most clearly seen this past week with the controversy over Tamaki Makaurau candidate Kerrin Leoni's visit to a Mongrel Mob function and her subsequent resignation. RNZ political editor Jo Moir says you can see Hipkins "driving towards middle New Zealand" in his firm criticism of any campaigning with gang members, but also trying to acknowledge the different standards Māori and Pasifika MPs are held to. "He was trying to almost talk out of both sides of his mouth".

Chris Hipkins (L) and Kerrin Leoni. RNZ

Leoni is still on the ballot in Tamaki Makaurau however and she's now running as an independent. The break-up with Labour means TPM's Oriini Kaipara should be a shoe-in. But if Leoni wins she will by law be a Labour MP as voting sheets are printed and it's too late to change her party affiliation. It will be fascinating to see whether Labour will forgive all in that case, given how tight this election could be.

The gang controversy hasn't moved the polls though and the Caucus hosts agree this is a cost of living election and nothing else going to change votes at this stage. National, so enthusiastic at first to link Labour to the gangs, seems to have clocked this. Last week senior minister Paul Goldsmith interrupted discussion on pay equity at an Epsom candidates' debate saying, "when are we going to talk about the Mongrel Mob? I want to talk about the Mongrel Mob". Barely six days later on Morning Report he was changing the subject again, but in the opposite direction. "After 10 days of talking about gangs, people are sick of it," he said.

The electorate that may be the least predictable in the country is Te Tai Tokerau. Wilcox says it's "too close to call". Vote-splitting means it could go any which way. Green list MP Huhana Lyndon leads in the Whakaata Māori poll and could become the first from her party to win a Māori electorate. But Labour's Willow-Jean Prime is on 18 percent, TPM's Aperahama Edwards 17 percent, and Te Tai Tokerau Party's Mariameno Kapa-Kingi 12 percent. Fully 22 percent are undecided.

Te Tai Tokerau candidates, from left: Hūhana Lyndon, Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, Willow-Jean Prime and Aperahama Edwards. RNZ / Supplied

"It's opened up the middle to Willow-Jean Prime, who I didn't think was going to get anywhere near that," says Wilcox. "But I think she will now because we've seen votes splitting between those who are picking up Aperahama and Mariameno, who won't get on the list. Add Huhana, who was ahead in the poll but will get in on the list with the Greens, and Willow-Jean's all of a sudden come through the middle."

Labour is confident of victory in Te Tai Tonga and Ikaroa-Rawhiti with Mananui Ramsden and Cushla Tangaere-Manual respectively. Wilcox says they've both favoured because they're following the Parekura Horomia playbook - "be everywhere, at everything".

Caucus this week also looks at the significant impact overhang seats could have this election and discusses the latest variations in polls and what that tells us.

World.title: 'I don't see how you have the resources': Veteran reporter bows out, fearing for local news
World.content:
Audio player for " Journalist retiring after 45 years fears for reporting's future " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/regions/2226304%2Fi-don-t-see-how-you-have-the-resources-veteran-reporter-bows-out-fearing-for-local-news

Journalist retiring after 45 years fears for reporting's future Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Journalist Janine Rankin first walked into a workplace filled with cigarette smoke, ink and clanking typewriters.

Forty-five years later she is this week leaving an industry completely changed. Not only has the smoke gone, the printing press long closed and computers taken over, she has far fewer colleagues.

And after a life's work devoted to covering local news in depth, she's not confident vigorous reporting on community issues will survive.

'We're down to such a small team now'

Rankin is full of stories, after decades writing them for readers of the Manawatū Standard newspaper in Palmerston North.

From Timaru, she studied in Christchurch and ended up in the lower North Island because she wanted to move away from home, and the Otago Daily Times wasn't that year taking female graduate reporters. So, she looked north.

"There was a family feel to the newsroom," she said of her early days.

"Everybody supported everybody else. We had to get on with each other, because we were four to a telephone line. We had to make appointments to make phone calls and you had to get in touch with Mrs R at reception if you wanted to make a toll call."

The 66-year-old has covered all sorts of local council rounds, building relationships spanning decades.

"And I also did the health round because that's what they did with the newest young female reporter in the room, because they thought it was an easy gig. Never was. Still isn't. Has got harder."

Career highlights include the newspaper campaign to open a hospice in Palmerston North - Rankin has even written two books about the Arohanui Hospice. She covered flooding in 1988, local government reform - in the 1980s and now - and what to do with wastewater.

RNZ asked if she's confident these sorts of issues will continue to be reported.

"No, not really. We're down to such a small team now of three reporters. With me going away there will be only two. I don't see how you have the resources to follow a developing story over months or years."

News deserts are a phenomenon hitting many parts of the globe. Palmerston North isn't one now, but there is significantly less local reporting in cities like it than even a decade ago.

"Because there are so few of us and there is still that imperative of filling those few blank pages every day we tend to give priority to the stories you know you can seize on and probably get done today, and move on to something else tomorrow," Rankin said.

'End of an era'

After covering smaller local bodies, Rankin began writing about the Palmerston North City Council in the mid-1980s, forming a tag team with fellow reporter Neil Nelson. Rankin and Nelson married in 1985, but he died of a heart attack in Perth in 1996.

"He came through the different way into journalism, by playing cricket with the right people," Rankin said.

This week Rankin made the city council agenda herself as councillors paused normal business on Wednesday to pay tribute to her reporting, institutional knowledge and scrutiny - and Mayor Grant Smith made sure to mention Nelson as well.

Palmerston North Mayor Grant Smith says Janine Rankin's retirement is the end of an era. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Rankin even walked down from her usual perch on the press bench, leaving behind a notebook full of neat shorthand, to sit at the council table, as friends, current and former colleagues and former councillors filled the public gallery.

She was gifted a bunch of flowers and a framed special cover of the council's Palmy Proud magazine, featuring a younger Rankin hard at work.

Smith told RNZ it was the end of an era. To put in context her longevity, when Rankin began at the Standard in December 1981, Smith said he was still a pupil at Palmerston North Boys' High School.

There's a sense, though, that as Rankin and reporters like her retire, something will be lost for local democracy.

"The whole demise of local reporting, actually media in general - it's not healthy for society," Smith said.

"If people don't know about things and things are scrutinised that's when things can go wrong."

Janine Rankin began reporting at the Manawatū Standard newspaper in 1981. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Massey University media research associate Dr Cathy Strong is also watching on with unease.

"I am very concerned about the coverage and the transparency about what's going on in local government. I've been following this for several decades and it's getting harder and harder for the average ratepayer - the resident - to know what's going on."

As well as fewer reporters on the ground, local government had become more secretive. She advocates for more specialist civics reporters.

"A lot more journalists that can cover that would do a whole lot, because once it's got the light shone on it a lot of things are then taken care of."

That's a role Rankin has played down the years as the winds of change buffeted once thriving daily provincial newspapers.

She remembers about 300 people at her Christmas party at the Standard, which included the large commercial team and printing press operators. Circulation was well above 20,000 copies a day.

When she leaves on Friday Rankin will wave goodbye to an editor, two fellow reporters and two photographers, who have recently moved from the Standard's long-time office on The Square to a small office in a shared workspace. Circulation figures aren't published for the newspaper any more, but it would likely be a few thousand.

Weathering decades of change

Rankin said she'd been flexible while working through many changes she'd seen in the industry down the years.

These include the introduction of computers in the late 1980s and early 1990s; the closure of Palmerston North's printing press; a newspaper name change from Evening Standard to Manawatū Standard; the growth of online news and decline of print; the newspaper moving from an afternoon daily to a morning edition, and to a weekday tabloid; sharing of content; and many rounds of restructuring. The latest is ongoing.

On the internet: "It was weird having this Stuff website where we gave away our copy. A lot of us struggled getting our heads around that idea. It seems there might have been some good reasons for our hesitance around that.

"It became a lot more immediate. That was quite fun, to be able to get news up really promptly. But then, of course, when I started we had our own printing press and you could come into work in the morning, bang out a story, then you could go and collect it fresh off the press, smelling of nice ink."

She admits recent changes, such as the office move and the Standard now getting printed in Christchurch, meaning the deadline for a newspaper is mid-morning the day before, convinced her it was time to go.

"Most of our news is now two days old. It's hard. We've got our website where we can do the breaking news things, but we're not getting much national coverage.

"That was fun at one stage - to be able to write for Stuff and see your stories go up on the screen and how many people had read it in the last 10 minutes."

As retirement sinks in, she ponders the future of provincial daily newspapers.

"I really don't know. I've spent my whole career with people telling me that one day the Manawatū Standard will be a liftout in what used to be the Dominion, now The Post.

World.title: Gotta catch 'em all: Police seize Pokemon cards in gang bust
World.content:
The police Gang Disruption Unit has seized cash, cars and a stolen Pokémon card collection worth more than $30,000 in the Auckland suburb of Glen Eden.

It comes as part of an investigation into a patched Head Hunters member.

Assisted by the Armed Offenders Squad and the Specialist Search Group, Police descended on the property early yesterday morning.

On top of the Pokemon cards, officers seized a loaded firearm, $50,000, some high-value vehicles and an ounce of methamphetamine.

World.title: Te tiriti, gangs and grocery prices: Parties clash in Kaupapa Māori Debate
World.content:
Seven political parties have gone head to head in TVNZ's Kaupapa Māori Debate, clashing over Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the cost of living, and the future of te reo Māori.

Labour's Willie Jackson, National's Tama Potaka, ACT's Nicole McKee, Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson, NZ First's Shane Jones, Opportunity's Eden Skipper, and Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi all took part in the debate,

You can watch the full debate here:

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407581309112

Jackson: This is 'the most anti-Māori government of my lifetime'

Te Tiriti took centre stage at the start of the debate, with NZ First's Shane Jones questioned over his party's plans to abolish the Waitangi Tribunal.

Jones defended the policy, saying politics was "dynamic" and arguing that 50 years after the tribunal was established "it's not an institution that should remain away from the pressures and the democratic process".

Labour's Willie Jackson hit back, describing the Government as "the most anti-Māori government of my lifetime".

Waititi: 'Gangs have been politically manufactured'

The focus then quickly moved on to gangs - a hot topic in recent days.

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi said gangs had been "politically manufactured".

"They are the product of state abuse of our people, church abuse of our people, through the 70s and the 80s."

Jackson was also quick to push back against claims his party supports gangs, pointing to campaign billboards linking Labour, Te Pāti Māori and the Greens with gangs.

"We do not support gangs ... but we will always support whānau, we will always support communities."

ACT 'don't support a Pak'n'Soviet'

The cost of living was a major topic, with parties keen to push their own solutions to grocery prices - and criticise others' proposals.

Marama Davidson backed breaking up the supermarket duopoly, but said the Greens would go further with a publicly-owned supermarket focused on affordable prices.

ACT's Nicole McKee rejected that approach.

"We don't support a Pak'n'Soviet."

She argued reducing bureaucracy and the costs involved in getting new supermarkets established would help increase competition, referencing a supermarket in Christchurch that had to spend years and millions of dollars just to get the doors open.

Labour and Te Pāti Māori both set out their plans to deal with grocery prices at the debate. Screenshot / TVNZ

Rawiri Waititi pushed Te Pāti Māori's plan to put more money into whānau pockets through tax changes and a food credit, alongside greater competition in the supermarket sector, including a Māori-owned supermarket.

Willie Jackson said Labour would target price gouging, accusing supermarkets of "ripping off the customers".

Shane Jones hit back, saying he had been willing to take on the supermarket giants long before others.
