"In 2014, there was only one politician who stood up and took on Countdown. That was Shane Jones."

Opportunity weighs in on healthcare

As the debate turned to healthcare, Opportunity challenged the other parties to support a 10-year plan to address the problems in the system.

There was no definitive answer from any candidate on that challenge, except for Shane Jones, who asked why Eden Skipper - who is much younger than Jones - was questioning him, given Jones is his elder.

'We're going to mine', says NZ First

Jobs were the next flashpoint in the debate, with Shane Jones challenged over high unemployment in Kaikohe.

Jones said: "It's not government that generates jobs, it's the private sector."

He said creating well-paid jobs meant backing industry.

"We're going to mine," he announced.

That sparked pushback from Labour and the Greens, with Jones accusing his opponents of being "too scared to support industry" because of "woke" politics.

National's Tama Potaka criticised the Greens at the debate, decrying "Robin Hood politics". Harley Peters

Greens and National clash over 'Robin Hood politics'

As the debate turned to climate resilience and the role of marae during extreme weather events, Marama Davidson and Tama Potaka clashed over the Greens' proposed $2.4 billion investment in marae.

Davidson said strong marae meant stronger communities, and said decisions over how that money was distributed should sit with Māori rather than government.

Potaka pointed to funding already provided to marae, arguing the Government had delivered "results" rather than rhetoric.

"This is what we're talking about, supporting marae, where suitable in a sustainable arrangement - not Robin Hood politics."

Parties discuss future of te reo

The last major topic of the night was te reo, with the parties challenged over what they would do to grow and protect the language.

McKee pointed to Māori participation in charter schools, but said learning te reo should be a choice.

"One thing we won't do is take it away, but we don't want it being compulsory."

Jones defended NZ First's move to make English an official language when asked if "English was ever under threat" by moderators, and pointed to New Zealand's changing demographics. He said migrants needed to know "this is an English-speaking country".

Potaka was challenged over claims the Government had removed or reduced te reo Māori across parts of the public sector.

Coalition parties defended their record in government on Thursday night. Screenshot / TVNZ

He rejected that characterisation, saying the Government had "reinforced our commitment" to te reo through initiatives including Te Matatini and Māori broadcasting.

Waititi said Māori should be prioritised for spaces in te reo Māori classes and went further, calling for the language to be compulsory.

"We need to make Māori compulsory. But we won't strap you into it."

He spoke about the punishment Māori ancestors faced for speaking their language, and said the aim was to create a bilingual country.

"We will treat you with a lot of kindness and welcome you to our language, but we won't do what you did to our ancestors ... to learn English."

World.title: Wellington councillors mull free weekend parking over festive season
World.content:
Wellington City councillors are proposing free weekend parking in council-owned parking buildings in the city for over a month during the festive period.

Under the plan, parking would be free on weekends between 5 December and 10 January at Barnett Street, Clyde Quay, Frank Kitts, Clifton Terrace and Tory Street carparks.

Current time restrictions would remain.

Mayor Andrew Little and northern ward councillor Andrea Compton said the move would help the city's businesses.

Compton lodged a notice of motion for the move, advocating for a range of independent stores in the central city.

Little said the council wanted the central city "bustling" this Christmas, and free weekend parking gave people a reason to travel in.

The city's Chamber of Commerce said the move would help retailers and hospitality businesses after a tough year.

World.title: Live: Australia pass 400 as lead over South Africa builds
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Playing his first Test of the series in Cape Town, Cameron Green had to come into the line up in the crucial number four batting spot.

But if he had any nerves, he did not show them.

After taking 15 balls to get off the mark, Green crushed a lofted cover drive off the final ball of the morning session from Marco Jansen.

Then, he smashed three boundaries off as many balls against the off-colour Kagiso Rabada.

Matt Renshaw noted that sort of flurry could have led to the tall all rounder losing his head.

World.title: Brewers complete underdog story with maiden World Series title
World.content:
The small-ball Milwaukee Brewers, playing in the smallest market in the majors, are World Series champions for the first time.

Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings, rookie Cooper Pratt had two more hits and two runs batted in (RBIs), and the Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field.

"It's the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here. I know the city's waited a long, long time for this," Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said.

"We're so happy to bring it home to them. I can't wait to get back there and celebrate."

World Series MVP William Contreras hit an RBI double and Misiorowski allowed just two hits before leaving the game because of a right calf cramp. He got a standing ovation from the Brew-Crew fans, who took over the section behind Milwaukee's dugout for the last three games.

The 22-year-old Pratt set a series rookie record with six straight hits before a sacrifice fly in the sixth. Jackson Chourio set a five-game series record with 11 hits.

"This is one of the greatest moments of my life. Oh my gosh. It doesn't even feel real," said Pratt, who made his major league debut in June.

"This is surreal. It only took four months."

The championship comes in the 58th season for a franchise that began as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 and moved to Milwaukee the following year. The Brewers' only previous trip to the World Series in 1982 ended in heartbreak when they blew a 3-1 lead in the sixth inning of Game 7 and lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals.

But this team displayed the toughness and resilience of 67-year-old manager Pat Murphy, who survived a heart attack in 2020 and was the NL Manager of the Year in his first two full seasons at the helm in 2024 and 2025.

"This group of guys right here, the 2026 team, will be remembered forever — and they deserve that because they were a team," Murphy said.

"When you talk about this team, you've got to talk about people who care about each other. They're not worried about their own stats. No-one cares about that. They care about coming together and winning tonight."

AP

World.title: Aussie captain most expensive player at WPL auction
World.content:
Australia captain Sophie Molineux has proved the most expensive buy in India's Women's Premier League auction, and she'll suit up for a UP Warriorz side captained by former national team skipper Meg Lanning.

With many of the world's top players having already been retained for the 2027 edition of the lucrative Indian league, Molineux's signature was the most coveted one still left and the Lucknow-based franchise captured the T20 World Cup-winning skipper for the biggest price, INR 1.1 crore ($A164,000).

The spinning all-rounder won't be leading the team in the January 14-February 7 tournament, though.

Instead, Molineux will be playing under the captaincy of 34-year-old Lanning, the inspirational figure who skippered Australia when she first came into the side, in a T20I in India eight years ago.

Big life changes for WBBL winning duo A lot has changed since Nicola Carey and Elyse Villani lifted the WBBL trophy last year, as the Hobart Hurricanes prepare to defend their title.

Molineux's base price in the auction in Kochi was 50 Lakh ($A75,000) but she eventually went for over twice that price as a bidding battle began between Royal Challengers Bengaluru and the Warriorz.

With their superior budget, UP also snapped up big-hitting all-rounder Grace Harris going for $45,000, meaning that the side will have four Australians in their ranks with Phoebe Litchfield already on board.

Intriguingly, national skipper Molineux has been bought for less than both Lanning and Litchfield and four others among the 14-strong Australian contingent in the league.

The most expensive Australian in the league — each of the five teams has at least one Aussie World Cup winner in its ranks — will be Ash Gardner, captain of the Gujarat Giants, who was retained for $523,000 in a side that also includes four Aussies.

Gardner is the joint most-lucrative retention, alongside Royal Challengers Bengaluru captain Smriti Mandhana and Mumbai Indians' England skipper Nat Sciver-Brunt.

Of the 11 Australians up for grabs in Wednesday's auction, only three were sold.

Heather Graham, Tayla Vlaeminck, Tess Flintoff, Charli Knott, Samantha Bates, Maitlan Brown, Maddie Penna and Milly Illingworth were the ones to miss out.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Gold Coast Suns AFLW finals feat faces home-ground headache
World.content:
The Gold Coast Suns have earned their place in the AFLW finals — but their reward could be a home final away from home.

After back-to-back seasons near the bottom of the ladder, the Suns have surged into fourth spot with eight wins, booking their first finals appearance since 2023.

A victory over GWS on Sunday would strengthen their grip on a double chance, guaranteeing a home final during the series.

But there's a catch.

Carrara Stadium is unavailable for weeks two, three and four of the finals series, due to Australia's T20 clash with England, leaving the Suns and the AFL searching for an alternative venue.

Springfield, home of Queensland rivals the Brisbane Lions and an hour's drive up the highway, and Southport's Fankhauser Reserve are among the alternatives being considered.

Southport however comes with a significant caveat — any final would need to be played during the day, when November temperatures average around 28 degrees and humidity can hover around 70 per cent.

A spokesperson for the club said it is "working with all stakeholders on home venues for each week of the finals" where Carrara is not available.

"Our playing group and staff have been resolute all season in their efforts to play anywhere, anytime, across eight different venues and we know they'll take that attitude into any scenario that presents throughout the post-season campaign," the spokesperson said.

Despite this, coach Rhyce Shaw said on Tuesday the club is embracing the excitement of a long-awaited finals campaign.

Michael Voss Oval in Springfield is being considered as one option for an alternative venue. (Supplied: Brisbane Lions)

"I took [my son] Henry to swimming the other day and all the staff were getting behind us," Shaw said.

"It is exciting for our footy club … It's been a bit of a tough year all round, but for our girls to pick up the slack a little bit and get going and make finals is really, really cool."

"We've got a big job against the Giants and then we'll think of finals after that."

If the Suns were to fall to GWS on Sunday, there is the potential for them finish as low as seventh on the ladder.

However, a fifth or sixth place finish would mean they would earn a home final next weekend and the ABC can confirm Carrara Stadium would be available in this instance.

Rhyce Shaw, Senior Coach of the Suns, says it's been a "tough year" for the club. (Getty Images: Maya Thompson)

ABC Sport AFLW expert Chyloe Kurdas said regardless of the ladder outcome, the lack of venue certainty is an unwanted distraction.

"I think it is such a valuable home ground advantage [finishing in the top four] but it's also not just that, it's the distraction of this conversation right now that happens in the lead up to," she said.

"It occupies bandwidth and it occupies energy from the playing group and the coaching group and the staff."

Kurdas said not being able to play at Carrara, a venue the side has won their last three games at, would be a missed opportunity.

"I think there's a real sweet spot right now with the number of talented kids that are Gold Coast born and raised … that are now playing at the Suns," Kurdas said.

"Fan engagement is going to be such an important part of this Gold Coast Suns women's team journey … they're so talented."

The Suns have had a 75 per cent increase in AFLW memberships for this season.

A familiar problem

The Suns aren't the only club caught in a scheduling squeeze.

Second-placed Geelong, one win away from securing a top-two finish, also faces a venue clash, with Kardinia Park unavailable next weekend due to the AUSX Supercross Championship.

While, the AFLW Grand Final, should it be played in Melbourne, has already been locked in for Princes Park — with a capacity of 13 thousand that has sold out for the showpiece game within hours in recent seasons.

Docklands Stadium, with a 53,343-capacity is unavailable, with Harry Styles booked across the weekend, despite players calling for a bigger venue.

The Geelong Cats are facing a similar venue problem. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Grand Final has also been scheduled for Friday night, November 27, to avoid a clash with the Victorian State Election.

It's a familiar problem that's haunted the competition since it started in 2017.

In the inaugural season, the Brisbane Lions earned the right to host the Grand Final but were forced to play at Carrara, with the Gabba unavailable due to cricket.

Now in its 11th season, the debate continues about where the AFLW competition belongs in the sporting calendar.

The AFL is reportedly considering an earlier start to align the women's season with the end of the men's competition.

"You do your due diligence and you look at where is there likely to be these kind of clashes," Chyloe Kurdas said.

"But ultimately, whenever you choose to play it, you then have to live and die by those decisions."

She says clubs and the AFL must also be prepared to make commercial decisions that put their women's programs first.

" You can't just buy in when it suits you. "

The AFL and Stadiums Queensland were contacted for comment.

World.title: WBBL winning duo on eve of big life changes
World.content:
A lot has changed since Nicola Carey hit the winning runs for the Hobart Hurricanes in last year's WBBL final.

Cricket-wise, her partner Elyse Villani retired and handed over the captaincy.

Life-wise, they're building a house together and are expecting their first child.

"Now that you've pointed it out, I am a bit overwhelmed," Carey joked.

"We've got a bit going on, don't we?

"Poor thing, Elyse has to carry the baby and do all the admin for the house. We're both very much looking forward to having a little one.

"People keep asking me if I'm excited, but I don't think I know fully what's coming."

The desire to start a family influenced Villani's decision to call time on her WBBL career.

The 37-year-old played in every season since the competition started in 2015 and skippered three different clubs during that time.

Elyse Villani retired last year, and Nicola Carey has since taken over the Hurricanes' captaincy. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"Elyse would've played cricket forever, but I don't think her body would've allowed it," Carey said.

"It definitely did play a part, but it's not a guaranteed thing that you'll fall pregnant either."

Following successful IVF treatment, Villani is due to give birth to a boy in November.

Loading Instagram content

It was a fairly straightforward process, and Carey said she was grateful knowing how tricky fertility could be for some people.

They are adjusting to the new chapter in their lives, as the Hobart Hurricanes open their season against the Melbourne Stars tonight.

Name game

In February, all-rounder Carey played her first match for Australia in four years.

There has been a lot of interstate travel since and overseas tours to the Caribbean and the UK.

Nicola Carey played in Australia's recent T20I series against New Zealand in Sydney. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"Elyse came over to England for about seven weeks because I was there for the T20 World Cup and The Hundred, and she was calling it a baby moon," Carey laughed.

"She knows a lot of the players obviously, so it was a huge social get-together and cruisy for her.

"While I was stressed playing terrible cricket she was living her best life."

"No-one misses pre-season do they. Maybe when we start playing again here for Tassie, she'll miss it a bit more."

The couple is aligned when it comes to baby names.

"We've got a few names picked out but we haven't nailed one down yet," Carey said.

"Every male that we walk past seems to have an opinion though.

"Our CEO [at Cricket Tasmania] Dominic Baker is like, 'Dom's a good name,' and I'm thinking, that's not even top 100 for us, but thank you for your input."

Reflecting on the final

The Hurricanes' victory last December at Bellerive Oval was a dream come true: playing in front of their home fans, claiming a maiden title and sending off Villani in style.

The Hurricanes celebrate last year's WBBL title. (Getty Images: Steve Ball)

Although Carey was the batter that sealed the result with a boundary, she concedes she had "the easy part" thanks to a record-breaking innings from teammate Lizelle Lee.

The South African opener was the star of the night, as the team chased down 138 runs.

Blasting 77 off 34 balls, Lee equalled the highest individual score in a WBBL finals match.

The women were inspired after watching their male counterparts lift the BBL trophy in January that same year.

It also followed the achievements of a core group of players in the 50-over Women's National Cricket League (WNCL), clinching three consecutive titles from 2022 to 2024.

The result capped off a wonderful career for Villani, who had previously played in three losing WBBL finals.

The Hurricanes' WBBL title win last season was a special occasion for the players. (ABC News)

She caught the team by surprise, deciding to retire on the spot and go out on a high.

"I sort of knew it was Elyse's last season," Carey said.

"What I didn't know was that she was going to announce it right then and there.

"She was panicking because she told the TV broadcast in an interview first and was then like, 'Oh no, now I need to tell the girls.'

Loading Instagram content

"That caught me off guard.

"To finally win one in your last season adds to that fairytale narrative.

"We had a great group and really good people, which made it enjoyable, so to cap it off with that win was really special."

Despite originally hailing from NSW and Victoria, the couple has now been living in the Apple Isle for a long time and is passionate about ensuring the next generation of the state's talent is set up for sustainable success.

"It's been a nice period of cricket in Tasmania," Carey said.

"A lot of us aren't from there originally, but they've taken us in and welcomed us.

"Because it's so small, everyone lives five minutes away, so you spend a lot more time together than you would in the bigger cities, where you're more spread out.

"It's got a real family feel, so it's nice to be able to give back."

World.title: Scans reveal extent of Steve Smith's neck injury ahead of Test summer
World.content:
Australia expects to have Steve Smith back for the home summer after scans confirmed joint damage to the vice-captain's neck in South Africa.

Australian team officials said Smith had scans on Friday before failing in his bid to play in the third and deciding Test.

Those scans detected an injury to a "cervical facet joint", which connects to the spine and acts to guide and stabilise neck movement.

"Due to this and his limited range of motion, he was unfit to participate in the current Test," Cricket Australia said in a statement.

On a day that could have ended Test careers, a few young ones flourish With a reshuffled line-up in questionable form, Australia's batting stocks show the sort of fight and flair the team has been lacking of late.

"Steve will continue to receive treatment and rehabilitation, with a full return to availability anticipated for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand."

Smith has six weeks to recover for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, which will begin a long run of virtually uninterrupted cricket through to mid-March, with a five-Test tour of India (January 21 to March 3) and the 150th anniversary Test against England at the MCG (March 11-15).

Australia will want Smith available for that stretch of 10 Tests in 14 weeks, just as they had hoped to have him for the return to Cape Town this week.

Even well after Friday's scans on arrival in Cape Town, Australia's coaching staff had been extremely confident Smith would be fit to face South Africa.

The 37-year-old batted in the nets for around 35 minutes on Sunday, two days out from the third Test, before sitting down and stretching his neck.

He then briefly returned to batting, before growing increasingly frustrated and walking out of the nets.

Smith also attempted to bat on Tuesday morning just 90 minutes before the match, then determining he was not able to get his neck right.

"He is huge, one of the greatest batters we have ever had," Cummins said the day before the start of play.

"You don't play 100-odd Test matches without playing Test matches where you're not 100 per cent fit.

"Even though he is probably not going to be 100 per cent, hopefully he can compartmentalise that, like he has done 100 times before with other things, and come out and contribute like he does every week."

The injury means Smith is likely to never play another Test at Newlands, the venue of the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 that cost him the captaincy and a 12-month ban.

AAP

World.title: A three-ball statement gives Australia hope of a flourishing future
World.content:
The vague suspicion before play on day two of the Cape Town Test was that Australia — out of form, stalked by rumours of disharmony in the ranks, its batting line-up restocked and reshuffled for the umpteenth time — was one more calamitous batting collapse away from the end of an era.

The day of perfectly calm and controlled Test batting that took place instead was no less arresting, and in the context of this topsy-turvy series, far more surprising. For 90 overs, Australia batted diligently, adaptively, intelligently and at changing tempos, building a series of reassuring partnerships that put it in control of the game.

Elevated to the opening slot, Matt Renshaw looked safe as houses. Slotted into Steve Smith's number four position, Cameron Green hit a commanding half-century. Drafted in at the 11th hour, Josh Inglis was closing in on a century by stumps and had dragged Alex Carey along in his slipstream.

Josh Inglis took the baton from Cameron Green and Matt Renshaw. (AP: Halden Krog)

It all meant that Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada, who probably woke up feeling comfortable with the expectation it would be his day to wreak some havoc — perhaps even end some careers — went wicketless, as did too many of his mates.

Thanks to stands of 126 between Renshaw and Green and an undefeated 145 between Inglis and Carey, Australia reached 4-330 by stumps and walked away probably feeling in the box seat on a pitch offering very little assistance to the bowlers.

The weight of numbers was one thing, the problem-solving another. In two testing periods, South Africa made double-strikes and threatened to blow the game back open, only for the tourists to consolidate and rebuild.

Monster Carey-Inglis stand keeps Australia in driver's seat in Cape Town Alex Carey and Josh Inglis put together a handy partnership late on day two in Cape Town to put Australia in firm control of the third Test against South Africa.

The crunch moments came in the 18th over, when off-spinner Simon Harmer ripped out Travis Head and Marnus Labuschagne, and just before tea, when Renshaw and Green were removed by Marco Jansen in the space of a few overs.

Both times Australia took a deep breath, regrouped and pushed on in the same direction as before.

The only major negative of the day for Australia — although the many unkind souls who wish him bad luck will not view it so — was Labuschagne's duck. Out-of-form players often have a knack for attracting unplayable balls. At the moment, poor old Marnus can make almost anything look unplayable.

For a team that has not produced a single 100-run opening partnership in the past three years, Renshaw's 74 from 139 deliveries was a welcome return to normalcy at the top of the order. In a 58-run stand with Travis Head (41) to start off, the Queenslander was deferential and circumspect, showing they could be a fire and ice combination.

But it was Renshaw's union with Green, which stretched across 32 overs, that provided the most welcome glimpse of the future of this Australian team.

At 27 and 30, Cameron Green and Matt Renshaw are the babies of this team. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

They were a study on contrasts: surely no batsman as big as Renshaw has ever made himself such a small target for bowlers; heavy-footed Green, on the other hand, has the awkward tendency to turn himself into a fast bowler's piñata, swaying and ducking into bouncers, and in this case wearing a few painful body blows from the shorter stuff South Africa threw at him in large doses.

In the latter sense, Green again showed he had guts. And as he got going, his fluent stroke play more than made up for the cobwebs he was destined to display after three and a half weeks without a competitive hit.

As Aiden Markram had treated Pat Cummins's bowling with disdain on day one, Green took it upon himself to take down Rabada, who has lorded it over Australia in the past.

The killer blow on that front was when Green moved into the 40s with a trio of swivel-pulls that brought six, six and four off consecutive deliveries.

Green punished a trio of Kagiso Rabada short balls. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

Renshaw, as in his Durban epic, was more watchful and unassuming, content to press, deflect, dab, flick and generally accumulate — precisely the sort of calm, unhurried Test batting Australia has been crying out for in the past two years, and which is the bedrock of the big, defendable totals Australia will need to post when it can no longer rely on its brilliant but aging bowling unit.

As well as re-emphasising Labuschagne's redundancy, the Renshaw-Green partnership might also, in the wash-up, accelerate the conversation about how Australia tactfully moves on from the Smith and Labuschagne era.

What more is there to say about Marnus at this point? Harmer, who weeded him out this time, is a canny bowler and has proved himself a big-moment performer in this series. But geez, his wicket ball this time was not exactly a jaffa.

Labuschagne shuffled back to what might otherwise have been a half-volley, pushed at it with hard hands, his slicing bat plane again a horror story, and Markram gobbled the edge at slip.

And what Labuschagne had made look impossible in that brief and tortured innings was, by the end of the day, looking entirely straightforward thanks to Inglis and Carey, undefeated on 85 and 51 respectively.

Loose and a little too eager to play his shots earlier in the series, Carey took a leaf out of Renshaw's book with nudges, nurdles and strike rotation. Inglis, whose finger injury prevented even net sessions for most of the past two weeks, clobbered nine fours and two sixes to poleaxe a tiring Proteas attack.

Tomorrow, both or either batsmen could feasibly take the game and the series away from South Africa in the space of an hour or two. But then, we've said that before, haven't we?

World.title: Quick hits: Green survives Rorschach test as Aussies put Cape Town to sleep
World.content:
Cam Green has fallen on the right side of a line-ball call and "that annoying number three" has collected another unwanted record as the Aussies sent Cape Town to sleep on a dominant second day.

Here are the quick hits from the third Test at Newlands.

1. Unwanted record for 'annoying number three'

The South Africans were eagerly awaiting Labuschagne's entrance on day two. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

The Aussies were cruising.

Starting their innings at the beginning of day two, the tourists raced out of the blocks in glorious mid-morning sun, just as South Africa's openers had done 24 hours earlier.

But things changed with Simon Harmer's entrance into the attack, with the off spinner promptly removing Travis Head for 41 and exposing the under-pressure Marnus Labuschagne.

The South Africans had been clearly looking forward to welcoming Labuschagne to the middle all morning, with the stump mic having earlier picked up an unknown fielder encouraging his bowler to "get that annoying number three in here".

Loading Instagram content

But the hosts did not get much of an opportunity to enjoy Labuschagne's company, with the Queenslander spending four deliveries trying to work a single before edging to slip to be out for a five-ball duck.

Harmer wheeled away in celebration, joined by a horde of ravenous teammates, as Labuschagne's career crisis continued.

The Queenslander's latest failure was his 48th Test innings without a century, making it the longest run without a ton for a top-four batter in Australia's history.

2. Green survives third umpire's Rorschach test

The Proteas were convinced they had their man.

Cam Green had made his way to 22 when he pushed tentatively to a Gerald Coetzee length ball, with his thick edge flying to a stooping Harmer at second slip.

At first glance, it looked to be a regulation grab, with the off-spinner rising then roaring in celebration, but Green was not going anywhere.

After a brief consultation, the umpires decided to send the decision upstairs, where the footage was combed over frame-by-frame.

It was close, with the two camera angles telling two different stories.

The two angles told two different stories. (Fox Cricket)

Straight on, it could be argued the ball had kissed turf as it nestled into Harmer's hands, but side on, the ball looked to have been collected cleanly.

It was something of a Rorschach Test for the third umpire, and unfortunately for the hosts, he saw the image that kept Green out in the middle.

Only a matter of moments later, it was Renshaw's turn to survive a very close call, with a line-ball LBW decision going the Aussies' way.

3. Sandpaper in the stands

The only remaining member of the trio that was punished for the Sandpapergate scandal in 2018, Steve Smith's 11th hour withdrawal robbed cricket fans of one of the most eagerly anticipated returns in Test history.

But if the Australians thought that meant they wouldn't be reminded of one of their darkest days, some in the Cape Town crowd have ensured they were mistaken.

Video emerged of Nathan Lyon taking his place on the boundary at fine leg on day one, with a cackling spectator leaning forward while holding out a sheet of what looked to be sandpaper.

Lyon declined the offer.

Another fan, wearing a shirt with Smith's sobbing face emblazoned across it, told the Herald Sun he was disappointed the batter wasn't playing, and that he had been looking forward to some "banter".

4. Magic Marco joins rare air

With both Renshaw and Green set and with the luck appearing to go their way, South Africa was in need of something special.

Marco Jansen provided it.

South Africa vs Australia third Test, day two live Alex Carey and Josh Inglis put together a handy partnership late on day two in Cape Town to put Australia in firm control of the third Test against South Africa.

The world's number one ranked bowler provided a fearsome spell in the shadows of tea, dismissing both batters to swing the momentum once again.

Renshaw stood his ground as he just about middled one through to Ryan Rickelton behind the stumps, but was rightly given out for 74 on review, and Green (65) was caught — this time fairly — by Harmer at second slip.

With neither the ball nor pitch appearing to offer very much, it was a seriously impressive five-over spell, and one that saw the 26-year-old take his 100th Test wicket.

In terms of balls bowled, Jansen's 3,864 deliveries saw him become the fifth-fastest bowler to claim a century of scalps, and the third fastest since the 19th century.

5. Carey and Inglis put Cape Town to sleep

Coming together after that Jansen double strike and with Australia's innings at a crossroads at 4-185, Alex Carey and Josh Inglis were composed and circumspect in building their partnership.

The pair were for the most part untroubled in pushing their stand past 100, playing only the shots that were presented to them and offering up few opportunities to the increasingly desperate South Africans.

Not even the second new ball could interrupt their rhythm, with Jansen and Kagiso Rabada unable to emulate Mitchell Starc's stunning spell from late on day one.

But where Starc had low clouds and fading light, the South African spearheads had a placid pitch and still sparkling evening sun.

And in the dying embers of a taxing, 90-over day, some in the Newlands crowd couldn't help but nod off.

Carey and Inglis pushed Australia into a lead and put some in the Newlands crowd to sleep in the process. (Fox Cricket)

Carey (51*) and Inglis (85*) will resume on day three having batted the entire final session and with Australia one run in front.

Tech.title: AI has come for Arizona’s water
Tech.content:
AA hulking gray giant rises from the desert. Inside, engineers create the force behind our phones and computers and appliances, our streaming services and search engines and chatbots and vibe-coded apps and websites. The complex is simultaneously massive and squat, dwarfed by the mountains that surround it, and it is endless. I drive past one building, and then another, and then the ground opens up where construction crews have dug up the earth so a third building can rise. There is a parking lot, and then another, and then another. There is an empty lot on the other side of the street, full of cars and the occasional food truck to feed the thousands of laborers who are busy transforming this expanse of desert into an industrial park. There is dust, so much of it, choking the air.

I stand before the savior of Arizonaâs economy. Like all great deities, it demands sacrifice. In the desert, nothing is more precious than water, and water is what must be given â nearly 5 million gallons a day, every day, sourced from Phoenixâs municipal supply. The offering has been well worth it.

All of this is the fruit of the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the worldâs leading producer of microchips. Its Arizona operation is the result of a pre-pandemic gamble Phoenix made to revive its sluggish economy, which never quite rebounded from the Great Recession. Now TSMCâs foundry looms over the cityâs outskirts.

TSMC is a success story, one that some local leaders may have hoped to repeat with hyperscale data center developments. The progression may have seemed natural: The Grand Canyon State is not only home to the largest chip factory this side of the Pacific but also 172 data centers, neither of which faced much pushback. But the newer, larger developments being proposed from Phoenix to Tucson demand more of everything â more water, more power, more land â than Arizonans are willing to give. Where TSMC was welcomed with open arms and the first wave of data centers was largely ignored, new developments are facing mass backlash in Arizona, where a grassroots, surprisingly bipartisan coalition of residents has united against data centers.

Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. âChips.â

In reporting this story, I spoke to local activists and economic developers, elected officials and their angry constituents. I sat in on city council meetings where people lined up by the dozens to speak up against data center projects, and in cozy suburban homes where tight-knit groups of former strangers told me about the struggle that brought them together. I pored over maps of Arizonaâs dry, cracked landscape with laypeople who, over the past two years, have made themselves experts on zoning and land use and water consumption so they can understand the beast theyâre trying to fight. The locals on both sides of this debate claim to want the same thing: a better, more prosperous Arizona. Their visions for achieving it, however, are completely at odds.

In Arizona and elsewhere, data center developers have tried to win over locals by making enticing promises about the jobs, tax revenue, and infrastructure theyâll bring with them. All they ask for in exchange is water â and, they swear, not nearly as much of it as youâd expect. Some hyperscale data centers, like Googleâs facility in The Dalles, Oregon, use about 1.5 million gallons a day, about one-third of what TSMCâs Arizona complex consumes in the same timeframe. Those reassurances, however, arenât enough to assuage Arizonans, who now have to contend with the fact that the state will soon lose access to nearly 30 percent of the water it receives from the Colorado River.

Even now, as people across the country sour on AI and fight against data centers in their communities, TSMCâs Arizona operation hums along without significant opposition. And yet itâs impossible to make sense of why Arizonans are so opposed to new data center development without first understanding why they eagerly welcomed TSMC, even though both industries must contend with the issue that has plagued Arizona since its founding: There isnât enough water.

An irrigation canal that is part of the Central Arizona Project, which brings water to Phoenix from the Colorado River.

For as long as anyone could remember, business in Arizona revolved around the storied âfive Câsâ: cattle, copper, cotton, citrus, and climate, a catchall for the regionâs mild, salubrious winters, which locals say often more than make up for the sweltering summers. Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. âChips.â The TSMC development is, in a sense, Mackayâs doing. As the head of Phoenixâs economic development office, she spearheaded the effort that brought the Taiwanese giant to the Sonoran Desert. In 2020, while the global economy was all but shut down, TSMC made an announcement. The same forces that brought the world to a standstill had created even more demand for TSMCâs products, and in response, TSMC would be opening an advanced semiconductor foundry â a âfab,â in industry jargon â in Phoenix. Initially, TSMC predicted that it would pour $12 billion into Arizonaâs economy by 2029. Since then, TSMCâs projected expenditure in the state has ballooned to $265 billion, what the company touts as the largest foreign direct investment in US history. The TSMC Arizona headquarters in Phoenix. TSMC just put the finishing touches on its second fab in a formerly desolate swath of north Phoenix, with a third under construction and plans for several more underway. This buildout has been more than a decade in the making. TSMC started shopping around for a US location in 2016. That year, Mackay said, the company put out a request for proposals through a codename. No one won. âWe arenât a group that takes no for an answer,â Mackay said proudly. Her office asked TSMC executives what they thought Arizona was missing, and then spent the next three years addressing their concerns. In 2019, Phoenix sent a delegation to Taiwan to share a new development plan for a science and technology park, the nucleus of which would be a factory, ideally one of TSMCâs fabs. âThey agreed they needed to come back and take another look at Phoenix,â Mackay told me. Her team showed them two locations: Laveen, Arizona, a suburb southwest of Phoenix, and, just north of the city, an undeveloped area roughly the size of Manhattan called Biscuit Flats, so named, Mackay told me, because âitâs as round and flat as a biscuit.â âThat very day,â she recalled, âthey said, âThis could work.ââ What followed was a flurry of development unlike anything the state has ever seen. TSMC has brought more than 3,500 jobs to the state, and an entire economy has sprung up to support the companyâs Arizona operation. Much like in Taiwan â where the company accounts for nearly one-tenth of Taiwanâs gross domestic product â TSMC has become, if not the center of the universe, then at least a galaxy unto itself. The company controls an estimated 70 percent of the global chip market, and its contracts with Apple and Nvidia alone make up more than one-third of its annual revenue. (Apple and Nvidia design their own chips, but they donât produce them. The complex manufacturing process is instead largely outsourced to TSMC.) This semiconductor manufacturing facility has more than 3,500 employees. TSMC has changed swaths of Phoenix â its landscape, its industries â and it has brought with it jobs and prosperity. Locals fear that the new hyperscale data center developments will do the former but not the latter, consuming resources while contributing little to the community. Mackay, who has worked as an economic developer for over 30 years, didnât experience significant pushback when she helped court data center developments in the past. âThe first 10 data centers I did look like pretty little office buildings,â she said. The new developments being proposed are neither pretty nor little. Where earlier data centers were inconspicuous, the hyperscale facilities developers want to build in Arizona â often on rural farm or desert land â are both massive and incongruous. Despite the stateâs recently acquired reputation for sprawl, there are still plenty of places where, in the quiet desert stillness, you can sometimes hear a pack of coyotes howl in the middle of the night. There are dark-sky corridors and wild animals, ghost towns and saguaro forests. All of this, some locals say, could be sacrificed for the benefit of an industry that also poses an existential threat to humanity. There are ethical questions and environmental ones, debates over zoning and taxes and, most of all, over water. Yet the cities and the outlying suburbs keep growing, spreading in all directions until theyâre constrained by geography or bureaucracy or Indigenous sovereignty. And industry, somehow, keeps arriving, thirstier than ever.

In Mesa, Arizona, the EdgeCore PH03 data center â the largest data center in the state â stands right beside a residential neighborhood.

Year-round but especially in the summers, Arizonans tailor their routines to the elements. Drivers are careful not to get stuck in dust storms or monsoons. Joggers avoid going out in late mornings and early afternoons, when the heat is at its most intense. And on August 1st, at the peak of monsoon season, the No Desert Data Center Coalitionâs protest began in the early evening, when the sunâs punishing rays were starting to give way to a muted desert sunset.

About a dozen people showed up to the rally on the outskirts of Tucson, in front of the 290-acre site where Beale Infrastructure is building a 600-megawatt data center. Every few minutes, Vivek Bharathan, one of the organizers, reminded the protesters to stay hydrated. Children sprayed each other with water guns and dutifully accepted drinks from their parents. Mayra Duron, one of the attendees, brought a cooler of agua de jamaicato share with the group. The magenta beverage, she said, was full of electrolytes. Water â the lack of it, the need for it, the amount required to build a massive data center in the middle of the desert â was top of mind. A hand-painted banner expressed the overarching sentiment: BEALEâS DATA CENTER WILL SUCK US DRY.

âIf you feel the heat, please head home,â Bharathan told the small crowd. âIt is a hot day, and if they succeed in building a data center here, itâll be even hotter. We know these things create heat islands that can affect the surrounding area by over 10 degrees Fahrenheit.â Duron, a local macrame artist who incorporates cactus spines into her weaving, said she worried about how rising temperatures would affect the regionâs saguaros. âIn Phoenix, itâs hyper-industrialized,â she said, âand theyâve seen saguaros die left and right.â

Cars honked in support. Some drivers pumped their fists out their windows as they sped by. Arizonans werenât riled up about AI in 2019, when the TSMC project was announced, nor did they notice or care much about the previous data centers that were quietly built throughout the state. Things have changed. Tucson, it appears, is united in its opposition to the data center complex dubbed Project Blue. But the buildings are going up anyway.

Members of the No Desert Data Center Coalition pose for a portrait near the site of the Project Blue data center. From left: Reed Spurling, Vivek Bharathan, Margo, Pablo, and Glenda Avalos.

âWe take it as normal because itâs been that way for so long. But it isnât normal. Itâs a catastrophe.â

Information about Project Blue began slowly trickling out in the spring of 2025. First came the name, and some clues: The development, whatever it was, would be on a county-owned plot of land; it would create 3,000 temporary construction jobs and 200 well-paying positions down the road; it would generate $152 million in tax revenue over the next decade; it would be big, and it would be thirsty, and new water lines would be built to keep it satiated. That was all anyone in the know would say, because the county government, which owned the land, signed a nondisclosure agreement with the would-be developer.

The news came out in a mundane, bureaucratic way, as information about prospective land sales in midsize cities often does. In June 2025, Jan Lesher, the Pima County administrator, submitted a 44-page memo to the Board of Supervisors. The words âdata centerâ did not appear until the fourth page. This data center would provide an âunprecedentedâ $3.6 billion opportunity for Tucson and for the county. There were other details, and there was flattery, and there were promises. Project Blue would use â100% renewable water resources.â Its developer, Beale Infrastructure, would build critical infrastructure at its own expense, including an 18-mile pipe extension and an aquifer recharge facility.

âThe boost it could provide to our local economy may well be transformative,â Rex Scott, one of five members of the County Board of Supervisors, said at the time. His colleagues were split. They voted 3-2 to rezone the 290-acre tract, and voted again to sell it to Beale for around $20 million. But it wasnât a guarantee yet. One of the terms of the deal required Tucson to annex the land and approve the sale, since the city would be on the hook for the landâs water service.

The honeymoon, if there even was one, didnât last. Just hours after the boardâs vote, Tucson Electric Power announced it was looking into a rate hike that would increase customersâ bills by an average of 14 percent. The utility claimed the decision was unrelated to the forthcoming data center. Even still, one of the commissioners who voted to rezone the land and sell it to Beale officially asked to reconsider the rezoning.

Perhaps it was the fact that Tucsonans learned of the data center and the rate hike in such quick succession, coupled with the inescapable news of data centers raising localsâ utility bills, that catalyzed their mass opposition. Maybe it was the Arizona Mirrorâs report that Project Blue, combined with another proposed data center, would not only be TEPâs biggest customer but also consume more than four golf coursesâ worth of water each year. The fact that Amazon Web Services was reportedly the end client â and that county officials had been discussing the project since 2023, and, according to public records obtained by Arizona Luminaria, signed NDAs prohibiting them from naming the companies involved â certainly didnât help. Whatever the reason, Beale executives probably werenât prepared for just how angry the public would be.

Around 200 people showed up to a public information meeting Beale hosted in the auditorium of a local high school in July 2025. Most of them were furious about the data center, or they were worried, or they were scared. Tensions were even higher at the follow-up meeting held at the Tucson Convention Center. Over a thousand people showed up. The boos started before Bealeâs representatives got through their introductions, and they continued throughout the night.

Giant saguaro cactuses dot the Arizona landscape â they need minimal water but are still dying off.

Keri Silvyn, one of the attorneys representing Beale, tried to warm up the crowd. âWe all have cellphones, we have computers, a number of us have multiple of those in our households,â she said. âMany of the various signs that Iâve seen have QR codes, that if you click on, will take you through a data center in order to get to different sites. The internet is housed in data centers. Thatâs what they are.â Bealeâs team explained that they selected the site because it was far from residential areas, and then they reiterated the now familiar pitch data center developers make to wary communities. Beale said it would pay for a pipeline, and once the pipeline was built the data center would run on reclaimed water. (Until then, however, it would rely on potable water.) The company would pay to clean up contaminated water. It would inject any extra water into local aquifers, eventually making the whole thing âwater-positive.â None of this mollified the thousand or so people in the audience, who booed every few minutes.

To no oneâs surprise, the opposition mostly came down to water. Locals worried that if the data center came to town, the resource, already so scarce and so precious, would vanish. They cited the fact that Arizona would likely lose more of its Colorado River allotment. They conjured images of even hotter, drier summers.

A commercial water well being dug on the site of the Project Blue data center.

âCan you guarantee us water for future generations?â When it was her turn to speak, Melanie Cooley, an education specialist at the Watershed Management Group, a local habitat restoration nonprofit, conjured up a past familiar to few Tucsonans. âWhere we are sitting right now was a forest 125 years ago that adjoined a flowing river that flowed year-round,â she said. âThere are people alive today who grew up swimming in the Santa Cruz River.â Average temperatures in Tucson are now 11 degrees Fahrenheit higher than they were a century ago, Cooley said. About six degrees of that rise can be attributed to global warming. The other five, Cooley explained, are because of changes in the local ecosystem, including the felling of forests and the drying up of rivers like the Santa Cruz. âWhat we see today when we drive across that river that looks like a big, dry ditch, we take it as normal because itâs been that way for so long. But it isnât normal. Itâs a catastrophe. Itâs a catastrophe that was brought on by overpumping of our groundwater and bad development decisions, and Project Blue is another bad development decision.â Another speaker compared Project Blue to industrial projects of decades past. âThis is like dÃ©jÃ vu for me,â he said, listing off economic development projects that were supposed to turn things around for the city: Raytheon; Hughes, the military contractor that preceded it; the Air National Guard. âWhat did they do? They contaminated our water. To this day, weâre having to deal with that.â Tucsonans had gone to great lengths to conserve their water. âWe took our landscaping out, we took our swimming pools out.â He waved over a relative who was holding an infant in a sling. âCan you guarantee us water for future generations?â he asked the Beale representatives. âCan you guarantee water for her generation, my kidsâ generation, my grandkidsâ generation, and this little babyâs generation?â Photo: Wild Horizons / Universal Images Group via Getty Images At a public forum in Tucson to discuss the pros and cons of Project Blue, protesters questioned the long-term feasibility of building a water- and power-hungry facility in Tucsonâs desert. Two days after this contentious hearing, a unanimous vote by the Tucson City Council shut down the annexation of the land. At a subsequent meeting, the city adopted new rules for data centers and other large water users. Residents were relieved, but not for long. Three weeks after the city stopped the annexation, effectively killing the development, local reporters confirmed that Beale was moving forward with the data center anyway. County officials and Beale representatives had previously said that the deal was contingent on Tucsonâs annexation of the land. Suddenly that was no longer an issue. (Beale declined to comment on why annexation was no longer necessary for the deal.) Over time, there were other adjustments to the plan: The data center would no longer be water-cooled and would instead rely on closed-loop air cooling. If the shift was intended to win over Bealeâs critics, it didnât work. Members of the No Desert Data Center Coalition claim that air-cooled facilities use more electricity, and, since power plants also use water to cool their systems, air-cooled data centers may actually be more water-intensive, just indirectly, an allegation Beale denies. âThe use of air-cooled technology for this project does not increase overall energy use; while the energy allocation is different, the energy use is the same,â Beale spokesperson Tony Burkart, the Beale spokesperson, told The Verge. (Energy generation does require water, though thereâs little data on just how much water Arizonaâs power plants consume.) The change also cost Beale a tenant: Amazon reportedly pulled out of the project, saying an air-cooled facility wouldnât meet its needs. Beale declined to disclose whether it has since found a new tenant for Project Blue. âItâs up to our tenants when they choose to announce their investment in a project,â Burkart said. Still, the project moved forward. The county completed its deal with Beale on Christmas Eve, and Beale promised to bring even more gifts in the form of $15 million in donations, some of which would go toward local STEM and trade school programs. The new year brought more challenges. The stateâs attorney general filed an appeal against the Arizona Corporation Commission, the state agency that oversees public utilities, over its approval of a special energy agreement between Beale and TEP. Members of the No Desert Data Center Coalition filed a separate lawsuit alleging that the countyâs dealings with Beale violated the stateâs open meeting law.

Image 1 of 4 In the Ahwatukee area of Phoenix, locals push back against data center construction. Protesting locals pointed to past economic development projects from Raytheon and Hughes that they say contaminated their water. Tucson is 11 degrees hotter on average than it used to be; five of those degrees can be chalked up to changes in the local ecosystem, not just climate change. Less than 100 years ago, the Santa Cruz River still flowed in Tucson. Today itâs long gone.

The coalitionâs suit got tossed, but the data centerâs opponents found other ways to voice their displeasure. They staged a protest inside the offices of Lazarus and Silvyn, the law firm representing Beale in its dealings with the county. When construction crews broke ground on the site, dozens of people were there, blocking vehicles while chanting, âWe respect the workers, we donât respect the work.â The data centerâs opponents havenât been able to stop construction altogether, but theyâve managed to slow it. After observers affiliated with No Desert Data Center noticed that contractors with Ames Construction were using city-owned hydrants, officials demanded that Beale give the city water credits to replenish the approximately 651,702 gallons of drinking water used for dust control. (A host of local ordinances require construction crews to spray water to mitigate the air pollution caused by blowing dust.) Burkart, the Beale spokesperson, said the contractor âfollowed standard procedures and the City issued a permit for temporary water per the normal course of business.â After Ames stopped using city water, officials with the Pima County Department of Environmental Quality also found the contractors in violation of their âfugitive dust permitâ on two separate occasions, each of which could carry a fine of up to $10,000. And when Ames turned to a Tucson green waste facility for water, protesters flooded the subcontractor with phone calls until its owner dropped the contract.

None of this grassroots opposition, however, has been enough to actually stop Project Blue. To facilitate construction, the Arizona Department of Water approved a request to build two wells on the site, allowing the facility to draw up 31 million gallons of groundwater a year. Burkart said this water will only be used for construction. Once the data center is up and running, Burkart said, water use âwill be limited to ordinary domestic purposes, such as restrooms, employee kitchens and health and safety.â

Some local leaders have since worked to regain the communityâs trust. After a contentious meeting in August, the Tucson City Council implemented new, stringent limits on data centers, making them one of the most regulated developments in the city. But residents want more, and theyâve vowed to keep showing up until they get a full ban. Even the county government has been surprisingly amenable of late. In September, the Pima County Board of Supervisors imposed a 120-day moratorium on new data center projects. But that doesnât mean other developments are off the table. In March, the county announced it would be putting some of the proceeds of the Beale land sale toward hiring an economic developer. The goal of the job, which comes with an annual salary of $150,000, would be to bring foreign direct investments to Tucson. The city, it seems, is looking for a Christine Mackay of its own â and maybe a TSMC, too.

Rebecca Chen understood the promise of TSMC well before most other Arizonans. A Phoenix resident since 2015, she started working as a Realtor in 2019, just before the company arrived. âTSMC may not be a huge household name for a lot of Americans, but it is for Asians,â Chen said. âTSMC is basically like Apple or Tesla for Taiwanese.â The covid-19 pandemic sent the industry into a frenzy: Americans, largely confined to their homes, wanted space and sunshine and relocated to the Sun Belt in droves, and Arizona was no exception. Still, Chen knew this was nothing compared to what TSMC would bring. She was introduced to her first Taiwanese client by an industry friend in California, and soon the referrals were piling up. She sold homes virtually, showing them to clients via video call; some TSMC workers bought houses sight unseen.

âI feel like Iâm way more than a Realtor,â Chen told me. âIâm like a guide to them.â Sheâs helped clients set up utility bills, get their driverâs licenses, recommended places to eat and shop. âIâm an immigrant myself,â she explained, so she knows how hard it can be to feel settled in a new place. Arizonaâs Taiwanese immigrants have risked a lot in coming to America, staking their futures on a new project in an unknown place at a time of extreme nativist backlash. Itâs a leap of faith, and it appears to have worked out.

Real estate agent Rebecca Chan poses for a portrait in front of a warehouse she recently sold in Phoenix. TSMC and other tech companies have purchased warehouses in the area.

TSMCâs presence in Arizona has revived a way of life some thought had vanished in America: a prosperous household where one partner (usually male) works at a factory and earns enough to support a family. Think of it as the midcentury ideal with a new global twist, suburban idyll propped up by industrial manufacturing. TSMC now has more than 3,500 employees in Arizona, according to spokesperson William Moss, who said the company doesnât disclose the number of international workers it has, which can fluctuate depending on the project. Early reports claimed that about half of TSMCâs 2,200 employees at a single fab were from Taiwan. Still, itâs undeniable that TSMCâs presence in Arizona has led to an influx of Taiwanese immigrants in the Phoenix metro area â all while the Trump administration wages a full-fledged attack on legal immigration. TSMC is now working to cultivate local talent. In May, the company announced it was starting a semiconductor technician training program at Arizona State University, and the university recently signed on to a White House initiative to build up Americaâs manufacturing workforce. As part of the partnership, ASU will organize a âFoundry Schoolâ taught by experts from Japan, South Korea, India, and Taiwan.

New businesses have popped up to cater to Arizonaâs growing Taiwanese community, further bolstering the local economy. North Phoenix now has a Little Taipei. Restaurants have opened to cater to these new Arizonans, some opened by the newcomers themselves. Buildings have popped up seemingly overnight to house them. Mandarin-speaking real estate agents like Chen have found a lucrative niche selling luxe new-build homes to well-compensated tech workers, including employees of TSMC suppliers. The state has added a new holiday to its unofficial calendar: October 10th, or Double Ten Day, a commemoration of the uprising that felled the Qing dynasty. Phoenix is now home to the largest Double Ten celebration in North America. Each year, thousands of spectators ooh and aah at a drone show sponsored by TSMC. China Airlines started offering direct flights between Phoenix and Taipei in 2025. Taiwanâs Starlux Airlines soon followed suit. The Hilton Garden Inn I stayed in, located just 10 minutes from the TSMC campus, served congee for breakfast. Scottsdale now has a Din Tai Fung. Reservations are hard to get.

âWe call it the economic value of a gallon of water.â

Some of these changes happened organically; others resulted from meticulous planning. Mackay, the economic developer, told me that the local grocery chain Fryâs reached out to her office to ask what products Taiwanese customers might want to see on its shelves. Mackay set up a meeting between Fryâs and TSMC, and she set up another with a Taiwanese attorney who worked with the state Department of Transportation to ensure Taiwanese immigrantsâ driverâs licenses would be valid in Arizona. Working along Phoenix Sister Cities, a nonprofit that started in 1972, Mackayâs office put together a team of Mandarin-speaking doctors and nurses to serve Taiwanese immigrants in their native language.

Phoenix and Taipei have been sister cities since 1979, a designation that, until recently, was largely ceremonial. As is the case in all sororal relationships, there have been conflicts, some of them over shared resources. Given the industryâs demands and the stateâs historic drought, critics ask, is it wise to build water-guzzling factories in the middle of the desert?

TSMC hasnât faced nearly as much pushback for its water use as data centers have, but semiconductor manufacturing nonetheless requires massive amounts of water, and this water must be of a specific grade â free of contaminants organic or otherwise, and so devoid of minerals that itâs actually not recommended for human consumption. It takes 1.4 to 1.6 gallons of municipal water to create a single gallon of ultrapure water, since some is inevitably lost to evaporation in the process.

Water storage facilities that are part of the Avra Valley aquifer in Phoenix. Supply to the aquifer has historically come from the Colorado River.

Each chip requires 50 to 250 wash cycles, Paul Westerhoff, the director of ASUâs Global Center for Water Technology, told me. âIf thereâs a little particle in there, or an ion-like chloride in there, the thing doesnât work,â Westerhoff said, âso they need to use a lot of water in each of these cleaning cycles.â This process requires 4.75 million gallons of water each day, which TSMC obtains through Phoenixâs municipal water supply. The Arizona Republic reports that TSMC mostly uses reclaimed wastewater, with some groundwater as well.

Westerhoff compared the process of semiconductor manufacturing to washing dishes. And just like you wouldnât reuse your sink water to wash a second round of pots and pans, chip manufacturers canât reuse their dirty water to wash other chips. But this water isnât totally lost. âIf you want to reuse sink water, maybe you throw it out on your lawn,â Westerhoff said. He explained that TSMC uses 20 percent or so of its recycled water to power its evaporative cooling systems. Part of Westerhoffâs role is to figure out new ways for TSMC to use its excess wastewater â hopefully, someday, as part of the chip manufacturing process itself.

Sarah Porter, the director of ASUâs Kyl Center for Water Policy, explained that while 15 to 20 percent of the water TSMC uses is lost to evaporation, much of the rest is processed in the companyâs recycling plant. According to Porter, TSMC recycles 60 to 65 percent of the water that flows through its first Arizona fab and is planning for 90 percent reuse by 2028. To get there, TSMC is building an on-site reclamation facility. The ultimate goal, however, is to figure out how to use reclaimed water in the manufacturing process. Westerhoff has called this the âholy grail.â

âWhen weâre talking about semiconductor manufacturing, thatâs very different from, say, a golf course.â

The fact that TSMC can recycle most of the water it consumes differentiates it from some of the stateâs traditional industries. And even if TSMC were to someday use more water than some of Arizonaâs more conventional enterprises, the regionâs leaders say the tradeoff would be well worth it. âWe call it the economic value of a gallon of water,â Mackay told me. âThat gallon of water can do a huge amount for the region, or it can do nothing for the region.â In Mackayâs estimation, TSMC has earned its keep and then some.

TSMC brought with it an entire industry. So far, 55 TSMC suppliers have set up shop in Arizona, as per Mackay, and more are on their way. Topco Scientific, a Taiwanese materials integrator that works closely with TSMC, opened an outpost in Phoenix in 2022, operating at a loss for years until TSMCâs first fab was up and running. Chang Chun, a Taiwanese petrochemical firm, now manufactures electronic-grade hydrogen peroxide in Casa Grande, a city of some 70,000 people halfway between Phoenix and Tucson. Rebecca Chen, the Phoenix-based real estate agent, has moved into the commercial and industrial market, which she said is hotter than ever. Applied Materials, another supplier, opened a $270 million research and development facility at ASU last fall. New construction projects are underway, many of them clustered around TSMCâs growing campus. Among them is Halo Vista, a $7 billion, 2,300-acre master-planned community developed by a New York real estate firm. Business is booming. TSMC reported $514 million in profit at its Arizona site in 2025, its first full year of production. And the average hourly wage in the Phoenix metro area climbed to $33.48 from $22.85 a decade earlier, outpacing inflation.

The TSMC complex uses more water in nine days than Project Blue is expected to consume in a year, but TSMC has also boosted the state economy in a way no data center could. Data center developers used to pitch the projects to local governments by emphasizing the fact that they donât create many permanent jobs; communities would get infrastructure and tax revenue but none of the congestion that comes with rapid population growth. But now, after years of AI executives warning that the product theyâre building could vaporize entry-level work â and potentially cause a literal apocalypse â more communities see data centers as a lose-lose proposition. TSMCâs chips make the generative AI boom possible, but unlike data centers and AI itself, they actually create jobs.

Work continues at the TSMC Arizona headquarters in Phoenix.

âWhen weâre talking about semiconductor manufacturing, thatâs very different from, say, a golf course,â Porter said. Arizonaâs golf courses, in fact, have historically used far more water than the state allows, much of it sourced from the rapidly drying Colorado River. An investigation by The Arizona Republic found that the stateâs golf courses consumed nearly 39 billion gallons each year between 2002 and 2022. âThat water,â Porter added, âis not reclaimed.â Where TSMC can go through as much as 1.7 billion gallons of water a year, much of which is recycled, golf clubs and courses in Arizonaâs active management areas consumed upwards of 41 billion gallons of water in 2020 alone â and that water is largely lost to evaporation. And still, golf courses use just 2 percent of Arizonaâs water, or 9 percent of water in municipal areas. When it comes to overall water use, putting greens and semiconductor manufacturers are, to use an apt turn of phrase, a drop in the bucket.

But critics of semiconductor manufacturing say that the amount of water the industry uses is just part of the problem. âThereâs water quality, and thereâs water quantity â or water use and water contamination,â Judith Barish, the coalition director of CHIPS Communities United, told me. The coalition, made up largely of labor and environmental groups, was founded in the wake of the CHIPS and Science Act, which designated $52.7 billion in funding for domestic semiconductor manufacturing. Its goal is to ensure that communities, not corporations, reap the benefits of the tech boom.

Semiconductor manufacturing involves the use of hundreds of different per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, which are commonly referred to as forever chemicals because they donât naturally break down. The durability of these chemicals means they wonât be degraded during the manufacturing process, which can involve hundreds or even thousands of steps. But the qualities that make PFAS so essential to chipmaking are precisely what make them so dangerous to people. Some researchers have linked forever chemicals to liver and kidney issues, high cholesterol, birth defects, and various cancers. The use of forever chemicals isnât limited to chip manufacturing, or to the tech industry writ large â PFAS have been found in nonstick pans, dental floss, shampoo, menstrual care products, food packaging, and even food itself â but the semiconductor industry, by nature of the manufacturing process, uses a significant amount of chemicals that are detrimental to human health.

Some researchers have linked chip manufacturing to thyroid and liver diseases, fertility problems, and cancer â an especially ironic outcome, given AI boostersâ claims that the technology will cure cancer within our lifetimes. Women who worked in chip fabs during the â80s manufacturing heyday were twice as likely to suffer miscarriages than women who didnât, and their children were also more likely to experience birth defects. And because each step of semiconductor manufacturing requires thousands of gallons of water, these chemicals ultimately become liquid waste. A single fab can produce tens or hundreds of thousands of gallons of wastewater a day, discharge one bimolecular researcher described as a veritable âsoupâ of forever chemicals.

Traditional wastewater treatment methods often fail to detect forever chemicals, and most semiconductor manufacturers arenât required to monitor or test for PFAS. Compounding the problem, the exact chemical cocktails used in chip fabs are closely guarded trade secrets. But TSMC says it has âcontinuously optimizedâ its in-house PFAS detection systems and is developing technologies to remove PFAS from its wastewater streams. The company also says itâs studying how and when it can use non-PFAS alternatives in the manufacturing process. And Porter pointed out that unlike Tucson, where groundwater has been contaminated by military bases and manufacturing, Phoenix doesnât have much of a PFAS problem, and city leaders are interested in keeping it that way. Phoenix requires TSMC to treat its water before putting it back into the municipal wastewater system, Porter said. And all Arizona cities are required to comply with standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency.

Still, for organizers like Barish, wastewater disposal remains a concern. While TSMC and other chip manufacturers have to comply with city and EPA standards, Donald Trump has largely defanged the EPA and eased restrictions on PFAS in drinking water since returning to office. But concessions for chip manufacturers have been largely bipartisan. The Building Chips in America Act â sponsored by Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) and signed into law by President Joe Biden â exempted semiconductor manufacturing from key environmental review.

Arizonans have gone to great lengths to reduce their water consumption and to roll back the industrial pollution that has tainted groundwater in Tucson and surrounding communities for decades. Still, experts say the mess caused by PFAS could take generations to clean up. And as the stateâs economy becomes increasingly tied to tech â which not only uses huge amounts of water but also produces industrial waste â some residents fear an even more parched Arizona, a drought exacerbated by the promise of industry.

The culprit there isnât population growth or heavy industry, at least not in the way most people think of it. Itâs agriculture

Arizonaâs historic megadrought was set in motion well before any part of the tech industry gained a foothold in the Grand Canyon State. Itâs an almost cartoonishly simple issue of supply and demand, one whose consequences are complex and still uncertain. Hotter and drier summers in the Rocky Mountains are drying up the Colorado River, the source of more than one-third of Arizonaâs water. At the same time, Arizonaâs aquifers are being drained far faster than they can be replenished. The latter is a problem of demand, the former one of supply. Together, they add up to a crisis over a century in the making.

The 1922 Colorado River Compact â the agreement that determines how much of the riverâs water to allocate to seven states â simultaneously overestimated the long-term supply of water and underestimated the demand. Legislators in 1922 could not have foreseen the midcentury population boom or the severity of climate change. But this alone does not explain Arizonaâs current water woes. Thereâs also the matter of Arizonaâs dwindling aquifers. The culprit there isnât population growth or heavy industry, at least not in the way most people think of it. Itâs agriculture, an extractive, hyperindustrialized process unto itself. Arizonaâs now romanticized five Câs were largely brought to the state from elsewhere, and they continue to use far more water than a casual observer imagines or expects. You canât grow cotton and citrus in the desert, nor can you raise cattle, without water â lots of it.

Over the past decade, one commodity crop, increasingly dominated by hedge funds and foreign investors, has become a sort of scapegoat for the stateâs water woes: alfalfa. Its presence is incongruous and inescapable, shocks of green in a sea of clay. Every few dozen miles, the earth-toned monotony that surrounds I-10, the artery connecting Tucson and Phoenix, is interrupted by fields of the stuff. The plant â technically a legume â is grown as cow feed, fueling one of the stateâs oldest and most romanticized industries. More recently, however, deep-pocketed outsiders started getting in on the game, growing alfalfa to produce hay for herds overseas. Until 2011, almost all of Arizonaâs alfalfa crop was consumed inside the state. And then Fondomonte moved in.

Image 1 of 3 An alfalfa field along Interstate 10 in Arizona. Interstate 10 runs between Tucson and Phoenix. A solar array near the site of a proposed data center in Marana, around 20 miles northwest of Tucson.

Fondomonte, a subsidiary of the Saudi dairy company Almarai, bought a 14,000-acre plot of land just off the I-10 in 2014, as part of what the Middle East Policy Council described as a strategy of âdeveloping farm resources in land-rich, cash-poor countries around the world.â Other foreign investors soon followed. The United Arab Emirates-based Al Dahra opened an alfalfa farm of its own in La Paz County, on the stateâs border with California; a massive Minnesota-owned dairy bought up more than 50,000 acres in Cochise County.

One could look at this outside investment as a continuation â or perhaps an escalation â of the cattle economy that has sustained Arizona since the arrival of the first Catholic missionaries. But these industrial megafarms are consuming more water than ever before, at a time when the resource has never been more scarce. For over a decade, Arizonans have urged the government to do something about these industrial alfalfa farms. This year, they finally got their way. In January, the backlash became so pronounced that Gov. Katie Hobbs reduced Fondomonteâs water access. Still, the company is just one among many. All told, the animal feed industry has a significant presence in Arizona, where alfalfa alone accounted for 35 percent of crops harvested in a single year.

âItâs a legacy of the way the West was settled,â said Porter. âI feel like itâs important to respect the historical context, but most of that water use is not sustainable. And the only way to move away from that is to have different economic activities â like data centers and chip manufacturing.â

The 31 million gallons per year granted to Project Blue for construction pales in comparison to the 11 billion gallons Fondomonte guzzled in 2023, and this water comes from different places. Rural farms rely on groundwater; Arizonaâs urban and suburban data centers rely on municipal water, much of it sourced from the Colorado River. And Project Blueâs water allotment adds up to a tiny fraction of the water governed by the Tucson Active Management Area, a state-designated region with specific conservation measures in place, including a provision requiring developers to prove they can guarantee a 100-year supply of water for their projects.
